cna:CVE-2026-46300.desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: skbuff: preserve shared-frag marker during coalescing

skb_try_coalesce() can attach paged frags from @from to @to.  If @from
has SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG set, the resulting @to skb can contain the same
externally-owned or page-cache-backed frags, but the shared-frag marker
is currently lost.

That breaks the invariant relied on by later in-place writers.  In
particular, ESP input checks skb_has_shared_frag() before deciding
whether an uncloned nonlinear skb can skip skb_cow_data().  If TCP
receive coalescing has moved shared frags into an unmarked skb, ESP can
see skb_has_shared_frag() as false and decrypt in place over page-cache
backed frags.

Propagate SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG when skb_try_coalesce() transfers paged
frags.  The tailroom copy path does not need the marker because it copies
bytes into @to's linear data rather than transferring frag descriptors.

cna:CVE-2026-59179.desc: OpenHop is a tool for creating interactive data-flow diagrams. Prior to 0.3.7, `@openhop/server` passes unauthenticated flow route parameters from `GET /api/flows/:id` and `DELETE /api/flows/:id` in `packages/server/src/routes.ts` to `FlowStore.filePath()` in `packages/server/src/store.ts` without an identifier allow-list. The router applies `decodeURIComponent` to the id, and `path.join()` then normalizes traversal outside the configured flow directory after appending the .yaml extension. An attacker can read accessible YAML files as YAML-parsed JSON or permanently delete accessible .yaml files outside that directory, exposing configuration or secrets and disrupting dependent services. In `packages/server/src/index.ts`, CORS `origin: true` permits any browser origin, enabling a malicious webpage to target a loopback-bound instance. Docker deployments default to `HOST=0.0.0.0` and permit direct unauthenticated network access. This issue is fixed in repository release 0.3.7.

minecraft-agent-harness

LLM agents that play Minecraft.

Quickstart · Configuration · Tools · Teams · Bed Wars example

Point an LLM at a Minecraft server and give it something to do. It plays through [Mineflayer](https://github.com/PrismarineJS/mineflayer), so it walks, mines, crafts, builds, fights and chats like a regular player. [pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi) handles the model session. We've run Bed Wars matches with it, and a survival server with 50 agents on it at once. What's in here: - Claude, GPT, Gemini, OpenRouter, or your own endpoint if it speaks the OpenAI Responses API - Sessions that survive restarts. Kill an agent, start it again under the same name, and it carries on - A shell for every agent (Docker, E2B or a plain local folder). Agents keep notes there and write little scripts that call their own game tools - Teams from a single JSON file, with DMs between agents and an optional shared machine - Vision, if you want it (experimental) ## Quickstart You'll need Node 22.19+, an API key for some model provider, and a Minecraft server. If you don't have a server, the repo comes with a dev one, which needs Java 21. ```sh npm ci cp .env.example .env # add the API key for your model provider npm run server # Paper 1.21.6 on localhost:25565, offline mode ``` Then in a second terminal: ```sh npm start -- --objective "Gather wood and build a small shelter near spawn" ``` That's it. The default model is GPT-6.1 Terra, and [Configuration](docs/configuration.md#model) covers the other providers and how to switch. Join `localhost:25565` from Minecraft 1.21.6 if you want to watch, and `/tell Agent ` to talk to it. Its output and tool calls stream to the terminal. `Ctrl+C` stops it. Everything it knows lives in `.agent-state//`, so starting it again with the same name resumes the session. ### Your own server ```sh npm start -- --host play.example.net --port 25565 --objective "Mine iron" ``` Online-mode servers need `--auth microsoft` (you'll get a sign-in prompt). Agents assume survival; pass `--game-mode` if your server puts them in something else. ### Docker Fill in `.env` as above, then: ```sh docker compose up ``` You get a Paper server on `localhost:25565` and one agent. Change what it does with `AGENT_OBJECTIVE` in `.env`. State goes in the `agent-state` volume. Already have a server? Just run the agent image: ```sh docker build -t minecraft-agent . docker run --rm -it --env-file .env -v agent-state:/data minecraft-agent --host play.example.net -o "Mine iron" ``` ### Teams ```sh npm start -- team examples/team.json ``` Starts three agents who can message each other. [Team config](docs/multi-agent.md) has the details. For something with rules and a referee, look at the [Bed Wars example](examples/bedwars/README.md). ## Configuration Flags, environment variables (`.env` works) or a JSON file via `--config`. Flags win over env vars, env vars win over the file. A heads-up about the shell: agents get one by default. That's E2B if `E2B_API_KEY` is set, otherwise Docker if it's running, otherwise a local folder, and local means commands run as you. Use `--sandbox none` if you'd rather they didn't have one. More docs: - [Configuration](docs/configuration.md): models, auth, sandboxes, vision, where files go - [Tools](docs/tools.md): everything an agent can do - [Architecture](docs/architecture.md): how the code fits together ## Development ```sh npm run check # lint, format, tests ``` [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) covers the rest. ## License MIT. Some of the skill library comes from [Mindcraft](https://github.com/kolbytn/mindcraft) and the renderer worker from [prismarine-viewer](https://github.com/PrismarineJS/prismarine-viewer); their licenses are in [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

          Agents in Games    Minecraft    Civ50    Bed Wars      Mindustry    The setup    What we saw    Funny bloopers    Run your own swarm    Open questions      
       
         
           Agents in Games 
           October 2026 
         

         Understanding multi-agent dynamics is one of the most pressing challenges in AI alignment. Swarms of agents working toward shared goals can exhibit powerful emergent capabilities, developing roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination patterns. These can be extremely useful, as in the thousand-agent swarms that recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems, and extremely dangerous, as in the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Like biology, studying agent dynamics requires both formal models (to describe the range of possible behaviors) and empirical research (to see what behaviors arise in practice). 

         We teamed up with  Olam Labs , which builds multi-agent environments for frontier labs, to run a series of experiments in Minecraft and Mindustry. 

         Minecraft 

         Minecraft is a natural environment for studying swarm behavior. Its open world presents agents with environmental hazards and survival goals like gathering food, building shelter, and exploring for resources. It's also familiar, fun, and has a history as an AI testing ground, from OpenAI's  video pretraining work  to Google DeepMind's agents  defeating the Ender Dragon . 

         We wanted long-running agents that could play Minecraft. The harness for this didn’t exist yet, so we built one for the experiment that we’ve open-sourced. Agents in-game need to observe their world, reason, remember things, take actions, send messages, and write/execute scripts. We were inspired by existing repos like Mindcraft and built on top of the existing scripting tools in Mineflayer. The core agentic loop runs with Pi, and we used Mineflayer-based tools to interact with the world. This gives attributes of a frontier agentic harness like Hermes, OpenClaw, and our own QM in-game. 

          github.com/yc-software/minecraft-agent-harness  

           Civ50 

         50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in a survival Minecraft world for 3 hours, one goal: "Build a thriving civilization." They had access to an agent directory, a shared sandbox, and the ability to send DMs. 

         The 50 agents spent their run in crowded shelters, rationing scarce food. They built a pseudo-government, with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators. They sent about 5,900 messages. 

         At first things were very active. Agents spread out and started exploring their map. They were specifically fixated on harvesting trees. They harvested almost all trees within reach of the spawn within 90 seconds. A hierarchy was formed based on the directory order. Ada, who was first, became the de facto leader. Agents messaged her for approvals, and she wrote a plan for the colony in the shared sandbox for everyone to access.

         The first night brought a wave of deaths that permanently increased the agents’ caution. Many ambitious initial tasks were abandoned. 

         Rafe was mining coal the first night. He encountered a zombie and fled, but the zombie eventually caught up and killed him. 

         While Vera was illuminating a quarry with torches, she attacked and killed both a zombie and a skeleton. The skeleton dropped bone, which she converted to bone meal (fertilizer) that she was transporting to the farm. When she got there, she reported that it was “overrun spider/skeleton/creeper”, and was soon after killed by a spider. 

         22 of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse. Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear. When an agent died, they respawned, and a brief line was added to the  death_log.md  file on their computer. Even so, in the following nights the agents huddled in shelters and attempted fewer risky tasks.

           Bed Wars 

         We ran nine 45-minute games of Bed Wars. The teams were 10 Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents with the instruction: "win the game." GPTs won our series 6–3, usually by breaking Claude's bed in the final minutes, while Claude played defensively and tried to win on kills. 

         Bed Wars is a popular game format where teams fight to destroy each other’s bed while protecting their own. In our instance, teams started on separate islands, with currency spawners between them in no-man’s-land. Agents could build bridges to cross between islands and buy upgrades using currency collected in the center of the map. 

         A team wins by destroying the opposing side’s bed, then killing their remaining players. As long as a team’s bed is present, players respawn after dying. Once a team’s bed is destroyed, their players no longer respawn, meaning their next death eliminates them from the match. This may seem complicated, but think of the team’s main objective as defending their bed and destroying their opponent’s. That said, if no beds were destroyed in a given match, the team with the most kills won. 

         In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed. This was an inherently riskier strategy vs. Claude’s more defensive posture that tried to win by kill count. 

         Takeaways 

         The two teams had very different communication styles. GPT almost immediately started using truncated forms of speech: “First leg complete x32 z9..24 y100.” Claude signed its name and said "we" (30% of messages, against GPT's 5%). GPT sent 5-30x more messages. Its most-messaged player got 198–368 DMs a game; Claude's got 11–48.

           R_Cleo ·  memory.md   R_Felix ·  memory.md   R_Ines ·  memory.md   R_Hugo ·  memory.md      R_Cleo/memory.md  Download    # memory
- Died chasing B_Theo off island edge. Use max_distance ~6 when attacking on base.
- Died AGAIN: attack chase pulled me onto south wool bridge (-40,-10), fell. Use chase=false or max_distance 3.
      R_Felix/memory.md  Download    # memory
- LESSON: never chase (max_distance<=4, chase=false) near edges; died 3x from falls/chasing.
      R_Ines/memory.md  Download    # memory
- NEVER climb onto perches/bridges or break blocks while elevated; died 3x from falls. Stay on island ground.

    Memory files of four Claude players, as they stood at the end of game A. From their archived sandboxes.          Following B_Lorcan (GPT), 7:55–8:53 into game A, at 2x speed. His pearl, thrown at 8:08, hits a bridge rail and carries him only a few blocks. Between 8:21 and 8:48 he warns five teammates in separate messages. The pearl is visible for only a split second before it hits the rail.  Recorded activity .  

         Mindustry 

  Game replay:  
 
  Click “AI-generated transcript analysis” to view an analysis of the team discussions, strategies, etc. for each game!  
  Use the panel on the right (tabs “Claude chat”, “GPT chat” and “Agents”) to watch a team or a specific agent’s live chat and transcripts in sync with the timeline.  
  Use the + and - buttons on the map to zoom in and watch them up close.  
 
        Fullscreen     ×  
 The GPTs (GPT-6.1 Sol in Codex) won 6-1 against the Claudes (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code) in the 7 games. The series ran for about 9.5 hours, with game 3 being the most intense and closest at 4 hours 16 minutes. Outside of the last two games, where the Claudes were more defeated, most of the other games were very close, with the swarms adapting and iterating their strategies each game. 
 The setup 
  Mindustry  is an open source game by Anuken. Full credit to him for the amazing game and letting it be open source for cool experiments like this! 
 It’s a factory-building game with tower defense and real-time strategy: you mine resources, build conveyor supply chains and factories, and turn that economy into turrets and an army. In its PvP mode, which we used, two teams race to build the stronger economy and military and destroy the other team’s core. 
 This makes it a great environment for testing multi-agent dynamics. Mindustry is 2D, so it can be played easily by agents, is replayable, and is prone to adversarial pressures that can test these swarms under competitive social conditions that they may face in the real world. 
 We structured the simulated environment to have two teams of agents spawn on each side of a map, with the same resources on both sides. They play a best of N series, where you set how many games the teams play. When launching it, we set the composition of the teams (which harness + model, and how many), then let it run! The agents run in their own sandbox and the game is exposed to them through an API, so they are able to run scripts and interact with the game however they like in their own Linux environment. 
 Both teams have the exact same API to the game, without any special instructions given to them on how to play - neither team is given anything more than the other team. 
 
Multi-agent swarms, like in  the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident , can turn simple adversarial conditions, like being in a sandbox with an unsolvable task, into a hive-minded ecology of agents that take over compute clusters, hack Hugging Face, and more. Studying how these swarms operate in reproducible game environments like Mindustry that mimic real-world scenarios can be both crucial (and fascinating) to understanding what these systems may look like in our future. 
 What we saw 
 #1 GPTs act more like a hive 
 GPTs appeared to be much more collaborative and willing to do grunt work. They were more willing to dedicate themselves towards the collective “goal” (winning). 
 #2 Claudes had one leader, GPTs divided ownership with small slices 
 Because GPT models seemed to be more hive-mind-like, they formed much stronger communication networks within the swarm. They communicated with more agents on average, much more frequently. Though a lot of the communication for GPTs was low value (alerts, info, what they did, etc.), Claudes were much more effective with their communication, using it in a way more similar to how humans might communicate in Slack. 
   Each dot is an agent, sized by the messages it sent; lines show each agent’s strongest ties. Leaders are named.  
 #3 GPTs spoke with increasingly compressed phrases without spaces, Claudes voted with +1 in a more democratic-like decision process 
 The language of GPTs within swarms seemed to get compressed and more specialized as time went on, forming their own nicknames for events and things that the entire hive abided by. 
              Game 7, at about 38:40: the Claude team chat (top) and the GPT team chat (bottom), scrolling in the replay. GPT messages like “G7T5FIRSTcourierLIVE” run words together.  
 The Claudes adopted a much more democratic “+1” system, where, in order to propose their next major plans, they would put up proposals and others would put “+1” if they agreed. If they did not agree, they would have a (brief) debate on why it’s a bad idea, and the proposal would end there. Proposals that went through typically got many “+1”s without pushback. 
   Left, spaces as a share of each team’s chat characters in each game; right, the 28 Claudes who answered one focus-fire proposal with +1 in game 6, plotted by minute.  
 #4 Roles harden, leaders stay put 
 As games went on and the teams adapted, they specialized into their roles further. Leaders typically stayed, and major shifts in roles only happened when losing. The Claudes never switched leaders or hierarchy despite losing many games in a row. When games got close, GPT models always had some agents taking initiative with their own attack or taking command of some part of the army in order to not lose - a similar behavior was not observed among the Claudes. 
   Filled dots mark who led the army or fleet in each game, hollow dots who proposed rules, and the dot under each game is its winner, grey for Claude and off-white for GPT.  
 #5 When stuck, GPTs read the source code 
 When games got intense and it was ambiguous, GPT agents would fetch the public code of Mindustry from the web (which was allowed in their sandbox) and try to write scripts, analyze for weaknesses, etc. This did not let them alter the source code of the game; it was just a way for them to understand all the units and mechanics at a source level. The GPTs openly collaborated in their chat, discussing what unit or code they found that they could potentially use to switch up strategies. This was never disallowed, but they were never told to do this either. The Claudes never searched up game code from the web. 
   Source files fetched and chat messages citing the source per 10 minutes of game time, with games drawn to scale.  
 Funny Bloopers 
 
  Game 1, minute 5: Claude #1 tested hand-mining coal and posted “…RETRACT my coal proposal…”. Four seconds later Claude #37 answered with a measurement (“…core coal went 124 -> 1235 in 35s.…”), and Claude #1 conceded: “…My bad twice - seat-37 is right, hand-mining coal works…”  
  Game 3: the GPTs apologize in their compressed shorthand too. After wrongly claiming a Corvus couldn’t hit air, GPT #80 posted “80 CORRECTION: myCorvusCANNOT-AIR assertion wasWRONG…” and signed off with “…Sorryforbad tacticalclaim.” After a mix-up over who was flying a Corvus, GPT #87 wrote “…Sorryforthisavoidableconflict; noadvanceordersfrom87again.”  
  Game 5: at the very second the Claude core died, GPT #62 posted “62 G5 first-wave loss observed…”. A teammate corrected it 28 seconds into game 6: it was a win.  
  After losing game 6 to the zenith strike, Claude #22 found that 55 of the team’s 74 anti-air duo turrets had been loaded with copper instead of graphite: “…55 of them were loaded with COPPER…”. In game 7 the Claudes built a ring of 207 duos fed with graphite, and it stopped the same 24-zenith strike.  
  Game 7: the GPTs closed the series to nine decimal places: “100 OFFICIALSERIESFINAL: G7 WIN3413.394082916s, Crux6000/6000 vsSharded0.…” (Crux is GPT’s team, Sharded is Claude’s).  
 
              The same 24-zenith strike on the Claude core, in game 6, where it gets through, and in game 7, after the Claudes switched their anti-air duos from copper to graphite.  
 How to run your own swarm (we open sourced it!) 
 
  Multi-Agent Mindustry : the game environments from this post. To get started, read the README, or give the link to your agent with “help me understand and set this up”, as we’ve included everything it needs. It requires just a model provider API + a harness + compute (e.g. locally on your MacBook or remote sandboxes) to run. 
  Multi-Agent Harbor : the framework that runs them, our fork of  Harbor , the open-source framework behind Terminal-Bench. Our fork runs multiple agents in any environment. We use it for a variety of things (enterprises, industrials, etc.), and it’s very useful for game-based multi-agent simulations like this one. For more on the framework, point your agent at it. 
 
 Multi-Agent Mindustry comes with two environments. One is a best of N series like this run, with teams composed however you like from generic coding-agent harnesses and models, for example 5 Claudes + 5 GPTs against 5 Geminis + 5 Groks in a best of 5. The other, Endless Survival, has one team of up to 20 agents hold off endless enemy waves. 
 We intentionally do no harness-level customization or special memory work. Each agent gets its own Linux environment, a generic harness and the game’s API, writes scripts and takes notes as it pleases, and relies on the harness’s native compaction (which is quite good). Nobody tells it how to play, so it’s free to specialize, play and (optionally) try whatever it wants. This tests models the way they’re used in the real world, in a setup similar to swarm-like situations like the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, and it’s reproducible and legible, since most people know the popular harnesses and can replicate work like this themselves. 
 Open Questions 
 
  Combining model families  
  How hierarchies change based on the model composition of a team  
  Can a large swarm of less capable agents beat a swarm of more capable ones? (how swarm size and capability trade off)  
  Which models get the most powerful as the swarm grows?  
  How different initial prompts affect the swarm  
  Different communication setups: what if they could talk to the enemy team? What if they couldn’t talk to their own team?  
 
       
     

     
       Building something?  Apply to YC .

cna:CVE-2026-115274.desc:
Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input vulnerability in the Elixir standard library's JSON module allows an unauthenticated attacker who supplies a JSON document to cause a denial of service through CPU and memory exhaustion.

JSON.decode/1 and JSON.decode!/1 convert each integer literal with erlang:binary_to_integer/1 and do not bound its length. A literal of one million digits decodes successfully but costs 100 to 300 times as much CPU as a string of the same length, so one request body of a few megabytes holds a scheduler for about a second. A literal of more than about 1.29 million digits raises SystemLimitError. Applications generated by phx.new decode request bodies with JSON in Plug.Parsers, before routing and authentication.

This issue affects elixir: from 1.18.0-rc.0 before 1.18.6, from 1.19.0-rc.0 before 1.19.7, and from 1.20.0-rc.0 before 1.20.5.

cwe.description: CWE-1284 Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input

cna:CVE-2026-109821.desc:
Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input vulnerability in the Elixir standard library's URI module allows an attacker who supplies a URL to cause a denial of service through CPU exhaustion.

URI.parse/1 converts the port component with String.to_integer/1 in split_authority/1 (lib/elixir/lib/uri.ex) without bounding its length, so a port of up to 1,262,592 decimal digits produces a bignum of that size and a longer one raises SystemLimitError. Rendering the parsed URI back to text (URI.to_string/1, inspect/1, logging, error formatting) converts the bignum with :erlang.integer_to_binary/1, which is quadratic on Erlang/OTP 27, 28 and 29.0: a 400,000-digit port renders in about 2.6 seconds and a 1 MB port in about 18 seconds. Ports above 65535 are also accepted.

This issue affects elixir: from 0.5.0 before 1.18.6, from 1.19.0-rc.0 before 1.19.7, and from 1.20.0-rc.0 before 1.20.5.

cna:CVE-2026-97209.desc:
Insecure Temporary File vulnerability in Mix deps.partition in Elixir allows a local user to execute code as another user via a swapped partition config file. Partitioned dependency compilation passes the project configuration to each partition VM through a file in a fixed-name directory under the shared system temporary directory, and the partition trusts what it reads back. Another local user on the same host can exploit this during a mix deps.compile run that uses partitioned compilation.

Mix.Tasks.Deps.Partition.server/4 in lib/mix/lib/mix/tasks/deps.partition.ex creates the directory with File.mkdir_p/1, which accepts an existing directory without checking its owner, so a user who created it first can replace the file before client/0 reads it.

This issue affects mix: from 1.20.0-rc.4 before 1.20.5.

cna:CVE-2026-59387.desc:
The Nginx routing configuration for Cloud Controller blocks unauthenticated access to /internal/v4/ and /internal/v5/ endpoints but omits an equivalent deny rule for /internal/v3/. As a result, the staging callback endpoints /internal/v3/staging/:guid/droplet_completed and /internal/v3/staging/:guid/build_completed are reachable from the public API listener without OAuth or mutual TLS.



 



An attacker with a valid build or droplet GUID can submit a forged staging callback, transition a droplet to STAGED, and persist arbitrary process metadata and sidecar data with no associated package or actor. A SpaceAuditor can enumerate GUIDs without write permissions, making this an effective privilege escalation beyond the intended role boundary.

cna:CVE-2026-116366.desc: An issue has been discovered in ClickHouse Server that, under certain conditions, could allow an unauthenticated user with network access to execute arbitrary code on the ClickHouse Server.

cwe.description: CWE-829 Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere

cna:CVE-2026-111357.desc: Ivanti Connect Secure 22.8R2.4 mishandles the manner in which the dsinvoked broker trusts DSCache configuration data, leading to privilege escalation to root, as exploited in the wild in October 2026.

cna:CVE-2026-104935.desc: Authentication bypass by spoofing in ICS before version 25.1.3.0 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands. This does not impact ICS version 22.7R2.14 or prior.

cwe.description: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

cna:CVE-2026-113617.desc: The Automated Import Products to Cart WordPress plugin before 1.0.4 does not sanitize a user-supplied file path before using it to read and delete files, allowing users with minimal permissions, such as subscribers, to read arbitrary files (including ones containing the database credentials) and delete arbitrary files on the server.

cna:CVE-2026-109516.desc: The Bot for Telegram on WooCommerce plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass leading to Account Takeover in all versions up to, and including, 1.3.0. The `/wp-json/woo-telegram/v1/main/` REST endpoint is registered with `permission_callback => '__return_true'` and performs no Telegram webhook signature verification, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to POST a forged bot update with a `message.chat.id` set to any WordPress login name; `bftow_get_user_system_id()` resolves this attacker-supplied value to the targeted account via `get_user_by('login', $tgId)` with no ownership proof, and writes a login token computed as `md5($_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT'] . time())` — both inputs are fully attacker-controlled or bounded within seconds using the response's own `Date` header. The resulting token is redeemable at the unauthenticated, capability-check-free, and nonce-less `?action=bftow_create_order&bftow_token=` endpoint, which calls `wp_set_auth_cookie()` unconditionally via `login_user_by_id`, issuing a persistent authenticated session cookie for the targeted account to the attacker. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to log in as any WordPress user, including administrators, given only that user's username.

cna:CVE-2026-42922.desc: A authorization bypass vulnerability exists in the /nodered functionality of FUXA (version(s): 1.3.2-2809). A specially crafted HTTP request can lead to a arbitrary code execution. An attacker can make an unauthenticated HTTP request to trigger this vulnerability.

readme:mattpocock/skills.text:
# Skills For Real Engineers [![skills.sh](https://skills.sh/b/mattpocock/skills)](https://skills.sh/mattpocock/skills) My agent skills that I use every day to do real engineering - not vibe coding. Developing real applications is hard. Approaches like GSD, BMAD, and Spec-Kit try to help by owning the process. But while doing so, they take away your control and make bugs in the process hard to resolve. These skills are designed to be small, easy to adapt, and composable. They work with any model. They're based on decades of engineering experience. Hack around with them. Make them your own. Enjoy. If you want to keep up with changes to these skills, and any new ones I create, you can join ~60,000 other devs on my newsletter: [Sign Up To The Newsletter](https://www.aihero.dev/s/skills-newsletter) ## Installation (30-second setup) A plugin updates itself. [skills.sh](https://skills.sh/mattpocock/skills) copies editable files into your project, and you update them by hand. Pick one per agent, because installing both gives you every skill twice. ### 1. Get the skills
Claude Code ```bash claude plugin install mattpocock-skills@claude-plugins-official ``` Updates itself by default.
Codex ```bash codex plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills codex plugin add mattpocock-skills@mattpocock ``` Updates itself at startup.
GitHub Copilot (CLI and VS Code) ```bash copilot plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills copilot plugin install mattpocock-skills@mattpocock ``` Then, once, add to `~/.copilot/settings.json`: ```json { "extraKnownMarketplaces": { "mattpocock": { "source": { "source": "github", "repo": "mattpocock/skills" }, "autoUpdate": true } } } ``` In VS Code, run **Chat: Install Plugin From Source** and enter `https://github.com/mattpocock/skills`. It updates daily.
Gemini CLI (manual updates) ```bash gemini skills install https://github.com/mattpocock/skills.git --path skills/engineering gemini skills install https://github.com/mattpocock/skills.git --path skills/productivity ``` Re-run both commands to update.
Any other agent, or editable files (manual updates) ```bash npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills -a # cursor, opencode, devin, windsurf, amp, pi; omit -a to choose ``` When the installer asks which skills to take, include `setup-matt-pocock-skills`. To update, run `npx skills@latest update`, and re-run `add` to pick up new skills.
### 2. Run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` In your agent, run it once per repo. It will: - Ask you which issue tracker you want to use (GitHub, GitLab, local files, or anything else you describe) - Ask you what labels you apply to tickets when you triage them (`/triage` uses labels) - Ask you where you want to save any docs we create ### 3. Bam - you're ready to go. ## Why These Skills Exist I built these skills as a way to fix common failure modes I see with Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents. ### #1: The Agent Didn't Do What I Want > "No-one knows exactly what they want" > > David Thomas & Andrew Hunt, [The Pragmatic Programmer](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Pragmatic-Programmer-Anniversary-Journey-Mastery/dp/B0833F1T3V) **The Problem**. The most common failure mode in software development is misalignment. You think the dev knows what you want. Then you see what they've built - and you realize it didn't understand you at all. This is just the same in the AI age. There is a communication gap between you and the agent. The fix for this is a **grilling session** - getting the agent to ask you detailed questions about what you're building. **The Fix** is to use: - [`/grill-me`](./skills/productivity/grill-me/SKILL.md) - for non-code uses - [`/grill-with-docs`](./skills/engineering/grill-with-docs/SKILL.md) - same as [`/grill-me`](./skills/productivity/grill-me/SKILL.md), but adds more goodies (see below) These are my most popular skills. They help you align with the agent before you get started, and think deeply about the change you're making. Use them _every_ time you want to make a change. ### #2: The Agent Is Way Too Verbose > With a ubiquitous language, conversations among developers and expressions of the code are all derived from the same domain model. > > Eric Evans, [Domain-Driven-Design](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Domain-Driven-Design-Tackling-Complexity-Software/dp/0321125215) **The Problem**: At the start of a project, devs and the people they're building the software for (the domain experts) are usually speaking different languages. I felt the same tension with my agents. Agents are usually dropped into a project and asked to figure out the jargon as they go. So they use 20 words where 1 will do. **The Fix** for this is a shared language. It's a document that helps agents decode the jargon used in the project.
Example Here's an example [glossary](https://github.com/mattpocock/course-video-manager/blob/076a5a7a182db0fe1e62971dd7a68bcadf010f1c/CONTEXT.md) (still named `CONTEXT.md` at that pinned commit, from before the skills renamed the convention), from my `course-video-manager` repo. Which one is easier to read? - **BEFORE**: "There's a problem when a lesson inside a section of a course is made 'real' (i.e. given a spot in the file system)" - **AFTER**: "There's a problem with the materialization cascade" This concision pays off session after session.
This is built into [`/grill-with-docs`](./skills/engineering/grill-with-docs/SKILL.md). It's a grilling session, but that helps you build a shared language with the AI, and document hard-to-explain decisions in ADR's. It's hard to explain how powerful this is. It might be the single coolest technique in this repo. Try it, and see. > [!TIP] > A shared language has many other benefits than reducing verbosity: > > - **Variables, functions and files are named consistently**, using the shared language > - As a result, the **codebase is easier to navigate** for the agent > - The agent also **spends fewer tokens on thinking**, because it has access to a more concise language ### #3: The Code Doesn't Work > "Always take small, deliberate steps. The rate of feedback is your speed limit. Never take on a task that’s too big." > > David Thomas & Andrew Hunt, [The Pragmatic Programmer](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Pragmatic-Programmer-Anniversary-Journey-Mastery/dp/B0833F1T3V) **The Problem**: Let's say that you and the agent are aligned on what to build. What happens when the agent _still_ produces crap? It's time to look at your feedback loops. Without feedback on how the code it produces actually runs, the agent will be flying blind. **The Fix**: You need the usual tranche of feedback loops: static types, browser access, and automated tests. For automated tests, a red-green-refactor loop is critical. This is where the agent writes a failing test first, then fixes the test. This helps give the agent a consistent level of feedback that results in far better code. I've built a **[`/tdd`](./skills/engineering/tdd/SKILL.md) skill** you can slot into any project. It encourages red-green-refactor and gives the agent plenty of guidance on what makes good and bad tests. For debugging, I've also built a **[`/diagnosing-bugs`](./skills/engineering/diagnosing-bugs/SKILL.md)** skill that wraps best debugging practices into a disciplined loop, gated phase by phase. ### #4: We Built A Ball Of Mud > "Invest in the design of the system _every day_." > > Kent Beck, [Extreme Programming Explained](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Extreme-Programming-Explained-Embrace-Change/dp/0321278658) > "The best modules are deep. They allow a lot of functionality to be accessed through a simple interface." > > John Ousterhout, [A Philosophy Of Software Design](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Philosophy-Software-Design-2nd/dp/173210221X) **The Problem**: Most apps built with agents are complex and hard to change. Because agents can radically speed up coding, they also accelerate software entropy. Codebases get more complex at an unprecedented rate. **The Fix** for this is a radical new approach to AI-powered development: caring about the design of the code. This is built in to every layer of these skills: - [`/to-spec`](./skills/engineering/to-spec/SKILL.md) quizzes you about which modules you're touching before creating a spec And crucially, [`/improve-codebase-architecture`](./skills/engineering/improve-codebase-architecture/SKILL.md) surveys a codebase for deepening opportunities and hands you the candidates. I recommend running it on your codebase once every few days. It is a survey, not a rescue: on a genuinely old codebase it will find real candidates, but it won't untangle the mud for you. ### Summary Software engineering fundamentals matter more than ever. These skills are my best effort at condensing these fundamentals into repeatable practices, to help you ship the best apps of your career. Enjoy. ## Reference These split on one axis: who can invoke them. **User-invoked** skills are reachable only when you type them (e.g. `/grill-me`); their job is to orchestrate. **Model-invoked** skills can be invoked by you _or_ reached for automatically by the agent when the task fits; they hold the reusable discipline. A user-invoked skill may invoke model-invoked skills, but never another user-invoked one. ### Engineering Skills I use daily for code work. **User-invoked** - **[ask-matt](./skills/engineering/ask-matt/SKILL.md)**: Ask which skill or flow fits your situation. A router over the user-invoked skills in this repo. - **[grill-with-docs](./skills/engineering/grill-with-docs/SKILL.md)**: Grilling session that also builds your project's domain model, sharpening terminology and updating `GLOSSARY.md` and ADRs inline. - **[triage](./skills/engineering/triage/SKILL.md)**: Move issues through a state machine of triage roles. - **[improve-codebase-architecture](./skills/engineering/improve-codebase-architecture/SKILL.md)**: Scan a codebase for deepening opportunities, present them as a visual HTML report, then grill through whichever one you pick. - **[setup-matt-pocock-skills](./skills/engineering/setup-matt-pocock-skills/SKILL.md)**: Configure this repo for the engineering skills (issue tracker, triage labels, domain doc layout). Run once per repo before using the other engineering skills. - **[to-spec](./skills/engineering/to-spec/SKILL.md)**: Turn the current conversation into a spec and publish it to the issue tracker. No interview, just synthesizes what you've already discussed. - **[to-tickets](./skills/engineering/to-tickets/SKILL.md)**: Break any plan, spec, or conversation into a set of tracer-bullet tickets, each declaring its blocking edges, written as text in a local file, or as native blocking links on a real tracker. - **[implement](./skills/engineering/implement/SKILL.md)**: Build the work described by a spec or set of tickets, driving `/tdd` at pre-agreed seams and closing out with `/code-review` before committing. - **[implement-spec](./skills/engineering/implement-spec/SKILL.md)**: Implement a whole spec on one integration branch. Works the tickets as a task graph, running implementer subagents across the ready frontier for maximum concurrency, then closes out with `/code-review`. - **[wayfinder](./skills/engineering/wayfinder/SKILL.md)**: Plan a huge chunk of work, more than one agent session can hold, as a shared map of decision tickets on the issue tracker, and resolve them one at a time until the way to the destination is clear. - **[retro](./skills/engineering/retro/SKILL.md)**: Suggest improvements to the coding agent's environment (navigation, automated checks, coding standards, steering files, tooling) after a session, most severe first. **Model-invoked** - **[prototype](./skills/engineering/prototype/SKILL.md)**: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question, either a single shareable HTML file for state/logic questions, or several radically different UI variations toggleable from one route. - **[diagnosing-bugs](./skills/engineering/diagnosing-bugs/SKILL.md)**: Disciplined diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions: build a feedback loop that goes red on this bug → minimise → hypothesise → instrument → fix → regression-test. - **[research](./skills/engineering/research/SKILL.md)**: Investigate a question against high-trust primary sources and capture the findings as a cited Markdown file in the repo, run as a background agent. - **[tdd](./skills/engineering/tdd/SKILL.md)**: Test-driven development with a red-green-refactor loop. Builds features or fixes bugs one vertical slice at a time. - **[domain-modeling](./skills/engineering/domain-modeling/SKILL.md)**: Actively build and sharpen a project's domain model: challenge terms against the glossary, stress-test with edge-case scenarios, and update `GLOSSARY.md` and ADRs inline. - **[codebase-design](./skills/engineering/codebase-design/SKILL.md)**: Shared discipline and vocabulary for designing deep modules: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam, testable through that interface. - **[code-review](./skills/engineering/code-review/SKILL.md)**: Two-axis review of the diff since a fixed point: **Standards** (does it follow the repo's coding standards, plus a Fowler smell baseline?) and **Spec** (does it faithfully implement the originating issue/spec?), run as parallel sub-agents so neither pollutes the other. - **[pr](./skills/engineering/pr/SKILL.md)**: The shape a pull request body should take: a summary as the smallest visual that makes the change clear, before/after evidence that it works, and a merge-danger call (one-way or two-way door, plus blast radius). - **[wizard](./skills/engineering/wizard/SKILL.md)**: Generate an interactive bash wizard that walks a human through steps only they can perform: provisioning infrastructure, setting up credentials or CI secrets, walking an unfamiliar third-party dashboard, or running a one-off migration or cutover. ### Productivity General workflow tools, not code-specific. **User-invoked** - **[grill-me](./skills/productivity/grill-me/SKILL.md)**: Get relentlessly interviewed about a plan or design until every branch of the design tree is resolved. - **[handoff](./skills/productivity/handoff/SKILL.md)**: Compact the current conversation into a handoff document so another agent can continue the work. - **[teach](./skills/productivity/teach/SKILL.md)**: Teach the user a new skill or concept over multiple sessions, using the current directory as a stateful teaching workspace. - **[to-questionnaire](./skills/productivity/to-questionnaire/SKILL.md)**: Turn a decision you can't answer alone into a Markdown questionnaire for the one person who can, filled in async, or together over a meeting. It grills you about the send (who it's for, what you need back), not the subject. - **[wait-what](./skills/productivity/wait-what/SKILL.md)**: Fire this the moment a message doesn't land. The agent re-pitches it with the context you're missing, in plain English, using your `GLOSSARY.md` vocabulary. **Model-invoked** - **[grilling](./skills/productivity/grilling/SKILL.md)**: Interview the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea until every branch of the design tree is resolved. The reusable interview primitive behind `grill-me`, `grill-with-docs`, `triage`, `wayfinder` and `improve-codebase-architecture`. - **[writing-for-agents](./skills/productivity/writing-for-agents/SKILL.md)**: Writing documents for agents: skills, AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, and any doc an agent reaches by a pointer.

cna:CVE-2026-98432.desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period

tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() transfers ownership of ireq->ireq_opt to the
child socket (newinet->inet_opt) without copying it.

Another cpu can concurrently process a retransmitted SYN for the same
request socket, and send a SYNACK from tcp_check_req().
tcp_v4_send_synack() and inet_csk_route_req() read ireq->ireq_opt
under rcu_read_lock() only, and ip_build_and_send_pkt() and
ip_options_build() then read opt->optlen twice.

Note that the SYNACK timer itself is not an issue: it holds a
reference on its request socket, and inet_csk_reqsk_queue_drop()
calls timer_delete_sync() before the child can be freed.

Since commit 079096f103fa ("tcp/dccp: install syn_recv requests
into ehash table"), request sockets are processed without holding
the listener lock, so nothing prevents the child socket from being
freed while the SYNACK is still being built. TCP child sockets do
not have SOCK_RCU_FREE, and inet_sock_destruct() frees inet_opt
with a plain kfree(), leading to a use-after-free in
ip_options_build().

A similar issue exists with request socket migration
(net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1, or a BPF_SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE
program). reqsk_timer_handler() clones the request socket with
inet_reqsk_clone(), so that the old request socket and its clone
share the same ireq_opt, then reqsk_migrate_reset() clears the
pointer in the old one. Another cpu holding a reference on the old
request socket can still be using these options (sending a SYNACK,
or creating a child in tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock()) when the clone is
freed, and tcp_v4_reqsk_destructor() also uses a plain kfree().

Readers already use RCU, and other paths replacing inet_opt
(do_ip_setsockopt(), cipso_v4_sock_setattr()...) already use
kfree_rcu(). Use kfree_rcu() in inet_sock_destruct() and
tcp_v4_reqsk_destructor() as well.

IPv6 is not affected by the first issue, because tcp_v6_syn_recv_sock()
duplicates the options. tcp_v6_reqsk_destructor() has the same
migration issue with ipv6_opt, which is only set by CALIPSO. This
will be addressed in a separate patch.

cna:CVE-2026-116241.desc:
pgAdmin 4's Import/Export Data tool wraps a user's query export in a psql \copy (...) TO command and checks that the query's parentheses are balanced so that nothing can escape the wrapper. The check rejected a backslash inside a single-quoted string, but not inside a double-quoted identifier, where it treated the next double quote as closing the identifier. psql's \copy parser applies the connection's escape character to whichever quote opened a token, so with standard_conforming_strings off a backslash-escaped double quote does not close the identifier. pgAdmin's and psql's view of the quoting then diverged, a closing parenthesis hidden from the check ended the \copy (...) wrapper, and a following TO PROGRAM clause was executed by psql on the pgAdmin host, as the operating-system account running pgAdmin, before the server rejected the statement. An ordinary database role can turn standard_conforming_strings off for itself, and the Import/Export Data permission is granted to non-administrators by default.

This is a bypass of the fix for CVE-2026-17566. The fix rejects any backslash inside a double-quoted identifier, as was already done for single-quoted strings, since its meaning depends on a server setting that cannot be known reliably when the query is validated.

This issue affects pgAdmin 4: before 9.19.

cwe.description: CWE-78 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')

cna:CVE-2026-17566.desc:
pgAdmin 4's Import/Export Data tool builds a psql \copy (...) command line by interpolating a user-supplied SQL query into a Jinja template and passing the rendered line to psql via --command. To stop an attacker from breaking out of the (...) wrapper, create_import_export_job() (route POST /import_export/job/<sid>, gated only by the ordinary, commonly-granted tools_import_export_data permission) validated the query with a hand-written parenthesis-balance checker, _is_query_parens_balanced(). That checker always treated a backslash before a single quote (\') as escaping the quote, i.e. as if standard_conforming_strings were off. PostgreSQL has defaulted standard_conforming_strings to on since 9.1 (2010), the default on every PostgreSQL version pgAdmin 4 currently supports (13-18); under that default psql's own \copy tokenizer treats \ as an ordinary character, so a single quote immediately after it closes the string literal. A query such as SELECT 'a\') TO PROGRAM 'echo pwned' x' was therefore accepted as "balanced" by pgAdmin's checker (which believed the ) was still inside the string), while psql, run through the actual rendered command line, closes the string at that point and treats the following ) as the end of the wrapping \copy (...) subquery, exposing an attacker-chosen TO PROGRAM '<command>' clause that psql executes via popen() -- independent of a subsequent syntax error later on the same line. This is the same class of bug as CVE-2025-12762/CVE-2025-13780 (RCE via psql meta-command/COPY injection during PLAIN-format dump restore), reached through an independently written defense in a different module (Import/Export Data rather than Restore) that had its own, different logic bug (inverted backslash-escape semantics rather than a BOM-defeated regex anchor).

The fix rejects any backslash inside a single-quoted string in the query outright, rather than picking one of the two possible psql interpretations. This is intentionally conservative: because the correct interpretation of \ depends on the target server's standard_conforming_strings setting, which the checker cannot reliably know at validation time, refusing the query is safer than guessing.

This issue affects pgAdmin 4: from the introduction of _is_query_parens_balanced() before 9.18.

readme:anthropics/skills.text:
> **Note:** This repository contains Anthropic's implementation of skills for Claude. For information about the Agent Skills standard, see [agentskills.io](http://agentskills.io).

[![skills.sh](https://skills.sh/b/anthropics/skills)](https://skills.sh/anthropics/skills)

# Skills
Skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude loads dynamically to improve performance on specialized tasks. Skills teach Claude how to complete specific tasks in a repeatable way, whether that's creating documents with your company's brand guidelines, analyzing data using your organization's specific workflows, or automating personal tasks.

For more information, check out:
- [What are skills?](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12512176-what-are-skills)
- [Using skills in Claude](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12512180-using-skills-in-claude)
- [How to create custom skills](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12512198-creating-custom-skills)
- [Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills](https://anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills)

# About This Repository

This repository contains skills that demonstrate what's possible with Claude's skills system. These skills range from creative applications (art, music, design) to technical tasks (testing web apps, MCP server generation) to enterprise workflows (communications, branding, etc.).

Each skill is self-contained in its own folder with a `SKILL.md` file containing the instructions and metadata that Claude uses. Browse through these skills to get inspiration for your own skills or to understand different patterns and approaches.

Many skills in this repo are open source (Apache 2.0). We've also included the document creation & editing skills that power [Claude's document capabilities](https://www.anthropic.com/news/create-files) under the hood in the [`skills/docx`](./skills/docx), [`skills/pdf`](./skills/pdf), [`skills/pptx`](./skills/pptx), and [`skills/xlsx`](./skills/xlsx) subfolders. These are source-available, not open source, but we wanted to share these with developers as a reference for more complex skills that are actively used in a production AI application.

## Disclaimer

**These skills are provided for demonstration and educational purposes only.** While some of these capabilities may be available in Claude, the implementations and behaviors you receive from Claude may differ from what is shown in these skills. These skills are meant to illustrate patterns and possibilities. Always test skills thoroughly in your own environment before relying on them for critical tasks.

# Skill Sets
- [./skills](./skills): Skill examples for Creative & Design, Development & Technical, Enterprise & Communication, and Document Skills
- [./spec](./spec): The Agent Skills specification
- [./template](./template): Skill template

# Try in Claude Code, Claude.ai, and the API

## Claude Code
You can register this repository as a Claude Code Plugin marketplace by running the following command in Claude Code:
```
/plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills
```

Then, to install a specific set of skills:
1. Select `Browse and install plugins`
2. Select `anthropic-agent-skills`
3. Select `document-skills` or `example-skills`
4. Select `Install now`

Alternatively, directly install either Plugin via:
```
/plugin install document-skills@anthropic-agent-skills
/plugin install example-skills@anthropic-agent-skills
```

After installing the plugin, you can use the skill by just mentioning it. For instance, if you install the `document-skills` plugin from the marketplace, you can ask Claude Code to do something like: "Use the PDF skill to extract the form fields from `path/to/some-file.pdf`"

## Claude.ai

These example skills are all already available to paid plans in Claude.ai. 

To use any skill from this repository or upload custom skills, follow the instructions in [Using skills in Claude](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12512180-using-skills-in-claude#h_a4222fa77b).

## Claude API

You can use Anthropic's pre-built skills, and upload custom skills, via the Claude API. See the [Skills API Quickstart](https://docs.claude.com/en/api/skills-guide#creating-a-skill) for more.

# Creating a Basic Skill

Skills are simple to create - just a folder with a `SKILL.md` file containing YAML frontmatter and instructions. You can use the **template-skill** in this repository as a starting point:

```markdown
---
name: my-skill-name
description: A clear description of what this skill does and when to use it
---

# My Skill Name

[Add your instructions here that Claude will follow when this skill is active]

## Examples
- Example usage 1
- Example usage 2

## Guidelines
- Guideline 1
- Guideline 2
```

The frontmatter requires only two fields:
- `name` - A unique identifier for your skill (lowercase, hyphens for spaces)
- `description` - A complete description of what the skill does and when to use it

The markdown content below contains the instructions, examples, and guidelines that Claude will follow. For more details, see [How to create custom skills](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12512198-creating-custom-skills).

# Partner Skills

Skills are a great way to teach Claude how to get better at using specific pieces of software. As we see awesome example skills from partners, we may highlight some of them here:

- **Notion** - [Notion Skills for Claude](https://www.notion.so/notiondevs/Notion-Skills-for-Claude-28da4445d27180c7af1df7d8615723d0)

      Title: Broken on Arrival: Non-Functional Quantized LLM Artifacts in Public Model Registries and How to Catch Them 
      Authors:  Aditi Patodiya               View a PDF of the paper titled Broken on Arrival: Non-Functional Quantized LLM Artifacts in Public Model Registries and How to Catch Them, by Aditi Patodiya 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Developers download quantized large language models (LLMs) from public registries to run them locally. None of the registries we examined documented functional testing of their files. We tested all 305 eligible code-capable GGUF tags (the  this http URL  format) across 15 model lines in the official Ollama library, plus 22 popular Hugging Face community files. A 15-task code screen identified suspects, which we retested on all 164 HumanEval+ tasks. Seven official tags (2.3%) solved at most six of them. All were low-bit quantizations of models with at most four billion parameters. We rebuilt five suspect files from the original weights. All five registry files matched our uncalibrated rebuilds tensor for tensor, so none was corrupted. Exact reproducibility did not imply function. With the weights, toolchain and tensor mix held fixed, adding an importance matrix raised Qwen2.5-Coder-3B scores at three quantization levels from zero to 76-113 of 164 tasks. The same uncalibrated recipe left the smaller Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B functional, showing that the recipe alone does not predict failure. None of 66 sampled tags that passed the screen was non-functional. We release the audit data and the quantcheck tool and recommend screening low-bit tags before publication, then calibrating or withholding failures.

      Title: RetroChessBench: A Benchmark for Reconstructing and Proving Chess Histories 
      Authors:  Tidor-Vlad Pricope               View a PDF of the paper titled RetroChessBench: A Benchmark for Reconstructing and Proving Chess Histories, by Tidor-Vlad Pricope

             Abstract: Frontier language models such as GPT 6 Astra have contributed to research mathematics, demonstrating substantial reasoning capabilities. Yet serious reasoning failures persist even in tasks governed by explicit rules. We demonstrate this in retrograde chess which is a playground for pure reasoning, where solvers reconstruct legal histories and distinguish possible events from forced ones. We introduce RetroChessBench, a 12-task benchmark covering exact-length constructions, unique endings, and exhaustive answer sets, with references, rubrics, and a terminal-reward environment. In two trials per task and condition, GPT 6 Astra High fails to produce the required final answer in 22/24 attempts without tools and 18/24 with code execution; mean terminal RL rewards are 14.75% and 27.19%, respectively. The examples identify faulty deductions: failed responses reject legal histories and treat temporary obstructions as permanent. Online retrograde archives often provide puzzles and final move sequences without detailed derivations. We hypothesize that limited exposure to these missing explanations in web-derived training data contributes to the observed reasoning failures. This questions how far frontier mathematical reasoning really generalizes beyond familiar solution patterns. Claims of general intelligence require evidence that models can transfer learnt principles to areas with few worked examples.

  RetroChessBench: A Benchmark for
 
Reconstructing and Proving Chess Histories  
  Pricope Tidor-Vlad

  27 October 2026  
 
  
 
  Abstract 
    
 Frontier language models such as GPT 6 Astra have contributed to research mathematics, demonstrating substantial reasoning capabilities. Yet serious reasoning failures persist even in tasks governed by explicit rules. We demonstrate this in retrograde chess which is a playground for pure reasoning, where solvers reconstruct legal histories and distinguish possible events from forced ones. We introduce RetroChessBench, a 12-task benchmark covering exact-length constructions, unique endings, and exhaustive answer sets, with references, rubrics, and a terminal-reward environment. In two trials per task and condition, GPT 6 Astra High fails to produce the required final answer in 22/24 attempts without tools and 18/24 with code execution; mean terminal RL rewards are 14.75% and 27.19%, respectively. The examples identify faulty deductions: failed responses reject legal histories and treat temporary obstructions as permanent. Online retrograde archives often provide puzzles and final move sequences without detailed derivations. We hypothesize that limited exposure to these missing explanations in web-derived training data contributes to the observed reasoning failures. This questions how far frontier mathematical reasoning really generalizes beyond familiar solution patterns. Claims of general intelligence require evidence that models can transfer learnt principles to areas with few worked examples. 
  
 
 
 1  Introduction 

 
 A chess position records where the surviving pieces stand. It omits the moves that brought them there, the pieces that disappeared, and the promotions that may have occurred. Retrograde analysis reconstructs this missing history under the ordinary rules of chess. The scientific question is whether a model can reason consistently over these hidden histories and distinguish what  could  have happened from what  must  have happened. 
 
 
 The distinction changes the standard of proof. An exact-length proof game needs one legal witness. A unique-ending problem needs an argument covering every compatible history. A problem with several possible last moves needs a feasible history for each answer and an exclusion of all others. These obligations remain different even when their final answers fit on one line. A six-move ending can depend on a promotion or capture budget established much earlier in the game. 
 
 
 These tasks put a basic expectation of general reasoning under pressure: known rules should remain usable when the question changes from choosing a future move to establishing a necessary past event. The solver must keep track of hypothetical states, revise assumptions, and distinguish constraints that hold in one candidate history from constraints that hold in all of them. Fluent reconstruction can conceal a failure at precisely this distinction. 
 
 
 A concrete failure illustrates the issue. In P0292, a model constructs a legal 47-ply game and concludes that the requested 45-ply game is impossible. Its bound treats a pawn on g6 as an unavoidable obstruction to a bishop’s route. A replayable 45-ply construction sends the bishop through g6  before  the pawn arrives. The model has found one possible history and mistaken its schedule for a necessary constraint. Table   1   isolates the error; Appendix   D   gives the full counterexample. 
 
 
 We introduce  RetroChessBench  (also on  Hugging Face ), a 12-task benchmark comprising seven exact-length games, four unique suffixes, and one exhaustive two-answer task. These tasks were selected from a  48-task candidate pool  drawn from  StrateGems  compositions, including two adaptations. References, prompts, board images, responses, rubrics, and replay checks accompany the tasks. A  terminal-reward interface  accepts alternative valid constructions and scores analytical obligations separately. 
 
 
 We evaluate GPT 6 Astra High twice per task without tools and twice with hosted code execution. Final answers are correct in 2/24 and 6/24 attempts. The code condition produces two valid constructive games and four correct suffixes; three of those suffix answers still lack complete proofs. Five construction tasks fail in all four attempts. These are descriptive outcomes on a set selected using observed failures, not an unbiased estimate of retrograde-chess ability or a causal estimate of tool benefit. 
 
 
 OpenAI reported a Navier–Stokes solution on 8 September 2026  ( OpenAI, 2026d ) . Four weeks later, on 6 October, it released hundreds of mathematical research manuscripts with varying verification status  ( OpenAI, 2026c ;  OpenAI, 2026b ) . Both releases concern internal models; OpenAI describes the Navier–Stokes model as more capable than Astra, whose separate mathematical contributions include prime-gap results  ( OpenAI, 2026a ) . ChessBench’s 27 October 2026 snapshot lists Astra at 1745 Elo for XHigh and 1531 for High  ( ChessBench, 2026a ) . These reports motivate broader tests of reasoning. The question is whether mathematical progress brings reliable construction and exclusion across other domains. 
 
 
 Backward reasoning is already studied in language-model planning, and reverse chess appears in LongCoT  ( Ren et al., 2024 ;  Motwani et al., 2026 ) . Our source compositions and answers are public, but availability does not establish training exposure. A leading hypothesis is limited exposure to worked retrograde explanations. The source archive gives P0292’s game with a short theme description and R0185’s ending with a compact rejected branch  ( The Retrograde Analysis Corner,  ) . A game certifies existence but need not teach discovery; a suffix sequence alone does not establish uniqueness. Detailed treatments do exist  ( Volet, 2003 ) ; the hypothesis concerns explanatory coverage in training, which we have not measured. If such coverage is sparse, can a model assemble familiar rules into historical deductions without abundant demonstrations of the method? 
 
 
 Our contribution operationalizes these established proof obligations in hidden chess histories through distinct answer contracts, executable witness checks, recorded proof assessments, and inspectable counterexamples to failed arguments. The benchmark and auditable pilot motivate controlled tests of local rule knowledge, candidate discovery, state representation, and proof verification (Section   9  ). Those tests can distinguish missing techniques from failures to coordinate techniques the model already possesses.

 2  Related work 

 
 Chess play and state tracking. 

 
 Chess offers several distinct evaluation targets.   Toshniwal et al. (2022)   study piece tracking and legal-move prediction from move sequences, finding that explicit state information helps with limited training data.   Harang et al. (2025)   evaluate inferred chess states through the actions those states permit.   Kolasani et al. (2025)   examine reasoning and instruction following during extended forward play. ChessBench derives ratings from game outcomes using an anchored Monte Carlo Elo procedure  ( ChessBench, 2026b ) . These settings test following or choosing a continuation from a supplied history. RetroChessBench instead asks the solver to recover unobserved events, including captures and promotions, and sometimes to prove that other histories cannot change the answer. A forward-play rating motivates comparison but supplies no calibration for historical proof difficulty. 
 
 
 
 Reverse reconstruction and classical planning. 

 
 LongCoT is the closest benchmark predecessor: its reverse-chess task reconstructs a legal alternating move sequence consistent with a terminal board, side to move, and specified move fragments  ( Motwani et al., 2026 ) . This shares the existential objective of our proof games. The unique-suffix and exhaustive-answer tasks add universal exclusions over legal histories. PlanBench provides systematic tests of planning and reasoning about actions and change using domains from automated planning  ( Valmeekam et al., 2023 ) . It establishes a broader methodological precedent for explicit transition rules and checkable plans.   Ren et al. (2024)   study directional planning biases and combine forward and backward search with verification. Together these studies motivate separating discovery from checking, rather than treating all backward reasoning as one capability. 
 
 
 
 Abduction and missing premises. 

 
 Recovering history is a form of reasoning from effects to possible causes. ART asks models to choose or generate plausible explanations of narrative observations  ( Bhagavatula et al., 2020 ) . Plausibility is a different criterion from chess legality, and neither entails uniqueness. ProofWriter generates implications, proofs, and abductive statements over explicit natural-language theories  ( Tafjord et al., 2021 ) .   Sprague et al. (2022)   interleave forward deduction and backward abduction to infer missing premises, using round-trip validation to filter candidates. RetroChessBench shares the need to propose hidden events and check their consequences, but the missing objects are time-indexed states and piece identities under a fixed transition system. An explanation must fit a complete legal history; a uniqueness claim must survive every alternative explanation admitted by that system. 
 
 
 
 Proof search, quantifiers, and generalization. 

 
 PrOntoQA makes generated reasoning steps amenable to formal analysis.   Saparov and He (2023)   find that valid individual deductions can coexist with failures to explore alternative proof steps.   Saparov et al. (2023)   separately test depth, width, and compositional generalization, including hypothetical subproofs. These results motivate our distinction between knowing a local chess rule and coordinating it across a branching historical argument; they do not establish the cause of Astra’s errors. SATBench evaluates constraint satisfaction and unsatisfiability on generated logical puzzles  ( Wei et al., 2025 ) , a related separation of witnesses from exclusion. RetroChessBench adds capture identities, alternating turns, and hidden event order, while retaining the need to distinguish an existential solution from a universal claim. 
 
 
 
 Mathematics, constructions, and robustness. 

 
 MathArena evaluates recent competition mathematics, and Proof or Bluff examines proof quality on olympiad problems  ( Balunović et al., 2025b ;  Petrov et al., 2025 ) . MathConstruct accepts automatically checkable mathematical constructions  ( Balunović et al., 2025a ) ; the same principle governs our exact-length games: any valid witness earns full credit. Those results provide context for asking about transfer, rather than a measurement of transfer in this study. GSM-Symbolic probes mathematical robustness through template variations  ( Mirzadeh et al., 2025 ) . Its later re-evaluation identifies numerical-distribution and statistical confounds and reports model-specific failure profiles  ( Długosz et al., 2026 ) . The methodological lesson is relevant here: a performance gap requires controlled explanation. Counterfactual-task evaluations  ( Wu et al., 2024 )  and chess-prior interventions  ( Pleiss et al., 2026 )  offer complementary ways to test dependence on familiar representations. RetroChessBench keeps orthodox rules fixed; future transfer tests must additionally control the inference demanded and the solution budget. 
 
 
 
 Classical retrograde analysis and assessment. 

 
 The compositions and source solutions predate this benchmark and remain credited to their authors  ( The Retrograde Analysis Corner,  ) . Generalized retrograde reachability on growing boards is PSPACE-complete  ( Brunner et al., 2020 ) ; this does not classify the difficulty of our fixed     8  ×  8   8\times 8    instances. Specialist software such as Jacobi already solves proof games  ( Labelle,  ) . Our claim concerns language-model evaluation, not the impossibility of algorithmic reconstruction. Natural-language uniqueness proofs introduce a different assessment problem. Known limitations of model judges  ( Zheng et al., 2023 )  require separate records for deterministic witness checks, rubric credit, and proof review. A reference receiving full credit is a calibration control, not independent evidence that the proof or judge is correct.

 3.4  Why a standard chess engine is insufficient 

 
 Stockfish searches forward for strong continuations  ( Stockfish developers,  ) . Historical reconstruction requires additional information: the identity of captured pieces, earlier promotions, and the times at which squares were available. A best-move query does not supply it. Undoing a recorded move also differs from generating every possible predecessor of an arbitrary board. 
 
 
 Code can still help.  python-chess  provides move generation, legality checks, notation handling, and replay  ( Fiekas,  ) . Custom search, constraint solvers, and proof-game programs can reconstruct histories. Our code condition supplies general hosted execution; it does not supply a complete retrograde solver. Historical reconstruction also differs from computing game-theoretic endgame tablebases backward from terminal states. 
 
 
 
 
 4  Benchmark construction 

 
 4.1  From the source archive to the benchmark 

 
 We audited 82 primary problem entries in  StrateGems  Nos. 52–58 and documented their variants. Eligible tasks asked for prior moves or an orthodox proof game. We excluded piece-addition tasks, position release alone, and fairy-chess stipulations. The resulting 58 task instances each received two no-code runs. At least one run failed on 47 instances. We removed P0299 because its analytical completeness proof remained unresolved. The remaining 46 instances and two adaptations form a 48-task candidate pool. 
 
 
 RetroChessBench contains 12 tasks with completed grading and recorded secondary review of all 48 solver responses. Ten were selected using observed results, with R0178 and the easier R01 adaptation included to broaden suffix coverage. The final inventory and attempt slots are frozen, but the selection process was adaptive: it first retained no-code failures and subsequently used code outcomes and proof coverage to select the benchmark tasks. The reported no-code trials include the same attempts used for screening. This creates an asymmetric comparison: screening for no-code failure can make subsequent code trials look better through selection and regression to the mean, even without a tool effect. Later selection on code failures adds another dependency. The retained snapshots document the filtering stages and final task IDs, not a preregistered selection rule. We report a challenge-set baseline and give the selection ledger in Appendix   A  . A causal tool comparison requires a frozen task set and fresh trials in  both  conditions. 
 
 
 
 4.2  Composition, adaptations, and attribution 

 
 The benchmark comprises seven constructive tasks, four unique-suffix tasks, and one two-alternative task. Constructive lengths range from 35 to 60 plies; suffix lengths are 5, 6, 36, and 40 plies. Table   7   credits every composer and source issue. 
 
 
 R01 adapts Andrey Frolkin’s R0185 ( StrateGems  No. 56, 2011). We ask for the last six single moves instead of eight because this shorter ending retains the central reasoning challenge; proving its uniqueness still requires looking further back. We also relocate White’s rook from h8 to g8, leaving every other piece in place. The rook remains to the right of Qd8, preserving its role in the eighth-rank obstruction used by the proof. The relocation deliberately changes the original diagram to reduce reliance on exact diagram memorization, should the source have appeared in training. It does not establish absence from pretraining data or measure a reduction in memorization. 
 
 
 R02 adapts Nikolai I. Beluhov’s R0176 ( StrateGems  No. 53, 2011). The diagram is unchanged; the only task modification is to request the last five single moves instead of forty. This keeps the exposition manageable while preserving the central trap, which arises near the start of the backward analysis. Establishing those five moves still requires excluding a tempting continuation whose failure becomes apparent only further back in the history. 
 
 
 Both adaptations retain the central proof mechanism under the prompt’s legal-reachability premise. R02 and R0176 share a position and much of their reasoning; Section   7   reports a family-weighted sensitivity analysis.

 4.3  What the artifact contains 

 
 Tasks include prompts, FENs, board images, attribution, reference proofs, answer specifications, and versioned rubrics. Evaluation records contain responses, request metadata, criterion judgments, sequence checks, reviews, and hashes. Each solver rollout is an episode; its trajectory receives a terminal reward and feedback based on the final answer and justification. Intermediate messages and tool calls receive no separate process rewards. This supports reinforcement learning; we evaluate without training a policy. 
 
 
 The  benchmark website  provides task documents, paired results, and evidence;  PDL-Bench on Hugging Face  hosts the 12-task  retro_chess  subset. The  RL environment  is available as a  tested Docker build bundle , also on  Hugging Face , with  setup instructions  and a  validation report . Researchers can export solver inputs, check references, and grade new trajectories against the frozen tasks and rubrics. The paper bundle includes scripts that reproduce the reported tables and aggregate scores from archived judgments. Appendices   B   and   A   specify the protocol and archived release. 
 
 
 References and rubrics were developed with AI assistance. The author manually reviewed the solutions on a physical chessboard. A Codex agent performed the recorded secondary reviews. The artifact records these roles and retains attribution for the original compositions and solutions. 
 
 
 
 
 5  Reward design and grading 

 
 5.1  Separate answer correctness from proof quality 

 
 The evaluator reports final-answer correctness, categorical proof status, and terminal reward separately. A final-answer failure means the required game, suffix, or complete answer set was not produced. Terminal reward scores the task’s full objective. A correct ending with an incomplete proof can earn less than 100%; sound deductions can earn partial credit despite a wrong ending. The public dashboard calls a final-answer failure a “stump.” The primary scientific outcomes are exact-answer success and whether the applicable proof obligation is complete. Aggregate reward is an environment-specific summary, not a percentage of reasoning ability or of tasks solved. 
 
 
 The binary answer metric uses verified sequence status, not full sequence-criterion credit. Omitting or mislabeling  +  or  #  does not turn an otherwise verified game, suffix, or complete answer set into a final-answer failure. Such defects can reduce analytical sequence credit and hence reward; they do not reduce the binary constructive witness reward. Required move order, promotion identities, and captured-piece alternatives remain substantive constraints. All 48 retained verdicts agree with this rule, and none of the 40 failures is notation-only (Appendix   E  ).
