 5.4  Calibration and corrections 

 
 All 12 reference controls (the “golden answers”) score 100%. Because those references were used to develop the rubrics, this checks calibration rather than independent judge accuracy. Solver and judge also use the same model family, leaving room for correlated errors. 
 
 
 Secondary audits cover all 48 answers and 12 controls. One retained score changed: R0178 code run 1 rose from 82.5% to 88% after review found inconsistent credit for a valid blocker-exclusion argument. The record preserves both scores and the correction. R0171 required a reference repair: an earlier grading bundle loaded an obsolete incomplete draft. We synchronized the completed reference, versioned its task and rubric, and regenerated its five grades. That reference includes both full feasibility witnesses and the analytical exclusion argument. 
 
 
 
 
 6  Experimental setup 

 
 We evaluate GPT 6 Astra High using RetroChessBench’s terminal-reward RL environment. The study uses 48 archived Azure solver rollouts, subsequently scored as episodes: 12 tasks, two runs, and two solver tool presets. Each trajectory’s final answer and written justification determine its terminal reward     r  ∈   [   0  ,  1   ]    r\in[0,1]   , alongside separate final-answer and proof-status assessments. Analytical tasks allow partial reward; constructive games use the binary witness reward (Section   5  ). Intermediate messages and tool calls receive no process rewards, and this study performs no policy updates. 
 
 
 Calls were made on 26–27 October 2026 through Azure with deployment alias  gpt-6-astra  and reasoning effort  high . We call this configuration GPT 6 Astra High. The response metadata identifies the alias, not an immutable weight snapshot. Separate ChatGPT XHigh experiments are excluded. 
 
 
 The two solver presets share task and reward definitions:  no code  supplies no tools;  code enabled  supplies Azure’s hosted code interpreter with an automatically provisioned 4 GB container. The grading pipeline is the same in both presets. The system prompt specifies only a JSON object containing one  solution  string and adherence to the task. All four runs for a task receive identical text after newline normalization, including FEN, and the same high-detail board image. Solvers receive no reference, rubric, or chess strategy. Web search is unavailable. Requests leave seed, temperature, and maximum output tokens unset, using provider defaults. 
 
 
 All selected responses completed, and every code-enabled rollout invoked the tool. The archive records 219 completed code calls and none in the no-code preset. It retains code payloads but no console outputs, so we cannot confirm library installation, useful verifier feedback, or whether a solver used or ignored that feedback. In particular, the record does not establish successful Stockfish use. 
 
 
 Median output-token usage, including reasoning tokens, is 42,295 without code and 58,443 with code. Compute is therefore unmatched; tool access, token usage, and search behavior vary together. The comparison uses the frozen completed pair for each task. Technical retries, two later R01 no-code runs, and separate ChatGPT outputs remain outside the 48-episode analysis. 
 
 
 The analysis pins task IDs, answer hashes, references, rubrics, and reviewed grades. A local script regenerates every numerical summary, task table, and plot. It also replays the constructive references and successful model games, checking legality, length, final placement, and premature automatic termination. Analytical proofs retain their separate rubric assessments.

 7.4  Sensitivity and interpretation 

 
 The R0178 correction changes the code mean from 26.96% to 27.19%, a 0.23-point increase. To reduce double weighting of the R02/R0176 position, we average their task means and give each of the resulting eleven families equal weight. The means become 12.52% without code and 26.33% with code. Dropping R02 gives 10.82% and 26.80%; dropping R0176 gives 14.23% and 25.86%. The aggregate contrast survives each adjustment. 
 
 
 Omitting any one task gives a code-minus-no-code difference between 7.82 and 15.98 percentage points. This is a sensitivity range, not a confidence interval. Two runs per task, shared source families, and selection on observed performance prevent a precise population interpretation. 
 
 
 Reward design has a larger effect than the grading correction. Substituting diagnostic rubric credit for binary construction reward raises the means to 20.06% and 32.88%. That measures a different objective. We retain binary reward for construction because the requested deliverable is a valid exact-length witness, and keep diagnostic credit available for studying partial progress. 
 
 
 
 
 8  Failure mechanisms 

 
 Saved answers make the failures inspectable. Each case below identifies the disputed claim and the move or history that defeats it. The analysis concerns observable arguments; it does not infer hidden model states or estimate the frequency of each mechanism outside this set. 
 
 
 8.1  R01: applying king safety to the wrong time step 

 
 The six-move ending is 
 

  
  
          Kb6  ×  Bb7   ,    c7  −  c8   =   B  +    ,   Kb7  −   b8  +     ,          Bc8  −   b7  +    ,   Kb8  ×  Bb7   ,   a5  −   a6  #     .      \begin{gathered}\mathrm{Kb6}\times\mathrm{Bb7},\quad\mathrm{c7-c8}=\mathrm{B}^{+},\quad\mathrm{Kb7-b8}^{+},\\
\mathrm{Bc8-b7}^{+},\quad\mathrm{Kb8}\times\mathrm{Bb7},\quad\mathrm{a5-a6}^{\#}.\end{gathered}    
    
 
 Code run 1 rejects b8 as the origin of Black’s penultimate king move because White’s queen attacks it. The king can legally  start  its turn in check, then capture the bishop on b7 to escape. The rule concerns safety after the move. Applying it before the move leads to a false impossibility claim. The response earns 7.5% for a sound preliminary pawn-provenance argument. 
 
 
 No-code run 1 makes the same kind of error earlier. Black vacates b7, opening the bishop’s a8–b7–c6–d5 diagonal against White’s king. White then plays Bc8-b7, blocking that check and uncovering a queen check against Black. The response declares the intermediate check impossible instead of testing White’s reply. Its capture accounting earns 22.5%; its no-history conclusion is false. 
 
 
 The reference required a related repair. To exclude a  knight  as the earliest b7 victim, it is insufficient to observe that White was in check before a hypothetical Nc5-b7: that move could block the check. The corrected proof examines whether Black’s preceding move could have created it. The grader must enforce the same temporal standard on the reference and the submission. 
 
 
 
 8.2  R02: a temporary lock mistaken for a permanent constraint 

 
 The required five moves are 
 

  
  
       Bc6  −  a4   ,   b3  −  b2   ,   Ba4  −  c2   ,    b2  −  b1   =  B   ,   Rf2  ×   Nf3  +     .   \mathrm{Bc6-a4},\quad\mathrm{b3-b2},\quad\mathrm{Ba4-c2},\quad\mathrm{b2-b1}=\mathrm{B},\quad\mathrm{Rf2}\times\mathrm{Nf3}^{+}.    
    
 
 Code run 2 derives useful capture and promotion constraints, including the final promotion/capture pair. It then declares the central group locked until an earlier pawn capture is undone, missing a release through a knight-screen exchange. It also fixes capture squares from the white pawns’  final  ranks without establishing their ranks at the time. These assumptions create a false shortage of turns. The answer concludes that the position is impossible and earns 47% for its valid deductions. 
 
 
 The release moves the bishop away from c2, routes the a6 knight backward through b4 and c2 to e1, and coordinates the restored f3 knight. Each step depends on squares becoming available at the right time. A shortest geometric knight route is only a candidate; it must fit the alternating turns. Those deadlines force the early bishop moves in the answer. 
 
 
 
 8.3  P0292: a near witness does not establish a lower bound 

 
 Both code runs reach the board legally in 47 plies; the task requires 45. Run 1 claims that 47 is minimal because a bishop cannot travel from e8 to h5 through the pawn on g6. The reference sends the newly promoted bishop through g6  before  g7-g6, then plays g6   ×  \times   Bh5. The supposed obstruction exists only after the route has been used. 
 
 
 Replay confirms the proposed 47-ply games. It cannot certify the claimed lower bound. The 45-ply reference refutes that claim directly and is printed in Appendix   D  . Any valid 45-ply alternative would earn full credit; the submitted games fail the length requirement. 
 
 
 
 8.4  R0171 and R0178: a final answer is not a proof certificate 

 
 R0171’s answers are b7   ×  \times   Rc8=R# and b7   ×  \times   Nc8=R#. Writing b7   ×  \times   Xc8=R# identifies the mechanism but leaves the victim identities and completeness unresolved. The reference supplies legal histories for both the rook and knight branches and excludes the other victims. The two-move answer set carries both existence and exclusion obligations. 
 
 
 Both code runs on R0178 give the correct ending and omit parts of its uniqueness proof. One reaches the 90% incompleteness cap. Retaining the final-answer check alongside the reward makes this distinction visible. 
 
 
 
 
 9  Validation priorities and follow-up tests 

 
 The archived responses expose failures of temporal consistency and historical exclusion. Establishing their cause requires validated references and controlled comparisons; the present pilot supplies neither a causal tool effect nor a transfer estimate. 
 
 
 Complete witness coverage and assess the grader. 

 
 The remaining reference-evidence work is to supply a legal start-to-diagram witness for each suffix position (Table   14  ). A separate blinded evaluation of the grader should assess solver answers, valid alternative proofs, and minimally corrupted proofs without model or condition labels. Report criterion-level disagreement, false acceptance, false rejection, and adjudication; retain unresolved cases as such. Full-score reference controls establish calibration and cannot replace these checks. 
 
 
 
 Separate discovery from justification. 

 
 The most direct diagnostic compares free solving with a condition that supplies the correct suffix and asks whether it is forced. This holds the position fixed and removes answer discovery; a separate incorrect-candidate arm tests automatic endorsement. Persistent exclusion errors with the true ending supplied would locate a failure beyond discovery. Complement this with unrelated local-rule probes and blinded proof-verification trials. Score final answers and proof validity separately, and keep assisted results outside the unassisted benchmark score. 
 
 
 
 Test explanatory coverage. 

 
 Compare an unadapted baseline with adaptation on final-answer sequences or fully worked proofs for the same training tasks. Match total training tokens and compute; test fresh composition families and new combinations of mechanisms. Measure answer recovery and proof completion separately. Gains from worked proofs would establish their usefulness, not their absence from the original training corpus. 
 
 
 
 Test mechanism-specific predictions. 

 
 Appendix   F   specifies the interventions and safeguards for state tracking, search, and compositional transfer. A transfer claim requires demonstrated source competence, a defined target shift, and improvement from a targeted intervention that does not reveal the answer. Architectural explanations additionally require controlled comparisons with comparable training and inference budgets; improvement from an external state ledger alone would not isolate architecture. Freeze fresh composition families and primary outcomes before evaluation. These are proposed experiments, not results of this study. 
 
 
 
 
 10  Limitations and Reproducibility 

 
 Selection and scale. 

 
 The 12 tasks were selected using the model results reported here, including no-code screening trials retained in the comparison. This asymmetry can favor code without a causal tool benefit. Composers, mechanisms, and the repeated R02/R0176 position create dependencies. Two runs per condition and unmatched compute support descriptive scores, not population success rates or a causal estimate of code’s benefit. A broader evaluation needs tasks fixed in advance, more runs, multiple model families, and matched budgets. 
 
 
 
 Ground truth and grading. 

 
 Complete constructive witnesses can be replayed. The author manually reviewed the solutions, including the analytical uniqueness and exclusion arguments, on a physical chessboard. These arguments are presented as natural-language proofs rather than formal certificates. The four suffix references additionally lack full reachability witnesses in this bundle; their arguments are conditional on the prompt premise. Solver and judge may share errors. Reference controls calibrate the rubric; they do not measure independent judge accuracy. The recorded reference repair and score correction show why versioned evidence and review matter. 
 
 
 
 Exposure and adaptation. 

 
 Source problems and answers are public. We have measured neither the volume of public worked explanations nor Astra’s exposure to them. Changing a rook square or suffix length cannot guarantee that a task is absent from training. Future splits should keep shared position families together and include newly composed problems with documented creation dates. We also lack a matched mathematics evaluation of this deployment. The results do not identify memorization, an architectural limit, or a general-intelligence boundary as the cause of failure. 
 
 
 
 RL environment and replication. 

 
 Researchers can download the 12-task benchmark and tested RL environment from  https://app.poindexterlabs.net/docs/retro-chess  or  PDL-Bench on Hugging Face , under  retro_chess . The  Docker ZIP , also  mirrored on Hugging Face , contains build files, all 12 tasks, board images, reference solutions, rubrics, and the grading runtime. Follow the  setup instructions  to build the container, run offline checks, export solver inputs, and grade new model trajectories with provider credentials. The paper bundle’s analysis scripts reproduce the reported tables and aggregate scores from archived judgments. Appendix   B   specifies the experimental settings; the  validation report  records the Docker and grading checks. Replication should record the downloaded release hash and actual grading provider. 
 
 
 
 Provenance and attribution. 

 
 The manuscript bundle preserves the prompts, diagrams, references, rubrics, answer evidence, scoring scripts, and analyses used here; the  candidate pool  records selection provenance. Composition attribution and applicable third-party rights must accompany redistribution. The bundle does not grant a blanket license to the original compositions. 
 
 
 
 
 11  Conclusion 

 
 RetroChessBench tests three obligations: constructing a legal history, proving a forced ending, and identifying every possible answer. On this selected challenge set, Astra High gives correct final answers in 2/24 attempts without code and 6/24 with code. Mean terminal rewards from the RL environment are 14.75% and 27.19%, respectively. The benchmark remains far from saturated in both solver presets, even with code execution. 
 
 
 We expect the  three hardest tasks  to resist reliable solution for some time, while the others approach saturation as models improve. Progress requires both better answers and complete proofs: only one of the four correct code-enabled suffix answers receives full proof credit under the archived review. 
 
 
 The model rules out legal histories for the wrong reasons. It rejects a king for starting its turn in check even though it can escape legally, excludes a route because a square is occupied later, and uses a valid construction to claim a false lower bound. A restriction on one moment or candidate does not establish a claim about every legal history. 
 
 
 Limited exposure to worked retrograde proofs is a leading hypothesis to test. Generality requires evaluating how efficiently a model learns from such explanations and transfers the method to new compositions. Matched tests must distinguish missing domain instruction from failures to combine familiar rules. Claims of artificial general intelligence require evidence of reliable reasoning across new, independently validated problems, beyond saturation of a fixed public set. The standard is a legal construction when one history suffices, and rigorous exclusion when every history matters.

 Sequence partial credit. 

 
 The deterministic R01/R02 policy awards half of C1 only for the explicitly specified near-complete cases, including at least four correct moves in their chronological slots; R02 additionally permits a specified single ordering repair. It does not convert a different final conclusion into the expected sequence. Missing identity or annotation details may prevent full notation credit even where the underlying moves agree. The full JSON policy distinguishes these cases. 
 
 
 
 Judge input and feedback. 

 
 The judge receives the task, reference proof, expected answer or set, rubric, and submission as separate inputs. Credited reasoning requires evidence in the submission. The environment checks the quoted evidence and computes scores locally. Anchoring verifies that the text exists; judging its logic remains a separate responsibility. Instructions embedded in a submission must be treated as answer data.

  analysis/reviewer_audit.py  maps the 20 archived analytical grades and review comments to Table   4  , retaining submission/reference hashes. It changes no rewards and requests no new judgments. The 28 constructive answers use the replay categories above: a valid witness suffices. Partial reasoning credit is not a proof-validity probability. 
 
 
 
 Notation and headline counts. 

 
  analysis/notation_audit.py  checks all 48 retained verdicts against archived sequence status: accepted answers are exactly those marked verified. None of the 40 failures is notation-only. Two P0295 answers have a check/mate-marker defect, but both supply 48 plies instead of the required 46. Thirteen annotation-removal checks on reference strings using the archived runtime retain verified status; analytical sequence credit can fall from full to half. The audit records these checks without new model calls or changes to the saved scores. It does not validate global reachability or analytical proofs. 
 
 
 
 Why 27.5% diagnostic credit can coexist with zero reward. 

 
 P0332 no-code run 1 reaches the target legally in 46 plies; the task requires 44. Route, check, and material deductions earn 27.5% diagnostic credit. Terminal reward remains zero because the construction misses the move budget. The artifact preserves both values so that analysis of partial progress can use the diagnostic without changing the exact-task score. 
 
 
 
 Reference-control interpretation. 

 
 All 12 current references score 100%. Full-game replay verifies the constructive controls. Analytical controls satisfy the calibrated rubric under the current judge and review. R01 includes the expanded earliest-knight exclusion; R0171 uses its completed v2 reference. Reproduction must use those versions. 
 
 
 
 One explicit correction. 

 
 Review raised R0178 code run 1 from 82.5% to 88%: its tracked position and argument excluded competing c8 blockers, meeting the standard accepted in run 2. Other omissions prevent full credit. Run 2 totals 95.5% before the incomplete-proof cap reduces it to 90%. Raw judgments, caps, and overrides are stored separately. 
 
 
 
 What an independent replay checks. 

 
 Replay starts from the standard position and checks UCI moves for legality, exact length, final placement, and premature automatic termination. All seven constructive controls and both successful model games pass. Replay can establish these properties of a supplied witness. Lower bounds and complete exclusions require additional arguments. 
 
 
 
 
  Appendix F  Controlled follow-up study 

 
 Following the validation priorities in Section   9  , freeze fresh tasks and keep composition families within one split. Use the same model snapshot and explicit token/tool budgets across paired conditions. Predefine source competence, target shift, and primary outcomes; report uncertainty over families. The interventions below are proposed controls, not completed experiments.

  Compare no adaptation, answer-only examples, and worked proofs on the same training tasks; test disjoint families and new mechanism combinations.

cna:CVE-2026-61738.desc: SOCFortress CoPilot focuses on providing a single pane of glass for all your security operations needs. Prior to 0.1.77, `POST /api/scoutsuite/generate-gcp-report` in `backend/app/integrations/scoutsuite/routes/scoutsuite.py` admits admin and analyst users and validates the uploaded content as `GCPScoutSuiteJSON`, but passes raw `file.filename` from the multipart header to `save_file_to_directory` in `backend/app/integrations/scoutsuite/services/scoutsuite.py`. The writer combines this filename with `scoutsuite-report` using `os.path.join` without sanitization or a resolved-path containment check. A traversal filename therefore writes the supplied JSON outside the intended report directory. In the reported root-running backend, the researcher demonstrated root-owned writes outside that directory and into the application source directory. This permits host-file overwrite subject to the accepted JSON-content constraint and can disrupt application operation; the demonstrated primitive does not establish unrestricted executable contents or unconditional cross-tenant confidentiality loss. Version 0.1.77 removes caller-controlled filenames from the affected route; unrestricted-content and direct-code-execution claims require separate curator reconciliation.

cna:CVE-2026-61826.desc: Bazarr is a companion application to Sonarr and Radarr. Prior to 1.5.7-beta.14, the `api_ns_plex` namespace in `bazarr/api/plex/oauth.py` omits `@authenticate` on its Resource handlers, while normal APIs require an API key and no global authentication hook compensates. Anonymous callers can invoke `POST /api/plex/oauth/logout` to clear credentials and disable the integration, or `POST /api/plex/apikey` to persist an attacker-selected key, without a PIN, account or state precondition. `POST /api/plex/oauth/pin` and `GET /api/plex/oauth/pin/<pin_id>/check` additionally allow an attacker who completes a PIN with an attacker-controlled Plex account to bind that account's token to the instance. `PlexPinCheck` skips state validation when `state_param` is absent and merely logs a mismatch without stopping execution. `POST /api/plex/select-server`, `POST /api/plex/oauth/servers`, `POST /api/plex/webhook/create`, `POST /api/plex/webhook/delete` and `POST /api/plex/encrypt-apikey` expose further `write_config()` operations. Attacker-controlled server URLs feed later outbound requests carrying the configured API key in `X-Plex-Token`, enabling server-side request forgery and credential exposure in addition to persistent configuration tampering and integration denial of service. Version 1.5.7-beta.14 closes the anonymous API-mutation path by adding authentication; complete OAuth state validation is not established and remains a separate residual for curator review.

cwe.description: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

cna:CVE-2026-63377.desc: TAKO AI Agent for Okta is a local-first AI agent that helps Okta administrators query tenant data using natural language. Prior to 3.0.1-beta, `POST /api/auth/setup` in `src/api/routers/auth.py` allows an unauthenticated network attacker to create the first administrator account before the legitimate owner completes initial setup. The `initial_setup` function checks only the `is_setup` completion flag and requires no authentication, one-time bootstrap token, or network restriction. The default `docker-compose.yml` publishes port 8001 on all interfaces, the `Dockerfile` starts the listener on 0.0.0.0, and `src/api/main.py` mounts the authentication router without a global authentication guard. The endpoint invokes `create_auth_user` with `UserRole.ADMIN` and `set_auth_cookie`, issuing a valid `fctr_session` JWT cookie. Localhost-only CORS rules do not restrict non-browser HTTP clients, and the setup operation does not require access to a real Okta tenant. The attacker becomes the sole administrator and prevents legitimate first-run setup, can read Okta-synced user data, API tokens, chat history, and application configuration, modify users and Okta integration credentials, and lock out administrators or disable the service. Already completed setup is rejected. This issue is fixed in version 3.0.1-beta.

cna:CVE-2026-61620.desc: HoneySQL turns Clojure data structures into SQL. From 2.0.0 until 2.7.1392, applications that pass user input or other arbitrary data into the HoneySQL `DSL` by calling `keyword` or `symbol` on that input can produce SQL strings that facilitate SQL injection when executed unchanged by a `JDBC` driver. Some formatters do not apply the existing suspicious-character check to the resulting entity names. The impact depends on the privileges of the database connection executing the generated statement. Input validation before constructing `keyword` or `symbol` entities is a workaround. The maintainer-designated fixed version is 2.7.1392.

      Title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery 
      Authors:  Jiarui Yao ,  Ruida Wang ,  Tong Zhang               View a PDF of the paper titled OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery, by Jiarui Yao and 2 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in research-level problem solving, yet a comprehensive collection of such problems is still missing, and evaluating them on research-level problems remains challenging. We introduce OpenFrontiers, a cross-disciplinary resource that combines a structured corpus of open research problems with a retrospective benchmark of recently resolved problems in mathematics. The corpus records problem statements, context, progress, and other information for 12,151 problems. The benchmark contains 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean~4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; a subset HQ-50 further filters based on quality score, etc. Our evaluation protocol grades formal proofs with two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on the HQ-50 subset under a standardized budget, we find that closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, whereas live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions. By linking a broad research-problem corpus to a formally graded evaluation subset with documented solutions, OpenFrontiers provides a foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and studying progress toward solving currently open scientific problems. The dataset and benchmark could be found in  this https URL .

          Title: 
          LRMoE: Demand-Side Load Re-Calibration for Efficient MoE Training on Memory-Constrained Nodes
         
          Jiaming Hu ,  Zhida Jiang ,  Zhaolong Xing ,  Yu Li ,  Zhen Chen ,  Ke Zhang  



          Subjects: 
           Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
         

         
          Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer scalable capacity for Web applications, but uneven routing creates computation and communication bottlenecks. Existing placement and replication methods redistribute this workload, yet additional expert copies compete with token-related buffers for limited GPU memory. We present LRMoE, a memory-aware MoE training system that jointly recalibrates backward demand and balances the retained workload. During forward execution, it plans retention quotas and expert placement under resource constraints while preserving all routed computations. During backpropagation, a load recalibration metric estimates each token-expert pair's contribution to the expert update and selects pairs within these quotas. A capacity-aware routing algorithm distributes retained pairs among eligible instances of their original experts. Physical compaction then forms smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs, reducing backward traffic, computation, and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B show that LRMoE reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2-44.8% relative to SYMI.

          Title: 
          Amortized Localized Posterior Inference for Model Calibration with Application to an Ocean Turbulence Closure
         
          Exaucé Luweh Adjim Ngarti  (AIRSEA),  Élise Arnaud  (AIRSEA),  Léo Nicoletti ,  Victor Trappler  (Mines Saint-Étienne MSE, LIMOS, FAYOL-ENSMSE, FAYOL-ENSMSE),  Arthur Vidard  (AIRSEA) 



          Subjects: 
           Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG); Machine Learning (stat.ML)
         

         
          Model discrepancy may prevent a single calibration parameter from reproducing a physical response across the context domain. In addition, uncertainties in observations and contexts affect calibration and must be accounted for and quantified. We construct a family of localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods according to their proximity to a target context. Gaussian localization weights incorporate context uncertainty through covariance inflation, with reflection at domain boundaries and an optional correction for uneven context sampling. A conditional normalizing flow approximates the family of posteriors through amortized variational inference. Integrating the localized posteriors under a prescribed context measure gives the marginalized parameter distribution. In a twin experiment with the Branin-Hoo model, we compare global and localized inference under uniform and skewed context distributions. Localization reduces the reported aggregate predictive errors relative to the global posterior. An application to the k-$\epsilon$ turbulence closure in a single-column ocean model, with atmospheric surface forcing as context, shows that localized posterior calibration reduces temperature and zonal-velocity errors relative to deterministic and global-posterior calibration. Both twin experiments are constructed to admit local compensation.

          Title: 
          ThinkJev: One Thought, Every Budget for Calibrated Typed Decisions
         
          Xiaolu Ding ,  Kai Yang ,  Dongdong Liu  

          Comments: 
          31 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables
         


          Subjects: 
           Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
         

         
          Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. Reading those probabilities from one forward pass is fast but often wrong on decisions that take several steps, such as arithmetic, counting, and date comparison. Letting the model think first fixes most of these errors, but costs seconds per decision instead of milliseconds. To pay for thinking only where it helps, ThinkJev builds a fast and a slow system from one open hybrid-thinking model that can answer directly or after a thought. System 1 reads the model's probabilities for the option letters when it answers directly; System 2 reads the same letters after the model has thought on the same cached prompt, so escalating repeats no work and both systems give probabilities over the same options. Because the letters can be read after any number of thought tokens, one sampled thought also gives the answer under every thinking budget. Without training, ThinkJev lets System 1 answer alone only where a statistical test on labeled dev data guarantees that its accepted answers stay under a target error rate. At a 5% target, Qwen3.5-27B answers 24.5% of 8359 test decisions this way with a realized error of 3.9% (Qwen3.5-4B and 9B: 6.5% and 0.0%). For the rest, stopping each thought as soon as its answer is confident reaches 81.6% accuracy, against 82.7% for always thinking, with 72% of the thought tokens. Choosing when to think from System 1's confidence alone saves less, because the decisions System 1 is least sure of are often not the ones thinking fixes. On the public items of JevBench, an independent benchmark of typed-decision services, Qwen3.5-27B thinks on 29.4% and is not distinguishable in accuracy from the two thinking APIs listed (exploratory). Speculative decoding does: a drafter proposes several future tokens, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass that reuses the same weight read. Because every drafted token must be verified whether or not it is accepted, the energy speculation saves depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted. This saving is hard to pin down. It varies across target models from different attention families and across drafting schemes, and it depends on the text being served. Every drafter we evaluate accepts fewer tokens on conversation than on code, and every trained drafter accepts fewer on Romansh, a low-resource language, than on English. On dense models, verification, not drafting, dominates the energy cost. The saving shrinks as the batch grows, because batching has already shared the weight read that speculation would divide among the accepted tokens. At large batch sizes, block drafters push verification past the balance point between arithmetic and memory traffic into the compute-bound regime, where the saving becomes a loss, and a drafter with low acceptance raises energy per token.           Title: 
          Anti-coherence Regularized Absolute Scaling for Out-of-Distribution Detection
         
          Donghwan Kim ,  Youngwoong Jin ,  Hyunsoo Yoon  

          Comments:

          Subjects:

          Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is recognized as a critical problem in AI safety. SCALE is an effective post-hoc OOD detection method in the activation-shaping family that requires no training data and rescales penultimate activations using a percentile-based magnitude ratio. However, this ratio is ill-defined when negative activations are present, since positive and negative contributions cancel within the underlying sum, causing SCALE to degenerate on backbones such as ViT. We address this with an Absolute Fix that computes the ratio over absolute-valued activations rather than discarding negative activations through ReLU. Building on this corrected scale, we propose Anti-coherence regularization, which penalizes the scaling factor by the fraction of a sample's max-logit contributions to the max logit that are sign-mismatched and thereby suppresses unreliable evidence for the predicted class. Despite requiring no access to training data or training labels, our method ties or outperforms activation-shaping methods that rely on training data in terms of AUROC and FPR@95 on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet under the OpenOOD v1.5 protocol.

          Xiaodi Huang ,  Zilin Wang ,  Jinpeng Liu ,  Pengchuan Xiao ,  Zhenlei Shao ,  Zhang Zhang

          Embodied perception requires positional representations that capture both physical geometry and the spatial and temporal extent of observations.           Title: 
          A Sign Law for Entropy Drift under Sampler Mismatch in RLVR
         
          Zhiyuan Wang ,  Jacob Steeves ,  Chang Liu

          In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), whether entropy rises or falls can depend on choices that matter little under exact sampling, such as whether over-length responses are masked or counted as failures. We trace this to sampler mismatch: rollouts are drawn with top-k/top-p truncation or at a temperature the learner does not apply. We prove that a constant advantage shift then changes the entropy of a softmax policy, at first order and in expectation, with a sign fixed by the sampler. Positive shifts sharpen the policy under any sampler whose likelihood ratio to the policy increases with token probability, including top-k, top-p, min-p, and temperatures below one, and flatten it under flatter samplers. In group-based RLVR with token-level losses, the baseline-dependent part of this drift is set by the token-weighted net advantage, which masking and failing can push to opposite signs. The rest comes from a covariance between advantages and the sampler's sharpness gap and feeds back on itself: in a two-level model, a push away from a sharper sampler takes off in finite time, while a pull toward it saturates. On a 2B model, the entropy slope is linear in shifts of the net advantage under truncated sampling and indistinguishable from flat under exact sampling. Token-level importance ratios leave 98% of the drift, and four clipped minibatch updates per batch amplify it sevenfold. In 100-step runs, a net-zero baseline only delays an entropy explosion, and entropy raised at the start keeps rising only under truncation; cancelling the first-order drift at every step keeps entropy bounded without changing the learner.           A long-lived assistant that brings up memories without being asked must decide at every turn whether anything in its store is worth an interruption.           Crowd-counting models deployed on edge devices face two challenges: inputs are degraded along the capture and transmission pipeline, while models are often quantized to satisfy resource constraints of the edge. Yet corruption robustness and deployment quantization are typically evaluated separately. We evaluate TensorRT engines at FP32, FP16, and post-training INT8 precision on an A100 GPU, alongside throughput and energy measurements on corresponding Jetson Orin~NX configurations. The corruptions span six families, with head annotations adjusted when geometry or visibility changes. Our results show that capture-chain corruptions consistently cause the largest degradation across evaluated models, while crowd density affects absolute and relative errors differently. Accuracy on clean images does not reliably predict performance on the corresponding corrupted images. INT8 changes corruption robustness more than FP16, without a consistent direction, and does not consistently improve latency or energy efficiency. INT8 inference efficiency is strongly associated with reformat overhead in the compiled engine, with slowdowns also observed under limited INT8 coverage.           Scientific drilling has produced large archives of physical, chemical and magnetic measurements linked to descriptions of the rock recovered. These archives are mostly incomplete: instruments sample at different intervals, recovery is partial, and destructive analyses preclude later measurement of the same material. We train an self-supervised embedding model on the LILY ocean drilling database using six routinely logged properties (bulk density, magnetic susceptibility, natural gamma radiation, and red, green and blue reflectance) across 236,963 observations from 296 boreholes, with a masked variational autoencoder that has a heteroscedastic Gaussian decoder and learnable mask tokens. The labels are recoverable from the measurements geologists use to assign them, so training on them adds nothing. Lithological categories compress continuous measurements into classes, and compressing them discards what the measurements record about the processes that produced the rock. The embeddings also predict physical properties that were absent from training, on boreholes the model has never seen. While depth should account for this since sediments compact with burial, it does not.           Title: 
          Proposing Better Rollouts for On-Policy Distillation
         
          Sirui Chen ,  Yunzhe Qi ,  Haobo Xu ,  Jiaru Zou ,  Mengting Ai ,  Zihao Li ,  Jingrui He  



          Subjects: 
           Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
         

         
          On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model post-training by letting the student learn from its own sampled trajectories under teacher supervision, aligning the training process with inference-time behavior. However, the rollout policy in OPD is usually treated as fixed: each round samples directly from the current student. We show that this choice can create a compounding teacher--student mismatch, because it requires the teacher to provide effective supervision on whichever trajectories the student samples, including ones less reachable by the teacher itself. On such trajectories, teacher supervision can become noisy or even misleading, leading to undesirable student patterns such as repetition. Moreover, since the updated student in turn defines the rollout policy of subsequent rounds, these patterns persist and potentially amplify over training. This failure mode suggests that improving OPD requires treating the rollout policy itself as an optimization target, rather than only modifying the distillation objective. We propose Mixture Proposal On-Policy Distillation (MPOPD), which derives a student-anchored, teacher-guided rollout distribution from a local trust-region objective based on relative teacher support. The resulting target is a geometric mixture of the student and teacher policies, and we introduce a proposal policy that approximates this mixture, enabling rollout generation in a single forward pass. Experiments on 16 math, knowledge, and medical reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over OPD and recent variants. On math reasoning, our method improves average accuracy by 6.91 over OPD on Qwen3-4B-Base while reducing average generation length by 41%, suggesting that rollout policy design provides an effective way to improve OPD.

          Activation steering offers an effective and efficient way to modify an LLM's behavior at inference time. However, it remains unclear how to apply steering such that the signal is consistently strong and the steering strength has a universally interpretable meaning. We address this first by identifying the most steerable interval for each steering vector and rescaling the steering range accordingly. Building on this, we introduce a more interpretable method for steering, called parameterized steering which instead of pushing activations in a direction, it sets them at the desired trait strength.           REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
         
          Yuxi Huang ,  Silin Zhou ,  Chenhao Wang ,  Zihan Li ,  Gangming Guo ,  Pei Ke ,  Shen Gao ,  Shuo Shang

          Personalized recommendation depends on learning semantic and collaborative relations among items from online content and user interactions. Generative recommendation (GR) offers a promising paradigm by autoregressively generating discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) of items. However, randomly initialized SID token embeddings and GR models trained from scratch do not directly inherit the semantic relations inherent in items, while inter-item collaborative relations are learned largely implicitly through token-level attention and next-token supervision. To address this limitation, we propose REGER, a unified framework that explicitly incorporates inter-item relations into semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation. We pretrain the GR model through generative semantic retrieval, enabling it to inherit inter-item semantic similarity by learning to generate semantic neighbors' SIDs. We combine global attention with local attention aligned with SID boundaries to capture historical context and directed transitions between adjacent items. We further develop a theoretical framework for hierarchical preference decomposition over the SID prefix tree, proving an exact factorization of collaborative preference distributions and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into prefix-conditional KL divergences. Building on this analysis, we distill a discriminative teacher's full conditional distributions over all legal next tokens at ground-truth prefixes along the target SID path, jointly optimizing this objective with cross-entropy. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over existing GR baselines and support the effectiveness of the proposed preference distillation.

Recommended sampling settings are **Temperature 1.0** and **Top\_P 0.95** in both thinking enabled and disabled modes. ```py from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY") MODEL = "nemotron-bolt" ``` Bolt-E4B exposes reasoning control through chat-template kwargs: thinking enabled (the default), thinking disabled for direct answers, and a runtime thinking budget. #### Reasoning On ```py response = client.chat.completions.create( model=MODEL, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a haiku about GPUs"}], max_tokens=16000, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, extra_body={ "skip_special_tokens": False, "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": True}, } ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` #### Reasoning Off ```py response = client.chat.completions.create( model=MODEL, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of Japan?"}], max_tokens=16000, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, extra_body={ "skip_special_tokens": False, "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}, } ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` #### Streaming ```py stream = client.chat.completions.create( model=MODEL, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain speculative decoding in two sentences"}], max_tokens=16000, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, stream=True, extra_body={"skip_special_tokens": False}, ) for chunk in stream: print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content or "", end="", flush=True) ``` #### Tool Calling For vLLM, add the following to any serve command above: ```sh --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser gemma4 \ --reasoning-parser gemma4 \ ``` Sample request with tool-calling enabled: ```py tools = [{ "type": "function", "function": { "name": "get_weather", "description": "Get the current weather for a city", "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["city"], }, }, }] response = client.chat.completions.create( model=MODEL, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in Santa Clara?"}], tools=tools, max_tokens=16000, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, extra_body={ "skip_special_tokens": False, "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": True}, }, ) print(response.choices[0].message.tool_calls) ``` #### Conversational Mode Bolt-E4B supports a conversational mode. If enabled, Bolt-E4B responds concisely and without as much textual formatting. This mode is suitable for conversational and spoken interaction-based applications. Conversational mode can be toggled as follows: ```py response = client.chat.completions.create( model=MODEL, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of Japan?"}], max_tokens=16000, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, extra_body={ "skip_special_tokens": False, "chat_template_kwargs": {"conversational_mode": True}, } ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` Conversational mode can be combined with thinking enabled and disabled mode, as well as tool-calling. #### Runtime Thinking Budget Control With llama-server you can control thinking budget by specifying the `--reasoning-budget` argument: ``` docker run --rm --gpus all \ -p 8000:8000 \ -v "$MODEL_DIR:/models:ro" \ ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-cuda13-b11459 \ -m "/models/$MODEL_FILE" \ --alias nemotron-bolt \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 8000 \ -c 65536 \ -ngl 999 \ --jinja \ --reasoning on \ --reasoning-budget ``` ##### Limits and Recommendations for Runtime Budget Control - Restricted token allocations may truncate thought processes mid-sentence. While output clarity is typically maintained, task-specific output evaluation remains necessary. - The client halts execution immediately upon reaching the pre-configured initial generation ceiling, ignoring subsequent line boundaries. - Conduct systematic allocation sweeps using standard evaluation prompts prior to establishing deployment parameters. - Illustration: To maintain a strict 500-token overall threshold, evaluate unconstrained model generation metrics (e.g., averaging 200 tokens). Assigning a dedicated 300-token reasoning parameter alongside a 500-token global ceiling forces thought termination at 300 tokens, reserving 200 tokens for output synthesis. - To encourage brief output (excluding internal reasoning steps), incorporate explicit word- or sentence-count constraints within system prompts. #### Asynchronous Tool Calling Bolt-E4B's chat template currently does not allow stray tool responses (`messages` with `tool` role that do not immediately follow a message with `assistant` role and `tool_calls`). However, this model can support asynchronous tool-calling with in the following manner:
Asynchronous tool-calling usage If the model invokes a tool in `message.tool_calls` that has a later arriving result, respond with a `tool` message in the immediate next turn that acknowledges the tool-call and shows the tool result as pending. Example: Assistant tool-call ```json { "role": "assistant", "tool_calls": [{ "id": "call_1", "type": "function", "function": { "name": "build_report", "arguments": "{\"_task_id\":\"task_1\",\"scope\":\"weekly\"}" } }] } ``` Immediate acknowledgement with pending result ```json { "role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "call_1", "content": "{\"status\":\"pending\",\"task_id\":\"task_1\",\"function\":\"build_report\"}" } ``` The model can continue the conversation with the user after this acknowledgement `tool` result message. Once the tool result is available, respond with a `user` message that provides the tool result in a structured format, prefixed with something like `"TOOL RESULT:"` Example: Later tool result completion result ```json { "role": "user", "content": "TOOL UPDATE: {\"status\":\"completed\",\"task_id\":\"task_1\",\"function\":\"build_report\",\"response\":\"Report is ready.\"}" } ``` The model processes the finalized payload to resume the conversation.
## Prompting Guidelines General guidelines for using Bolt-E4B in conversational and interactive agent applications. ### Prompt Structure and Content - Put persistent role definitions, behavioral constraints, and operating rules in the system prompt. - Use consistent headings which clearly identify the purpose of a section of the prompt, Example: ROLE, IDENTITY, INPUT FORMAT, TASK RULES, PERSONALITY, SPEECH EXAMPLES, etc. - State the primary objective clearly. Define what counts as completion for multi-step workflows. - Write instructions as conditions and actions: “After crafting succeeds, call the delivery tool.” - Remove redundant instructions rather than repeatedly adding stronger versions. - Use response-length limits that fit the application. A one- or two-sentence limit can suit spoken replies; it will not restrict tool arguments or reasoning. - Use explicit constraints (e.g., `"limit responses to 1-2 sentences"`) instead of vague requests (e.g., `"be brief"`). - Preserve genuine conversation history. Do not insert fabricated assistant actions, promises, or tool calls as if they occurred. - If using few-shot examples, identify them as examples. Test whether the model copies their wording or themes and adjust instructions accordingly. - Strictly adhere to standard `system/user/assistant/tool` turn sequences. ### Identity, Ownership, and Perspective - Define the agent and user as separate entities with separate actions, locations, possessions, and knowledge. - Explain pronouns when both entities appear in state: “In the state update following a user turn, ‘my’ refers to the user; but in a state update after an assistant turn, ‘my’ refers to you.” - Use explicit labels such as YOUR INVENTORY, PLAYER VIEW, and SHARED CHEST to reinforce ownership. - Distinguish unavailable information from empty state. An inaccessible user inventory is unknown, not empty. - Distinguish visible resources from possessed resources. A nearby item or chest does not mean the agent owns its contents. - Make character lore consistent with available information and tools. Explain any restrictions on what the character can perceive or use. ### Conveying Environment State - Mark state blocks clearly, for example with # CURRENT STATE. - Explain that state is operational context, not a new request or text to repeat aloud. - Share state updates via new `user` or `system` messages. The model supports consecutive `user` and `system` messages. It is important to maintain correct chronology when conveying state information/updates and continuing the conversation. For example, for a user message that is conditioned upon a state update, the state update `user` or `system` message must come *before* the user response: ``` # CURRENT STATE ... ---------------- ``` OR in two user/system messages: ``` [..., {"role": "user/system", "content": "# CURRENT STATE..."}, {"role": "user", "content": ""}, ...] ``` But, for conveying an updated state that occurs after a tool is executed, the state update `user` or `system` message must come *after* the tool execution response: ``` [..., {"role": "tool", "content": ""}, {"role": "user/system", "content": "# CURRENT STATE... "}, {"role": "user", "content": ""}, ...] ``` ### Tool Definitions and Calling - Send tools through the native tools array and read actions from message.tool_calls. - Use stable function names and parameter schemas. Describe prerequisites, argument meanings, units, defaults, effects, and failure conditions. - Make tool descriptions match actual behavior. “Drops an item toward the player” must not be described as guaranteed placement in the player’s inventory. ## Training, Testing, and Evaluation Datasets ### Training #### Dataset Overview **Data Modality:** Text **Training Data Size:** More than 20 Trillion Tokens **Dataset partition:** *Training [100%], testing [0%], validation [0%]* **Time period for training data collection:** 2013 to December 2025 **Time period for testing data collection:** 2013 to December 2025 **Time period for validation data collection:** 2013 to December 2025 **Data Collection Method by dataset:** Hybrid: Automated, Manually-Collected, Synthetic **Labeling Method by dataset:** Hybrid: Automated, Manually-Labeled, Synthetic The post-training corpus for NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB consists of high-quality curated and synthetically-generated data. Primary languages used for post-training include English, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Spanish, and Chinese. These datasets, such as FinePDFs, EssentialWeb, HotpotQA, SQuAD, and HelpSteer3, do not collectively or exhaustively represent all demographic groups (and proportionally therein). For instance, these datasets do not contain explicit mentions of demographic classes such as age, gender, or ethnicity in 64-99% of samples, depending on the source. In the subset where such terms are present, document-based datasets (FinePDFs and EssentialWeb) contain representational skews, such as references to "male" outnumbering those to "female", and mentions of "White" as the most frequent among ethnic identifiers (comprising 43-44% of ethnicity mentions). To mitigate these imbalances, we recommend considering evaluation techniques such as bias audits, fine-tuning with demographically balanced datasets, and mitigation strategies like counterfactual data augmentation to align with the desired model behavior. This evaluation used a 3,000-sample subset per dataset, identified as the optimal threshold for maximizing embedder accuracy. During post-training, we generate synthetic data by distilling trajectories, solutions, and translations from strong teacher models and agent systems, often grounded in real tasks or documents and aggressively filtered for quality. For math, code, and science, we start from curated problem sets and use open source permissive models such as GPT-OSS-120B to produce step-by-step reasoning traces, candidate solutions, best-of-n selection traces, and verified CUDA kernels. For long-context and science, we build synthetic QA and reasoning data by retrieving passages from long documents, generating MCQ/OpenQA questions and answers, and paraphrasing them into multiple prompt/response formats to ensure diversity. Across all pipelines we stack automated verification—compilers, numerical checks, language identification—to ensure our data is high quality. For all domains, we apply a unified data filtering pipeline to ensure that only high-quality, license-compliant, and verifiable samples are used for post-training. We first discard malformed examples using structural checks (e.g., missing tool definitions when tool calls are present). We then aggressively filter reasoning traces exhibiting pathological repetition, such as repeated n-grams within a sliding window or across the entire trajectory, which we found to be a strong indicator of malformed or low-quality reasoning. Finally, based on internal audits of synthetically generated datasets, we observed that some teacher models occasionally produce reasoning traces and final responses that implicitly align with specific political entities or promote nationalistic narratives. To mitigate this, we apply targeted keyword- and regex-based filters and remove all trajectories matching such behavior. Alongside the model, we release our final pre-training and post-training data, as outlined in this section. For ease of analysis, there is a sample set that is ungated. For all remaining code, math and multilingual data, gating and approval is required, and the dataset is permissively licensed for model training purposes.

![image](bolt-smart-and-fast.png) ## Description **NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB** is a small language model (SLM) further post-trained from [Gemma-4-E4B-it](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-E4B-it) by NVIDIA. Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B carries forward Gemma’s strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/edge interfaces. Designed for low-memory, low-TTFT operation, the model allows agents to respond quickly while preserving headroom for applications or adjacent model pipelines. ![demo](reachy-bolt.gif) For speculative decoding, use the companion [DFlash drafter](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB-DFlash). For the full-precision (BF16) version, see [NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-BF16](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-BF16). This model is ready for commercial or non‑commercial use. ## Model Summary | | | |:---|:---| | **Total Parameters** | 8B (4B effective) | | **Architecture** | Gemma-4-E4B | | **Precision** | Q4_K_M | | **Context Length** | Input: up to 64K tokens; output: up to 64K tokens | | **Inputs / Outputs** | Text / text | | **Deployment** | llama.cpp (recipe pending) | | **Reasoning Mode** | Chat-template controls (`enable_thinking=True/False`) and runtime thinking budget | | **Conversational Mode** | Chat-template controls (`conversational_mode=True/False`) | | **Recommended Sampling** | Temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95 in both thinking modes | | **Best For** | Local voice and device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded interfaces | | **License** | [OpenMDW-1.1](https://github.com/OpenMDW/OpenMDW/blob/main/1.1/LICENSE.OpenMDW-1.1) | ## Model Overview **Model Developer:** NVIDIA Corporation **Model Dates:** December 2025 - May 2026 **Data Freshness:** * The post-training data has a cutoff date of May 2026. ### What is Nemotron? NVIDIA Nemotron™ is a family of open models with open weights, training data, and recipes, delivering leading efficiency and accuracy for building specialized AI agents. ## Quick Start ``` export MODEL_REPO=nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB export MODEL_FILE=Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-Q4_K_M.gguf export DRAFTER_REPO=nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB-DFlash export DRAFTER_FILE=Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-DFlash-BF16.gguf export MODEL_DIR="$PWD/bolt-models" hf download "$MODEL_REPO" "$MODEL_FILE" \ --local-dir "$MODEL_DIR" hf download "$DRAFTER_REPO" "$DRAFTER_FILE" \ --local-dir "$MODEL_DIR" ``` ### Without drafter ``` docker run --rm --gpus all \ -p 8000:8000 \ -v "$MODEL_DIR:/models:ro" \ ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-cuda13-b11459 \ -m "/models/$MODEL_FILE" \ --alias nemotron-bolt \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 8000 \ -c 65536 \ -ngl 999 \ --jinja ``` ### With DFlash drafter ``` docker run --rm --gpus all \ -p 8000:8000 \ -v "$MODEL_DIR:/models:ro" \ ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-cuda13-b11459 \ -m "/models/$MODEL_FILE" \ --spec-draft-model "/models/$DRAFTER_FILE" \ --spec-type draft-dflash \ --spec-draft-n-max 7 \ --spec-draft-ngl 999 \ --alias nemotron-bolt \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 8000 \ -c 65536 \ -ngl 999 \ --jinja ``` ``` curl --fail-with-body -sS \ http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "model": "nemotron-bolt", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 multiplied by 23?"} ], "temperature": 0.0, "max_tokens": 512, "chat_template_kwargs": { "enable_thinking": true } }' ``` For more details on how to deploy and use the model — see the [Quick Start Guide](#quick-start-guide) below! ## License/Terms of Use **Governing Terms:** Use of this model is governed by the [OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1](https://github.com/OpenMDW/OpenMDW/blob/main/1.1/LICENSE.OpenMDW-1.1).
