All tied highest scores are bold. - Accuracy numbers are measured by NVIDIA under a consistent harness ([NeMo Gym](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym)); they may differ from vendors' self-reported numbers. ### Deployment Geography: Global ### Use Case NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB is designed for fast local voice and device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded interfaces, with an emphasis on multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding. ### Release Date - Hugging Face 10/23/2026 via https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB - Build.NVIDIA.com 10/23/2026 via https://build.nvidia.com/nvidia/nemotron-3.5-bolt-e4b ## Reference(s) * [NVIDIA Nemotron 3 model family on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/nvidia-nemotron-v3) * [NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB Technical Report](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/files/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB-Technical-Report.pdf) * [NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB Technical Blog](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB/) ## Model Architecture - **Architecture Type:** Gemma 4 - **Network Architecture:** Gemma-4-E4B - **Number of model parameters:** 8B (4B effective parameters) ## Model Design The model was further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it. ## Training Methodology Reinforcement Learning * The model underwent multi-environment reinforcement learning using GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) across instruction following, multi-step tool use, multi-turn conversations, and structured output environments. It utilized an asynchronous RL architecture that decouples training from inference. * Software used for reinforcement learning: [NeMo RL](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/RL), [NeMo Gym](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym) NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB is a result of the above work. ## Input - **Input Type(s):** Text - **Input Format(s):** String - **Input Parameters:** One-Dimensional (1D): Sequences - **Other Properties Related to Input:** Maximum context length up to 64K tokens. Supported languages include English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, and Japanese, among others. ## Output - **Output Type(s):** Text - **Output Format:** String - **Output Parameters:** One-Dimensional (1D): Sequences - **Other Properties Related to Output:** Maximum context length up to 64K tokens Our AI models are designed and/or optimized to run on NVIDIA GPU-accelerated systems. By leveraging NVIDIA's hardware (e.g. GPU cores) and software frameworks (e.g., CUDA libraries), the model achieves faster training and inference times compared to CPU-only solutions. ## Software Integration - **Runtime Engine(s):** PyTorch - **Supported Hardware Microarchitecture Compatibility:** NVIDIA Ampere - A100; NVIDIA Blackwell; NVIDIA Hopper - H100-80GB - **Supported Operating System(s):** Linux The integration of foundation and fine-tuned models into AI systems requires additional testing using use-case-specific data to ensure safe and effective deployment. Following the V-model methodology, iterative testing and validation at both unit and system levels are essential to mitigate risks, meet technical and functional requirements, and ensure compliance with safety and ethical standards before deployment. ## Model Version(s) * GA (10/23/2026) ## Quick Start Guide ``` export MODEL_REPO=nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB export MODEL_FILE=Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-Q4_K_M.gguf export DRAFTER_REPO=nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB-DFlash export DRAFTER_FILE=Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-DFlash-BF16.gguf export MODEL_DIR="$PWD/bolt-models" hf download "$MODEL_REPO" "$MODEL_FILE" \ --local-dir "$MODEL_DIR" hf download "$DRAFTER_REPO" "$DRAFTER_FILE" \ --local-dir "$MODEL_DIR" ``` ### Without drafter ``` docker run --rm --gpus all \ -p 8000:8000 \ -v "$MODEL_DIR:/models:ro" \ ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-cuda13-b11459 \ -m "/models/$MODEL_FILE" \ --alias nemotron-bolt \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 8000 \ -c 65536 \ -ngl 999 \ --jinja ``` ### With DFlash drafter ``` docker run --rm --gpus all \ -p 8000:8000 \ -v "$MODEL_DIR:/models:ro" \ ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-cuda13-b11459 \ -m "/models/$MODEL_FILE" \ --spec-draft-model "/models/$DRAFTER_FILE" \ --spec-type draft-dflash \ --spec-draft-n-max 7 \ --spec-draft-ngl 999 \ --alias nemotron-bolt \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 8000 \ -c 65536 \ -ngl 999 \ --jinja ``` ``` curl --fail-with-body -sS \ http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "model": "nemotron-bolt", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 multiplied by 23?"} ], "temperature": 0.0, "max_tokens": 512, "chat_template_kwargs": { "enable_thinking": true } }' ``` ### API Client The examples below use the OpenAI-compatible client and work with the serving backend above. Recommended sampling settings are **Temperature 1.0** and **Top\_P 0.95** in both thinking enabled and disabled modes. ```py from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY") MODEL = "nemotron-bolt" ``` Bolt-E4B exposes reasoning control through chat-template kwargs: thinking enabled (the default), thinking disabled for direct answers, and a runtime thinking budget. #### Reasoning On ```py response = client.chat.completions.create( model=MODEL, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a haiku about GPUs"}], max_tokens=16000, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, extra_body={ "skip_special_tokens": False, "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": True}, } ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` #### Reasoning Off ```py response = client.chat.completions.create( model=MODEL, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of Japan?"}], max_tokens=16000, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, extra_body={ "skip_special_tokens": False, "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}, } ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` #### Streaming ```py stream = client.chat.completions.create( model=MODEL, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain speculative decoding in two sentences"}], max_tokens=16000, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, stream=True, extra_body={"skip_special_tokens": False}, ) for chunk in stream: print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content or "", end="", flush=True) ``` #### Tool Calling For vLLM, add the following to any serve command above: ```sh --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser gemma4 \ --reasoning-parser gemma4 \ ``` Sample request with tool-calling enabled: ```py tools = [{ "type": "function", "function": { "name": "get_weather", "description": "Get the current weather for a city", "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["city"], }, }, }] response = client.chat.completions.create( model=MODEL, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in Santa Clara?"}], tools=tools, max_tokens=16000, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, extra_body={ "skip_special_tokens": False, "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": True}, }, ) print(response.choices[0].message.tool_calls) ``` #### Conversational Mode Bolt-E4B supports a conversational mode. If enabled, Bolt-E4B responds concisely and without as much textual formatting. This mode is suitable for conversational and spoken interaction-based applications. Conversational mode can be toggled as follows: ```py response = client.chat.completions.create( model=MODEL, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of Japan?"}], max_tokens=16000, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, extra_body={ "skip_special_tokens": False, "chat_template_kwargs": {"conversational_mode": True}, } ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` Conversational mode can be combined with thinking enabled and disabled mode, as well as tool-calling. #### Runtime Thinking Budget Control With llama-server you can control thinking budget by specifying the `--reasoning-budget` argument: ``` docker run --rm --gpus all \ -p 8000:8000 \ -v "$MODEL_DIR:/models:ro" \ ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-cuda13-b11459 \ -m "/models/$MODEL_FILE" \ --alias nemotron-bolt \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 8000 \ -c 65536 \ -ngl 999 \ --jinja \ --reasoning on \ --reasoning-budget ``` ##### Limits and Recommendations for Runtime Budget Control - Restricted token allocations may truncate thought processes mid-sentence. While output clarity is typically maintained, task-specific output evaluation remains necessary. - The client halts execution immediately upon reaching the pre-configured initial generation ceiling, ignoring subsequent line boundaries. - Conduct systematic allocation sweeps using standard evaluation prompts prior to establishing deployment parameters. - Illustration: To maintain a strict 500-token overall threshold, evaluate unconstrained model generation metrics (e.g., averaging 200 tokens). Assigning a dedicated 300-token reasoning parameter alongside a 500-token global ceiling forces thought termination at 300 tokens, reserving 200 tokens for output synthesis. - To encourage brief output (excluding internal reasoning steps), incorporate explicit word- or sentence-count constraints within system prompts. #### Asynchronous Tool Calling Bolt-E4B's chat template currently does not allow stray tool responses (`messages` with `tool` role that do not immediately follow a message with `assistant` role and `tool_calls`). However, this model can support asynchronous tool-calling with in the following manner:
Asynchronous tool-calling usage If the model invokes a tool in `message.tool_calls` that has a later arriving result, respond with a `tool` message in the immediate next turn that acknowledges the tool-call and shows the tool result as pending. Example: Assistant tool-call ```json { "role": "assistant", "tool_calls": [{ "id": "call_1", "type": "function", "function": { "name": "build_report", "arguments": "{\"_task_id\":\"task_1\",\"scope\":\"weekly\"}" } }] } ``` Immediate acknowledgement with pending result ```json { "role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "call_1", "content": "{\"status\":\"pending\",\"task_id\":\"task_1\",\"function\":\"build_report\"}" } ``` The model can continue the conversation with the user after this acknowledgement `tool` result message. Once the tool result is available, respond with a `user` message that provides the tool result in a structured format, prefixed with something like `"TOOL RESULT:"` Example: Later tool result completion result ```json { "role": "user", "content": "TOOL UPDATE: {\"status\":\"completed\",\"task_id\":\"task_1\",\"function\":\"build_report\",\"response\":\"Report is ready.\"}" } ``` The model processes the finalized payload to resume the conversation.
## Prompting Guidelines General guidelines for using Bolt-E4B in conversational and interactive agent applications. ### Prompt Structure and Content - Put persistent role definitions, behavioral constraints, and operating rules in the system prompt. - Use consistent headings which clearly identify the purpose of a section of the prompt, Example: ROLE, IDENTITY, INPUT FORMAT, TASK RULES, PERSONALITY, SPEECH EXAMPLES, etc. - State the primary objective clearly. Define what counts as completion for multi-step workflows. - Write instructions as conditions and actions: “After crafting succeeds, call the delivery tool.” - Remove redundant instructions rather than repeatedly adding stronger versions. - Use response-length limits that fit the application. A one- or two-sentence limit can suit spoken replies; it will not restrict tool arguments or reasoning. - Use explicit constraints (e.g., `"limit responses to 1-2 sentences"`) instead of vague requests (e.g., `"be brief"`). - Preserve genuine conversation history. Do not insert fabricated assistant actions, promises, or tool calls as if they occurred. - If using few-shot examples, identify them as examples. Test whether the model copies their wording or themes and adjust instructions accordingly. - Strictly adhere to standard `system/user/assistant/tool` turn sequences. ### Identity, Ownership, and Perspective - Define the agent and user as separate entities with separate actions, locations, possessions, and knowledge. - Explain pronouns when both entities appear in state: “In the state update following a user turn, ‘my’ refers to the user; but in a state update after an assistant turn, ‘my’ refers to you.” - Use explicit labels such as YOUR INVENTORY, PLAYER VIEW, and SHARED CHEST to reinforce ownership. - Distinguish unavailable information from empty state. An inaccessible user inventory is unknown, not empty. - Distinguish visible resources from possessed resources. A nearby item or chest does not mean the agent owns its contents. - Make character lore consistent with available information and tools. Explain any restrictions on what the character can perceive or use. ### Conveying Environment State - Mark state blocks clearly, for example with # CURRENT STATE. - Explain that state is operational context, not a new request or text to repeat aloud. - Share state updates via new `user` or `system` messages. The model supports consecutive `user` and `system` messages. It is important to maintain correct chronology when conveying state information/updates and continuing the conversation. For example, for a user message that is conditioned upon a state update, the state update `user` or `system` message must come *before* the user response: ``` # CURRENT STATE ... ---------------- ``` OR in two user/system messages: ``` [..., {"role": "user/system", "content": "# CURRENT STATE..."}, {"role": "user", "content": ""}, ...] ``` But, for conveying an updated state that occurs after a tool is executed, the state update `user` or `system` message must come *after* the tool execution response: ``` [..., {"role": "tool", "content": ""}, {"role": "user/system", "content": "# CURRENT STATE... "}, {"role": "user", "content": ""}, ...] ``` ### Tool Definitions and Calling - Send tools through the native tools array and read actions from message.tool_calls. - Use stable function names and parameter schemas. Describe prerequisites, argument meanings, units, defaults, effects, and failure conditions. - Make tool descriptions match actual behavior. “Drops an item toward the player” must not be described as guaranteed placement in the player’s inventory. ## Training, Testing, and Evaluation Datasets ### Training #### Dataset Overview **Data Modality:** Text **Training Data Size:** More than 20 Trillion Tokens **Dataset partition:** *Training [100%], testing [0%], validation [0%]* **Time period for training data collection:** 2013 to December 2025 **Time period for testing data collection:** 2013 to December 2025 **Time period for validation data collection:** 2013 to December 2025 **Data Collection Method by dataset:** Hybrid: Automated, Manually-Collected, Synthetic **Labeling Method by dataset:** Hybrid: Automated, Manually-Labeled, Synthetic The post-training corpus for NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB consists of high-quality curated and synthetically-generated data. Primary languages used for post-training include English, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Spanish, and Chinese. These datasets, such as FinePDFs, EssentialWeb, HotpotQA, SQuAD, and HelpSteer3, do not collectively or exhaustively represent all demographic groups (and proportionally therein). For instance, these datasets do not contain explicit mentions of demographic classes such as age, gender, or ethnicity in 64-99% of samples, depending on the source. In the subset where such terms are present, document-based datasets (FinePDFs and EssentialWeb) contain representational skews, such as references to "male" outnumbering those to "female", and mentions of "White" as the most frequent among ethnic identifiers (comprising 43-44% of ethnicity mentions). To mitigate these imbalances, we recommend considering evaluation techniques such as bias audits, fine-tuning with demographically balanced datasets, and mitigation strategies like counterfactual data augmentation to align with the desired model behavior. This evaluation used a 3,000-sample subset per dataset, identified as the optimal threshold for maximizing embedder accuracy. During post-training, we generate synthetic data by distilling trajectories, solutions, and translations from strong teacher models and agent systems, often grounded in real tasks or documents and aggressively filtered for quality. For math, code, and science, we start from curated problem sets and use open source permissive models such as GPT-OSS-120B to produce step-by-step reasoning traces, candidate solutions, best-of-n selection traces, and verified CUDA kernels. For long-context and science, we build synthetic QA and reasoning data by retrieving passages from long documents, generating MCQ/OpenQA questions and answers, and paraphrasing them into multiple prompt/response formats to ensure diversity. Across all pipelines we stack automated verification—compilers, numerical checks, language identification—to ensure our data is high quality. For all domains, we apply a unified data filtering pipeline to ensure that only high-quality, license-compliant, and verifiable samples are used for post-training. We first discard malformed examples using structural checks (e.g., missing tool definitions when tool calls are present). We then aggressively filter reasoning traces exhibiting pathological repetition, such as repeated n-grams within a sliding window or across the entire trajectory, which we found to be a strong indicator of malformed or low-quality reasoning. Finally, based on internal audits of synthetically generated datasets, we observed that some teacher models occasionally produce reasoning traces and final responses that implicitly align with specific political entities or promote nationalistic narratives. To mitigate this, we apply targeted keyword- and regex-based filters and remove all trajectories matching such behavior. Alongside the model, we release our final pre-training and post-training data, as outlined in this section. For ease of analysis, there is a sample set that is ungated. For all remaining code, math and multilingual data, gating and approval is required, and the dataset is permissively licensed for model training purposes.

    Security Advisories  
 This page provides timely updates on software vulnerabilities, patches, and security-related issues that may impact our products or services. We’re committed to transparency and proactive communication to help you stay informed and protected. 
 Check back regularly for the latest advisories, mitigation guidance, and best practices to ensure your systems remain secure.   

  
  
  

 
 
 
 

  
  
 
  
    
     
       
         Secret Server JWT issuance error - CVE-2026-115830 
     
     
            Copy Link  
   
 
  In Secret Server versions earlier than 12.3.1, a user under certain conditions could submit an unsigned JWT and receive cloudadmin permissions in response.   
 
     
  Affected product and version:  
 
 
 Delinea Secret Server on-prem and cloud 
 
 12.2.7 or earlier 
 
 
 
   Resolution:   
 
  Upgrade to Secret Server version 12.3.1  
 
 
   
   CVE Details   
 
  CVE ID:  CVE-2026-115830 
  Published Date:  October 30, 2026 
  Vulnerability Type:  Incorrect Authorization 
  CWE:  863 
  CVSS V4 Score:  8.7 
  CVSS V4 Vector:  AV:N/AC:H/AT:N/PR:H/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:H/SI:H/SA:N 
  References:   https://docs.delinea.com/online-help/secret-server/release-notes/ss-rn-12-3-000001.htm  
 
 
     
  
    
     
       
         Secret Server partial login bypass - CVE-2026-115829 
     
     
            Copy Link  
   
 
  In Secret Server versions earlier than 12.3.1, a user could bypass the initial login step and authenticate by successfully negotiating the second factor login step only.   
 
     
  Affected product and version:  
 
 
 Delinea Secret Server on-prem and cloud 
 
 12.2.7 or earlier 
 
 
 
   Resolution:   
 
  Upgrade to Secret Server version 12.3.1  
 
 
   
   CVE Details   
 
  CVE ID :     CVE-2026-115829 
  Published Date : October 30, 2026 
  Vulnerability Type:  Authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel 
  CWE: 288  
  CVSS V4 Score:  8.7 
   CVSS V4 Vector:    AV:N/AC:H/AT:N/PR:H/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:H/SI:H/SA:N

## 1. Model Introduction Kimi K2 is a state-of-the-art mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model with 32 billion activated parameters and 1 trillion total parameters. Trained with the Muon optimizer, Kimi K2 achieves exceptional performance across frontier knowledge, reasoning, and coding tasks while being meticulously optimized for agentic capabilities. ### Key Features - Large-Scale Training: Pre-trained a 1T parameter MoE model on 15.5T tokens with zero training instability. - MuonClip Optimizer: We apply the Muon optimizer to an unprecedented scale, and develop novel optimization techniques to resolve instabilities while scaling up. - Agentic Intelligence: Specifically designed for tool use, reasoning, and autonomous problem-solving. ### Model Variants - **Kimi-K2-Base**: The foundation model, a strong start for researchers and builders who want full control for fine-tuning and custom solutions. - **Kimi-K2-Instruct**: The post-trained model, best for drop-in, general-purpose chat and agentic experiences. It is a reflex-grade model without long thinking.
## 2. Model Summary

• Kimi K2 achieves 65.8% pass@1 on the SWE-bench Verified tests with bash/editor tools (single-attempt patches, no test-time compute). It also achieves a 47.3% pass@1 on the SWE-bench Multilingual tests under the same conditions. Additionally, we report results on SWE-bench Verified tests (71.6%) that leverage parallel test-time compute by sampling multiple sequences and selecting the single best via an internal scoring model.
• To ensure the stability of the evaluation, we employed avg@k on the AIME, HMMT, CNMO, PolyMath-en, GPQA-Diamond, EvalPlus, Tau2.
• Some data points have been omitted due to prohibitively expensive evaluation costs. --- #### Base model evaluation results

• All models are evaluated using the same evaluation protocol. ## 4. Deployment > [!Note] > You can access Kimi K2's API on https://platform.moonshot.ai , we provide an OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible API for you. > > The Anthropic-compatible API maps temperature by `real_temperature = request_temperature * 0.6` for better compatiblity with existing applications. Our model checkpoints are stored in block-fp8 format, you can find it on [Huggingface](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K2-Instruct). Currently, it is recommended to run Kimi-K2 on the following inference engines: * vLLM * SGLang * KTransformers * TensorRT-LLM Deployment examples for vLLM and SGLang can be found in the [Model Deployment Guide](docs/deploy_guidance.md). --- ## 5. Model Usage ### Chat Completion Once the local inference service is set up, you can interact with it through the chat endpoint: ```python def simple_chat(client: OpenAI, model_name: str): messages = [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are Kimi, an AI assistant created by Moonshot AI."}, {"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Please give a brief self-introduction."}]}, ] response = client.chat.completions.create( model=model_name, messages=messages, stream=False, temperature=0.6, max_tokens=256 ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` > [!NOTE] > The recommended temperature for Kimi-K2-Instruct is `temperature = 0.6`. > If no special instructions are required, the system prompt is a good default. --- ### Tool Calling Kimi-K2-Instruct has strong tool-calling capabilities. To enable them, you need to pass the list of available tools in each request, then the model will autonomously decide when and how to invoke them. The following example demonstrates calling a weather tool end-to-end: ```python # Your tool implementation def get_weather(city: str) -> dict: return {"weather": "Sunny"} # Tool schema definition tools = [{ "type": "function", "function": { "name": "get_weather", "description": "Retrieve current weather information. Call this when the user asks about the weather.", "parameters": { "type": "object", "required": ["city"], "properties": { "city": { "type": "string", "description": "Name of the city" } } } } }] # Map tool names to their implementations tool_map = { "get_weather": get_weather } def tool_call_with_client(client: OpenAI, model_name: str): messages = [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are Kimi, an AI assistant created by Moonshot AI."}, {"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather like in Beijing today? Use the tool to check."} ] finish_reason = None while finish_reason is None or finish_reason == "tool_calls": completion = client.chat.completions.create( model=model_name, messages=messages, temperature=0.6, tools=tools, # tool list defined above tool_choice="auto" ) choice = completion.choices[0] finish_reason = choice.finish_reason if finish_reason == "tool_calls": messages.append(choice.message) for tool_call in choice.message.tool_calls: tool_call_name = tool_call.function.name tool_call_arguments = json.loads(tool_call.function.arguments) tool_function = tool_map[tool_call_name] tool_result = tool_function(**tool_call_arguments) print("tool_result:", tool_result) messages.append({ "role": "tool", "tool_call_id": tool_call.id, "name": tool_call_name, "content": json.dumps(tool_result) }) print("-" * 100) print(choice.message.content) ``` The `tool_call_with_client` function implements the pipeline from user query to tool execution. This pipeline requires the inference engine to support Kimi-K2’s native tool-parsing logic. For streaming output and manual tool-parsing, see the [Tool Calling Guide](docs/tool_call_guidance.md). --- ## 6.      Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer 

     
         
             By  
                 Ryan Fetterman 
         

         
         
            Saturday, October 31, 2026 08:00
         

         
                             
                                AI
                             
                                                     
                                Threat Spotlight
                             
                                                     
                                Stealer
                             
                                 
     

     
         
              VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value.  If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails.   This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator.     There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the   CAIRN research effort  , is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage.  After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token.  The bundle is serialized and POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt that instructs the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY'RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets.     Figure 1. The VOLTA-AUTODOXER workflow.    The AI configuration: “Go deep, not wide... Be blunt, specific, accurate.”   VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model’s refusal, checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models. 
 
         Endpoint               https[  :]//  openrouter  [  .]ai/  api  /v1/chat/completions                 Default model               anthropic/claude-opus-4.6                 Fallback chain               moonshotai  /kimi-k2 → google/gemini-2.5-flash                 Temperature               0.2 — deterministic, consistent output                 Request format               Hand-assembled JSON; no SDK; User-Agent Mozilla/5.0            
 
    Figure 2. Hardcoded model selection.       Figure 3. Failover model selection to kimi-k2, and then gemini-2.5-flash.    Model temperate controls the randomness and predictability of LLM-generated text. The low hardcoded temperature value (0.2) suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency. The malware also employs a chain of cascading models in the event of failures. This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models.  The system prompt directly reveals the operator’s use case: Produce a concise analytical assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations.     Figure 4. VOLTA's raw system prompt.    The prompt also asks for something out of the ordinary, but that agents excel at: making connections between sparse and disparate data. For example, encouraging connections like the victim’s names, addresses, or universities to patterns in their passwords. In this case, the model isn't being asked to find data; rather, it’s being asked to stretch the data and make useful inferences that extend the value of what has been scraped.  Stealer capabilities   VOLTA’s capabilities are directly aligned with the records produced in modern digital life, and well beyond basic credential theft. In a single pass, the stealer can extract browser credentials, cookies, and saved payment cards across Chromium-based browsers. It hits Firefox and Thunderbird, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, Steam and Battle.net sessions, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, Roblox accounts, and SSH and cloud-provider config files (gcloud, OpenVPN, Hide.me). VOLTA doesn’t just copy cryptocurrency wallets, but runs an embedded cracker against the vault inline, writing the result to a WALLET VAULTS CRACKED line in its own report.    Every saved Wi-Fi password on the machine is pulled via a direct call to  WlanGetProfileList  and dumped to plaintext.     Figure 5. VOLTA dumps plaintext passwords for every saved Wi-Fi network on the host.       Figure 6. The organized collection targets.    What really sets VOLTA apart from commodity stealers is what comes after the initial collection. There is a live enrichment pass that leverages stolen sessions to deep dive the victim’s data. For example, using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal, then review those receipts to establish a confirmed home address. Stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions are called directly for order history. The Discord token is re-used to enrich the victim's account profile. Roblox inventory is valued via a live “Rolimons[.]com” lookup.     Figure 7. That’s right: Your Uber Eats history is now a potential liability.    After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called “Identity_Report.txt”. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as “AI_Analysis.txt”. Both files exfil together in “volta_dox.zip”.     Figure 8. VOLTA’s exfil can happen in three stages: 1) after the stealer runs (“volta_log.zip”), 2) after the AI call (“volta_dox.zip”), (3) if the network enrichment produces anything (“volta_doxnet.zip”).    The inference round-trip happens entirely through the victim's own network connection, on their own machine, before the result is exfiltrated.   Deployment model   Instead of hardcoding its Telegram channel, API keys, and settings directly into the code (which is likely what someone writing a tool for personal use would do) VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots, filled in at build time.    This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way. The key is SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary, but it's presumably there because customers expect their API keys not to be sitting in plaintext, not because it provides real protection. Anyone who reverses the file can recover them.    If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations. It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox.    All the observed endpoints for this malware are third-party controlled. There is no actor-owned infrastructure.  Countermeasures   Much of the token-stealing capability of VOLTA relies on techniques to bypass App-Bound Encryption (ABE) in Chrome. An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with  --headless  would block the ABE decryption path entirely. At minimum, you can also alert when Chrome is launched with  --headless  from any process not in a known developer. Best practices for storing credentials in hardware backed stores also apply.   In the event of compromise, the main executable may have deleted itself, but users should attempt to preserve the “APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt” file. This is a timestamped harvest log and contains a record of exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device.   Conclusions   VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in   CLOSEDQUORUM  , though applied to a different phase. These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next.     Figure 9. End-to-end VOLTA workflow.    The second trend to watch is the anticipation of hitting model refusals, and the approaches to building in resiliency. In this case, it includes a fallback chain from Claude to Kimi to Gemini and the ability to run without the LLM stage altogether if no key is present. As AI integration in malware matures, refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement.   The open question underlying both trends is whether effort displacement in crimeware changes the landscape in a meaningful way: lowering the operational floor, raising the ceiling on scale, or both. Cybercrime operations have always been opportunistic, and the sophistication bar has always been lower than assumed, but there is a difference between a wide net and a wide net that sorts itself.    Sample details

  This is the kind of stuff that keeps me up at night. Claude, ArtCraft, tons of other auto-downloading tools, are rolling 10'000's of code changes a month. If one compromised update snuck this guy in, it's kind of game over. The windows of opportunity for an attack like this seem to be widening the faster we "develop" software. Makes me want to have like 5 separate computers: - one for banking only - one for development only - one for web browsing only - one for gaming only - one for socials only How else can you stay safe against a threat that exfiltrates your entire digital life in like 10 seconds?      reply                             DotNetCorePowa    11 hours ago       |  parent  |  next   [–]       
  You can thank the npm and the like. Before, people were responsible for the dependencies they were importing. With npm and all the javascripters flooding the market, it became normal to be irresponsible "because everybody is doing it". Fast-forward a couple of years, now everything is web based, even the stand-alone app version. No one knows what is running on own computer, even the Devs themselves don't know what the are asking you to run... With a pinch of vibe coding on top, and thats the end. We took 40 years for our industry to be taken seriously, it's all gone now.      reply                             hibikir    11 hours ago       |  root  |  parent  |  next   [–]       
  Shared code repositories for OSS are much older than npm. See at least maven central for Java. What makes npm a more relevant target is a much smaller standard library and thinner dependencies, leading to more chances that a random project will have code of suspicious provenance. The vast majority of what a backend Java project depends on was probably written either by the same 3 companies, or large, established OSS repos. So this is relatively solvable if people in steering committees decided they cared. It's improving, but I'd argue not fast enough.      reply                             ctkhn    10 hours ago       |  root  |  parent  |  next   [–]       
  I noticed this a lot with java where most of what I needed that wasn't specific to our company's business logic was already available in the standard library, and a lot of the OSS libraries I needed were relatively reputable and well-known. I did a few personal backend projects with js and the amount of functionality I had to crate-dig from npm drove me insane, on top of the more complicated chain of trust for how many layers packages from npm can have.      reply                             hoppp    11 hours ago       |  root  |  parent  |  prev  |  next   [–]       
  Generally we don't hear much about attacks in Java like that. But they probably exist but python and javascript are targeted mainly because everyone uses them. They cover a lot of ground.      reply                             td521534f12    10 hours ago       |  root  |  parent  |  next   [–]

  All the extra code isn't really the problem, it's the insanely easy to attack "programming language package ecosystems", like NPM, PyPI, etc, compared to something like the Linux package ecosystem. But this is a much less common problem than malware and phishing. Supply chain is more of a concern than it used to be, but thousands of people get infected with malware or phished every day, versus relatively few supply chain attacks that get caught fairly quickly. For your own user security, my suggestion is to stop using SaaS wherever you can. None of them are secure, and exfiltration is child's play. All SaaS I've worked for had terrible security. Malware typically depends on two things: 1) Unpatched software. OS, apps, routers, etc. Always keep everything up to date on patches. 0-day exploits are rarely used because it burns a valuable resource. If you can use an OS that has very little malware (like Linux, MacOS) it reduces your risk. Malware also tends to lurk in certain spaces on the internet (porn sites, pirated media, shareware downloads, malicious ads), so staying clear of them also reduces your risk. 2) Persistent credentials. Most malware (at least when I was looking at it years ago) isn't very advanced/persistent. An advanced persistent threat may sit on your machine indefinitely until you login using credentials, but they may not use those credentials immediately. Sign in and out quickly (don't "stay signed in") and always use MFA, ideally a second device. Secured Android and iPhone devices are ideal for checking bank statements etc... but you must be vigilant not to install untrusted apps from App Stores (anything not from a major company), as they are more likely to infect you than your browser on normal/safe websites. If you can, try to use virtual credit card numbers, and use a credit rather than debit card for purchases. Phishing largely depends on clicking a link in an email, but also SMS "alerts" and browser pages that look like OS pop-ups. To defend against these, use a password manager to generate random unique passwords everywhere, use MFA everywhere. For login, set up and use 1-click-login and passkeys, especially for the most important logins (bank, email). Don't share or reuse passwords or API keys for more than one thing; not only does it reduce the impact, but it helps you identify where the compromise came from. I personally play "fast and loose" on my Linux desktop and don't run things in isolation. But if you want rock-solid security, the only real option is running applications in dedicated VMs, and only mounting files needed for that application. Don't depend on containers or sandboxes for security. If you want a "lightweight" alternative to VMs/containers, you can have multiple user accounts on your computer, lock each user account down (no reading/writing from other user accounts), and either login to different ones for different tasks, or run apps as that user and have them display in your current user's desktop.      reply                             qaq    11 hours ago       |  parent  |  prev  |  next   [–]

Jepsen: ParticleDB 1.1.4 
     
     
     
     
     

     
     
     

     
   

   
     
       
          JEPSEN  
       

         Blog  Analyses  Talks  Consistency  Services    Ethics   

      

        
   
     
   

       ParticleDB 1.1.4 
    
     
       
        Kyle Kingsbury
       

               2026-10-31 
           
   

   
      ParticleDB  is a multi-model
    database designed for AI workloads. We tested versions 1.1.4 through
    1.1.18.11.rc-22 and found that ParticleDB’s claims of “Full ACID”
    were somewhat premature. We present 96 issues in ParticleDB, ranging
    from the pedestrian (crashes, deadlocks, data loss, etc.) to the
    piquant (partially-invisible rows which could not be deleted,
     WHERE 4 = 5 , dropped tables re-emerging in distorted
    forms, confused columns, strings turning into integers, and so on).
    Most issues required just a single server, single client, and no
    faults. By version 1.1.18.11.rc-22, all but ten of those issues
    appeared resolved. However, ParticleDB continued to lose committed
    writes during normal operation with the default  occ 
    transaction mode, and allowed internal anomalies and Lost Update
    with  serializable , the strongest setting. Orkes, the
    makers of ParticleDB, have since released version 1.1.19-rc.13;  they
    claim  that it resolves all remaining issues discussed in this
    report. This research was funded by Orkes, Inc., and conducted in
    accordance with the  Jepsen ethics
    policy . 
   


 
   
  1  Background 
 Modern applications often spread state across a variety of systems:
databases, caches, queues, data warehouses, search indices, and so on.
Coordinating these systems is challenging: caches are often stale, the
analytics platform might lag days behind the primary database, the
search index might lose data, and transactional updates across disparate
systems  remains
an open research problem . 
 ParticleDB  1   aims to unify these workloads in a
single engine with a special focus on AI agents and applications. It
offers transactional SQL, a key-value store, vector search, live
analytics, and user-defined functions called  Particles .  2   To integrate with existing systems,
clients can connect through  a variety of
interfaces , including the Postgres and Redis protocols, as well as
its own gRPC and HTTP2 APIs. Written from the ground up in Rust,
ParticleDB claims to be orders of magnitude faster than  Postgres  while preserving the
same safety characteristics. 
 ParticleDB was built by  Orkes  to
support their workflow orchestration platform,  Conductor .
Conductor was initially built to store data in Redis and Postgres, but
to improve performance, Orkes opted to write their own database.
ParticleDB 1.0.0 offered a limited feature set specifically for
Conductor’s queries, and was deployed as the backing database for some
of their Conductor clusters. A few Orkes customers followed suit. In
preparation for a broader release, Orkes undertook a major refactoring
of ParticleDB, adding a custom wire protocol, more datatypes, additional
OLAP queries, and more. While Orkes and their customers continued to run
1.0.0, they soft launched the refactored versions on  particledb.ai . Orkes engaged Jepsen to
test these versions of ParticleDB, beginning with 1.1.4. 
 While ParticleDB could run as a single node, it also offered a
replicated cluster using the  Raft 
consensus protocol. This replication feature was available only in
enterprise cloud deployments. The builds Orkes provided did not support
replication, so this report covers only single-node behavior. 
  1.1  Safety 
 ParticleDB’s home page  advertised 
that ParticleDB was “formally proven” with a TLA+ proof. However, during
our collaboration no TLA+ specification was available. It is unclear
what properties might be proven, or whether they described ParticleDB as
built. 
 ParticleDB offered  three
tactics  for syncing its Write-Ahead Log (WAL). The  sync 
mode called  fsync  on each commit,  groupsync 
batched multiple transactions into a single  fsync , and
 nosync  skipped  fsync  altogether. The  Transaction
Engine documentation  described  sync  as offering
“stronger durability” than  groupsync . On the other hand,
 particledb start --help  said the  groupsync 
mode ensured that “COMMIT waits for flush”, and Orkes’ internal operator
guide concurred:  groupsync  offered the “same durability as
 sync ”. 
 ParticleDB’s home page proudly claimed “Full ACID. 159K TPS.”
However, the text immediately below this said “snapshot isolation”,
which is  not fully
isolated . 
 Most SQL databases use the
 SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL  statement to control the
concurrent semantics of a transaction. However, ParticleDB  ignored
or rejected these statements . In some cases it instructed users to
choose  READ COMMITTED , a relatively weak isolation level.
In other cases it accepted requests for different isolation levels, and
silently ignored them (despite documentation to the contrary). 
 Instead, transaction isolation was governed by the
 --txn-mode  setting passed at startup. The transaction
engine documentation  described
four modes : 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Mode 
 Behavior 
 When to use 
 
 
 
 
  fast  
 No locks; commit-on-write 
 Bulk loads, single-writer benchmarks 
 
 
  occ  
 Overlay + commit-time OCC validation
(default) 
 General OLTP — safe under concurrency 
 
 
  zero-copy-occ  
 Partition-pinned OCC; single-partition
txns skip cross-partition coordination 
 High-throughput OLTP on partition-affine
workloads (TPC-C, key-value) 
 
 
  table-2pl  
 Exclusive table locks at first touch 
 Strictest serialization, simple
semantics 
 
 
 
 This table was difficult to interpret. While the  best
practices documentation  warned that users should “pick
 --txn-mode  deliberately”, since “it changes correctness and
throughput characteristics more than SQL text does”, the documentation
did not explain what these modes actually guaranteed. The
 fast  mode was clearly intended for weaker isolation, but
was that Read Atomic, Read Uncommitted, or something else? The
 occ  mode was similarly unclear. “Commit-time OCC
validation” could describe a broad spectrum of consistency models from
Read Uncommitted to Strong Serializable, but “safe under concurrency”
suggests it might be Serializable. The  zero-copy-occ  mode
described a performance optimization which could be as safe as
 occ , but it was  not  described as “safe under
concurrency”—raising the question: in what ways was it unsafe? Finally,
if  table-2pl  offered the “strictest serialization”, was
 occ  some weaker isolation level? 
 The  CLI
reference page  contained another table which described
 occ  and  table-2pl  as “Jepsen-safe”, whereas
 fast  was not “Jepsen-safe”, but did not explain their
safety properties. Since Jepsen evaluates safety with respect to
documentation and marketing claims, it is not clear how to interpret
these terms.  3   
 Running  particledb start --help  provided the following
table: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Mode 
 Description 
 
 
 
 
  fast  
 No locks, maximum OLTP throughput (unsafe
under concurrency) 
 
 
  occ  
 Table locks + commit-time validation (safe
for most OLTP) 
 
 
  row-2pl  
 Alias for  occ  
 
 
  zero-copy-occ  
 Partition-pinned OCC (highest throughput
safe mode) 
 
 
  table-2pl  
 Exclusive table locks, full serialization
(strictest) 
 
 
  serializable  
 Alias for  table-2pl  
 
 
  serializable-ssi  
 Adaptive SSI (Cahill 2008), PL-3 with
optimistic semantics (v1 scaffolding — see SSI_ADAPTIVE_DESIGN.md) 
 
 
 
 The point of Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) is generally to
 avoid  taking locks, so the mention of table locks and a
 row-2pl   4   alias was surprising. Moreover,
“safe for most OLTP” undermines the claim that  occ  was
“safe under concurrency”; it suggests there are some OLTP workloads
which are unsafe! 
 Orkes explained that this documentation was wrong:  occ 
was actually optimistic, and the  row-2pl  alias was to
preserve compatibility with an earlier two-phase locking mechanism. They
also provided an unpublished operator guide with detailed descriptions
of the various transaction modes. This document was  difficult
to interpret , but did specify the following consistency models: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Mode 
 Consistency Model 
 
 
 
 
  fast  
 Unknown 
 
 
  occ-v3  (a.k.a.
 occ ,  occ-v2 ,  row-2pl ) 
 Snapshot Isolation 
 
 
  zero-copy-occ  (a.k.a.
 zocc ) 
 Snapshot Isolation 
 
 
  serializable-ssi  (a.k.a.
 ssi ) 
 Serializable 
 
 
  table-2pl  (a.k.a.
 serializable ) 
 Strong Serializable 
 
 
 
 Sources disagreed about the default transaction and WAL sync modes,
but in general,  occ-v3  and  groupsync  appeared
to be the default. 
  2  Test Design 
 We wrote a  test
suite  for ParticleDB using the  Jepsen testing library .
We ran ParticleDB versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 on individual
Debian 13 nodes, both in containers and EC2 VMs. Our test harness could
simulate process crashes by killing ParticleDB, simulate the loss of
un- fsync ed writes using  LazyFS , and truncate or
corrupt disk files. We ran ParticleDB using each transaction mode and
all three WAL sync modes. 
 We first tried ParticleDB’s official Java SDK. While the  documentation
indicated  that the library was available as a Maven dependency,
neither the JAR nor source code were actually available. Instead, we
began with the official Postgres JDBC client, version 42.7.11, and later
added support for the  ParticleDB Java SDK ,
versions 1.0.0 through 1.0.2. 
  2.1  Workloads 
 We used several Jepsen workloads from other SQL databases, and
designed new ones specifically for ParticleDB. 
 The   rw 
workload  performed randomly generated transactions involving reads
and writes of integer values identified by unique integer keys. We
stored each value in a single row and accessed them both via primary and
unindexed secondary keys. Keys and values were encoded as a variety of
datatypes, including integers, decimals, and strings. We assumed that
writes followed reads within each transaction, and that individual keys
were sequentially consistent, and used these assumptions to infer
constraints on the  version orders and
transaction dependency graphs . Jepsen’s transactional checker,  Elle , then searched for
cycles in that dependency graph, as well as a variety of non-cyclic
phenomena like  G1a
(Aborted Read) . 
 The   append  
workload also performed randomly generated transactions over rows
identified by unique integer keys, but the values were lists of
integers. Transactions could read one of these lists by key, or append a
unique integer to a list by key. We encoded each list as a
comma-separated  text  field, and used SQL
 concat  to append to them. Rows could be selected via
primary key or unindexed secondary key, or via a join to an indirection
table. From there, we used Elle to infer version orders and dependency
graphs, and searched for a variety of cyclic and non-cyclic
phenomena. 
 When these workloads revealed consistency violations within a single
transaction, we designed an   internal  
workload to stress internal consistency. This workload performed a
series of randomly generated transactions involving  INSERT ,
 UPDATE ,  DELETE , and  SELECT 
statements over a simple key-value table, and verified that within each
individual transaction, reads observed prior writes. 
 To investigate tantalizing anomalies in the  internal 
workload, we designed the   compare  
workload. This workload used Clojure’s  test.check  generative
testing library to  produce 
random tables and simple SQL statements over them, then executed those
statements against both ParticleDB and PostgreSQL. If ParticleDB’s
behavior was  not
equivalent  to PostgreSQL’s, the compare workload would  search 
for a simpler sequence of statements that could reproduce the same
divergence. Although our SQL generator was relatively simple—just a few
basic datatypes, literals, arithmetic, comparisons, boolean logic,
transactions, and some simple  LIMIT ,  OFFSET ,
and  ORDER BY  clauses—it proved remarkably fruitful. 
 Drawing on these successes, we devised a hybrid   internal-sim  
workload to search for violations of internal consistency in more
complex transactions. This workload  generated 
a random set of tables, then concurrently executed  random
transactions  over them. It then  checked
each transaction  independently to ensure that each of its statements
observed results consistent with those preceding. For example, if a
transaction executed  DELETE ... WHERE 2 < c , then
observed a row with  c = 3 , we could prove that transaction
was not internally consistent. 
  3  Results 
 We found 96 issues with ParticleDB, which we present in several
categories below. All but three of these issues occurred in healthy,
single-node instances of ParticleDB. Busy readers may wish to jump to
the  Discussion  section, which summarizes our
findings. 
 
  Availability and
Performance  
  Broken Features  
  Predicates  
  Constraints  
  Joins

A :
