  3.1  Availability and
Performance 
 Under normal operation, ParticleDB was slow, deadlocked, and crashed
without warning. 
  3.1.1  Abysmal Performance With
 table-2pl  (#62) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4,
 --txn-mode table-2pl  was so slow as to be essentially
unusable. While some transactions might complete in a few milliseconds,
most took 10, 20, or even 30 seconds, then failed. 
 For example, take  this
test run  with a single node running 1.1.18.4, transaction mode
 table-2pl , and WAL mode  groupsync . With ten
concurrent clients, most transactions blocked for tens of seconds before
throwing
 could not serialize access due to concurrent update , or an
IO error. 
 High latencies ( #62 )
appeared improved by 1.1.18.6, which could execute transactions with
sub-100 millisecond latencies for at least a few seconds. 
  3.1.2  Mystery Crash (#81) 
 While 1.1.18.6 improved latencies, it also crashed frequently.
Crashes occurred spontaneously with various transaction modes, WAL
modes, and client interfaces; there was no obvious cause. Nodes would
run for a few hundred to a few thousand seconds before exiting. No error
messages were printed. These crashes ( #81 ) no
longer appeared in 1.1.18.11.rc-18. 
  3.1.3  Deadlock After Two
Transactions (#27) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.18.8, submitting as few as two concurrent
transactions to a healthy, single-node deployment could cause it to
deadlock. This occurred both using the Postgres and ParticleDB
interfaces. The node would log an error message like
 [DEADLOCK] 1 cycles detected at SystemTime ... , and an
empty backtrace. In some cases new clients could attach and perform
transactions; in others, new clients would also hang indefinitely. This
may reflect multiple deadlock bugs. 
 With the  append  workload, version 1.1.18.9 generally
could not run for more than 45 seconds without locking up. Version
1.1.18.11.rc-1 could reliably run for two minutes without lockups, and
we declared the issue ( #27 )
resolved. 
  3.1.4  Deadlock With
 table-2pl  (#71) 
 While version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 fixed the most frequent deadlocks, we
continued to find deadlocks through 1.1.18.11.rc-6 when running with
 table-2pl . An otherwise healthy ParticleDB node would
execute transactions for about 30 seconds, then get stuck forever. The
node would log  a
similar deadlock error message  to #27, and all requests with the
ParticleDB client would throw  PDB JDBC: null  after a 100
second default timeout. These deadlocks ( #71 )
appeared resolved by 1.1.18.11.rc-7. 
  3.2  Broken Features 
 Orkes’  public
documentation  claimed broad support for Postgres features, and the
internal operator guide concurred: 
 
 The engine speaks PostgreSQL v3 wire protocol natively — anything
that speaks pgjdbc / libpq / psycopg2 / pq connects unchanged.
 BEGIN ,  COMMIT ,  ROLLBACK , prepared
statements, parameterised queries, and extended-query pipelining all
work as expected. 
 
 These claims were somewhat optimistic. ParticleDB was missing support
for a wide array of Postgres features, and others were badly broken. 
  3.2.1  No Aggregates Within
 CASE  (#20) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, aggregate expressions like
 COUNT(*)  were not supported within  CASE 
expressions. 
       SELECT  
      CASE  
        WHEN   COUNT ( * )  =   2  
          THEN   'CASE_COUNT_STAR_OK'  
          ELSE   'CASE_COUNT_STAR_BAD'  
      END  
    FROM  t;    
 This threw  Error: cannot evaluate wildcard expression .
ParticleDB gained support for this feature ( #20 ) by
version 1.1.18.6. 
  3.2.2  Unsupported Exponentiation
(#28) 
 ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 did not support the Postgres
exponentiation operator: 
      root =>   SELECT   2  ^  3 ; 
   ERROR:  unsupported binary  operator : PGExp    
 Version 1.1.18.9 added support for the  ^  operator ( #28 ). 
  3.2.3  Malformed Responses for
Prepared Statements (#2) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9, any attempt to execute a
prepared statement using the Postgres JDBC driver caused an exception
like
 Execution error (NoSuchElementException) at java.util.ArrayDeque/removeFirst .
Since the JDBC driver automatically switches to prepared statements
after the first few calls to  execute() , this rendered the
database essentially unusable. As a workaround, we disabled the client’s
use of prepared statements. 
 Prepared statements are executed using Postgres’  extended
query protocol , which takes place in several (potentially reusable)
phases: Parse, Bind, Execute, and so on. Orkes believes that ParticleDB
likely failed to return a response for one of those phases, or returned
an extra message, causing the client’s queue to underflow. By version
1.1.18.11.rc-1, this issue ( #2 ) appeared
fixed. 
  3.2.4  Most Postgres Queries Fail
(#83) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-7 through 1.1.18.11.rc-19, many queries
using the Postgres interface threw
 Bad value for type long: some_column . This rendered the
database largely unusable. 
       CREATE   TABLE  ints (a  int ); 
    SELECT   *   FROM  ints; 
      ->  Bad  value   for   type   long  : a    
 Orkes believes this issue ( #83 ) was
fixed in 1.1.19-rc.12. 
  3.2.5  Tuples Without Fields
(#111) 
 In 1.1.18.11.rc-18 and rc-19, queries with the Postgres interface
occasionally threw errors like
 Received resultset tuples, but no field structure for them .  5   For example, take  this
test  of version 1.1.18.11.rc-19, with no faults, a new
 strict-serializable  transaction mode, and WAL mode
 sync . It executed a transaction like: 
       BEGIN ; 
    SELECT   *   FROM  t_38; 
    INSERT   INTO  u_38 (d, a, c, b)  VALUES  
     ( null ,  null ,  false ,  "oudt1THxi" ); 
    INSERT   INTO  t_38 (d, b)  VALUES  
     ( false ,  "BCczDbueXLz9zXnpgbdCeFbC5y6XSEys3" ); 
    COMMIT ;    
 This complained of resultset tuples with no field structure,
suggesting an error in ParticleDB’s Postgres protocol state machine.
While Jepsen has not tested this version, Orkes reports this issue ( #111 ) was
fixed in version 1.1.19-rc.13. 
  3.2.6  Broken Postgres
Authentication (#1) 
 The Postgres wire protocol usually authenticates clients using a
username and password. ParticleDB had a  --pg-password 
option, but 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 lacked any option to set the
username.  Some
of the documentation  indicated the default username was
 admin , while  other 
 pages 
said it was  particledb . Neither appeared to work; the only
option was to use  --no-auth  to disable authentication
altogether. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 introduced a
 --pg-username  option ( #1 ). 
  3.2.7  Java Client Could Not Execute
Transactions (#3) 
 Version 1.0.0 of the official ParticleDB Java client refused every
attempt to execute a transaction. Any call to begin a JDBC transaction,
or to execute a  BEGIN  statement, would result in an error
message:
 PDB wire error 1064: SQL plan error: transaction/session statements do not produce a query plan . 
 ParticleDB 1.1.4 could execute transactions via its Postgres
interface, but using the official Java SDK was essentially impossible.
This issue ( #3 ) seems to
have been resolved by ParticleDB 1.1.15. 
  3.3  Predicates 
 ParticleDB struggled to interpret predicates.  WHERE 
clauses failed to match rows they should have, or matched unexpected or
nonexistent rows. These issues occurred with a single server, single
client, and no faults. 
  3.3.1   SELECT  Ignores
 WHERE  Clause (#40) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9,  SELECT  queries
without a table accepted a  WHERE  clause, but ignored
it. 
      root =>   SELECT   5   WHERE   FALSE ; 
     5  
    ---  
     5  
   ( 1   row )    
 This should have returned zero rows. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 seems to
have resolved this issue ( #40 ). 
  3.3.2 
 WHERE 1 < (a + 2)  (#47) 
 Version 1.1.1.18.9 introduced a new problem with predicates: inside a
transaction, a  WHERE  clause which performed sufficiently
complex floating-point operations would silently fail to match any rows.
For example: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  real ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 3 ); 
   root =>   BEGIN ; 
   root =*>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE   1   <  (a  +   2 ); 
    a 
    ---  
   ( 0   rows )    
 The same problem applied to  SELECT ,  UPDATE ,
and  DELETE : predicates like
 WHERE (a * 2) IS NOT NULL  would silently fail to match.
However, simpler predicates like  WHERE a IS NOT NULL  would
match correctly. The effect disappeared if the column was an integer.
Moreover, some predicates which would throw errors outside a transaction
would silently match zero rows within a transaction, suggesting these
predicates were not being evaluated at all: 
      root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE   1   <  ( 5.0  %  3 ); 
   ERROR:  internal error 
   root =>   BEGIN ; 
   root =*>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE   1   <  ( 5.0  %  3 ); 
    a 
    ---  
   ( 0   rows )    
 This issue ( #47 )
appeared resolved by 1.1.18.11.rc-1. 
  3.3.3   WHERE 4 = 5 
(#18) 
 ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 aggressively interpreted
 WHERE something = x  as a primary-key lookup of
 x , regardless of the value of  something . 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t 
          (a  int   primary   key , b  int ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t  VALUES  ( 4 ,  5 ), ( 5 ,  6 ); 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  b  =   4 ; 
    a | b 
    ---+---  
     4  |  5     
 ParticleDB would ignore a row with  b = 5  in favor of
 a = 5 : 
      root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  b  =   5 ; 
    a | b 
    ---+---  
     5  |  6  
   ( 1   row )    
 You could write predicates over non-existent columns: 
      root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t 
           WHERE  definitely_not_a_column  =   4 ; 
    a | b 
    ---+----  
     4  |  5  
   ( 1   row )    
 Or ask if  4 = 5 :  6   
      root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE   4   =   5 ; 
    a | b 
    ---+----  
     5  |  6  
   ( 1   row )    
 By version 1.1.18.4, ParticleDB had learned that not every equality
comparison involved a primary key ( #18 ). 
  3.3.4   SELECT  in a
Transaction Returns Nonsense (#35) 
 The behavior of  SELECT  within a transaction in
ParticleDB versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 was thoroughly confusing.
Consider a single client connected to a fresh single-node instance of
ParticleDB 1.1.18.8. It creates a simple table of integers with two
rows,  1  and  2 , and begins a transaction: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  INT   UNIQUE ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t  VALUES  ( 1 ), ( 2 ); 
   root =>   BEGIN ; 
   root =*>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
    a 
    ---  
     1  
     2  
   ( 2   rows )    
 So far, so good. But now consider: 
      root =*>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  a  =   1 ; 
    a 
    ---  
     2  
   ( 1   row ) 
    
   root =*>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  a  =   3 ; 
    a 
    ---  
     2  
   ( 1   row ) 
    
   root =*>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  a  IN  ( 1 ,  2 ); 
    a 
    ---  
     2  
   ( 1   row ) 
    
   root =*>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE   FALSE ; 
    a 
    ---  
     2  
   ( 1   row )    
 One might conclude that every  SELECT  with a predicate
returned a single row from the requested table—perhaps the most recently
inserted row. But this is not true, because many predicates evaluating
to  TRUE  returned nothing. 
      root =*>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE   TRUE ; 
    a 
    ---  
   ( 0   rows ) 
    
   root =*>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE   3   =   3 ; 
    a 
    ---  
   ( 0   rows )    
 This behavior ( #35 ) seemed
improved by ParticleDB 1.1.18.9. 
  3.4  Constraints 
 ParticleDB often violated constraints like  NOT NULL  or
 UNIQUE , even with a single server, single client, and no
faults. 
  3.4.1  Not-Null Constraints Allow
Null (#8) 
 While ParticleDB allowed users to add  NOT NULL 
constraints to columns, versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 ignored them,
resulting in bizarre states. 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  BOOLEAN   NOT   NULL ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( NULL ); 
    INSERT   0   1     
 While the resulting row existed in some sense, it was partly
invisible. 
      root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
    a 
    ---  
   ( 0   rows ) 
    
   root =>   SELECT   COUNT ( * )  FROM  t; 
     COUNT  
    -------  
         1  
   ( 1   row ) 
    
   root =>   SELECT   COUNT ( * )  FROM  t  WHERE  a  IS   NULL ; 
     COUNT  
    -------  
         0  
   ( 1   row )    
 In version 1.1.18.4, ParticleDB started to enforce null constraints
( #8 ). 
  3.4.2  Unique Constraints Allow
Duplicates (#9) 
 Similarly, while ParticleDB allowed users to add unique constraints
to columns, versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4 simply ignored them. 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  boolean   UNIQUE ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( TRUE ); 
    INSERT   0   1  
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( TRUE ); 
    INSERT   0   1  
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
    a 
    ---  
    t 
    t 
   ( 2   rows )    
 In version 1.1.18.6, ParticleDB partially enforced unique constraints
( #9 ). 
  3.4.3  Duplicate Primary Keys
(#29) 
 Although 1.1.18.6 made  UNIQUE  constraints somewhat more
robust, 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 allowed an  UPDATE  to produce
multiple rows with the same primary key. 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t ( id  text  PRIMARY   KEY , 
                           desc  text); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t  VALUES  ( 'a' ,  'a' ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t  VALUES  ( 'b' ,  'b' ); 
   root =>   UPDATE  t  SET   id   =   'c' ; 
    UPDATE   2     
 Selecting a row by primary key returned only one of the two rows, but
other predicates could return both: 
      root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE   id   =   'c' ; 
     id  |  desc  
    ----+------  
    c  | b 
   ( 1   row ) 
    
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE   id   LIKE   'c' ; 
     id  |  desc  
    ----+------  
    c  | a 
    c  | b    
 This issue ( #29 ) appears
to have been fixed by 1.1.18.9. 
  3.4.4  Null Primary Keys (#57) 
 Per the SQL standard, primary keys may not be null. This makes
intuitive sense, since  NULL  represents an unknown value.
ParticleDB would not allow you to insert null values for primary keys.
However, versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-1 were perfectly happy to
 update  the primary key of one (or more!) rows to
 NULL . 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  int   PRIMARY   KEY ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 3 ), ( 4 ); 
   root =>   UPDATE  t  SET  a  =   NULL ; 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
    a 
    ---  
    
    
   ( 2   rows )    
 ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-3 rejected attempts to set primary keys to
 NULL  ( #57 ). 
  3.4.5  Primary Key Conflicts with
Deleted Rows (#82) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.18.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-11, a transaction which
deleted a row, then inserted a new row with the same primary key, would
abort due to a primary key constraint violation. For example: 
       
    CREATE   TABLE  t (a  int   PRIMARY   KEY ); 
    INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 7 ); 
    BEGIN ; 
    DELETE   FROM  t; 
    INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 7 ); 
    COMMIT ;    
 The second  INSERT  would throw
 PDB wire error 1064: SQL execution error: duplicate key value violates unique constraint (key=7) ,
but only when using the ParticleDB interface—the Postgres interface was
unaffected. Orkes partially addressed this issue ( #82 ) in
version 1.1.18.11.rc-9, and fixed another case of it in
1.1.18.11.rc-18. 
  3.4.6  Lack of Primary Key Conflicts
with Extant Rows (#90) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-9, a transaction executing concurrently
with other transactions could read a row with a primary key, then
successfully insert a row with that same primary key. For example, take
 this
 internal-sim  test , which created a table with two
integer columns: 
  CREATE TABLE u_14 (b int, a int PRIMARY KEY);  
 A transaction ran  SELECT * FROM u_14  and observed
several rows, including  {:b 1020026655, :a -1} . It then ran
 INSERT INTO u_14 (b, a) VALUES (-27, -1) , which should have
conflicted with the extant primary key, but succeeded instead. It went
on to  SELECT * FROM u_14  again, and observed the newly
inserted row, but not the previously existent one. This is a violation
of internal consistency. 
 As of version 1.1.18.11.rc-19, we no longer observed these internal
consistency violations ( #90 ). 
  3.5  Joins 
 ParticleDB struggled to join tables together. The following issues
occurred with a single server, single client, and no faults. 
  3.5.1  Can’t Join Integers to Floats
(#58) 
 Even after agreeing that  2.0 = 2 , ParticleDB 1.1.4
through 1.1.18.9 refused to join two tables on an  int  and a
 real  column: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  real ); 
   root =>   CREATE   TABLE  u (a  int ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 2.0 ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  u (a)  VALUES  ( 2 ); 
   root =>   SELECT  t.a  FROM  t  JOIN  u  ON  u.a  =  t.a; 
   ERROR:   join   key  must be  integer   type     
 Databases like Postgres would return a single row here, since
 2.0 = 2 . ParticleDB gained the ability to join floats to
integers ( #58 ) by
1.1.18.11.rc-1. 
  3.5.2  Incorrect Column Names
(#54) 
 Because two tables can have a column with the same name, SQL
databases generally return both table and column names, so you can tell
which column belonged to which table. ParticleDB, with both the
ParticleDB and Postgres interfaces, neglected to return table names.
Instead, versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-1 renamed column
 a  in joined tables to  right.a ,
 right.right.a , and so on. Consider the following simple
join across two tables  t  and  u , both with an
integer column  a : 
       SELECT   *   FROM  t  FULL   OUTER   JOIN  u 
      ON  t.a  =  u.a;    
 In Postgres this produced rows like: 
      [{ :t/a   1 ,  :u/a   1.0 } 
    { :t/a   2 ,  :u/a   2.0 }]    
 Here the expression  :t/a  denotes column  a 
of table  t . In ParticleDB, this same query returned: 
      [{ :a   1 ,  :right.a   1.0 } 
    { :a   2 ,  :right.a   2.0 }]    
 The table names are completely missing, and ParticleDB has altered
the name of column  a  to  right.a . Programs
which expected typical SQL behavior would throw an error as they
attempted to read columns which were not present, or could silently read
null values. 
 ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-3 no longer munged columns, but the database
still omitted table names. The resulting name collisions destroyed
information. 
      [{ :a   1 } 
    { :a   2 }]    
 While Jepsen has not had a chance to test this version, Orkes claims
this issue ( #54 ) was
resolved by version 1.1.19-rc.13. 
  3.5.3  Coercing to Strings
(#76) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-19, joins would coerce some
values to strings in ParticleDB’s Postgres interface. For example,
consider the following join: 
       CREATE   TABLE  t (a  int ); 
    CREATE   TABLE  u (a  real ); 
    INSERT   INTO  u (a)  VALUES  ( 3.2 ); 
    INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 5 ); 
    SELECT  u.a  FROM  t  CROSS   JOIN  u;    
 With the ParticleDB interface, this produced the number
 3.2 . With the Postgres interface, it produced the string
 "3.2" . This issue ( #76 ) seemed
fixed by 1.1.18.11.rc-21. 
  3.5.4  Missing Rows (#59) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-1, outer joins of a
non-empty table to an empty one often returned no rows, even though the
query should have produced all rows in the non-empty table. For
example: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  int ); 
   root =>   CREATE   TABLE  u (a  int ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 1 ), ( 2 ); 
   root =>   SELECT  t.a  AS  t, u.a  AS  u 
           FROM  t  LEFT   JOIN  u  ON  u.a  =  t.a; 
    t | u 
    ---+---  
   ( 0   rows )    
 By version 1.1.18.11.rc-3, ParticleDB correctly returned rows when
joining to empty tables ( #59 ). 
  3.5.5  Column Confusion (#77) 
 Many tables in real databases contain columns with identical names,
like  id  or  created_at . When asked to join two
tables like this, ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-6 became
severely confused, even when all columns were fully qualified. For
example: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a text); 
   root =>   CREATE   TABLE  u (a text); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t  VALUES  ( 'this' ), ( 'that' ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  u  VALUES  
          ( 'is not the right column' ); 
   root =>   SELECT  t.a  AS  ta, u.a  AS  ua  FROM  t 
           CROSS   JOIN  u  WHERE  (u.a  =   'this' ); 
     ta  |           ua 
    ------+-------------------------  
    this |  is   not   the   right   column  
   ( 1   row )    
 This should not have matched anything—there are no rows in table
 u  where  u.a = 'this' . Instead ParticleDB
matched a row in table  t  which satisfied
 t.a = 'this' , then cross-joined it to all rows in
 u . To add insult to injury, 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9 appeared
to swap around the output columns, producing the following table: 
                 ta            |  ua 
    -------------------------+------  
     is   not   the   right   column  | this    
 If column  t.a  was of a different type than
 u.a , ParticleDB would try to coerce the types into
compatible forms, producing bizarre error messages or delightfully weird
results. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-7 was much less confused when joining
tables containing the same column name ( #77 ). 
  3.6  Zombies 
 ParticleDB often wound up with rows that could not be deleted or
updated, or which persisted in some (perhaps mangled) form after their
deletion. These issues occurred with a single server, single client, and
no faults. 
  3.6.1  Total Recall (#26) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.17 through 1.1.18.8, it appeared impossible to
delete rows within a transaction. For example: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  boolean ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( TRUE ); 
   root =>   BEGIN ; 
   root =*>   DELETE   FROM  t; 
    DELETE   0  
   root =*>   COMMIT ; 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
    a 
    ---  
    t 
   ( 1   row )    
 We were unable to find a predicate that allowed one to delete records
( #26 ).
Version 1.1.18.9 allowed transactions to mostly  7  
delete rows. 
  3.6.2  Memento Delere (#45) 
 1.1.18.9 resolved issue #26, but deleted rows still lingered on in
some capacity. While a transaction could not directly select deleted
rows, it could observe them via aggregate functions and various
predicates. 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  boolean ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( TRUE ); 
   root =>   BEGIN ; 
   root =*>   DELETE   FROM  t; 
    DELETE   1  
   root =*>   SELECT   COUNT ( * )  FROM  t  WHERE  a  =   TRUE ; 
     COUNT  
    -------  
         1  
   ( 1   row ) 
    
   root =*>   SELECT   COUNT ( * )  FROM  t  WHERE  a  =   FALSE ; 
     COUNT  
    -------  
         0  
   ( 1   row )    
 The row must still be present in some sense, because these aggregate
queries could observe its value via predicates. However, trying to read
the row directly returned nothing: 
      root =*>   SELECT  a  FROM  t  WHERE  a  =   TRUE ; 
    a 
    ---  
   ( 0   rows )    
 Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 no longer allowed shades of deleted records to
persist in aggregate queries ( #45 ). 
  3.6.3  Night of the Living Integers
(#23) 
 In versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.17, updating an integer column could
make rows impossible to delete. For example: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (i  int ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t  VALUES  ( 0 ); 
   root =>   UPDATE  t  SET  i  =   1.5 ; 
   root =>   DELETE   FROM  t; 
    DELETE   0  
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
    i 
    ---  
     1  
   ( 1   row )    
 While this row appears to contain the integer  1 , that
integer is  special , since the  UPDATE  statement
provided the value  1.5 . This row cannot be deleted. It does
appear in  SELECT , and is apparently equal to
 1 , rather than  1.5 . Oddly, updating a row by
primary key with the same  1.5  value did not create zombies;
the problem ( #23 ) was
somehow linked to predicates. ParticleDB 1.1.18.4 no longer exhibited
this behavior. 
  3.6.4  Team Rocket (#84) 
 Tables with a  double precision  column suffered from a
similar problem: they could be updated with integer values, but doing so
would produce zombie rows that could neither be updated nor deleted
again. 
      ROOT =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  double   precision ); 
   ROOT =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 1.0 ); 
   ROOT =>   UPDATE  t  SET  a  =   2 ; 
   ROOT =>   DELETE   FROM  t; 
    DELETE   0  
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
    a 
    ---  
     2  
   ( 1   row )    
 If the double precision column was a primary key, these updates would
produce duplicate copies of the updated row. This issue ( #84 )
affected ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-8, and was fixed
in 1.1.18.11.rc-9. 
  3.6.5  A Ghost is Technically Not a
Number (#78) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-6,  NaN 
values stored in  real  or  double precision 
columns could neither be updated nor deleted. 
       DROP   TABLE   IF   EXISTS  t; 
    CREATE   TABLE  t (a  real ); 
    INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 'NaN' ); 
    UPDATE  t  SET  a  =   5.0 ; 
      ->  # :next .jdbc{ :update  -  count   0 } 
    DELETE   FROM  t; 
      ->  # :next .jdbc{ :update  -  count   0 } 
    SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
      ->  [{ :a  ##NaN}]    
 This issue ( #78 ) did not
occur with the  psql  shell, but did happen with both
ParticleDB and Postgres JDBC clients. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-7 seems to
have fixed the problem. 
  3.6.6  Beached Strings (#74) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-6, fixed-width
strings were unmodifiable unless created with exactly the right number
of characters. While ParticleDB would correctly pad the string
 'hi'  to  'hi ' , the resulting row could neither
be updated nor deleted. 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  character ( 3 )); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 'hi' ); 
   root =>   DELETE   FROM  t; 
    DELETE   0  
   root =>   UPDATE  t  SET  a  =   'sup' ; 
    UPDATE   0  
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
     a 
    -----  
    hi 
   ( 1   row )    
 If a fixed-width column was used as a primary key, it could be
updated, but only once. Both old and new copies would appear as distinct
rows. 
       CREATE   TABLE  t 
          (a  character ( 3 )  PRIMARY   KEY ); 
    INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 'um' ); 
    UPDATE  t  SET  a  =   'no' ; 
    SELECT  a  FROM  t; 
    ->  [{ :a   "um " } { :a   "no " }]    
 Any further attempt to modify those rows would produce a duplicate
key error, despite all the values involved being distinct. Fixed-width
strings were also incomparable using the  =  operator.
Version 1.1.18.11.rc-7 resolved these issues ( #74 ). 
  3.6.7  Pet Sematary (#46) 
 In SQL, the  DROP TABLE  statement destroys a table
completely. In ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 through 1.1.18.11.rc-1, it left a
shadow of the table behind, whose rows would reappear in later tables
with the same name and more-or-less compatible schemata. To demonstrate
this behavior, let us create a table with a single row: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a text, b  real ); 
   root =>   BEGIN ; 
   root =*>   INSERT   INTO  t  VALUES  ( 'boo' ,  18.83 ); 
   root =*>   COMMIT ;    
 We then drop the table, and demonstrate that it no longer exists: 
      root =>   DROP   TABLE  t; 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
   ERROR:   table   not  found    
 If we then create a new table with the same name and a somewhat
compatible schema, rows from the deleted table reappear in the new one.
However, the resurrected rows are not exactly their former selves. The
floating-point value  18.83  has become the integer
 19 . 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a text, b  int ); 
   root =>   BEGIN ; 
   root =*>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
     a  | b 
    -----+----  
    boo |  19  
   ( 1   row )    
 This behavior ( #46 ) seemed
linked to transactions, and no longer appeared in 1.1.18.11.rc-3. 
  3.7  State Corruption 
 ParticleDB had many ways to create values which could not be read,
alter values unexpectedly, create rows with incorrect or missing
columns, or otherwise corrupt logical state. The issues in this section
involved only a single server, single client, and no faults. 
  3.7.1  Unreadable Infinities
(#15) 
 In versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.17, ParticleDB’s Postgres interface did
not correctly serialize floating-point values like
 Infinity . One could write infinite values, but trying to
read them would cause the client to throw an error. 
      CREATE TABLE t (a real) ;  
   INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES ( 'Infinity' ) ;  
   SELECT  *  FROM t 
      => PSQLException:  "Bad value for type  
          double : inf"     
 With Postgres, this correctly returned the JVM’s
 Double/INFINITY  value.  NaN  was serialized
correctly. At the  psql  shell, stored values came back as
 inf , rather than  Infinity . In version
1.1.18.6, ParticleDB serialized infinite values correctly ( #15 ). 
  3.7.2   NaN  Sometimes
Converted to 0.0 (#21) 
 ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4 would sometimes (but not always!)
convert the floating-point value  NaN  to  0.0 .
For example: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  real ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 2.5 ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 'NaN' ); 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
     a 
    -----  
     2.5  
       0  
   ( 2   rows )    
 Delightfully, whether this  NaN  corruption occurred
depended on the order in which rows were inserted. If the first value
inserted into the table was  NaN , that and later
 NaN s would be preserved. Version 1.1.18.6 seemed to store
 NaN  correctly ( #21 ). 
  3.7.3  Assignment of Incompatible
Types (#7) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, you could update a column of
one type to a column of a different, incompatible type—producing values
like  null  or  0 . For example: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  INT , b  BOOLEAN ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t  VALUES  ( 2 ,  FALSE ); 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  a  =  b; 
   ERROR:  arrow  compute : Invalid argument error: 
   Invalid comparison operation: Int64  ==   Boolean  
   root =>   UPDATE  t  SET  a  =  b; 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
    a | b 
    ---+---  
     0  | f    
 In Postgres, this UPDATE would throw
 ERROR: column "a" is of type text but expression is of type int .
ParticleDB refused to  compare  this string to an integer (at
least in this case), but was perfectly happy to make one equal to the
other, resulting in  NULL . Version 1.1.18.6 seemed to
resolve this issue ( #7 ). 
  3.7.4  Insert Column Order Table
Corruption (#16) 
 In SQL, one usually inserts a row into a table using a statement like
 INSERT INTO people (name, age) VALUES ('xanthippe', 15) .
ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 ignored the  INSERT 
statement’s columns, using whatever column order had been used to create
the table originally. This produced rows with titillating properties.
Consider the following pair of inserts: one with columns in the same
order as the table’s schema, and a second in a different order: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t 
          (a TEXT  NOT   NULL   PRIMARY   KEY , 
           b  boolean ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a, b)  VALUES  ( 'x' ,  TRUE ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (b, a)  VALUES  ( FALSE ,  'y' ); 
   root =>   SELECT   COUNT ( * )  FROM  t; 
     COUNT  
    -------  
         2  
   ( 1   row )    
 While ParticleDB thinks this table contains two rows, neither can be
read via  SELECT * : 
      root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
    a | b 
    ---+---  
   ( 0   rows )    
 In general, any query which happened to encounter a row inserted with
a different column order would silently produce zero results. However,
each row could be read by primary key! Note the different column orders
in the output: 
      root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  a  =   'x' ; 
    a | b 
    ---+---  
    x | t 
   ( 1   row ) 
    
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  a  =   'y' ; 
    b | a 
    ---+---  
    f | y 
   ( 1   row )    
 In the preceding example, the two columns were of (somewhat)
incompatible types. What happens if the types are compatible? 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  INT , b  REAL ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a, b) 
           VALUES  ( 1 ,  1.23E32 ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (b, a) 
           VALUES  ( 2.34E32 ,  2 ); 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
             a          |    b 
    ---------------------+---------  
                       1  |  1.23e32  
     9223372036854775807  |        2  
   ( 2   rows )    
 Now the table is readable, but the data is corrupt. The second row’s
 a  value appears under  b , and vice-versa. The
floating-point value  2.34E32  has become the integer  2 63  − 1 . 
 If we attempt to delete every row from the table, something very
strange happens. The  DELETE  leaves the differently-ordered
row in place, and its originally inserted values now appear intact! 
      root =>   DELETE   FROM  t; 
    DELETE   1  
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
    a |    b 
    ---+---------  
     2  |  2.34e32  
   ( 1   row )    
 A second  DELETE  statement—now that the table contains
only rows inserted with column order  (b, a) —could
successfully delete the remaining row. These column-order issues ( #16 ) no
longer appeared in version 1.1.18.4. 
  3.7.5  Updates Can Insert Corrupt
Rows (#24, #25) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8, an update which matched no rows
could instead create a new, possibly corrupt row in the table, with
baffling effects. Consider a table mapping integer keys to integer
values: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t 
          ( id   int   not   null   primary   key , 
           val  integer ); 
   root =>   BEGIN ; 
   root =*>   UPDATE  t  SET  val  =   10   WHERE   id   =   0 ; 
    UPDATE   1  
   root =*>   COMMIT ;    
 This table was just created. It contains no rows, so the update
should have affected zero, not one row. And yet it now contains a
row! 
      root =>   SELECT   COUNT  ( * )  FROM  t; 
     COUNT  
    -------  
         1  
   ( 1   row )    
 However, that row is invisible to typical queries: 
      root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
     id  | val 
    ----+-----  
   ( 0   rows ) 
    
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE   id   =   0 ; 
     id  | val 
    ----+-----  
   ( 0   rows ) 
    
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  val  =   10 ; 
     id  | val 
    ----+-----  
   ( 0   rows )    
 Although one cannot directly see the row by primary key, it can
conflict with some inserts. 
      root =>   INSERT   INTO  t ( id , val)  VALUES  ( 0 ,  100 ); 
    INSERT   0   1  
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t ( id , val)  VALUES  ( 10 ,  110 ); 
   ERROR:  duplicate  key   value  violates  unique  
            constraint  ( key  =  10 )    
 “Hang on,” an astute reader might exclaim. “The row we supposedly
updated had  id = 0  and set  val = 10 . Why did
it not conflict with an insert of  id = 0 ?” 
 Quite right, dear reader! And why did it instead conflict with
 id = 10 ? 
 These are excellent questions—which we do not know the answer to.
Pressing on: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t 
          ( id   int   not   null   primary   key , 
           val  integer ); 
   root =>   BEGIN ; 
   root =*>   UPDATE  t  SET  val  =   50   WHERE   id   =   5 ; 
    UPDATE   1  
   root =*>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE   id   =   5 ; 
    val 
    -----  
      50  
   ( 1   row ) 
    
   root =*>   COMMIT ;    
 Within the transaction, the row produced by this update is readable
by its primary key  id = 5 . Although this table has two
columns, the row is printed as if it had only one:
 val = 50 . 
 As in #16, these corrupt rows caused queries that encountered them to
silently return zero rows, even if there were other valid rows that
would have matched. 
      root =>   INSERT   INTO  t  VALUES  ( 6 ,  60 ); 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE   id   IN  ( 6 ); 
     id  | val 
    ----+-----  
      6  |   60  
    
   ( 1   row ) 
    
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE   id   IN  ( 6 ,  7 ); 
     id  | val 
    ----+-----  
   ( 0   rows )    
 Although our corrupt row had  id = 5  (or perhaps
 50 ), adding a second value to the  IN  predicate
seems to have caused ParticleDB to “notice” the corrupt row. It then
failed to return the valid row with  id = 6 . 
 Depending on the table structure and  UPDATE  statement,
rows created by updates might be structurally valid, but logically
corrupt: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  INT   UNIQUE ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t  VALUES  ( 1 ); 
   root =>   BEGIN ; 
   root =*>   UPDATE  t  SET  a  =   3   WHERE  a  =   2 ; 
    UPDATE   1  
   root =*>   COMMIT ; 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
    a 
    ---  
     1  
     3  
   ( 2   rows )    
 This bug ( #24 ) also
allowed updates which would have left a row’s value unchanged to instead
throw a duplicate key exception, as they (presumably) conflicted with
themselves ( #25 ). Both
issues appeared resolved as of version 1.1.18.9. 
  3.7.6  Sometimes, Strings That Are
Extensive… Are Cursed (#37) 
 In versions 1.1.15 through 1.1.17,  text  strings could be
unexpectedly transmogrified into eight-bit integers. We encountered this
in  append  tests using the official ParticleDB client, like
 this
one . The  append  workload stores a comma-separated list
of integers in an SQL  TEXT  column called  val ,
and appends values to it using  CONCAT . Most reads of
 val  sensibly returned strings: 
      [ "select (val) from txn2 where id = ? "   2946 ] 
      ->  [{ :val   "1" }]    
 However, after approximately 30 seconds, the ParticleDB client began
returning eight-bit integers for key  2946 . Here, the key’s
value has become the JVM  Byte   1 : 
      [ "select (val) from txn2 where sk = ? "   2946 ] 
      ->  [{ :val   1 }]    
 From this point on, some keys appeared as strings, while others
returned integers. A read of key  2961  returned the string
 "2" , while key  2865  returned the integer
 1 —then moments later, the string  "1,2" .
Sometimes the integer values corresponded to the string value produced
by earlier writes, but not always. For example, a transaction read key
 2980  as the integer  0 —when the only elements
appended to its string were  "1"  and  "2" .
Shortly thereafter, a single transaction read key  2980 
twice and found a string, then an apparently unrelated integer: 
      [ "select (val) from txn2 where id = ? "   2980 ] 
      ->  [{ :val   "2,1" }] 
   [ "select (val) from txn0 where sk = ? "   2981 ] 
      ->  [{ :val   "1" }] 
   [ "select (val) from txn2 where sk = ? "   2980 ] 
      ->  [{ :val   3 }]    
 This issue ( #37 ) seemed
to disappear by 1.1.18.11.rc-1. 
  3.7.7  Eternal Sunshine of the
Spotless Table (#72) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1,  append  tests of the
 table-2pl  transaction mode often threw errors like: 
 
 PDB wire error 1064: SQL execution error: failed to create
RecordBatch: Invalid argument error: Column ‘id’ is declared as
non-nullable but contains null values 
 
 This is odd. The  append  workload always picks a unique
integer ID for every write, and never tries to write a  NULL 
ID. It also never updates an ID—they are set only once, when the row is
created. Here’s  an
example  where a single  SELECT  statement, issued outside
of a transaction, complained of null primary keys. This suggests that
the table state had somehow become corrupt. 
 We no longer observed this error ( #72 ) in
1.1.18.11.rc-7. 
  3.8  Transactions and
Concurrency 
 We found several problems with ParticleDB’s transactions and
concurrency control. All of these occurred in single-node instances
without fault injection. 
  3.8.1  Nested Transactions Destroy
Ongoing Ones (#44) 
 ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9 allowed clients to begin nested
transactions, instead of warning that a transaction was already ongoing.
Any writes performed by the enclosing transaction would be lost, both
within the nested transaction and after commit. 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  int ); 
   root =>   BEGIN ; 
   root =*>   INSERT   INTO  t  VALUES  ( 3 ); 
   root =*>   BEGIN ; 
   root =*>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
    a 
    ---  
   ( 0   rows ) 
   root =*>   COMMIT ;    
 ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 seems to have resolved this issue ( #44 ):
issuing  BEGIN  within a transaction warned
 there is already a transaction in progress , and preserved
the ongoing transaction’s writes. 
  3.8.2  Aborted Transactions Can
Commit (#43) 
 Between versions 1.1.17 and 1.1.18.4, ParticleDB handled aborted
transactions irregularly. With the Postgres interface, an attempt to
commit an aborted transaction would throw an error, as one would
expect: 
      root =>   BEGIN ; 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 3 ); 
   root =>  THIS  IS   NOT  VALID SQL; 
   ERROR:  sql parser error: Expected: an SQL 
   statement, found: THIS  at  Line:  1 ,  Column :  1  
   root =>   COMMIT ; 
    ROLLBACK     
 Nevertheless, the writes performed by the aborted transaction
persisted: 
       SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
      ->  [{ :a   3 }]    
 The ParticleDB client had a different, also unexpected behavior:
executing a  COMMIT  statement on a failed transaction
returned  [#:next.jdbc{:update-count 0}] , rather than an
error. Although the transaction apparently committed, its effects were
invisible. Both interfaces, as of version 1.1.18.11.rc-18, returned
errors and did not expose the effects of aborted transactions ( #43 ). 
  3.8.3  Aggregates Sometimes Fail to
Observe a Transaction’s Rows (#48) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9, transactions which performed
aggregate queries, like  SELECT COUNT(*) , could miss rows
they should have matched, and return duplicate copies of rows, depending
on the predicate and previous queries in the transaction. For
example: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  int ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 2 ); 
   root =>   BEGIN ; 
   root =*>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 3 ); 
   root =*>   SELECT   COUNT ( * )  FROM  t; 
     COUNT   
    -------  
         1  
   ( 1   row )    
 This table clearly contains two rows:  2  and
 3 . Yet while the second row was visible to
 SELECT * , it was invisible to  SELECT COUNT(*) .
Oddly enough, aggregate functions which interacted with the column’s
value, like  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE a < 5 ,
sometimes observed correct state. In other circumstances,
 SELECT  queries appeared to create duplicate copies of rows
within the transaction, causing each query to observe more and more
rows. These behaviors ( #48 ) no
longer appeared in version 1.1.18.11.rc-1. 
  3.8.4  Double Trouble (#89) 
 ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-9 would occasionally return duplicate copies
of a single row, even though the row had a primary key which ought to
have ensured uniqueness. For example, take  this
append test , in which a read of key  10  returned two
rows, rather than one. 
      [{ :val   "1,2,5,10" } 
    { :val   "1,2,5,10" }]    
 We no longer observed duplicate rows ( #89 ) in
1.1.18.11.rc-18. 
  3.8.5  Updates to Zero Values
Sometimes Fail Silently (#91) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.18.4, a transaction could set all rows in a table
to some value, receive an acknowledgement that every row had been
updated, then read the table to find that some rows still had their
previous values. This bug seemed to hinge on inserting rows with a
special “zero” value:  0  for integers,  0.0  for
floats, and  ''  for various kinds of string columns. For
example: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  INT ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 0 ); 
   root =>   BEGIN ; 
   root =*>   UPDATE  t  SET  a  =   1 ; 
   root =*>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 0 ); 
   root =*>   UPDATE  t  SET  a  =   2 ; 
    UPDATE   2  
   root =*>   SELECT  t.a  FROM  t; 
    a 
    ---  
     2  
     0  
   ( 2   rows )    
 ParticleDB claimed that it updated all two rows in this table, but
showed the original value of  0  for one of them. This issue
( #91 )
seemed fixed by 1.1.18.11.rc-9.2. 
  3.8.6  Tables With a
 TEXT  Primary Key Are Mostly Invisible (#41) 
 Version 1.1.18.9 fixed several safety issues, but also introduced new
ones. For example, tables with a  text  primary key were
mostly invisible to transactions: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a TEXT  PRIMARY   KEY ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 'mood' ); 
   root =>   BEGIN ; 
   root =*>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
    a 
    ---  
   ( 0   rows )    
  SELECT ,  UPDATE , and  DELETE 
were all affected. Rows were invisible to a broad variety of predicates,
including  WHERE a LIKE 'moo%'  and
 WHERE a IS NOT NULL . However, rows were still accessible by
primary key: 
      root =*>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  a  =   'mood' ; 
     a 
    ------  
    mood 
   ( 1   row )    
 Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 no longer exhibited these mostly-invisible
tables ( #41 ). 
  3.8.7  A Thousand Tableaus (#38,
#66, #68, #69) 
 Perhaps owing to the single-threaded issues discussed above,
ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9 exhibited frequent, profound
transactional anomalies in essentially every way we could measure. We
routinely observed the loss of committed writes, internal consistency
violations, G1a (Aborted Read), G1b (Intermediate Read), and P4 (Lost
Update). In the  append  workload, successfully appended
values would routinely disappear from later reads of a given key. Our
test suite inferred every kind of cyclic anomaly including G0, G1c,
G-Single, and G2-item, but many of these can be attributed to more basic
issues, like write loss. These issues occurred with a single server and
without faults, and affected every transaction mode, interface, and WAL
mode tested.  8   
 Since we have already discussed single-threaded anomalies at length,
we omit detailed discussions of these issues. By version 1.1.18.11.rc-1,
ParticleDB’s most glaring examples of G1a ( #66 ), G1b
( #38 ),
internal consistency anomalies ( #68 ), write
loss ( #69 ), and so
on were much diminished. 
  3.8.8  G-Single (#73) 
 With versions 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22, we occasionally
observed  G-single , a
violation of Snapshot Isolation, in single nodes without faults. For
example, here are two transactions from  an
 append  test  using transaction mode  occ-v3 
and WAL mode  groupsync : 
   
 
 The top transaction read key  9  and found it did not
exist, then appended  8  to it. The bottom transaction
appended  6  to key  9 . Since every read of key

that the append of  6  happened before the append of

though the bottom must have occurred before the top. This is a similar
phenomenon to P4 (Lost Update), and violates Snapshot Isolation. 
 Similar behavior ( #73 )
occurred in  zero-copy-occ  and 1.1.18.11.rc-22’s
 occ . Orkes is investigating. Following our collaboration,
Orkes reports version 1.1.19-rc.13 no longer exhibits G-Single.

 In version 1.1.18.9, we found that queries for a specific row by a

Large Iced Coffee (#31) 
 Versions 1.1.18.8 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 exhibited perplexing
nondeterministic failures in the  compare  workload. Each

And yet sometimes, rows failed to appear in queries:

reported 1.1.19-rc.13 resolved this issue. 
  3.8.14  Read Skew With
 table-2pl  (#106) 
 With the ParticleDB interface, WAL mode  groupsync , and
 table-2pl , version 1.1.18.11.rc-18 exhibited  G-single 
under normal operation. Here’s  an
example : 
      T1: [[ :r   112   nil ] 
        [ :append   112   1 ] 
        [ :append   103   29 ] 
        [ :append   67   105 ]] 
    
   T2: [[ :r   110  [ 10   14   13   20   16   28   30   33   48   35 ]] 
        [ :r   112  [ 1 ]] 
        [ :r   110  [ 10   14   13   20   16   28   30   33   48   35 ]] 
        [ :r   103  [ 1   4   11   15   17   20   24   25 ]]]    
 The first transaction appended  1  to key  112 
and  29  to key  103 . The second transaction
observed the append to key  112 , but missed the append to
key  103 . Since it observed but also failed to observe
another transaction, this is  A5A (Read Skew) .
Since the first transaction read-write depends on the second, and the
second write-read depends on the first, it is also G-single. Both are
violations of Snapshot Isolation. 
 We no longer observed Read Skew with  table-2pl  ( #106 ) by
version 1.1.18.11.rc-19. 
  3.8.15  Stale Read With
 strict-serializable  (#109) 
 Version 1.1.18.11.rc-18 added a new transaction mode,
 strict-serializable , which may have been renamed to
 serializable  in 1.1.18.11.rc-22.  9  
Strict Serializability (also known as Strong Serializability) guarantees
that all transactions appear to execute in real-time order: if   T  1   completes before   T  2   begins, then   T  1   appears to execute
before   T  2  . However,
this was not true in 1.1.18.11.rc-18. Healthy ParticleDB nodes
infrequently but regularly exhibited  Stale
Read , even with WAL mode  sync . In one of our testing
environments, these anomalies appeared roughly every 300,000
transactions, using Elle’s exponential key distribution and 10
concurrent clients pushing ~80 transactions per second. 
 Stale reads all seemed to share the same structure: a cycle
comprising a real-time, read-write, then write-read edge. Here’s  an
example  involving a single key: 
   
 
 The top transaction appended  66  to key
 22209 , which was read by the middle transaction. After the
middle transaction completed, the bottom transaction began, and read key
 22209  without  66 . This is a violation of
Strong Snapshot Isolation, and therefore Strong Serializability as
well. 
 After the conclusion of our testing work, Orkes reported that version
1.1.19-rc.10 no longer exhibits stale read ( #109 ).

  3.9  With Faults 
 The issues described above occurred in healthy, single-node instances
of ParticleDB. When we introduced faults, new behaviors emerged. 
  3.9.1  Data Loss on WAL Bitflips
(#108) 
 ParticleDB uses checksums to detect corruption or incomplete writes
to its Write-Ahead Log (WAL) files. Sometimes these checks prevented the
server from starting up with corrupt data. In other cases, ParticleDB
would discover that its data files were corrupt, then start up anyway,
serving data to clients. 
 Take  this
 append  test  of 1.1.18.11.rc-18. At 09:25:09 we
introduced two single-bit errors into one of ParticleDB’s
 .wal  files. At 09:25:39 we read key  1754  and
observed a list of 44 elements:

               68   69   70   73   75   79   80 ]] ...

times. When the server came back online at 09:26:07, it logged:

recover_streaming{dir=/opt/particledb/data/wal}:
spanner_wal::segment: checksum mismatch in

2026-07-22T14:26:07.985235Z  WARN ThreadId(01)

While Jepsen has not tested this version, Orkes reports 1.1.19-rc.12

  3.9.2  Total Data Loss With
Simulated Misdirected Reads/Writes (#112) 
 One of our file corruption faults divided a file into four-kilobyte
chunks, then randomly replaced a small fraction of those chunks with
other chunks from the same file. The goal is to simulate  misdirected
reads or writes , a type of silent data corruption that happens in
some storage systems. In 1.1.18.11.rc-22, ParticleDB sometimes responded
to this type of fault by forgetting every table and (apparently)
deleting everything in its WAL file. 
 For example, take  this
test run . At 09:53:56, the test harness shuffled 13 four-kilobyte
chunks of the first  .wal  file around—approximately
one-tenth of the file’s contents. It then killed and restarted the node.
Although this file had hundreds of kilobytes in it, when ParticleDB
started up it logged that there was no data on disk: 
  2026-07-30T14:53:58.715589Z  INFO ThreadId(01)
spanner_exec::engine::context: No data found in
storage — starting fresh  
 At 09:53:58, ParticleDB began throwing
 ERROR: table not found  for every query. No request ever
succeeded after this time. 
 It appears that ParticleDB may have deleted the contents of its WAL
file. A few seconds later, the test found its size was zero bytes, and
the same held true at the end of the test. After we finished testing
Orkes released version 1.1.19-rc.12; they believe it resolves this issue
( #112 ).

  4  Discussion 
 ParticleDB 1.1.4 claimed to be a Postgres-compatible database which
offered Snapshot Isolation with its  occ-v3  and
 zero-copy-occ  transaction modes, Serializability with
 serializable-ssi , and Strong Serializability with
 table-2pl . 
 Instead, we found a library of confusion.  10  
In versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-19, basic functionality like
transactions (#3), prepared statements (#2), and Postgres auth (#1) were
unusably broken. The server spontaneously deadlocked (#27, #71) or
crashed (#81) every few minutes. Integers stood in for booleans (#30,
#50), comparisons to  NULL  threw errors (#13), and you could
assign multiple values to the same column (#5). Large floating-point
numbers quietly became infinite (#56);  Infinity ,
 NaN , and  NULL  arithmetic were broken (#36,
#92, #15, #21); and out-of-range values were improperly stored or
clipped to fit (#32, #11). In ParticleDB,  0.0  was not equal
to  0  (#63), but  0.90...  wasn’t  not 
equal to  5  (#80). Strings allowed too many (#52, #64) and
too few (#55) characters. A  WHERE  clause with
floating-point operations would silently fail to match any rows (#47),
 WHERE 4 = 5  returned rows with primary key  5 
(#18),  WHERE a = 1  matched the row  {a: 2} , and
 WHERE TRUE  matched nothing (#35). Null (#8) and unique (#9)
constraints did nothing, and primary keys could be duplicated (#29),
null (#57), or both. Primary keys failed to conflict with rows that did
exist (#90), and conflicted with rows that didn’t (#82). Joins returned
incorrect column names (#54), coerced values to strings (#76), failed to
return rows (#59), and confused similarly-named columns (#77). It was
impossible to delete rows within a transaction (#26, #45), rows with
integers set to floats (#23), or with floats set to integers (#84), or
those containing  NaN s (#78), or fixed-width strings
(#74).  11   Rows from dropped tables could
re-emerge in mangled forms (#46). Columns could be set to values of the
wrong type, silently altering or corrupting data (#7). Inserts ignored
provided columns, creating rows best described as “deeply cursed”
(#16).  12   Updates could create new, shambolic
rows where none existed (#24, #25). Strings sometimes turned into
eight-bit integers (#37), and primary keys occasionally became
 NULL  (#72). Aborted transactions could commit, or fail with
their effects still visible (#43). Queries sometimes missed (#48),
duplicated (#89), or returned the wrong (#67) rows. Tables with a
 text  primary key were mostly invisible (#41). Special
values were sometimes inalterable (#91). Entire columns occasionally
vanished for no obvious reason (#65). Uncontended statements on freshly
created tables observed nonsensical results or conflicted (apparently)
with themselves (#31). Each transaction and WAL mode exhibited
essentially every transactional anomaly our tests could detect: write
loss, internal consistency violations, G0, G1a, G1b, G1c, G-Single,
G-nonadjacent, P4, A5A, G2, and real-time variants thereof (#38, #66,
#68, #69, #73, #70, #96, #109, #110, etc.). 
 These behaviors occurred in single-node instances of ParticleDB,
without fault injection, often with just a single client. When we killed
ParticleDB, it allowed internal anomalies, P4 (Lost Update), and
G-single (#107), even with the new  serializable  transaction
mode. Corruption or truncation of WAL files caused partial data loss
(#108). Simulating misdirected reads or writes could cause total data
loss (#112). 
 As we concluded our engagement, version 1.1.18.11.rc-22 had just
become available. It abandoned the  table-2pl  and
 serializable-ssi  transaction modes in favor of
 fast ,  occ , and  serializable ,
which were intended to offer no consistency, Snapshot Isolation, and
Strong Serializability, respectively. While 1.1.18.11.rc-22 was
significantly safer than 1.1.4, we were still finding new issues. The
default  occ  mode regularly lost data in normal operation
(#110). The new  serializable  mode appeared significantly
safer, but still allowed stale read (#109) in normal operation, and with
process kills, sometimes failed to read extant rows. This led to
internal anomalies, Lost Update, and more (#107). 
 After we finished testing, Orkes updated ParticleDB’s documentation
to claim that every transaction mode discussed here was  “experimental” .
This claim is difficult to support. To the best of Jepsen’s knowledge,
none of the ParticleDB documentation  described
these modes  as experimental or unsupported during our engagement.
Orkes’ unpublished operator guide did describe one mode,
 serializable-occ , as an “internal A/B variant… do not use
for correctness runs”. We considered that mode experimental and omitted
it from this report. However, the others had no such caveats. 
 Orkes  appears to
have reworked  ParticleDB’s approach to consistency. It now supports
the standard SQL isolation level statements for
 READ COMMITTED ,  REPEATABLE READ  (meaning
Snapshot Isolation), and  SERIALIZABLE . The
 --txn-mode  option is gone, and a new
 --concurrency-control  setting has  none ,
 optimistic , and  strict-optimistic  options. The
 documentation
claims  that every mode discussed in this report has been removed
from version 1.1.19-rc.13. However, it goes on to say that
 occ-v3  and  strict-serializable  were “earlier
names” of the “optimistic engine” and “strict serializable mode”,
respectively. It is not clear whether these modes were removed or simply
renamed. 
 Jepsen has not evaluated versions of ParticleDB after
1.1.18.11.rc-22, and cannot speak to these isolation levels or
concurrency control modes. However, Orkes claims that all issues from
this report have been addressed as of version 1.1.19-rc.13. 
 As always, Jepsen takes an experimental approach to safety
verification: we can prove the presence of bugs, but not their absence.
While we make extensive efforts to find problems, we cannot prove
correctness. 
  4.1  Impact 
 Orkes believes that the issues we found in 1.1.4 were likely due to
an extensive refactor of ParticleDB in spring 2026, and that Orkes and
their customers, who continued to run an earlier version, were likely
unaffected. Near the end of our collaboration we briefly evaluated an
internal build of version 1.0.0. While it exhibited some string and
arithmetic issues, that version did not seem susceptible to most of the
serious safety errors we found in 1.1.4, and passed cursory
 rw  and  append  tests. We tested only a single
node at a time, so we cannot speak to the safety of the replication
system. 
 From May through July 2026, the ParticleDB  download page 
offered users (at least) versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-18.  13   All exhibited serious safety errors
during normal operation. It seems likely that users who ran these
versions of ParticleDB would have lost or corrupted data. In version
1.1.18.11.rc-22, using WAL mode  sync  and transaction mode
 serializable  significantly reduced the frequency and
severity of these issues, but did not prevent internal anomalies or Lost
Update. 
 Given the severity and extent of the safety errors we found, and the
process which produced them, Jepsen recommends users halt further
deployment of ParticleDB and migrate to other databases as soon as
possible. Consider checking and/or rebuilding database state from more
reliable sources, if available. 
  4.2  The Unreasonable Effectiveness
of Generative Testing 
 The  compare  workload generated random schemas and SQL
statements over them, then ran both against ParticleDB and Postgres to
see if they produced equivalent results. This should not have worked.
There are many ways in which two “Postgres-compatible” databases can
legitimately differ, such as floating-point details, which error message
takes precedence, or the order of unsorted results. The space of SQL
queries is large and difficult to cover. Many queries trivially return
equivalent results (e.g.  SELECT ... WHERE FALSE ) and
therefore tell us little information. We can test only sequential
behavior, which is easy for a database’s standard test suite to
check. 
 Nevertheless, roughly  two
thousand lines  of generative tests found a wealth of bugs in
ParticleDB, and unlike Jepsen’s typical workloads, the examples
generated were usually easy to reproduce. ParticleDB offered a good deal
of “low-hanging fruit” that should have been caught by example-based
tests—but the  compare  workload also found more subtle
errors. For example, the fact that  0.90...  was apparently
equal to  5  hinged on a high-precision floating-point
literal. Inspired by this success, we extracted part of the ParticleDB
SQL generator into  a shared
library  so it could be used in other tests, like the new
 internal-sim  workload. 
 Jepsen has traditionally focused on thorough analysis of a small set
of carefully chosen transactions. This is partly because checking (e.g.)
Serializability in general  is NP-complete ,
and also because we assume that if transactions of (e.g.) reads and
appends work correctly on strings, so will other operations on other
datatypes. Our intuition is that the “hard part” is in the concurrency
control mechanism, and sequential datatype behavior is generally covered
by existing tests. This was not the case in ParticleDB. We’ve expanded
Jepsen’s  list-append  and  rw  tests to use
alternate encodings and transaction structures, in an attempt to cover
more codepaths. This revealed new bugs in ParticleDB, and we hope it
will in other databases too. 
 Unfortunately,  compare  became less useful as Orkes fixed
major bugs and left smaller incompatibilities in place. For example,
Postgres checks unique constraints when updating each row of a table,
but ParticleDB only checks after all have been updated. This means that
a statement like  UPDATE bools SET x = NOT x  can swap the
values of  TRUE  and  FALSE  in ParticleDB without
violating a unique constraint. Toward the end of our engagement, the
 compare  test generally hit these minor inconsistencies
early, then spent most of its time searching for minimal cases of
them—potentially missing more serious bugs. 
  4.3  Quality Assurance 
 Orkes said they ran Jepsen’s existing Postgres test harness to find
and resolve issues in ParticleDB prior to this work. However, that same
test harness failed immediately when run against ParticleDB 1.1.4. Orkes
also stated they tested ParticleDB with  SQLancer , which generates far more
complex queries than the ones we tested. It is therefore perplexing that
nearly every feature we tested exhibited glaring errors, and that our
findings seemed to come as a surprise. 
 Most databases have a test suite which exercises at least basic
examples of each feature, and it is customary to run those tests before
release, if not continuously. Where were those tests for ParticleDB? How
does one add support for  NOT NULL  constraints without a
test which tries to insert at least one  NULL  value? What
development process adds a  CHARACTER(10)  type without
trying to write a string of (e.g.) five characters? 
 Our findings suggest structural deficiencies in the ParticleDB QA
process. Perhaps tests were not run prior to release. Perhaps the test
suite was run, but failed to exercise basic functionality. Perhaps
engineers entrusted Large Language Models with the work of testing. 
 Jepsen recommends that Orkes (and all database vendors!) build and
exercise an automated test suite for their database. This suite should
include at least simple, example-based tests covering important database
features. These tests should fail when the feature is unimplemented or
malformed, and pass when it is complete. Observing these failures is an
important part of the development process: it  validates that the
test measures something . Tests should be run at least once before
each release, and results disseminated to the team. Afterwards consider
more sophisticated generative tests, establishing adversarial QA and
implementation teams, and subtly breaking safety mechanisms to determine
whether the tests are still effective. 
  4.4  Documentation 
 ParticleDB’s website gave the appearance of a mature database
project. It made strong claims: a general-purpose OLTP/OLAP SQL database
a thousand times faster than PostgreSQL, “formally verified” by a TLA+
proof, multiple APIs, and client libraries in thirteen languages. It
offered a variety of deployment options and extensive documentation on
database features and operations. 
 On closer inspection, that documentation was riddled with omissions,
inconsistencies, and confabulations. The TLA+ proof was not published,
and in any event did not prevent disaster—perhaps it was incorrect,
formalized the wrong properties, or did not describe the system as
built. Safety-critical configuration settings like the transaction mode
were described in vague terms, like  “safe
under concurrency” . The documentation for the  Java
client library  referred to non-existent dependency coordinates and
seemed to make up class and package names which were nowhere to be found
in the library itself. The quickstart and client examples made up a
variety of default usernames for ParticleDB, all of which were wrong.
The stored procedure documentation even fabricated an  imaginary
email address  for the author of this report. In Orkes’ unpublished
operator guide, the descriptions of transaction modes omitted basic
phenomena like  G0  and confused  G1a  (Aborted
Read) with  G1c 
(Circular Information Flow). The Snapshot Isolation modes made no
mention of  G-single  or
the  other
boundary phenomena  proscribed by Snapshot Isolation, and
non-real-time models made no mention of the real-time phenomena they
allowed, like Stale Read.  14   
 Technical writing is important work that requires skill and care.
Jepsen recommends that Orkes work with a human technical writer to
rewrite ParticleDB’s documentation, with an eye toward concisely and
accurately communicating intended behavior and the guarantees users
should expect. 
 Jepsen is no stranger to working with early software projects, and
there is nothing intrinsically wrong with offering buggy or badly broken
software. However, it would be polite for a maintainer aware of serious
safety issues to display a prominent warning on the website. One might
place a large red box on the download page which reads, “This project is
in early development and is not suitable for production”, or more
bluntly, “This software has lost data and will do so again”. Orkes
should clearly explain the general status of ParticleDB, and advise
users of specific known safety issues. 
 Orkes has since published  a
release history  which describes versions 1.1.4 through
1.1.18.11.rc-22 as “unsupported pre-release builds”. It is not clear how
users would have understood versions like 1.1.4 or 1.1.18.9 as
“pre-release”. Pre-release software generally has a version number
beginning with 0, or including “rc”, “alpha”, etc. The documentation  did
not describe these versions  as pre-release or experimental at the
time. Indeed, the  Docker
install page  told users how to deploy these versions “for
production”. 
  4.5  LLM Tradeoffs 
 Large Language Models enable small teams to produce software and
documentation of staggering scope and complexity in a remarkably short
time. Five years ago, writing a distributed SQL database of this scope
might have taken hundreds of person-years.  15  
With LLM assistance, a handful of engineers at Orkes were able to
produce a highly sophisticated database system. 
 However, our work on ParticleDB (and other databases) suggests there
are serious tradeoffs to relying on LLMs. Quality suffered: ParticleDB
was a fractal of correctness errors. LLM tooling repeatedly claimed that
bugs had been fixed when, in fact, they had not. ParticleDB also seemed
more difficult to understand than typical databases. As with most Jepsen
analyses, Orkes engineers offered detailed explanations of the causes
and resolutions of the bugs we found in  Conductor .
However, Orkes seemed unable to explain the causes or resolutions of
nearly every issue we found in ParticleDB. New builds simply
materialized, sans changelogs, each hopefully containing a slew of
improvements. Why did ParticleDB sometimes turn strings into integers?
Why did it stop in 1.1.18.11.rc-1? Perhaps no one knows. With LLMs,  perhaps
no one needs to . 
 More broadly, the use of LLMs erodes trust in documentation, in
software, and in the organizations which produce them. Perhaps engineers
will begin to treat any new software project with suspicion—the signals
we used to rely on as markers of a mature system are now easier to
counterfeit. 
 Where correctness matters—and surely it ought to matter for
databases!—our industry must acknowledge and mitigate these tradeoffs.  16   In the age of LLMs, what can
maintainers do to ensure correct software and accurate documentation?
Having done that work, how can they demonstrate its quality to
users? 
  4.6  Future Work 
 As of 1.1.18.11.rc-22, our  append  and  rw 
workloads were still finding anomalies in every transaction mode. We
recommend further testing as development continues. The
 compare  workload also revealed a number of minor
compatibility bugs which we have not discussed here. These small
differences could mask more serious errors. Bringing ParticleDB into
closer alignment with Postgres could help the  compare 
workload reveal them. 
 Toward the end of our collaboration we tested ParticleDB’s on-disk
format, and found that corruption in WAL files could cause data loss.
The variety of error messages we found suggests that there might be
multiple paths to data loss—further tests should stress on-disk storage
more thoroughly. Furthermore, in almost all our tests ParticleDB wrote
only WAL files, and stored its tables entirely in memory. We recommend
Orkes add a configuration option to reduce the thresholds for on-disk
storage, so that future tests can exercise those codepaths. 
 The ParticleDB client has a number of slow network timeouts we did
not know how to change. These timeouts could conceal safety errors by
preventing the test from observing the database during a critical
moment. We worked around this by using the Postgres client (whose
timeouts are configurable), but we recommend testing the ParticleDB
client with lower timeouts as well. 
 ParticleDB offered a massive set of features, and we only tested a
small portion of them. The SQL specification and Postgres’ dialect of it
are astonishingly complex languages, and we used only a small fraction
of their syntax and vocabulary. We also did not evaluate ParticleDB’s
Redis or HTTP APIs, temporal or geospatial queries, materialized views,
vector search, or multi-tenant features. The replication system remains
to be tested. 
 Orkes is now adding stored procedures to ParticleDB. These
user-defined functions, called   Particles  ,
are written in Python or Rust and executed by the database server. Both
Rust and Python have large surface areas, and executing user-provided
binaries in a database environment seems like an exciting opportunity.
Our  previous
work  with stored procedures suggests this feature is worth further
investigation. 
 ParticleDB claimed to be “1087x faster than PostgreSQL”. In our tests
ParticleDB was nowhere near this fast, and over the course of an hour we
observed a linear decline in throughput and a significant increase in
median latencies—even over small datasets. Once ParticleDB reaches a
baseline level of correctness, revisiting performance benchmarks could
be worthwhile.
