  5  Appendix A 
 This appendix contains additional results involving types, syntax,
numbers, and strings. 
  5.1  Type Safety and Syntax 
 We found several incompatibilities or bugs involving static or
dynamic type safety, or behaviors that would normally have been caught
by static analysis of a query, such as referring to a nonexistent
column. These issues occurred with a single server, single client, and
no faults. 
  5.1.1  Ordering By an Unused Column
(#33) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8, you could order an aggregate
query’s results by a column that was not used in the aggregate
expressions or  GROUP BY  clause. This seems like a minor
issue, but it does differ from Postgres behavior: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  boolean ); 
   root =>   SELECT   COUNT ( * )  FROM  t 
           WHERE  (a  >=  a)  ORDER   BY  a  LIMIT   0 ; 
     COUNT  
    -------  
   ( 0   rows )    
 Orkes resolved this issue ( #33 ) in
1.1.18.9. 
  5.1.2  Comparison of Incomparable
Types (#6) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, you could write predicates for
 UPDATE  and  DELETE  which made equality
comparisons between columns of different types. 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a text, b  smallint ); 
   root =>   DELETE   FROM  t  WHERE  (a  =  b); 
    DELETE   0     
 In Postgres, this threw an error like
 ERROR: operator does not exist: text = smallint . You could
compare strings to boolean columns, or literal values like
 false . ParticleDB allowed these comparisons on empty
tables, but would throw an error if a record was present. In 1.1.18.6,
ParticleDB threw an error for empty tables as well ( #6 ). 
  5.1.3  Cannot Compare Decimals to
Floats (#94) 
 ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-9.2 forgot how to compare large decimal
literals to 64-bit floating-point numbers: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  double   precision ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 1.0 ); 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  
          (( 0   /   1.2002480805601245E26 )  >=  t.a); 
   ERROR: arrow  compute : Invalid argument error: 
          Invalid comparison operation: 
          Decimal256( 76 ,  44 )  >=  Float64    
 This issue ( #94 ) no
longer appeared by version 1.1.18.11.rc-18. 
  5.1.4  Filter Predicates Reject
 NULL  (#12) 
 SQL has three boolean values:  TRUE ,  FALSE ,
and  NULL , which represents an unknown value. In ParticleDB
1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, predicates in SELECT, UPDATE, etc. could not
evaluate to  NULL , even though the SQL specification states
that search conditions are boolean expressions. For example: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  boolean ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( TRUE ); 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE   NULL ; 
   ERROR:   filter  predicate must produce  boolean  
   result    
 In Postgres this would return an empty relation, because
 NULL  is not  TRUE . In 1.1.18.6,
 NULL  predicates evaluated correctly ( #12 ). 
  5.1.5  Cannot Compare Values to
 NULL  (#13) 
 Per the ANSI SQL standard, the value of comparing anything to
 NULL  is  unknown , represented as the boolean value
 NULL . However, ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 sometimes
refused to evaluate predicates which compared (e.g.) integers to
 NULL . 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  int ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 2 ), ( NULL ); 
   root =>   UPDATE  t  SET  a  =   5   WHERE  a  =   NULL ; 
   ERROR:  arrow  compute : Invalid argument error: 
   Invalid comparison operation: Int64  ==   Null     
 Oddly enough, ParticleDB correctly evaluated statements like
 SELECT 1 = NULL . Version 1.1.18.6 correctly compared
integers to  NULL  ( #13 ). 
  5.1.6  Boolean Logic on Integers
(#30) 
 The SQL standard is clear that boolean logical expressions like
 A AND B  evaluate to booleans. In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through
1.1.18.8, they could sometimes be other things: 
      root =>   SELECT   TRUE   AND   5 ;      #  =>   5  
   root =>   SELECT   5   AND   TRUE ;      #  =>   5  
   root =>   SELECT   5   AND   FALSE ;     #  =>   FALSE  
   root =>   SELECT   5   OR   TRUE ;       #  =>   TRUE  
   root =>   SELECT   'cat'   OR   FALSE ;  #  =>   'cat'  
   root =>   SELECT   'cat'   OR   'dog' ; 
   ERROR:   OR  requires  boolean  operands 
   root =>   SELECT   1   AND   2 ; 
   ERROR:   AND  conjunct must produce  boolean     
 By version 1.1.18.9, ParticleDB rejected boolean expressions over
non-boolean literals ( #30 ). 
  5.1.7  More Boolean/Integer
Confusion (#50) 
 ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 disallowed boolean logic on integer literals, but
allowed it on columns. 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  int ); 
   root =>   UPDATE  t  SET  a  =   NOT  a; 
    UPDATE   0     
 Likewise, you could do integer operations on booleans: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  boolean ); 
   root =>   UPDATE  t  SET  a  =  ((a  +  a)  IS   NULL ) 
           WHERE  a; 
    UPDATE   0     
 Orkes seems to have resolved this issue ( #50 ) by
version 1.1.18.11.rc-8. 
  5.1.8  Multiple Assignment to a
Single Column (#5) 
 The SQL standard specifies that an  UPDATE  statement
shall not contain a column name more than once. However, ParticleDB
1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4 allowed an  UPDATE  to assign multiple
values to the same column. It seemed to pick the last value,
lexically. 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  boolean , b  boolean ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a, b) 
           VALUES  ( FALSE ,  FALSE ); 
   root =>   UPDATE  t  SET  a  =   FALSE , a  =   TRUE ; 
    UPDATE   1     
 In Postgres this returned an error:
 multiple assignments to same column "a" . However,
ParticleDB applied the update, producing: 
      root =>   select   *   from  t; 
    a | b 
    ---+---  
    t | f 
   ( 1   row )    
 By version 1.1.18.6, multiple updates to the same column threw an
error ( #5 ). 
  5.1.9  Predicates Referring to
Non-Existent Columns (#10) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17, predicates in
 SELECT ,  UPDATE , and  DELETE 
statements could refer to columns which did not exist. For example: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  INT ); 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  b  =   1 ; 
    a 
    ---  
   ( 0   rows )    
 In Postgres, expressions like this would throw
 ERROR: column "b" does not exist . By version 1.1.18.6,
ParticleDB did as well ( #10 ). 
  5.2  Arithmetic 
 ParticleDB often performed arithmetic in unexpected ways. These
issues occurred with a single server, single client, and no faults. 
  5.2.1  No Large Integer Literals
(#14) 
 Postgres allows large integer literals like
 9223372036854775808  ( 2 63  ). However, ParticleDB 1.1.4
through 1.1.17 refused these literals, throwing an
 invalid integer  error: 
      root =>   SELECT   9223372036854775808 ; 
   ERROR:  invalid  integer :  9223372036854775808     
 In ParticleDB 1.1.18.6, one could write large integer literals ( #14 ). 
  5.2.2  To Infinity, and Beyond
(#85) 
 ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 gained an exponentiation operator  ^ ,
but could not apply it to  Infinity . 
       SELECT   'Infinity'  ^  2 ;    
 This returned  'Infinity'  in Postgres, but threw
 operator does not exist: ^ requires numeric operands  in
ParticleDB. By 1.1.18.11.rc-9, Orkes seems to have resolved this issue
( #85 ). 
  5.2.3   -1 ^ 0 = -1 
(#49) 
 ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 considered  -1 ^ 0  to be equal to
 -1 , rather than  1 . 
      root =>   select   -  1  ^  0 ; 
     -  1  
    ----  
     -  1  
   ( 1   row )    
 By version 1.1.18.11.rc-3, it correctly returned  1  ( #49 ). 
  5.2.4 
 1.0 + 1E-39 = 1.0  (#88) 
 ParticleDB 1.1.18.6 gained support for literals using scientific
notation—for example, using  3E12  to denote  3 × 10 12  . However, the parser
turned this notation into floating-point values, rather than precise
decimals, as in Postgres. This resulted in floating-point errors: 
      root =>   SELECT   1.0   +   1E-39   =   1.0 ; 
    ? column ? 
    ----------  
    t 
   ( 1   row )    
 This issue ( #88 ) was
fixed by 1.1.18.11.rc-9.2. 
  5.2.5  What’s the Largest Number You
Can Think Of? (#56) 
 ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-1 silently converted large
floating-point literals to infinities: 
      root =>   SELECT   -  4.56E500 ; 
    ? column ? 
    -----------  
     - Infinity 
   ( 1   row )    
 By version 1.1.18.11.rc-3, ParticleDB threw an error like
 "4.56E500" is out of range for type double precision  ( #56 ). 
  5.2.6  Exponent Underflow (#61) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.18.9, the exponent operator checked to see if its
arguments would cause an overflow, but did not check for underflow: 
      root=> SELECT  200  ^  200  ;  
   ERROR:  value out of range: overflow 
   root=> SELECT - 200  ^ - 200  ;  
    - 0  
   ---- 
      0  
   ( 1  row)    
 By version 1.1.18.11.rc-3, ParticleDB threw an underflow error ( #61 ). 
  5.2.7  Division by Integer Zero
(#34) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8, you could divide floating-point
values by integer  0  and receive  Infinity ,
rather than a  division by zero  error, as in Postgres. 
      root =>   SELECT   1.0   /   0 ; 
     1   /   0  
    -------  
      inf 
   ( 1   row )    
 ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 returned an error instead ( #34 ). 
  5.2.8  Modulo Operator Cannot Handle
Floats (#51) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.18.9, the modulo operator  %  threw an
internal error when either argument was a floating-point number. 
      root =>   SELECT   3.0  %  2 ; 
   ERROR:  internal error    
 The  MOD  function was unaffected, and this issue ( #51 ) was
fixed by 1.1.18.11.rc-1. 
  5.2.9  Broken  NaN 
Arithmetic (#36) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8, arithmetic operations on
 NaN  would throw an error: 
      root =>   SELECT   'NaN'   -   1.0 ; 
   ERROR:  arrow  compute : Invalid argument error: 
   Invalid arithmetic operation: Utf8  -  Float64    
 By 1.1.18.9, arithmetic on  NaN  correctly returned
 NaN  ( #36 ). 
  5.2.10  Broken  NULL 
Arithmetic (#92) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-9.2, arithmetic operations involving
sufficiently detailed scientific notation literals and  NULL 
threw internal errors: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  int ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( NULL ); 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  
          (t.a  +   2.0000000000000000E-23 )  IS   NULL ; 
   ERROR:  internal error: called `Option: :unwrap ()` 
            on  a `None`  value  ( at  crates /  exec  /.. .)    
 This error ( #92 ) no
longer appeared in version 1.1.18.11.rc-18. 
  5.2.11  UPDATE Can’t Do Math
(#60) 
 ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 introduced a new bug which rendered it unable to
do arithmetic operations on floating-point columns in an
 UPDATE  statement.  17   For example: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  real ); 
    CREATE   TABLE  
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 1.2 ); 
    INSERT   0   1  
   root =>   UPDATE  t  SET  a  =  a  +   1 ; 
   ERROR:  internal error    
 In 1.1.18.11.rc-1, ParticleDB was (mostly) able to add numbers ( #60 ). 
  5.2.12  Same Precision For
 real  and  double precision  (#32) 
 Per the SQL standard, the  double precision  data type
should have a greater precision than  real . In Postgres,
 real  and  double precision  are ( usually ) a
32-bit and 64-bit floating-point value, respectively. In ParticleDB,
both appear to be implemented as 64-bit floats. 
       CREATE   TABLE  t (a  real   NOT   NULL ); 
    INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 4.134917993754883E8 ); 
    SELECT   *   FROM  t  ORDER   BY  a; 
     ParticleDB: 
       [{ :a   4.134917993754883E8 }] 
     Postgres: 
       [{ :a   4.134918E8 }]    
 Version 1.1.18.9 seemed to introduce a 32-bit  real  type
( #32 ). 
  5.2.13  Big Integers (#11) 
 Similarly, integer fields (e.g.  smallint ,
 int , …) in ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 allowed values
much bigger than their typical ranges. It appeared as if ParticleDB
internally represented all integer types as signed 64-bit integers. For
example, here are four values too big to fit in a Postgres
 smallint : 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  smallint ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 32768 ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a) 
           VALUES  ( 9223372036854775807 ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a) 
           VALUES  ( 9223372036854775808 ); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( 1.234E40 ); 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
             a 
    ---------------------  
                   32768  
     9223372036854775807  
                       0  
     9223372036854775807  
   ( 5   rows )    
 In Postgres  smallint  is a 16-bit integer; each
 INSERT  would throw
 ERROR: smallint out of range . However, ParticleDB stored
each of these values with varying results. It preserved 32,768 and  2 63  − 1  (the largest
two’s-complement signed 64-bit integer).  2 63   and larger integers were
silently converted to  0 . On the other hand, the large
floating-point number was clipped to  2 63  − 1 . 
 Similar behavior occurred with  int  and
 bigint . ParticleDB 1.1.18.6 rejected oversized integers ( #11 ). 
  5.2.14  Dividing Nearby Numbers
(#86) 
 ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 through 1.1.18.11.rc-8 struggled to divide
floating-point numbers, often throwing  Numeric out of range 
when asked to divide values which were well within the range of a 32-bit
float. For example: 
      root =>   SELECT   81938.0   /   81937.82012987136848 ; 
   ERROR:   numeric   out   of   range     
 This value should be approximately  1.00000219 . Orkes
seems to have resolved this issue ( #86 ) in
version 1.1.18.11.rc-9. 
  5.2.15  Floating-Point Errors in
Integer Values (#87) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-8, adding small
numbers (e.g.  0.1 ) to large integer columns could cause
their values to change by surprising amounts. For example: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a bigint); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  
          ( 58950791971326900 ); 
   root =>   UPDATE  t  SET  a  =  (a  +   1E-1 ); 
   root =>   SELECT  a  FROM  t; 
            a 
    -------------------  
     58950791971326896     
 Adding  0.1  to this column actually subtracted
 4 . Jepsen suspects this bug ( #87 ) was
caused by performing these operations on floating-point values (which
cannot represent all integers) then coercing the result back to the
nearest integer value. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-9 seems to have fixed
this. 
  5.2.16  Floats Are Not Equal to
Quoted Forms (#19) 
 Postgres considers floating-point numbers like  0.0  to be
equal to their quoted representations—this is useful because some
floating-point values, like  'Infinity' , are written with
quotes. ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4 thought otherwise: 
       
   root =>   SELECT   0.0   =   '0.0' ; 
     false  
    -------  
    f 
   ( 1   row )    
 This issue ( #19 )
appeared resolved as of version 1.1.18.6. 
  5.2.17  Floats Are Not Equal to
Integers (#63) 
 In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.6, floats were not equal to
integers. 
      root =>   SELECT   0.0   =   0 ; 
     false  
    -------  
    f 
   ( 1   row )    
 By version 1.1.18.8, reasonably-sized integers were equal to their
floating-point counterparts ( #63 ). 
  5.2.18  Double Precision Floats
Appear Equal to Almost All Integers (#80) 
 Version 1.1.18.9 introduced a new bug which made predicates like
 WHERE x != y  fail to match for most double precision floats
in (-1.0, 1.0). It was as if all small floats were equal to all nonzero
integers. If we took a table containing a few integers, and performed
some simple queries that should return every row… 
       CREATE   TABLE  t (a  int ); 
    INSERT   INTO  t (a)  VALUES  ( -  1 ), ( 0 ), ( 5 ); 
    SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  a  !=  ( 0.1  ^  25 ); 
    SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  
   a  !=   0.90000000000000000000000000000000000000 ; 
    SELECT   *   FROM  t  WHERE  
   a  !=   -  0.34656654456890453890613489540952456545 ;    
 All three of these queries returned only a single row,
 0 —implying that  0.90...  was equal to
 -1  and  5 . The only exception seemed to be
 WHERE a != 0.0... , which returned no rows at all. This was
also wrong, but somewhat less so. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-9 seems to have
resolved the matter ( #80 ). 
  5.3  Strings 
 We found several problems with strings in ParticleDB, including
datatypes that could hold more or fewer characters than they ought, and
improper sort orders. These issues occurred with a single server, single
client, and no faults. 
  5.3.1   CHARACTER(n) 
Allows More Than  n  Characters (#64, #52) 
 The SQL standard defines a variety of fixed-width string datatypes
like  character(3) , which holds a string of exactly three
characters. Unfortunately, ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4 were happy
to store much larger strings in those columns.  18   
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a  character ( 3 )); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t 
           VALUES  ( 'large language model' ); 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
             a 
    ----------------------  
    large language model 
   ( 1   row )    
 Version 1.1.18.6 rejected inserts and updates of too-long string
literals ( #64 ), but
appeared to perform these checks only at runtime; one could still say
 UPDATE t SET a = 'far too long'  so long as it matched no
rows ( #52 ). That
issue was resolved in version 1.1.18.11.rc-3. 
  5.3.2   CHARACTER(n) 
Allows Fewer Than  n  Characters (#55) 
 While 1.1.18.6 rejected strings that were too large for a fixed-width
string column, 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9 also allowed strings that were too
short. Normally, shorter strings are padded with spaces to the specified
length, but in ParticleDB, short strings were returned unchanged. 
       CREATE   TABLE  t (a  character ( 16 )); 
    INSERT   INTO  t  VALUES  ( 'smol' ); 
    SELECT   *   FROM  t; 
      ->  { :a   "smol" }    
 This should have returned  "smol            " , with
padding spaces. ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 seems to have resolved the
issue ( #55 ). 
  5.3.3  Default Text Collation
(#22) 
 On a platform with  LC_COLLATE = en_US.UTF-8 , Postgres
uses that collation by default. ParticleDB appeared to collate strings
differently. Sorting via queries like
 SELECT ... ORDER BY name , or comparisons like
 'a' < 'B' , returned different results between the two
databases. Where Postgres considered  'a' < 'B' ,
ParticleDB believed the opposite. 
 Experiments suggest ParticleDB sorted by Unicode code point order,
rather than the  Unicode
Collation Algorithm  (UCA) with the locale’s collation rules. It may
have been compatible with  ucs_basic ,  C , or
 pg_c_utf8 . ParticleDB version 1.1.18.9 seemed to choose a
default collation more like UCA ( #22 ). 
  5.3.4  Mis-Sorted Text (#42,
#93) 
 Throughout our collaboration ParticleDB struggled to sort things.
Versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 accepted an explicit
 unicode  text collation, then ignored it: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (b text COLLATE unicode); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t (b) 
           VALUES  ( 'a' ), ( 'b' ), ( 'B' ); 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  ORDER   BY  b; 
    b 
    ---  
    B 
    a 
    b 
   ( 3   rows )    
 In Postgres’  unicode  collation, letters like
 a  and  A  sort similarly, despite being of
different cases. This query would have returned
 'a', 'b', 'B' . 
 ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 sorted English uppercase and lowercase letters
correctly, but only for some queries—adding a  LIMIT  clause
to a  SELECT  statement would cause it to revert to the old
sort order. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 resolved that, but sorted other
characters, like punctuation, oddly: 
      root =>   CREATE   TABLE  t (a text COLLATE unicode); 
   root =>   INSERT   INTO  t  VALUES  
          ( '_aa' ), ( 'a' ), ( 'aa' ), ( 'aaa' ); 
   root =>   SELECT   *   FROM  t  ORDER   BY  a  ASC ; 
     a 
    -----  
    a 
    _aa 
    aa 
    aaa 
   ( 4   rows )    
 Different sorting of whitespace and punctuation ( #42 ) seemed
better in version 1.1.18.11.rc-7, but reappeared in 1.1.18.11.rc-9
through 1.1.18.11.rc-19 ( #93 ). Text
sorting seemed improved in 1.1.18.11.rc-21. 
 
 
 
  There are also a handful of unrelated databases called
ParticleDB, mainly used in particle physics—for example, the  database
of particles  used in  the Belle II
physics experiment , or  this
one  at the Large Hadron Collider. ↩︎   
  The Particles feature was not available during our work;
we focus on ParticleDB’s SQL interfaces. ↩︎   
  One envisions a world of meta-recursive database
documentation in the style of  Raymond Smullyan . “One page of
the documentation always tells the truth. Another tells only lies…” ↩︎   
  Presumably  Two-Phase
Locking . ↩︎   
   With apologies to Deleuze & Guattari —Thus,
the tuple without fields is opposed less to fields as such than to the
organization of the fields insofar as it composes a row.  Le n-uplet
sans composants  is not a deleted tuple but a living tuple all the
more alive and teeming once it has blown apart the client and its memory
model. Structs commingling on the heap.  Self-modifying
Perl . The full tuple without fields is a tuple populated by
multiplicities. ↩︎   
  Madred, 2369. ↩︎   
   Cameron, 1986 . ↩︎   
  He explained that the Database—the Denormalized, the
Data Lakehouse, the giant Monad—is a table without tuples.  Le
tableau sans n-uplets  is permeated by unformed, unstable values, by
dataflows in all directions, by free JSON or nomadic singletons, by mad
or transitory transactions. That, however, was not the question at hand.
For there simultaneously occurs upon the database a very important,
inevitable phenomenon that is beneficial in many respects and
unfortunate in many others: schematization. Schemata are Layers, Belts.
They consist of giving form to values, of imprisoning arrays or locking
singletons into systems of record and replication, of producing upon the
body of the database records large and small and organizing them into
normal aggregates. Schemata are acts of capture, they are like “black
holes” or occlusions striving to seize whatever comes within their
reach. They operate by coding and normalization upon the database; they
proceed simultaneously by code and normality. The Schemata are
judgements of God; schematization in general is the entire system of the
judgement of God (but the database, or the table without tuples,
constantly eludes that judgement, flees and becomes deschematized,
destructured, denormalized). ↩︎   
  To make matters more confusing,
 serializable  in versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-11.2
was (depending on which version of the binary you asked) either an alias
for  table-2pl  or possibly  occ-v3 . In
1.1.18.11.rc-22,  serializable  reappeared as a new Strong
Serializable transaction mode, also based on Serializable Snapshot
Isolation (SSI), but perhaps not the  serializable-ssi  level
present in earlier builds, which was distinct from
 strict-serializable . ↩︎   
  De Lioncourt, 1793, presaging Borges, 1941. ↩︎   
  See ANSI/NISO Z39.19-2005 (R2010) “Celestial Emporium
of Benevolent Knowledge” for the full taxonomy of database records: rows
belonging to the DBA, tombstones, those which from afar look like JSON,
et cetera, etc. ↩︎   
  Jepsen encourages the consistency model research
community to come up with more official terms for this. ↩︎   
  Running  particledb --version  might not
return the actual version. For instance, 1.1.16 through 1.1.18.11.rc-18
all identified themselves as “spanner 1.1.16”. ↩︎   
  Barthes can rejoice: not only is the author dead, but
they were never alive to begin with. Nothing is true, everything is
permitted. ↩︎   
  MongoDB had  962
employees in 2018 , and Cockroach Labs had  400
in 2022 . Databases are hard! ↩︎   
  Or perhaps not. Not every application requires perfect
correctness. Vibrational Database Management Systems might be fine, at
least some of the time. ↩︎   
   Mattel,
1992 . ↩︎   
  Danielewski, 2000. ↩︎

             Abstract: Whether models trained on different modalities converge to the same representation of the world is central to AI. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) conjectures that they do as they scale, but without a proof it offers neither a guarantee nor a recipe. We turn the hypothesis into a theorem. First, we prove a \emph{Platonic Representation Theorem}: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) trained separately on any number of modalities learn the same representation up to one rotation whenever their positive pairs are two observations of one scene--\emph{good views}--and their misalignment is bounded otherwise. Second, we show that next-token prediction is a JEPA with \emph{bad views}, parts of a single document, which explains why language models align with vision only through scale. Third, we validate the theory from 145k captions to the texts of 940M web images, and uncover a scaling law of alignment that predicts unseen runs within seed noise. Good views need 42 times fewer training samples than next-token prediction on the same corpus to reach the same alignment, and a 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns with DINOv2 and CLIP's image encoders better than every language model we evaluated, up to 72B parameters, and than CLIP's text encoder: next-token prediction is a remarkably inefficient route to platonic representations. As a showcase, one rotation turns separately trained encoders into an image captioner (CIDEr .838 on COCO). Even that rotation needs no pair: on the latest pair-free benchmark, our text JEPA beats every zero-shot accuracy reported with language models up to 8B parameters, e.g., 64\% against at most 56\% top-5 on ImageNet-100. Positive views, and not scale alone, are thus the lever to build platonic representations.

Website | Blog | Documentation | imgproxy Pro

--- [imgproxy](https://imgproxy.net) is a fast and secure standalone server for resizing, processing, and converting images. The guiding principles behind imgproxy are speed, security, and simplicity. imgproxy is able to quickly and easily resize, process, and optimize images on the fly, and it's well-equipped to handle a large amount of image processing. imgproxy is a drop-in replacement for all the image processing code inside your web application (such as using image processing libraries or calling command-line tools). With imgproxy, you don’t need to repeatedly re-prepare images to fit your design every time it changes, as imgproxy does this on demand. To get an even better introduction and to dive deeper into the nitty-gritty details, check out this article by Evil Martians: [imgproxy: Resize your images instantly and securely](https://evilmartians.com/chronicles/introducing-imgproxy) ![imgproxy demo](assets/demo.gif) *Photo by [Joshua Patton](https://unsplash.com/@joshuapat)* ## ✨ Features imgproxy is packed with features to the brim to cover all your image processing needs: | Feature | imgproxy OSS | [imgproxy Pro](https://imgproxy.net/#pro) | |---|---|---| | Image formats | Basic formats: JPEG, PNG, GIF, WebP, AVIF, JPEG XL, [and more](https://docs.imgproxy.net/image_formats_support) | Preview generation for video, PDF, and Photoshop documents | | Processing | Resizing, cropping, rotating, watermarking, filters | Getting image info, advanced watermarking, color adjustment | | Optimization | Color profile and metadata stripping, PNG quantization | Advanced compression settings, GIF to MP4 conversion, SVG minification | | Smart features | Simple smart cropping, auto-quality by file size | Object detection, advanced smart cropping, auto-quality by SSIM, best format selection | Check out the [full feature list](https://imgproxy.net/features) for more details. ## 🛠️ How it works imgproxy works as a standalone HTTP server. You provide it with a source image URL and a set of processing options via a specially crafted URL, and imgproxy fetches the image, processes it according to your specifications, and serves the resulting image back to you. You can use imgproxy URLs directly in your HTML, CSS, or JavaScript code, just like you would with any other image URL. This way, imgproxy offloads all the image processing work from your application. The only thing your application needs to do is to [generate imgproxy URLs](https://docs.imgproxy.net/usage/processing) with the desired processing options.

## ⚖️ Main principles ### Simplicity > Keep it simple, stupid! We believe that software should be simple yet powerful. If your grandma can't get it up and running, you should make it simpler. That's why we designed imgproxy to be ready to use in a couple of minutes with minimal configuration. Check out the [Getting Started guide](https://docs.imgproxy.net/getting_started) to see how easy it is. > No code is better than no code. We believe in the single responsibility principle. If something can be done better outside of imgproxy, we won't reinvent the wheel. As a couple of examples: * HTTPS support sounds like a must-have feature for a web server. However, imgproxy will live behind a CDN, a load balancer, or a reverse proxy in a production environment anyway, so there is no need to implement HTTPS support inside imgproxy itself. * Rounding image corners or applying masks sounds useful, but doing this with CSS is way easier and more flexible. ### Speed We strive to tune every little piece of imgproxy to make it as fast as possible. imgproxy takes advantage of probably the most efficient image processing library out there – [libvips](https://github.com/libvips/libvips). It’s scary fast and comes with a very low memory footprint. Our extensive experience with libvips has enabled us to optimize our image-processing pipeline to its maximum. You can take a look at some benchmarking results and compare imgproxy with some well-known alternatives in our [benchmark report](https://imgproxy.net/blog/image-processing-servers-benchmark/). ### Security Image processing is a wide attack surface. That's why we treat security very seriously. imgproxy offers several security measures that enable you to strike the optimal balance between security and usability for your specific use case. For example: * imgproxy supports signing image URLs to prevent abusing your image processing server for denial-of-service attacks or simply using it for the attacker's own needs. * imgproxy checks the image type before fully downloading it to prevent unwanted resource consumption. * imgproxy checks the real image dimensions before decoding it to prevent so-called "image bombs", like those described in [this doc](https://www.bamsoftware.com/hacks/deflate.html). * imgproxy supports authorization by HTTP header to prevent direct access to it, bypassing your CDN or caching server. * imgproxy allows restricting image sources, maximum image file size, processing options, etc. Check out our documentation for more details on [security features](https://docs.imgproxy.net/configuration/options#security). ## 🚀 Getting started The easiest and recommended way to run imgproxy is using Docker. It's just a matter of a single command: ```bash docker run -p 8080:8080 -it ghcr.io/imgproxy/imgproxy:latest ``` That's it! imgproxy is ready to accept [image processing requests](https://docs.imgproxy.net/usage/processing) at `http://localhost:8080`. Check out the [Getting Started guide](https://docs.imgproxy.net/getting_started) for a step-by-step tutorial on how to get your first image processed with imgproxy. ## 📚 Documentation You can find the full documentation at [docs.imgproxy.net](https://docs.imgproxy.net). ## 💙 Supporting imgproxy imgproxy is not a side project; it's what we do for a living. We work hard to make it better every day. If you find imgproxy useful and want to support its development, here are some ways you can do that: * **imgproxy Pro subscription.** [imgproxy Pro](https://imgproxy.net/#pro) is a more feature-rich version of imgproxy. By subscribing to imgproxy Pro, you not only support the development of imgproxy but also get access to advanced features and priority support. * **Sponsorship.** If you don't need the Pro features but still want to support the project, consider sponsoring us on [GitHub Sponsors](https://github.com/sponsors/imgproxy). * **Spread the word.** If you like imgproxy, give it a shoutout. We don't spend much on marketing, and imgproxy's popularity is primarily a result of our valued users sharing it on social media and blogs. ## 🙏 Special thanks Many thanks to: * [Evil Martians](https://evilmartians.com) for providing a steady launch pad for imgproxy * [Roman Shamin](https://github.com/romashamin) for the awesome logo and website design * [John Cupitt](https://github.com/jcupitt) and [Kleis Auke Wolthuizen](https://github.com/kleisauke) for developing [libvips](https://github.com/libvips/libvips) and for helping me optimize its usage with imgproxy * [Kirill Kuznetsov](https://github.com/dragonsmith) for the [Helm chart](https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy-helm) ## 📄 License imgproxy is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. See [LICENSE](https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/blob/master/LICENSE) for the full license text. ## ⚠️ Security Contact To report a security vulnerability, please contact us at security@imgproxy.net. We will coordinate the fix and disclosure.

          Fixed 
 
 Fixed possible BMP loader heap buffer overflow. 
 (pro) Fixed SVG minifier failure on empty comments. 
 SVG sanitizator now strips dangerous href values in all the elements. 
 Fixed truncation of source image downloads when origins returned gzip-compressed responses. 
 The  Content-Length  header was previously ignored for S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, and Swift responses.

          Version 2.19.7 Release Notes 
 Compatible with OpenSearch and OpenSearch Dashboards version 2.19.7 
 Enhancements 
 
 Add upper bound for the hot_threads  snapshots  parameter with configurable  monitor.jvm.hot_threads.max_snapshots  cluster setting ( #23144 ) 
 Add  search.query.max_query_nesting_depth  setting to limit query_string parenthesis nesting depth and prevent StackOverflowError ( #22854 ) 
 Cap  max_determinized_states  in completion suggester regex and fuzzy options to prevent heap exhaustion ( #22925 ) 
 Disable Mustache partial template resolution in search templates ( #22440 ) 
 Reject out-of-range WLM node threshold updates at validation time ( #22678 ) 
 
 Bug Fixes 
 
 Fix unbounded recursion in JSON and binary deserialization that could cause StackOverflowError ( #22427 ) 
 Strengthen scroll_id validation to prevent OOM from crafted scroll IDs with oversized counts ( #22401 ) 
 Validate  base_path  in fs repository to prevent path traversal outside configured  path.repo  directories ( #22381 ) 
 Fix handling of unsupported zstd HTTP content encoding in netty4 and nio transports ( #23324 ) 
 
 Maintenance 
 
 Bump Jackson to 2.18.9 and Log4j to 2.25.5 ( #22990 ) 
 Bump Bouncy Castle bc-fips to 2.1.3 ( #23284 ) 
 Update Netty to 4.1.139.Final ( #22692 ,  #23003 ,  #23251 ) 
 Update bundled JDK to 21.0.12.1+1 ( #22572 ,  #22809 )

          Version 3.9.0 Release Notes 
 Compatible with OpenSearch and OpenSearch Dashboards version 3.9.0 
 Features 
 
 Add DELETE task API for removing stored completed task results ( #21727 ) 
 Add deployment drain and finish APIs for zero-downtime node deployments ( #21448 ) 
 Add adaptive per-action concurrency limiting module with Vegas, Gradient2, and AIMD algorithms ( #22312 ) 
 Add virtual thread-per-task executor support to ThreadPool ( #22485 ) 
 Add extensible payload decoder framework for pull-based ingestion ( #22364 ) 
 Add plugin SPI for dynamic field-type inference and dynamic-template types ( #22607 ) 
 Add pluggable PrimaryOperationPolicy to EngineConfig for cross-cluster replication ( #22886 ) 
 Add object-store fencing token for remote store primary term validation ( #22774 ) 
 Auto-restore remote store primaries on node loss when no valid copy survives ( #22904 ) 
 Add FieldDomain metadata producer API for enhanced can_match shard pruning ( #22483 ) 
 Add intra-segment search support for histogram, auto_date_histogram, and range aggregations ( #22531 ) 
 Add MPP-style distributed join and aggregation execution for the analytics engine ( #21844 ) 
 
 Enhancements 
 
 Add  cluster.blocks.read.auto_release  setting to prevent unconditional auto-release of user-set index read blocks ( #22610 ) 
 Add cluster-level remote-store flush settings for uncommitted segments ( #22935 ) 
 Restore size-based periodic flush on remote-store shards ( #22865 ) 
 Apply  index.periodic_flush_interval  changes to running shards dynamically ( #22991 ) 
 Use ordinals instead of byte values for bucket keys in multi-term aggregations ( #21033 ) 
 Optimize bucket counting and tracking in LongKeyedBucketOrds with O(1) lookups ( #22450 ) 
 Speed up reading history operations from Lucene via sequential stored-fields reader ( #22603 ) 
 Use  prefixQuery  to speed up  wildcardQuery  and  regexpQuery  for wildcard field type ( #22510 ) 
 Preserve  constant_score  through filtered aliases to maintain Lucene no-scoring fast path ( #22776 ) 
 Promote lowest-version replica on document-replication failover to prevent stuck replicas during rolling upgrades ( #22783 ) 
 Avoid cancellation checks on every  advance()  call for posting enums to reduce CPU overhead ( #22856 ) 
 Avoid quadratic identifier scan when removing snapshots ( #22968 ) 
 Stream translog parts instead of buffering the whole file for upload ( #23015 ) 
 Change tiered cache default partition count to 16 for improved hit rates on high-core instances ( #23032 ) 
 Bound Arrow native memory pools when  node.native_memory.limit  is unknown ( #22762 ) 
 Lower default  arrow.flight.channel.outbound_buffer_threshold  from 64 MB to 512 KB ( #22697 ) 
 Deprecate  RestHighLevelClient  in favor of  opensearch-java  client ( #23008 ) 
 Remove Jackson 2.x dependencies from OpenSearch core ( #22704 ) 
 Remove legacy client benchmark and noop API plugin modules ( #21839 ) 
 Preserve routing in  Translog.Delete  for CDC-based replication ( #22584 ) 
 Exempt server-injected preferences from strict weighted routing check and scope them per index ( #22571 ) 
 Reject out-of-range WLM node threshold updates at validation time ( #22649 ) 
 Return HTTP 400 for  too_many_clauses  and  too_many_nested_clauses  errors ( #21725 ) 
 Refactor  forPattern  if-else chains to switch on  FormatNames  enum for O(1) dispatch ( #22568 ) 
 Drain active streams before closing Flight channel to prevent spurious leak errors ( #22642 ) 
 Skip stream connections to nodes without a stream address in mixed-version clusters ( #22810 ) 
 Remove duplicate native memory limit setting from  NodeDuressSettings  ( #22620 ) 
 
 Bug Fixes 
 
 Fix  ApproximateScoreQuery.equals  for query cache correctness ( #22737 ) 
 Fix NPE on collapse with  search_after  sort using  _score  or  _doc  ( #23029 ) 
 Fix NPE when creating a match-all composable index template without an inline template ( #22421 ) 
 Fix NPE in routing table checksum when a shard has no primary ( #22723 ) 
 Fix  ClassCastException  in mixed rollup and raw index  avg  aggregation reduce ( #22658 ) 
 Fix parent-bucket scoping in  StreamStringTermsAggregator  for nested terms aggregations ( #21447 ) 
 Fix cache entries removed before promotion being retained indefinitely ( #22662 ) 
 Fix stale fielddata retention by invalidating exact key on reader close ( #22491 ) 
 Use point-in-time key snapshot for fielddata cache cleanup to prevent missed entries ( #22499 ) 
 Invalidate exact bitset filter cache keys on reader close ( #22498 ) 
 Make  ICache   keys()  iteration safe under concurrent mutation ( #22542 ) 
 Fix stranded snapshot markers on publish failure with bounded retry ( #22518 ) 
 Fix OpenSearch process not exiting when startup fails due to  StartupException  ( #22259 )

# OpenDeepWiki [中文](README.zh-CN.md) | [English](README.md)

AI-driven repository knowledge base with docs, chat, and MCP

OpenDeepWiki turns Git repositories, ZIP archives, and local directories into searchable knowledge bases. It generates structured repository docs, serves them through a public Next.js site, and reuses the same indexed content for chat, embed, and MCP workflows. Enterprise support and pricing: [docs.opendeep.wiki/pricing](https://docs.opendeep.wiki/pricing) ## What OpenDeepWiki Ships Today - Import repository sources from Git URLs, uploaded ZIP archives, or approved local directories. - Generate README summaries, project overviews, wiki catalogs, document content, multi-language translations, mind maps, and optional Graphify artifacts. - Publish public repository docs on SEO-friendly routes such as `/{owner}/{repo}`, `/{owner}/{repo}/mindmap`, and `/{owner}/{repo}/graphify`. - Expose repository knowledge through repository-scoped MCP endpoints, the built-in chat assistant, embedded chat APIs, and share links. - Manage repositories, users, roles, departments, API keys, AI providers/models, skills, MCP providers, and GitHub App imports from the admin console. - Run background workers for repository processing, translation, mind map generation, Graphify artifacts, and scheduled incremental updates. - Support incoming chat/webhook channels for Feishu, QQ, WeChat, and Slack. ## Architecture At A Glance | Layer | Current implementation | | --- | --- | | Backend | ASP.NET Core on .NET 10, MiniApis, background workers | | AI orchestration | `Microsoft.Agents.AI`, prompt assets under `src/OpenDeepWiki/prompts`, provider/model binding from settings | | Frontend | Next.js 16, React 19, App Router | | Database | SQLite or PostgreSQL | | Repo processing | `LibGit2Sharp`, ZIP/local-directory ingestion, incremental update pipeline | | Visualization | Mermaid mind maps plus optional `graphifyy` artifacts | | Deployment | Docker Compose, Makefile, optional Sealos deployment | ## Quick Start With Docker ### Prerequisites - Docker with Compose support - At least one LLM API key compatible with your chosen provider ### 1. Clone the repository ```bash git clone https://github.com/AIDotNet/OpenDeepWiki.git cd OpenDeepWiki ``` ### 2. Edit `compose.yaml` At minimum, set a real JWT secret and your AI credentials: ```yaml services: opendeepwiki: environment: - JWT_SECRET_KEY= - CHAT_API_KEY=your-chat-api-key - ENDPOINT=https://api.openai.com/v1 - CHAT_REQUEST_TYPE=OpenAI - WIKI_CATALOG_MODEL=gpt-4o - WIKI_CATALOG_ENDPOINT=https://api.openai.com/v1 - WIKI_CATALOG_API_KEY=your-catalog-api-key - WIKI_CATALOG_REQUEST_TYPE=OpenAI - WIKI_CONTENT_MODEL=gpt-4o - WIKI_CONTENT_ENDPOINT=https://api.openai.com/v1 - WIKI_CONTENT_API_KEY=your-content-api-key - WIKI_CONTENT_REQUEST_TYPE=OpenAI - WIKI_LANGUAGES=en,zh,zh-tw,ja,ko,es,fr,de,pt-br,pl,ru,ar - WIKI_PARALLEL_COUNT=5 ``` Notes: - `CHAT_*`, `WIKI_CATALOG_*`, and `WIKI_CONTENT_*` can point to the same provider. - Translation is optional. If `WIKI_TRANSLATION_*` is not set, translation falls back to the content-generation provider/model. - `compose.yaml` uses `Database__Type=sqlite` and `ConnectionStrings__Default=Data Source=/data/opendeepwiki.db` by default. ### 3. Start the stack ```bash docker compose up -d --build ``` Or use the Makefile shortcuts: ```bash make build make up ``` ### 4. Open the app - Web UI: [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000) - Backend health: [http://localhost:8080/health](http://localhost:8080/health) On a fresh database, the seeded admin account is: - Email: `admin@routin.ai` - Password: `Admin@123` Change the default JWT secret and admin password before any real deployment. ## PostgreSQL Instead Of SQLite The current runtime code supports `sqlite` and `postgresql`. To boot the bundled PostgreSQL stack: ```bash docker compose -f compose.pgsql.yaml up -d --build ``` If you prefer your own database, configure either of these equivalent pairs: ```yaml - Database__Type=postgresql - ConnectionStrings__Default=Host=your-host;Port=5432;Database=opendeepwiki;Username=postgres;Password=secret ``` or ```yaml - DB_TYPE=postgresql - CONNECTION_STRING=Host=your-host;Port=5432;Database=opendeepwiki;Username=postgres;Password=secret ``` ## Local Development ### Backend ```bash dotnet restore OpenDeepWiki.sln dotnet build OpenDeepWiki.sln dotnet run --project src/OpenDeepWiki/OpenDeepWiki.csproj ``` Useful local endpoints: - Backend API: [http://localhost:5265](http://localhost:5265) with the default `http` launch profile, or the URL printed by ASP.NET Core - Health: [http://localhost:5265/health](http://localhost:5265/health) - OpenAPI/Scalar: [http://localhost:5265/v1/scalar](http://localhost:5265/v1/scalar) when running in `Development` ### Web app Set the backend proxy first. The web app reads `API_PROXY_URL` from the environment, `web/.env.local`, or `web/.env`. ```bash cd web npm install echo API_PROXY_URL=http://localhost:5265 > .env.local npm run dev ``` ### Docs app (optional) ```bash cd docs npm install npm run dev ``` ### Tests and lint ```bash dotnet test tests/OpenDeepWiki.Tests/OpenDeepWiki.Tests.csproj cd web && npm test cd web && npm run lint ``` Common Makefile shortcuts: ```bash make dev make down make logs make test make build-arm make build-amd ``` ## Repository Processing Flow ```mermaid graph LR A["Git / ZIP / Local directory"] --> B["Prepare workspace"] B --> C["Analyze tree and existing repo context"] C --> D["Generate README, overview, and wiki catalog"] D --> E["Generate document content"] E --> F["Translation / mind map / Graphify / incremental workers"] F --> G["Public docs, chat, embed, and MCP"] ``` In practice, the main runtime path looks like this: 1. Normalize the repository source and prepare a workspace under `REPOSITORIES_DIRECTORY`. 2. Build or refresh repository metadata, branch/language state, and processing logs. 3. Generate documentation catalogs and document content with the configured AI provider/model bindings. 4. Queue follow-up work such as translation, mind map generation, Graphify artifacts, and incremental updates. 5. Serve the final repository knowledge through the public web app, admin tooling, chat APIs, and MCP endpoints. ## MCP Usage OpenDeepWiki registers official MCP endpoints at: - `/api/mcp` - `/api/mcp/{owner}/{repo}` You can scope the repository either by path or query string. Example: ```json { "mcpServers": { "OpenDeepWiki": { "url": "http://localhost:8080/api/mcp/AIDotNet/OpenDeepWiki" } } } ``` Query-based alternative: ```text http://localhost:8080/api/mcp?owner=AIDotNet&name=OpenDeepWiki ``` Optional: - Set `MCP_ENABLED=false` to disable MCP endpoints. - Set `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` and `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` if you want protected-resource MCP OAuth support. ## Optional Graphify Configuration The backend Docker image already installs `graphifyy`. To enable Graphify artifact generation, configure one of the optional provider groups already present in `compose.yaml`, such as: - `GRAPHIFY_BACKEND` - `GRAPHIFY_MODEL` - `GRAPHIFY_OPENAI_BASE_URL` - `GRAPHIFY_OPENAI_API_KEY` - `OPENAI_BASE_URL` / `OPENAI_API_KEY` - `OLLAMA_BASE_URL` / `OLLAMA_MODEL` ## Repository Layout - `src/OpenDeepWiki/`: ASP.NET Core entry point, endpoints, workers, AI/repository/chat/MCP services - `src/OpenDeepWiki.Entities/`: domain entities - `src/OpenDeepWiki.EFCore/`: shared EF Core model and context contract - `src/EFCore/OpenDeepWiki.Sqlite/`: SQLite provider - `src/EFCore/OpenDeepWiki.Postgresql/`: PostgreSQL provider - `web/`: public docs site and admin UI built with Next.js - `docs/`: separate documentation app - `tests/OpenDeepWiki.Tests/`: xUnit and FsCheck tests - `scripts/`: deployment and helper scripts ## Deployment Notes - Sealos: [One-click deployment guide](scripts/sealos/README.zh-CN.md) - Backend container definition: `src/OpenDeepWiki/Dockerfile` - Frontend container definition: `web/Dockerfile` ## Community - Discord: [join us](https://discord.gg/Y3fvpnGVwt) - Feishu QR code: ![Feishu](/img/feishu.png) ![WeChat](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/cb346569-2635-4038-a5cd-1c14485da7b2) ## License This project is licensed under the MIT License. See [LICENSE](./LICENSE) for details. ## Star History [![Star History Chart](https://star-history.dera.page/svg?repos=AIDotNet/OpenDeepWiki&type=Date)](https://star-history.dera.page/#AIDotNet/OpenDeepWiki&type=date)

readme:vercel-labs/agent-desktop.text:
# agent-desktop Computer use for AI agents: read and operate desktop apps through the OS accessibility tree.

A CLI and C library for macOS, Windows and Linux. A snapshot returns JSON with a ref for every element an agent can act on. The agent acts on a ref and snapshots again to check, with no pixel matching; the loop stays in your agent. On macOS, CLI calls reuse a private command host for each snapshot namespace and binary build. It retains native accessibility objects so a removed row cannot silently resolve to a surviving row with the same identifier. The host exits after 15 idle minutes. `TMPDIR` must be owned by the current user with mode `0700`; the standard macOS per-user temporary directory satisfies this requirement. Headless calls still prohibit foreground activation and synthesized input. Snapshots, clipboard reads, screenshots, command output and debug artifacts can contain private desktop content. Keep them out of public logs and uploads. The optional [JEV helper](skills/jev-desktop/SKILL.md) sends screen descriptions to a configured model provider; it is separate from the native CLI. See [privacy and data handling](docs/faq.md#what-data-can-contain-private-information). ## Installation Install on macOS, Windows or Linux with npm: ```bash npm install -g agent-desktop agent-desktop version ``` Bun, Yarn and pnpm can install the same package. It includes native binaries and platform helpers for x64 and ARM64. For direct execution without a JavaScript launcher, download the matching native archive from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop/releases) and keep its helper beside the executable. Official Homebrew and Scoop packages are being submitted; they are not yet available in the default catalogs. The repository no longer maintains a custom Homebrew tap or Scoop bucket. - **macOS** needs Accessibility permission: `agent-desktop permissions --guide`. - **Windows** needs no grant for apps at your terminal's integrity level. - **Linux** needs the user's graphical session with `at-spi2-core`. See [installation and permissions](docs/install.md) for package-manager behavior, release archives, and building from source. ## Quick start Observe, act on a ref, observe again. Any app name from `agent-desktop list-apps` works; Finder is the macOS example. Each command prints one JSON envelope; a trimmed snapshot follows the commands. ```bash agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # interactive elements, each with a ref agent-desktop click @s8f3k2p9:e8 # act on a ref from that snapshot agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # observe again to verify ``` ```json { "version": "2.5", "ok": true, "command": "snapshot", "data": { "app": "Finder", "window": { "id": "w-204749", "title": "Downloads" }, "snapshot_id": "s8f3k2p9", "ref_count": 59, "complete": true, "tree": { "role": "window", "name": "Downloads", "children": [ { "role": "treeitem", "name": "Documents", "ref_id": "@s8f3k2p9:e8", "available_actions": ["Click"] } ] } } } ``` - **Refs belong to their snapshot.** A bare `@e8` is rejected with `INVALID_ARGS`. When the UI changes, an action returns `STALE_REF` or `AMBIGUOUS_TARGET`: take a new snapshot and use its refs. - **Several windows** give `AMBIGUOUS_TARGET`; `snapshot` lists the candidate window ids in `error.details`. Pass one with `--window-id`. - **Dense apps:** map first with `snapshot --skeleton --app Slack -i --compact`, then drill into one region with `snapshot --root @s8f3k2p9:e3 -i --compact`. - **Headless by default.** Ref actions go through the accessibility API without moving the pointer or taking focus. The global `--headed` flag allows physical input. - **PowerShell.** Quote every ref (`'@s8f3k2p9:e8'`), because a bare `@token` is the splatting operator. ## For AI agents The binary carries its own docs, matched to its version: ```bash agent-desktop skills get desktop # the loop, refs, verification and retry rules agent-desktop skills get platform # what differs on the OS you run on agent-desktop --help # flags for one command ``` Install the skill into an agent harness from [skills.sh](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-desktop/agent-desktop): ```bash npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop --skill agent-desktop ``` Or add this to your `AGENTS.md`: ```markdown Use `agent-desktop` to see and operate desktop apps. Before the first use, run `agent-desktop skills get desktop` and `agent-desktop skills get platform`, and follow them. ``` Every command prints one envelope with `ok` and either `data` or `error`. An error carries a `code`, a `disposition` and usually a `suggestion`; retry only when `error.disposition.retry` is `safe`. The contract, error codes and exit codes are in [docs/json-output.md](docs/json-output.md). ## Commands It ships 60 command names, 56 operational commands. The other four (`key-down`, `key-up`, `mouse-down`, `mouse-up`) refuse to run until a daemon can release a held key or button. | Group | Commands | |---|---| | Observe | `snapshot`, `find`, `get`, `is`, `screenshot`, `list-surfaces` | | Act on a ref | `click`, `double-click`, `triple-click`, `right-click`, `type`, `set-value`, `clear`, `focus`, `select`, `toggle`, `check`, `uncheck`, `expand`, `collapse`, `scroll`, `scroll-to` | | Keyboard and mouse | `press`, `hover`, `drag`, `mouse-move`, `mouse-click`, `mouse-wheel`, `key-down`, `key-up`, `mouse-down`, `mouse-up` | | Apps and windows | `launch`, `close-app`, `list-apps`, `list-windows`, `list-displays`, `focus-window`, `resize-window`, `move-window`, `minimize`, `maximize`, `restore`, `open-system-surface` | | Notifications | `list-notifications`, `dismiss-notification`, `dismiss-all-notifications`, `notification-action` | | Clipboard | `clipboard-get`, `clipboard-set`, `clipboard-clear` | | Wait | `wait` | | Sessions | `session`, `trace`, `cursor-overlay` | | System | `status`, `permissions`, `version`, `batch`, `skills` | ## Platform support | | macOS | Windows | Linux | |---|:---:|:---:|:---:| | Accessibility tree | Yes | Yes | Yes (AT-SPI) | | Click / type / keyboard | Yes | Yes | AT-SPI; X11 / GNOME keys | | Mouse input | Yes | Yes | X11, `--headed` | | Screenshot | Yes | Yes | X11 windows; Wayland portal | | Clipboard | Yes | Yes | Yes; Wayland needs `wl-clipboard` | | App & window management | Yes | Yes | Launch/list; X11 window control | | Notifications | Yes | Yes | GNOME Shell | | Shell surfaces (`open-system-surface`) | Planned | Yes | GNOME tray, Action Center | The Windows surface and `launch` notes and the Linux X11 and Wayland notes are in [docs/install.md](docs/install.md#platform-notes). `agent-desktop skills get platform` prints the full capability table for the OS you run on. ## Language bindings Each release also ships `libagent_desktop_ffi` for macOS, Linux and Windows, so a program can call the tool in process instead of starting the CLI for each command. `agent-desktop skills get ffi` covers the entry points, memory ownership and threading rules. ```python import ctypes lib = ctypes.CDLL("./lib/libagent_desktop_ffi.dylib") lib.ad_adapter_create.restype = ctypes.c_void_p lib.ad_adapter_destroy.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p] assert lib.ad_init(6) == 0 # AD_RESULT_OK when the header's AD_ABI_VERSION_MAJOR matches the library adapter = lib.ad_adapter_create() lib.ad_adapter_destroy(adapter) ``` ## Development Each platform adapter builds only on its own OS, so scope cargo to the host's packages. On macOS: ```bash HOST_PKGS=(-p agent-desktop-core -p agent-desktop-macos -p agent-desktop -p agent-desktop-ffi) cargo test "${HOST_PKGS[@]}" cargo clippy "${HOST_PKGS[@]}" --all-targets -- -D warnings ``` On Windows, replace `agent-desktop-macos` in that list with `agent-desktop-windows`; on Linux, with `agent-desktop-linux`. [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) lists every gate. Build from source: [docs/install.md](docs/install.md#from-source). ## Documentation | I want to... | Read | |---|---| | Fix an install problem, grant permissions, verify a download or build from source | [docs/install.md](docs/install.md) | | Parse the JSON envelope, error codes and exit codes | [docs/json-output.md](docs/json-output.md) | | Drive the tool as an AI agent | `agent-desktop skills get desktop` ([skills/agent-desktop/](skills/agent-desktop/)) | | Learn what differs on one OS | [macOS](skills/agent-desktop-macos/), [Windows](skills/agent-desktop-windows/), [Linux](skills/agent-desktop-linux/) | | Call the C library | [skills/agent-desktop-ffi/](skills/agent-desktop-ffi/) | | Look up the vocabulary: refs, snapshots, sessions | [CONCEPTS.md](CONCEPTS.md) | | Contribute and pass the gates | [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) | | Read the engineering rules | [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) | | Learn from past bugs and lessons | [docs/solutions/](docs/solutions/) | | Find answers to common questions | [docs/faq.md](docs/faq.md) | | Report a vulnerability | [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) | | Get help | [SUPPORT.md](SUPPORT.md) | ## License Apache-2.0

           0.10.0  (2026-10-18) 
 ⚠ BREAKING CHANGES 
 
 the release carries these contract changes.
 
 The C ABI major version is 5. The legacy entrypoints that each have an 
*_exact replacement are removed: ad_list_surfaces, ad_surface_list_count, 
ad_surface_list_get, ad_surface_list_free, ad_list_windows, 
ad_window_list_count, ad_window_list_get, ad_window_list_free, 
ad_launch_app, ad_release_window_fields, ad_get_tree, ad_find, ad_is, 
ad_focus_window, ad_window_op, ad_resolve_element and 
ad_execute_ref_action_with_policy, with the AdSurfaceList and AdWindowList 
handles. AdScreenshotKind loses WINDOW (FULL_SCREEN keeps 2 and 1 is 
rejected); AdScreenshotTarget loses pid; AdExactSurfaceInfo is version 2, 
48 bytes, with a trailing unclassified field; the snapshot_id argument of 
ad_execute_by_ref and ad_execute_by_ref_timeout and the 
AdWaitPredicate.snapshot_id field are removed, so AdWaitPredicate is 40 
bytes and AdWaitArgs 104. Consumers must rebuild against the regenerated 
header. 
 Bare  @en  ref input is removed from every ref-taking CLI command, wait 
--element, snapshot --root, find --root, drag --from/--to, batch entries 
and the FFI. Only the snapshot-qualified @<snapshot_id>:eN is accepted, and 
a bare ref fails with INVALID_ARGS. The --snapshot flag that only qualified 
a bare ref is removed from every command, and batch entries carrying a 
snapshot or snapshot_id field are rejected as unknown fields. 
 get --property text no longer returns the same value as --property value. 
It prefers the value for textfield, combobox, listbox, datefield and 
timefield and falls back to the accessible name; every other role prefers 
the accessible name and falls back to the value. Blank strings count as 
absent. Ask for --property value explicitly to keep the previous answer. 
 An io error whose kind is PermissionDenied answers PERM_DENIED instead of 
INTERNAL, in the CLI envelope and in the FFI envelope, return code and 
last error alike. 
 A ref action whose element is gone no longer ends in TIMEOUT. A 
non-retryable resolution failure answers at once; a retryable one keeps 
polling, and if no later resolution succeeds the action answers the 
recorded STALE_REF or AMBIGUOUS_TARGET at the deadline. 
 
 
 
 Features 
 
 support Windows 10 1809+ and Windows Server 2019+ on x64 and ARM64 ( 483a31d )

# Molly [![Test](https://github.com/mollyim/mollyim-android/workflows/Test/badge.svg)](https://github.com/mollyim/mollyim-android/actions) [![Reproducible build](https://github.com/mollyim/mollyim-android/actions/workflows/reprocheck.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/mollyim/mollyim-android/actions/workflows/reprocheck.yml) [![Translation status](https://hosted.weblate.org/widgets/molly-instant-messenger/-/svg-badge.svg)](https://hosted.weblate.org/engage/molly-instant-messenger/?utm_source=widget) [![Financial contributors](https://opencollective.com/mollyim/tiers/badge.svg)](https://opencollective.com/mollyim#category-CONTRIBUTE) [![Cloudsmith](https://img.shields.io/badge/OSS%20hosting%20by-cloudsmith-blue?logo=cloudsmith&style=flat-square)](https://cloudsmith.com) Molly is a hardened version of [Signal](https://github.com/signalapp/Signal-Android) for Android, the fast simple yet secure messaging app by [Signal Foundation](https://signal.org). ## Introduction Back in 2018, Signal allowed the user to set a passphrase to secure the local message database. But this option was removed with the introduction of file-based encryption on Android. Molly brings it back again with additional security features. Molly connects to Signal's servers, so you can chat with your Signal contacts seamlessly. Before signing up, please remember to review the [Signal Terms & Privacy Policy](https://signal.org/legal/). We update Molly every two weeks to include the latest Signal features and fixes. The exceptions are security patches, which are applied as soon as they are available. ## Download You can download the app from GitHub's [Releases](https://github.com/mollyim/mollyim-android/releases/latest) page or install it from the [Molly F-Droid Repo](https://molly.im/fdroid/): [](https://molly.im/fdroid/) There are two versions available: **Molly** or **Molly-FOSS**. Learn the differences [below](#free-and-open-source) and download the right one for you. You can also get **Molly-FOSS** from [Accrescent](https://accrescent.app/): To [verify](https://developer.android.com/studio/command-line/apksigner#usage-verify) the APK, use the following signing certificate fingerprints: ``` SHA-256: 6aa80fdf4a8cc13737cfb434fc0cde486f09cf8fcda21a67bea5ee1ca2700886 SHA-1: 49ce310cdd0c09c8c34eb31a8005c6bf13f5a4f1 ``` ## Features Molly has unique features compared to Signal: - **Data encryption at rest** - Protect your app database with [passphrase encryption](https://github.com/mollyim/mollyim-android/wiki/Data-Encryption-At-Rest) - **Secure RAM wiper** - Securely shred sensitive data from device memory - **Automatic lock** - Lock the app automatically under user-defined conditions - **Multi-device support** - Link multiple devices to a single Signal account, including Android tablets - **UnifiedPush** - Receive push notifications without Google through the UnifiedPush protocol - **Block unknown contacts** - Block messages and calls from unknown senders for security and anti-spam - **Disappearing call history** - Clear call logs together with expiring messages - **Custom backup scheduling** - Set daily or weekly interval and the number of backups to retain - **SOCKS proxy and Tor support** - Tunnel app network traffic via proxy and Orbot - **Debug logs are optional** - Android logging can be disabled Additionally, you will find all the features of Signal, along with some minor tweaks and improvements. ## Free and Open-Source Molly is open-source just like Signal. But Signal depends on proprietary Google software for some features. To support a 100% free and auditable app, Molly comes in two versions: one with proprietary blobs like Signal, and one without. They are called Molly and Molly-FOSS, respectively. You can install the flavor of your choice at any time, and it will replace any previously installed version. The data and settings will be preserved so that you do not have to re-register. ### Feature Comparison Here's how some key features work in different versions of the app: | Feature | Molly-FOSS | Molly | Signal | | --------------------------------- | ---------------- | -------------------- | -------------------- | | Push notifications (1) | ✔ WebSocket
✔ UnifiedPush | ⚠ FCM
✔ WebSocket
✔ UnifiedPush | ⚠ FCM
✔ WebSocket | | Location sharing | ✔ OpenStreetMap | ⚠ Google Maps | ⚠ Google Maps | (1) You might need to turn off system-level battery restrictions for the app to receive messages when the app isn't open. ### UnifiedPush [UnifiedPush](https://unifiedpush.org/) is an open standard for delivering push notifications, offering a privacy-friendly alternative to Google's proprietary FCM service. It allows users to choose their own notification distributor. > [!IMPORTANT] > To use UnifiedPush notifications, you need access to a [MollySocket](https://github.com/mollyim/mollysocket) server to link your Signal account to UnifiedPush. You can either run MollySocket on a server you control (strongly advised) or use a public instance. Currently, UnifiedPush is unavailable for linked devices. ## Compatibility with Signal Molly and Signal apps can be installed on the same device. If you need a second number for messaging, you can register Molly with a different number while keeping Signal active. Any phone number capable of receiving SMS or calls can be used during registration. If you wish to use the same phone number for both Molly and Signal, you must register Molly as a linked device. Registering the same number independently on both apps will result in only the most recently registered app staying active, while the other will go offline. For Signal users looking to switch to Molly without changing the phone number, please refer to the [Migrating From Signal](https://github.com/mollyim/mollyim-android/wiki/Migrating-From-Signal) guide on the wiki. ## Backups Backups are fully compatible. Signal [backups](https://support.signal.org/hc/en-us/articles/360007059752-Backup-and-Restore-Messages) can be restored in Molly, and the other way around, simply by choosing the backup folder and file. However, to import a backup from Signal, you must use a matching or newer version of Molly. ## Feedback - [Submit bugs and feature requests](https://github.com/mollyim/mollyim-android/issues) on GitHub - Join us at [#mollyim:matrix.org](https://matrix.to/#/#mollyim:matrix.org) on Matrix (via space: [#mollyim-space:matrix.org](https://matrix.to/#/#mollyim-space:matrix.org)) - For news, tips, and tricks, follow [@mollyim](https://fosstodon.org/@mollyim) on Mastodon ## Reproducible Builds Molly supports reproducible builds, so that anyone can run the build process to reproduce the same APK as the original release. Please check the guide in the [reproducible-builds](https://github.com/mollyim/mollyim-android/blob/master/reproducible-builds) directory. ## Changelog See the [Changelog](https://github.com/mollyim/mollyim-android/wiki/Changelog) to view recent changes. ## License Licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3 only ([`AGPL-3.0-only`](LICENSE)). See [LEGAL.md](LEGAL.md) for legal and copyright information. ## Acknowledgements Molly is an independent project built on code published by Signal. We are deeply grateful to the Signal contributors for the work we build on. Thanks to the following organizations for supporting the **Molly** project.

            YSK Molly(Signal fork) has not been updated since 3 months and is vulnerable to attacks fixed in mainline Signal
             

         
             submitted  20 hours ago  by
                     
 
             
            beep
         
         
         
         

                    
                edited  20 hours ago  
             
         
             cross-posted from:  https://piefed.world/c/ysk/p/1503393/ysk-molly-signal-fork-has-not-been-updated-since-3-months-and-is-vulnerable-to-attacks-f  
 As of now, Molly  lastest release  was in 31 July (Version v8.19.2-4). 
 It contains vulnerabilities that had been simply fixed in mainline Signal. 
 Take for example the  latest exploit disclosed in October , it has been fixed in Signal 8.27.  1 . Meanwhile Molly remains vulnerable. 
 It’s currently recommended to use mainline Signal and delete Molly till they at least return to updating their app adequately, if they ever will.

             It’s just forward secrecy, not “perfect forward secrecy”, unless you are writing Signal press material. 
  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward_secrecy  
 I feel that such marketing can impart a false sense of security that has bitten Session users many a time. Ask Pete Hegseth, as much as I like to see him faceplant. 
 Not relying on the central server largely removes the need for forward security, since you can get a similar result by creating a new account (with a new private key) on your device as often as you like. It is Signal’s reliance on a fixed identity that complicates the matter of rotating keys. 
 In other words, Signal is not better because it has “perfect forward secrecy”. It is worse because it needs it. 
 Even so, it is such a talking point that Session does intend to implement “perfect forward secrecy”. 
  https://getsession.org/blog/session-protocol-v2  
 As for “store all messages in a blockchain”, I believe that is the alternative to storing them on a central server, as Signal does. They have to be stored  somewhere  until you are online to receive them. If they weren’t, someone would be replying in your stead and complaining that Session does not allow users to receive messages sent while they were offline. Of course the messages are stored encrypted in both cases but only Signal associates them with your metadata.

             Signal-FOSS as alternative 
 I use Signal-FOSS by twinhelix. It exists since many years and upatches are fully automated. 
 They are very simple, deblob signal, remove firebase messages and maps and whatnot. 
 Twinhelix has also added some of the  jw patches , which are nice to have. 
 It does not 
 
 remove donations (which is nice and kinda shit of molly) 
 remove payments with mobilecoin (kinda useless sadly as very few exchanges support it) 
 add blobfree firebase messaging 
 add unifiedpush support 
 support linking multiple phones 
 support encrypting the database 
 probably more 
 
 If you dont need those features, I   highly   recommend it. Signal shipping Google blobs and having no F-Droid repo is very bad and that shouldn’t be supported.  
  See the list of known 3rd party F-Droid repos  
 UnifiedPush issues 
 Note that UnifiedPush needs to be supported by the server. The server then sends the push message to a UnifiedPush  distributor  (like Conversations, ntfy or Sunup). That distributor wakes up the app, which sends you the notification. 
 There is a slight polling delay of about 1 minute, so notifications are delayed. 
 I measured the effect of this by comparing molly with UP and the Signal APK with websocket. On a Pixel 8a running GrapheneOS, 12 hours idle on Wifi, airplane mode on (as the modem uses  by far  the most battery). I configured to send 10 messages to the device using Signals “send later” feature. 
 Websocket used 3% of the batterylife. Thats it. 
 And that effect is only significant for people who rarely use Signal, so the likelyhood of a nerd configuring MollySocket falling into that category is pretty low. If you regularly open Signal, this only delays notification alerts for no benefit. 
 And because the Signal servers   don’t officially support this   you need to either selfhost MollySocket (which would be fine apart from potential update delays, what this post is about) or trust some server operator. MollySocket is registered as another device, so the Signal servers and any standard Signal client would treat it as a trusted device with its own decryption key.  
 Apparently MollySocket discards the key and only receives “you have a message” (and no other metadata? I have obviously not researched this a lot), and I suppose Molly ensures that the device will never get a decryption key either. Still, it increases attack surface for very limited benefit. 
 It would be great if Signal officially supported UP instead of Google FCM.
