# Orkas **An open-source team of AI agents on your desktop — it turns your goals into finished work and keeps it moving.** Orkas is an open-source (MIT), local-first multi-agent desktop app — an AI assistant that works as a team. Tell the **Commander** what you need: it finishes many tasks on its own, and for bigger work it plans the steps and brings in specialist agents along with the coding and personal agents you already use — **Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, OpenClaw and Hermes-Agent** — to work on it together. Orkas is built to keep a project moving, not just answer one prompt. A **project** holds the goal, rules, memory and files, so every new conversation picks up where the last one left off. **To-dos** split the work between people and agents, **Auto-advance** lets the team take on the next to-do by itself, and **scheduled automations** repeat routine work hourly, daily, weekly or monthly. All your data stays on your computer, and finished work comes back for your review — so you can trust Orkas with the ongoing work of your business. **[⬇ Download Orkas for macOS & Windows](https://orkas.ai/download/?source=gh-orkas&entry_point=github_readme&download=1)** — free, with 500 credits for the built-in Orkas model, so you don't need an API key to start. Prefer your own keys? Claude · OpenAI · Gemini · DeepSeek · Kimi · GLM · Qwen · MiniMax · Doubao, or a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint. [![Download for macOS & Windows](https://img.shields.io/badge/Download-macOS%20%26%20Windows-5b57d6?style=for-the-badge)](https://orkas.ai/download/?source=gh-orkas&entry_point=github_readme&download=1) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-green.svg)](./LICENSE) [![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/Orkas-AI/Orkas?style=flat&logo=github&label=Stars&color=yellow)](https://github.com/Orkas-AI/Orkas/stargazers) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/Orkas-AI/Orkas?color=blue)](https://github.com/Orkas-AI/Orkas/releases) [![X: @leochenpm](https://img.shields.io/badge/X-%40leochenpm-black?logo=x)](https://x.com/leochenpm) [![Website: orkas.ai](https://img.shields.io/badge/Website-orkas.ai-5b57d6)](https://orkas.ai/?source=gh-orkas) [English](./README.md) · [简体中文](./README.zh-CN.md) --- https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4f8b16c8-a192-45a4-b19f-80e8d02c3dab ![Orkas desktop — task conversation and deliverables](./resources/app-ui/task-en.png) --- ## What the team delivers - **Videos, voice-overs and images** — VideoStudio, VoiceStudio, ImageStudio - **Research reports, SEO audits and market analysis** — DeepResearcher, SeoGeoAgent, StockAnalyser - **Posts, articles, newsletters and slide decks** — ContentWriter, PptMaker - **Websites, UI and code** — UIDesigner, ProductDeveloper - **Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF files** — OfficeWorker - **E-commerce work** — product research, listings, review analysis, sales analysis and catalog changes, from five e-commerce agents - **Complex work that takes several agents** — the Commander splits it up, hands each part to the right agent and combines the results; for example, market research that becomes a report, a slide deck and a launch video 16 specialists ship with the app, each with its own skills, memory and tools. Browse 30+ agents in the [agent marketplace](https://orkas.ai/views/marketplace/gs/agents/?source=gh-orkas), or describe the role you need and the Commander builds a custom agent for you.
All 16 built-in agents | Area | Agent | What it delivers | | --- | --- | --- | | Research & analysis | **DeepResearcher** | Evidence-grounded research with verified sources, flagged contradictions and an auditable report | | | **SeoGeoAgent** | Give it a URL — technical audit, content quality, Core Web Vitals, AI-answer (GEO) citability, ranked fix list | | | **StockAnalyser** | Equity research, factor screens, backtests and portfolio risk checks, with traceable dashboards | | Content & media | **ContentWriter** | Publish-ready posts, articles, newsletters and case studies from a goal, sources or a rough draft | | | **PptMaker** | Editable, reviewable PPTX decks from a topic, outline or document | | | **ImageStudio** | Posters, covers, social images and infographics | | | **VideoStudio** | Narration, AI presenters, captions and dubbing, highlight clips, localization, and reference-video recreation with your own content and footage | | | **VoiceStudio** | Narration, multi-voice audio, transcripts and subtitles, audio editing and mixing | | | **UIDesigner** | Editable, HTML-first UI from product goals, PRDs, screenshots or Figma material | | Build & office | **ProductDeveloper** | Repo-aware engineering — implement a PRD, fix bugs, refactor, review, with verifiable results | | | **OfficeWorker** | Create, edit, check and deliver Word / Excel / PowerPoint / PDF files, one at a time or in batches | | E-commerce | **ECommerceResearcher** | Product selection by budget, market and sourcing limits — candidates, rejection reasons, validation plans | | | **ECommerceWriter** | Titles, detail pages, FAQs, image copy and video scripts in your brand voice | | | **ECommerceReviewer** | Review and reputation analysis — customer themes, root causes of bad reviews, priorities | | | **ECommerceAnalyzer** | Sales, profit, ads, refunds and inventory from your exports — reconciled metrics and decisions | | | **ECommerceOperator** | Plans catalog, price, promotion and inventory changes; executes only through tools you connect | More on each agent → [orkas.ai/agents](https://orkas.ai/agents/?source=gh-orkas)
### Recreate a reference video with your own content **VideoStudio** can recreate a viral video's narrative structure, visual style and editing pace using your own product, script and footage. Supply a reference video file and your assets: the agent analyzes the hook, information order, visual beats and call to action, then proposes what to preserve and what to replace before production. This works best for motion-graphic explainers, SaaS or app demos, and product ads built from your existing footage. Locally authored text, captions, narration and clips can be revised separately; text baked into AI-generated footage requires changing that footage. > "Use reference.mp4 as a reference for a 30-second vertical promo. Keep its hook, typography and pacing, replace the content with my product and screen recordings, and show me the breakdown and plan first." Start with a video file the agent can read; social-platform share-link downloading is not built in. Exact camera moves, human performances and frame-by-frame matching are not guaranteed. See the [reference-recreation workflow](./resources/builtin/marketplace/agents/79df9cc89f5f/skills/video-craft/references/reference-recreation.md). --- ## Keep the work moving One task is a good start. Orkas is built for the work that keeps going. - **Projects** — goals & rules, memory and files that every conversation in the project starts from, so you never brief from scratch. - **To-dos and Auto-advance** — every project has a to-do list for people and agents; with Auto-advance on, the team picks up the next item on its own and brings finished work back for your review. - **Scheduled automations** — run any task hourly, daily, weekly or monthly. Orkas runs on your computer. From v1.9, each automation catches up its most recent missed run within 12 hours when the computer wakes or Orkas starts. - **Connectors** — Gmail, Google Calendar, Sheets and Drive, Notion, Slack, Shopify, Stripe and many more. By default, Orkas asks before it sends, posts or deletes anything. - **Apps** — describe a tool and Orkas builds it as a local app inside the desktop app. In the packaged app, paid plans can also publish it as a web app with a public link. - **Shared projects** *(packaged app)* — invite a teammate or VA, and give each to-do to a person or an agent. > [!NOTE] > Shared projects, cloud sync and web-app publishing are only in the packaged app — the open-source build doesn't support them yet. To use them, **[download Orkas for macOS & Windows](https://orkas.ai/download/?source=gh-orkas&entry_point=github_readme&download=1)** (free, with 500 credits to start). Voice input also works in the source build. Configure an **Orkas API Key** in **Settings → Models**, then click the microphone beside a composer. Allow microphone access when prompted. Audio is sent to Orkas for recognition and uses the key owner’s Orkas credits. Click again to stop, review the text, and send it yourself. If access was denied, enable the microphone in your system settings. --- ## Run Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, OpenClaw and Hermes-Agent together Orkas runs the CLI agents you already have installed as local sessions, next to its own specialists — the coding agents **Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode**, and the personal agents **OpenClaw and Hermes-Agent**. The Commander hands each one the part it's best at and keeps one plan across all of them, so a single chat can fix the bug, review the change and draft the release note. Open-source tools such as HyperFrames plug in the same way. [Using Claude Code and Codex together →](https://orkas.ai/blog/claude-code-codex-together/?source=gh-orkas) --- ## Why Orkas - **A Commander that plans, delegates and does the rest** — it breaks down goals, picks the right agents, skills, connectors and tools, and handles analysis, writing, research and file work itself when no specialist is a better fit. - **Local-first by design** — conversations, files, knowledge bases and custom agents stay on your disk by default. Cloud sync is optional in the packaged app. With your own keys, model calls go straight from your machine to the provider; the built-in Orkas model runs through Orkas's managed model service. - **Any model, switch any time** — the Commander and built-in agents share one model setting: the built-in Orkas model, your own provider, or a local endpoint. External CLI agents keep their own model settings. - **Agents that get better** — each agent keeps private skills and memory. Background reviews examine new activity when the app is idle and can refine self-assessment, reusable methods and learned skills. - **Open source, no black box** — MIT licensed. Read exactly what Orkas and every agent and skill do. > ⭐ If Orkas is useful to you, a star helps more people find the project. --- ## Download | | Packaged app (recommended) | Run from source | | --- | --- | --- | | Platforms | macOS 12+ (Apple Silicon & Intel), Windows 10+ | macOS, Windows, glibc 2.34+ Linux x64/arm64 | | Account | Sign in — 500 free credits | None | | Models | Built-in Orkas model, or your own keys | Your own keys or a local endpoint | | Also includes | Project collaboration, app publishing, cloud sync, and more | — | | Get it | **[Download Orkas](https://orkas.ai/download/?source=gh-orkas&entry_point=github_readme&download=1)** | [Quick start](#quick-start) | The download link detects your system and starts the right installer. --- ## What people use it for - **Marketing content** — launch videos, product pages, posts and newsletters in your voice. [Content writing](https://orkas.ai/use/content-writing/?source=gh-orkas) · [Videos](https://orkas.ai/use/make-videos/?source=gh-orkas) - **Store operations** — weekly sales briefs, review replies, listings and competitor checks. [E-commerce](https://orkas.ai/use/ecommerce/?source=gh-orkas) - **Research and reports** — sourced reports and decks, on demand or every week. [Research](https://orkas.ai/use/researchers/?source=gh-orkas) · [Data analysis](https://orkas.ai/use/data-analysis/?source=gh-orkas) - **Chat with your documents** — answers grounded in your own files, with citations back to the source passages. [Chat with documents](https://orkas.ai/use/chat-with-documents/?source=gh-orkas) - **Client work** — meeting briefs, monthly client reports and update decks in your template. [Monthly client report template](https://orkas.ai/blog/monthly-client-report-template/?source=gh-orkas) - **Product launch** — landing pages, bug fixes with tests, changelogs and launch posts. [Developers](https://orkas.ai/use/developers/?source=gh-orkas) - **Build an app** — quote calculators, booking forms, internal tools. [Build apps](https://orkas.ai/use/build-apps/?source=gh-orkas) - **Small teams** — one project for people and agents. [Small teams](https://orkas.ai/use/small-teams/?source=gh-orkas) --- ## How Orkas compares | Tool | What it is | How Orkas differs | | --- | --- | --- | | **Claude Code** | Anthropic's agentic coding tool — in the terminal, IDE, desktop and web, built on Claude models. | Not either-or: Orkas runs Claude Code as one of its agents. Around it, Orkas adds a model-agnostic team for the work beyond code — research, content, video and more — with projects, to-dos and automations that keep it moving. [Orkas vs Claude Code →](https://orkas.ai/compare/orkas-vs-claude-code/?source=gh-orkas) | | **Codex** | OpenAI's coding agent — in the terminal, your editor and the cloud. | Not either-or: Orkas runs Codex as one of its agents, next to Claude Code and OpenCode. The Commander can hand the coding to Codex and the review to another agent, then cover the non-code half of a release — docs, launch posts and videos. [Orkas vs Codex →](https://orkas.ai/compare/orkas-vs-codex/?source=gh-orkas) | | **LangChain** | A developer framework/library for building LLM apps and agents — code-first, embedded in your own Python/JS app. | Orkas is a desktop app you direct through chat, not by writing orchestration code. Data stays local by default. | | **CrewAI** | A Python framework for orchestrating role-playing autonomous agents — you define crews and agents in code. | Orkas brings multi-agent orchestration into a desktop app, with projects, to-dos, automations and per-agent self-improvement built in. | | **OpenClaw** | A personal-agent platform with messaging integrations, multi-agent routing and sub-agents. | Orkas provides a desktop workspace for finished deliverables, with built-in specialists and coordination across Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and other CLI agents. OpenClaw can join that workflow as a CLI agent. | | **Hermes-Agent** | Nous Research's self-improving agent — one agent with memory and skills, available as a CLI, a messaging gateway and a desktop app. | Orkas coordinates a team: the Commander directs many specialists and other CLI agents, and Hermes-Agent plugs in as one of them. | **Orkas is for you if** you want a team of agents rather than one assistant, work that keeps moving across days, and your data, keys and agents on your own disk. **Not for you if** you just want a single all-purpose chatbot, or a pure code library to embed in your own app. **Choosing between coding agents?** [Codex vs OpenCode](https://orkas.ai/compare/codex-vs-opencode/?source=gh-orkas) · [Claude Code vs Codex vs OpenCode](https://orkas.ai/compare/claude-code-vs-codex-vs-opencode/?source=gh-orkas) · [Claude Code alternatives](https://orkas.ai/compare/claude-code-alternatives/?source=gh-orkas) **Full side-by-side comparisons →** [vs Claude Code](https://orkas.ai/compare/orkas-vs-claude-code?source=gh-orkas) · [vs Codex](https://orkas.ai/compare/orkas-vs-codex?source=gh-orkas) · [vs Cline](https://orkas.ai/compare/orkas-vs-cline?source=gh-orkas) · [vs LangChain](https://orkas.ai/compare/orkas-vs-langchain?source=gh-orkas) · [vs ChatGPT](https://orkas.ai/compare/orkas-vs-chatgpt?source=gh-orkas) · [vs OpenClaw](https://orkas.ai/compare/orkas-vs-openclaw?source=gh-orkas) · [vs Hermes-Agent](https://orkas.ai/compare/orkas-vs-hermes-agent?source=gh-orkas) --- ## Quick start Want a packaged installer instead? See [Download](#download) above. To run from source — currently the way to run Orkas on Linux: **Requirements**: Node 22.12+ · macOS / Windows 10+ / glibc 2.34+ Linux x64 or arm64. Keep Python 3 and a C/C++ build toolchain available for the uncommon native-module source-build fallback. ```bash git clone https://github.com/Orkas-AI/Orkas.git cd Orkas ./run.sh # macOS / Linux run.cmd # Windows ``` Linux source runs require glibc 2.34+. Alpine and other musl-based distributions are not supported. Local speech transcription downloads and verifies the target-native whisper.cpp runtime and multilingual model during the first source launch. `run.sh` / `run.cmd` installs the locked npm dependency tree and prepares the pinned Python, uv, Node, embedding model (~95 MB), OfficeCLI, FFmpeg, whisper.cpp, and multilingual speech model resources on first launch. Linux startup then verifies the platform-native modules and Whisper runtime under Electron's ABI before opening the app. OCR and Skill-specific Python packages are installed into isolated local environments when those features are first used. First launch creates a workspace under `~/.orkas/` (macOS / Linux) or `:\.orkas\` (Windows). Then open **Settings → AI Providers** to add an API key or OAuth. Native dependency errors: use Node.js 24 LTS (minimum 22.12.0), then run `npm run native:repair` from this checkout. This restores optional packages, repairs SQLite for Electron, prepares bundled Node for isolated image processing, and checks SQL, sqlite-vec and sharp before success. Use `npm run native:check` for a check without installation. See the [native dependency verification script](./scripts/verify-native-dependencies.cjs) for the checks performed. --- ## How it works ### Task routing The Commander handles general work itself and delegates specialist work through three tools: - **`dispatch_to`** runs a named agent and returns its result for continued work. It can wait for the result or run asynchronously and notify the Commander when the task finishes. - **`hand_off_to`** transfers the remaining work to a named agent and ends the current Commander turn. The agent delivers its own reply; an optional continuation lets the Commander resume a broader task afterward. - **`run_worker`** runs an anonymous, isolated sub-task and returns a private result. It does not receive conversation history or a named agent's skills. Named agent tasks and anonymous workers have separate concurrency controls. See the [dispatch implementation](./src/main/features/group_chat/bus.ts) and [execution locks](./src/main/util/locks.ts). ### Context management The runtime budgets context against the selected model's usable input capacity, accounting for prompts, tools and persistent runtime state. Completed dialogue uses a bounded recent-history window; long active tasks use checkpoints to condense earlier process messages while retaining recent work. File reads, file changes and command executions also have structured records that can survive context compaction. See [context budgets](./src/core-agent/src/agent/context-budget.ts), [session history and checkpoints](./src/core-agent/src/agent/session.ts) and [workspace records](./src/core-agent/src/agent/workspace-state.ts). ### Memory and the Library Durable notes keep user preferences, project facts and each agent's reusable knowledge in separate scopes. These notes are distinct from the Library's document index and the stored conversation history. The Library extracts documents into passages and stores a local SQLite vector index. Its embedding model runs on your machine; the `library` tool can list files, search relevant passages and read source content from the global or current-project Library. Earlier conversations are retrieved separately through `chat_history`. See [scoped memory](./src/main/features/memory.ts), [document extraction](./src/main/util/file_to_chunks.ts), [Library tools](./src/main/model/core-agent/kb-tools.ts) and [conversation retrieval](./src/main/model/core-agent/chat-history-tools.ts). ### Execution limits and recovery Session locks and concurrency limits bound parallel work. Tool-round budgets, progress checkpoints, repeated-call checks and phase-aware idle watchdogs help contain runs that stall or repeat work. Named agent tasks can be tracked and cancelled individually; an admitted or queued task is not treated as a completed result. See [actor budgets](./src/main/features/group_chat/actor-budgets.ts), the [agent runtime](./src/core-agent/src/agent/runner.ts) and the [desktop model adapter](./src/main/model/core-agent/client.ts). ### Learning from activity Background reviews examine new agent activity when the app is idle, subject to cooldowns and execution limits. A review may update an agent's self-assessment (`COMPETENCE.md`), reusable methods (`LEARNING_STRATEGIES.md`) or learned skills. Reviews depend on new activity rather than task count, and can conclude that there is nothing worth saving. See the [reflection scheduler](./src/main/features/reflection-orchestrator.ts) and [review prompt](./src/core-agent/src/evolution/metacognition.ts). --- ## FAQ **What is Orkas?** Orkas is an open-source (MIT), local-first multi-agent desktop app. Its Commander turns your goal into to-dos and coordinates 16 built-in specialist agents — plus Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, OpenClaw and Hermes-Agent — to deliver finished files. Not a single chatbot, not a code framework, not a hosted SaaS. **Do I need an API key?** No. The packaged app comes with 500 credits for the built-in Orkas model. After that, buy credits, choose a paid plan or add your own provider keys; provider charges are separate. **Is Orkas a local LLM?** No. Orkas runs on your machine and calls the models you choose — the built-in Orkas model, your own API keys, or a local model endpoint. It orchestrates agents and tools; it is not itself a model. **Can Orkas answer questions from my documents, with citations?** Yes. Add PDFs and documents to your local Library; Orkas can search them and answer with citations to source passages, so you can open the original and check. The index is built on your machine. **Can I use local models like Ollama or LM Studio?** Yes. Open **Account settings → Models → Chat → Add model → Custom**, select **OpenAI-compatible** or **Anthropic-compatible**, and enter the base URL, exact model ID, and API key. Choose the saved model from the task's model control. **Where are my API keys and data stored?** On your disk by default. Your own provider keys are encrypted locally and excluded from cloud sync. With your own keys, model calls go straight from your machine to the provider; the built-in Orkas model uses Orkas's managed service. Optional cloud sync and shared projects in the packaged app store the selected data on Orkas servers. [Security and data handling →](https://orkas.ai/security/?source=gh-orkas) **Does Orkas work offline?** The source build can run fully offline against a local model endpoint. The packaged app needs to sign in, and cloud models need a network connection. **Does it keep working when my computer is off?** No — Orkas runs on your computer, so Auto-advance and automations need the computer awake and Orkas running. From v1.9, each automation catches up its most recent missed run within 12 hours when the computer wakes or Orkas starts. **Can I build and publish apps?** Yes. Local apps that run inside Orkas are free. Publishing a web app to a public link needs a paid plan (Lite 5, Pro 8, Max 15 apps), and published web apps don't include every capability available inside Orkas. **Do I need an Orkas account?** The packaged desktop app asks you to sign in when you first launch it. The source build in this repository has no account layer at all — it boots straight into the app. **Can Orkas drive Claude Code and other CLI agents?** Yes. Orkas can drive five external CLI agents as local subprocesses — the coding agents Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, plus the personal agents OpenClaw and Hermes-Agent — and onboard open-source projects like HyperFrames, all directed from the same chat. **How is Orkas different from Claude Code / Codex / CrewAI / LangChain?** Claude Code and Codex are coding agents — Orkas runs both as members of its team, so you don't have to choose between them; CrewAI and LangChain are code-first frameworks. Orkas is an open-source desktop app where a Commander coordinates a team of specialist agents and your CLI agents, with any model provider, and keeps data and keys local. See the [full comparisons](https://orkas.ai/compare/?source=gh-orkas). **Which platforms does Orkas support?** macOS 12+ (Apple Silicon and Intel) and Windows 10+ have packaged installers. glibc 2.34+ Linux x64/arm64 runs from source today, with no installer yet. Local speech transcription is supported on Linux through the pinned whisper.cpp runtime prepared on first launch. Alpine and other musl-based distributions are not supported. The source bootstrap needs Node 22.12+; Python 3 and a C/C++ build toolchain are needed only when a native npm package has no compatible prebuilt binary and must be rebuilt locally. **Is Orkas free and open source?** Yes — the app is MIT licensed and free to use. The packaged app includes 500 credits for the built-in Orkas model; paid plans from $11.99/month add monthly credits, cloud sync, more shared projects and app publishing. With your own keys, model usage is billed by your provider; Orkas does not add a markup. [Pricing →](https://orkas.ai/pricing/?source=gh-orkas) --- ## License [MIT](./LICENSE)

        More  items                    Orkas     
  An open-source team of AI agents on your desktop — it turns your goals into finished work and keeps it moving.  
 Orkas is an open-source (MIT), local-first multi-agent desktop app — an AI assistant that works as a team. Tell the  Commander  what you need: it finishes many tasks on its own, and for bigger work it plans the steps and brings in specialist agents along with the coding and personal agents you already use —  Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, OpenClaw and Hermes-Agent  — to work on it together. 
 Orkas is built to keep a project moving, not just answer one prompt. A  project  holds the goal, rules, memory and files, so every new conversation picks up where the last one left off.  To-dos  split the work between people and agents,  Auto-advance  lets the team take on the next to-do by itself, and  scheduled automations  repeat routine work hourly, daily, weekly or monthly. All your data stays on your computer, and finished work comes back for your review — so you can trust Orkas with the ongoing work of your business. 
   ⬇ Download Orkas for macOS & Windows   — free, with 500 credits for the built-in Orkas model, so you don't need an API key to start. Prefer your own keys? Claude · OpenAI · Gemini · DeepSeek · Kimi · GLM · Qwen · MiniMax · Doubao, or a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

  Recreate a reference video with your own content     
  VideoStudio  can recreate a viral video's narrative structure, visual style and editing pace using your own product, script and footage. Supply a reference video file and your assets: the agent analyzes the hook, information order, visual beats and call to action, then proposes what to preserve and what to replace before production. 
 This works best for motion-graphic explainers, SaaS or app demos, and product ads built from your existing footage. Locally authored text, captions, narration and clips can be revised separately; text baked into AI-generated footage requires changing that footage. 
 
 "Use reference.mp4 as a reference for a 30-second vertical promo. Keep its hook, typography and pacing, replace the content with my product and screen recordings, and show me the breakdown and plan first." 
 
 Start with a video file the agent can read; social-platform share-link downloading is not built in. Exact camera moves, human performances and frame-by-frame matching are not guaranteed. See the  reference-recreation workflow . 
 
  Keep the work moving     
 One task is a good start. Orkas is built for the work that keeps going. 
 
  Projects  — goals & rules, memory and files that every conversation in the project starts from, so you never brief from scratch. 
  To-dos and Auto-advance  — every project has a to-do list for people and agents; with Auto-advance on, the team picks up the next item on its own and brings finished work back for your review. 
  Scheduled automations  — run any task hourly, daily, weekly or monthly. Orkas runs on your computer. From v1.9, each automation catches up its most recent missed run within 12 hours when the computer wakes or Orkas starts. 
  Connectors  — Gmail, Google Calendar, Sheets and Drive, Notion, Slack, Shopify, Stripe and many more. By default, Orkas asks before it sends, posts or deletes anything. 
  Apps  — describe a tool and Orkas builds it as a local app inside the desktop app. In the packaged app, paid plans can also publish it as a web app with a public link. 
  Shared projects   (packaged app)  — invite a teammate or VA, and give each to-do to a person or an agent. 
 
   Note  Shared projects, cloud sync and web-app publishing are only in the packaged app — the open-source build doesn't support them yet. To use them,   download Orkas for macOS & Windows   (free, with 500 credits to start). 
 
 Voice input also works in the source build. Configure an  Orkas API Key  in  Settings → Models , then click the microphone beside a composer. Allow microphone access when prompted. Audio is sent to Orkas for recognition and uses the key owner’s Orkas credits. Click again to stop, review the text, and send it yourself. If access was denied, enable the microphone in your system settings.

The Commander hands each one the part it's best at and keeps one plan across all of them, so a single chat can fix the bug, review the change and draft the release note.   A Commander that plans, delegates and does the rest  — it breaks down goals, picks the right agents, skills, connectors and tools, and handles analysis, writing, research and file work itself when no specialist is a better fit. 
  Local-first by design  — conversations, files, knowledge bases and custom agents stay on your disk by default.   How it works     
  Task routing     
 The Commander handles general work itself and delegates specialist work through three tools: 
 
   dispatch_to   runs a named agent and returns its result for continued work. It can wait for the result or run asynchronously and notify the Commander when the task finishes. 
   hand_off_to   transfers the remaining work to a named agent and ends the current Commander turn. The agent delivers its own reply; an optional continuation lets the Commander resume a broader task afterward. 
   run_worker   runs an anonymous, isolated sub-task and returns a private result. It does not receive conversation history or a named agent's skills. 
 
 Named agent tasks and anonymous workers have separate concurrency controls. See the  dispatch implementation  and  execution locks . 
  Context management     
 The runtime budgets context against the selected model's usable input capacity, accounting for prompts, tools and persistent runtime state. Completed dialogue uses a bounded recent-history window; long active tasks use checkpoints to condense earlier process messages while retaining recent work. File reads, file changes and command executions also have structured records that can survive context compaction. 
 See  context budgets ,  session history and checkpoints  and  workspace records . 
  Memory and the Library     
 Durable notes keep user preferences, project facts and each agent's reusable knowledge in separate scopes. These notes are distinct from the Library's document index and the stored conversation history. 
 The Library extracts documents into passages and stores a local SQLite vector index. Its embedding model runs on your machine; the  library  tool can list files, search relevant passages and read source content from the global or current-project Library. Earlier conversations are retrieved separately through  chat_history . 
 See  scoped memory ,  document extraction ,  Library tools  and  conversation retrieval . 
  Execution limits and recovery     
 Session locks and concurrency limits bound parallel work. Tool-round budgets, progress checkpoints, repeated-call checks and phase-aware idle watchdogs help contain runs that stall or repeat work. Named agent tasks can be tracked and cancelled individually; an admitted or queued task is not treated as a completed result. 
 See  actor budgets , the  agent runtime  and the  desktop model adapter . 
  Learning from activity     
 Background reviews examine new agent activity when the app is idle, subject to cooldowns and execution limits. A review may update an agent's self-assessment ( COMPETENCE.md ), reusable methods ( LEARNING_STRATEGIES.md ) or learned skills. Reviews depend on new activity rather than task count, and can conclude that there is nothing worth saving. 
 See the  reflection scheduler  and  review prompt . 
 
  FAQ     
  What is Orkas? 
Orkas is an open-source (MIT), local-first multi-agent desktop app. Its Commander turns your goal into to-dos and coordinates 16 built-in specialist agents — plus Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, OpenClaw and Hermes-Agent — to deliver finished files. Not a single chatbot, not a code framework, not a hosted SaaS. 
  Do I need an API key? 
No. The packaged app comes with 500 credits for the built-in Orkas model. After that, buy credits, choose a paid plan or add your own provider keys; provider charges are separate. 
  Is Orkas a local LLM? 
No. Orkas runs on your machine and calls the models you choose — the built-in Orkas model, your own API keys, or a local model endpoint. It orchestrates agents and tools; it is not itself a model. 
  Can Orkas answer questions from my documents, with citations? 
Yes. Add PDFs and documents to your local Library; Orkas can search them and answer with citations to source passages, so you can open the original and check. The index is built on your machine. 
  Can I use local models like Ollama or LM Studio? 
Yes. Open  Account settings → Models → Chat → Add model → Custom , select  OpenAI-compatible  or  Anthropic-compatible , and enter the base URL, exact model ID, and API key. Choose the saved model from the task's model control. 
  Where are my API keys and data stored? 
On your disk by default. Your own provider keys are encrypted locally and excluded from cloud sync. With your own keys, model calls go straight from your machine to the provider; the built-in Orkas model uses Orkas's managed service. Optional cloud sync and shared projects in the packaged app store the selected data on Orkas servers.  Security and data handling →  
  Does Orkas work offline? 
The source build can run fully offline against a local model endpoint. The packaged app needs to sign in, and cloud models need a network connection. 
  Does it keep working when my computer is off? 
No — Orkas runs on your computer, so Auto-advance and automations need the computer awake and Orkas running. From v1.9, each automation catches up its most recent missed run within 12 hours when the computer wakes or Orkas starts. 
  Can I build and publish apps? 
Yes. Local apps that run inside Orkas are free. Publishing a web app to a public link needs a paid plan (Lite 5, Pro 8, Max 15 apps), and published web apps don't include every capability available inside Orkas. 
  Do I need an Orkas account? 
The packaged desktop app asks you to sign in when you first launch it. The source build in this repository has no account layer at all — it boots straight into the app. 
  Can Orkas drive Claude Code and other CLI agents? 
Yes. Orkas can drive five external CLI agents as local subprocesses — the coding agents Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, plus the personal agents OpenClaw and Hermes-Agent — and onboard open-source projects like HyperFrames, all directed from the same chat. 
  How is Orkas different from Claude Code / Codex / CrewAI / LangChain? 
Claude Code and Codex are coding agents — Orkas runs both as members of its team, so you don't have to choose between them; CrewAI and LangChain are code-first frameworks. Orkas is an open-source desktop app where a Commander coordinates a team of specialist agents and your CLI agents, with any model provider, and keeps data and keys local. See the  full comparisons . 
  Which platforms does Orkas support? 
macOS 12+ (Apple Silicon and Intel) and Windows 10+ have packaged installers. glibc 2.34+ Linux x64/arm64 runs from source today, with no installer yet. Local speech transcription is supported on Linux through the pinned whisper.cpp runtime prepared on first launch. Alpine and other musl-based distributions are not supported. The source bootstrap needs Node 22.12+; Python 3 and a C/C++ build toolchain are needed only when a native npm package has no compatible prebuilt binary and must be rebuilt locally. 
  Is Orkas free and open source? 
Yes — the app is MIT licensed and free to use. The packaged app includes 500 credits for the built-in Orkas model; paid plans from $11.99/month add monthly credits, cloud sync, more shared projects and app publishing. With your own keys, model usage is billed by your provider; Orkas does not add a markup.  Pricing →

      Title: Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities 
      Authors:  Yunhang Shen ,  Zhangquan Chen ,  Xiaotian Li ,  Zhongpeng Cai ,  Qing Zhou ,  Zekai Zhang ,  Kun Zhang ,  Zezhong Wu ,  Jian Hu ,  Haihan Gao ,  Heting Gao ,  Xin Li ,  Yinsong Liu ,  Deqian Jiang ,  Di Yin ,  Haoyu Cao ,  Xing Sun ,  Bing Liu ,  Yanqiu Qu ,  Yunfei Wu ,  Kun Yin ,  Zhixiang Wei ,  Yongxiang Hua ,  Qianyu Li ,  Xiaoxing Hu ,  Peiyuan Zhang ,  Lijiang Li ,  Dong Xu ,  Zhenchuan Yang ,  Yiliang Jiang               View a PDF of the paper titled Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities, by Yunhang Shen and 29 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: We present Youtu-Parsing-Omni, an omni-modal parser that converts documents, images, audio, and video into structured records grounded in space and time, providing a perception layer for agents that read, locate, and cite evidence across modalities. Its design rests on one encoder for every modality and one schema for every task. Youtu-Omni-Encoder, initialized from a pre-trained language model to strengthen text reading, encodes all modalities with shared weights in a unified space-time coordinate system, and a few fusion layers let video frames attend to concurrent audio, bringing cross-modal fusion and temporal alignment into perception itself. OmniSchema unifies the outputs of all ten parsing tasks, allowing a single self-evolving post-training procedure, OmniSchema-Aware On-Policy Distillation (OSAD), to provide a shared token-role-based objective across tasks. In each round, the model is trained on its own rollouts against token-level targets from a reference-conditioned copy of itself, which is then refreshed with the trained weights, so that the parser and its supervision co-evolve. With a single 5 B-parameter checkpoint, Youtu-Parsing-Omni achieves state-of-the-art performance on OmniDocBench v1.6 (96.96 Overall) and leads all open-weight models on OmniParsingBench (75.08 Avg.), with its advantage concentrated on audio and video. It also achieves the best overall chart-parsing score (95.02) and the highest exact chemical-fingerprint agreement among compared systems, and matches a dedicated optical-music model in character-level transcription of typeset sheet music while staying far ahead of general-purpose systems. Code and model weights are publicly available.

Paper page - Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities Hugging Face Models Datasets Spaces Buckets Docs Enterprise Pricing Website Tasks HuggingChat Collections Languages Organizations Community Blog Posts Daily Papers Hardware Learn Discord Forum GitHub Solutions Team & Enterprise Hugging Face PRO Enterprise Support Inference Providers Inference Endpoints Storage Buckets Log In Sign Up Youtu-Parsing-Omni is a compact (5B) omni-modal parsing model. Given a single input — a document page, a natural image, a chart / flowchart, a geometry figure, an audio clip or an audio-visual video — it produces one structured JSON envelope that covers both perception (layout elements, text, tables, formulas, bounding boxes, timestamps, ASR, OCR, acoustic events, camera motion) and cognition (captions, narratives, reports).

Input --task modality / subtype Key contents
Document page document image / document layout elements with bbox, text / LaTeX / OTSL tables / Markdown charts / Mermaid flowcharts, reading order
Natural image natural_image image / natural_image entities and text with bbox, tags, captions, global description
Chart graphics_chart image / document one chart element: Markdown table, notes, caption
Flowchart graphics_flowchart image / document one flowchart element: Mermaid, caption
Geometry figure graphics_geometric image / document one geometric element: points, lines, arcs, shapes, geometric relations and measurements
Audio audio audio / – vocal / non-vocal segments with timestamps, speakers, ASR, timbre / scene captions, acoustic events
Natural video natural_video video / natural_video temporal segments with visual elements, actions, interactions, camera motion, audio track
Text-rich video textrich_video video / text_rich_video segments with OCR + ASR and a Markdown structured_report of the whole video

Highlights:

  • Unified schema – one JSON envelope for seven parsing families, driven by the task prompt.
  • Omni encoder – image, audio and interleaved audio-visual video inputs (frames + audio track) in a single model.
  • Strong results at a small size – state-of-the-art on OmniDocBench v1.6 (96.96 Overall), best open-weight model on OmniParsingBench (75.08 Avg., second only to Gemini-3-Pro), and competitive with specialized models on chemical-structure (ChemOCR) and music-score (PDMX-Synth) recognition (results).
  • Easy to serve – a vLLM plugin, pinned serving settings, task prompts and inference examples are included.

Generated by thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small We present Youtu-Parsing-Omni, an omni-modal parser that converts documents, images, audio, and video into structured records grounded in space and time, providing a perception layer for agents that read, locate, and cite evidence across modalities. Its design rests on one encoder for every modality and one schema for every task. Youtu-Omni-Encoder, initialized from a pre-trained language model to strengthen text reading, encodes all modalities with shared weights in a unified space-time coordinate system, and a few fusion layers let video frames attend to concurrent audio, bringing cross-modal fusion and temporal alignment into perception itself. OmniSchema unifies the outputs of all ten parsing tasks, allowing a single self-evolving post-training procedure, OmniSchema-Aware On-Policy Distillation (OSAD), to provide a shared token-role-based objective across tasks. In each round, the model is trained on its own rollouts against token-level targets from a reference-conditioned copy of itself, which is then refreshed with the trained weights, so that the parser and its supervision co-evolve. With a single 5 B-parameter checkpoint, Youtu-Parsing-Omni achieves state-of-the-art performance on OmniDocBench v1.6 (96.96 Overall) and leads all open-weight models on OmniParsingBench (75.08 Avg.), with its advantage concentrated on audio and video. It also achieves the best overall chart-parsing score (95.02) and the highest exact chemical-fingerprint agreement among compared systems, and matches a dedicated optical-music model in character-level transcription of typeset sheet music while staying far ahead of general-purpose systems. Code and model weights are publicly available.       Title: PAPERBENCHX: Can AI Reproduce Science Across Disciplines? 
      Authors:  Ruoyu Wu ,  Zengji Tu ,  Aolong Sun ,  Tianyi Ma ,  Junren Li ,  Xinbo Xu ,  Li Fu ,  Ziyan Zhang ,  Pinrui Huang ,  Xiaochen Wang ,  Chengda Wu ,  Yutao Zhou ,  Jianjun Wu ,  Lin Chang ,  Baobao Chang ,  Liang Chen ,  Kuan Li               View a PDF of the paper titled PAPERBENCHX: Can AI Reproduce Science Across Disciplines?, by Ruoyu Wu and 16 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Before AI can be trusted to discover new science, it should be able to reproduce what science already knows. Reproduction provides a rigorous checkpoint for an AI scientist: the target claim is known, yet recovering it still requires translating an incomplete scientific description into an executable experiment and producing evidence that can be independently verified. Existing research-reproduction benchmarks largely focus on AI and machine learning, where experiments share relatively homogeneous software stacks. Extending this capability across scientific disciplines introduces a different challenge: agents must operate domain-specific scientific software, make physical and numerical choices, diagnose long-running computations, and distinguish valid evidence from merely plausible outputs. We introduce PAPERBENCHX, a benchmark of 93 expert-constructed paper-reproduction tasks spanning 12 research areas across electromagnetics, photonics, chemistry, materials science, biology, and robotics. Each task provides the source paper, a public task specification, and a domain-native scientific environment involving specialized scientific software. Agents must reconstruct a key experiment, execute and diagnose it, and deliver a runnable workflow that supports the target scientific claim. To evaluate scientific validity rather than surface-level agreement, we replay every submission from scratch and score only regenerated evidence against expert-validated criteria. Across 10 frontier agent configurations, the best configuration fully reproduces only 14% tasks under the 90% threshold. Meanwhile, mean rubric scores range from 27.53% to 59.08%, indicating that substantial partial progress rarely translates into complete scientific reproduction. These results reveal a large gap between paper understanding and reliably producing reproducible scientific evidence.

  PaperBenchX : Can AI Reproduce Science Across Disciplines? 
 
 
 UniPat AI
   

  Abstract 
    
  Before AI can be trusted to discover new science, it should be able to reproduce what science already knows.  Reproduction provides a rigorous checkpoint for an AI scientist: the target claim is known, yet recovering it still requires translating an incomplete scientific description into an executable experiment and producing evidence that can be independently verified. Existing research-reproduction benchmarks largely focus on AI and machine learning, where experiments share relatively homogeneous software stacks. Extending this capability across scientific disciplines introduces a different challenge: agents must operate domain-specific scientific software, make physical and numerical choices, diagnose long-running computations, and distinguish valid evidence from merely plausible outputs.
We introduce  PaperBenchX , a benchmark of 93 expert-constructed paper-reproduction tasks spanning 12 research areas across electromagnetics, photonics, chemistry, materials science, biology, and robotics. Each task provides the source paper, a public task specification, and a domain-native scientific environment involving specialized scientific software. Agents must reconstruct a key experiment, execute and diagnose it, and deliver a runnable workflow that supports the target scientific claim.
To evaluate scientific validity rather than surface-level agreement, we replay every submission from scratch and score only regenerated evidence against expert-validated criteria. Across 10 frontier agent configurations, the best configuration fully reproduces only 14% tasks under the 90% threshold. Meanwhile, mean rubric scores range from 27.53% to 59.08%, indicating that substantial partial progress rarely translates into complete scientific reproduction. These results reveal a large gap between paper understanding and reliably producing reproducible scientific evidence. 
  
    
  
  Figure 1:   Frontier agents on  PaperBenchX .  Bars show full scores
(      >   90  %    >90\%   ); boxes show partial scores.
GPT-6-Astra and GPT-5.6-sol use Codex; all others use Claude Code. 
 
 
  1  Introduction 

 
 Reproducibility is one of the defining features of science: a result is meaningful not only because it has been reported, but because the assumptions, procedures, and evidence behind it can be reconstructed and independently examined. For AI systems, this makes reproduction a demanding test of scientific competence. An agent must go beyond understanding a paper’s conclusion to recover how the result was obtained, translate incomplete descriptions into executable procedures, operate specialized tools, diagnose failures, and determine whether the resulting evidence actually supports the claim. Existing reproduction benchmarks largely focus on AI and machine learning, while cross-domain scientific benchmarks typically isolate only parts of the workflow  ( Starace et al., 2025 ;  Siegel et al., 2024 ;  Geng et al., 2026 ) .  What remains underexplored is whether an agent can reproduce published experiments across disciplines, inside the environments native to the underlying science.  
 
 
 This distinction matters because, outside machine learning, the environment is not merely infrastructure. It is part of the scientific problem. Reproducing an antenna result may require constructing and solving an electromagnetic model in HFSS; reproducing a photonics result may depend on geometry, boundary conditions, mode extraction, and convergence behavior in Lumerical or Meep  ( Oskooi et al., 2010 ) ; reproducing a chemistry or materials result may require choosing basis sets, numerical tolerances, or electronic-structure settings; and reproducing a robotics result may require executing and validating behavior inside an embodied simulator. A workflow can run successfully, generate plausible numbers, and still represent the wrong physical system. Cross-disciplinary scientific reproduction therefore demands more than writing code that executes. 
 
  
  Figure 2:   From task package to replay-grounded score. 
An agent receives the paper, task specification, environment, and starter
submission; interacts with domain-native scientific software; and returns a
runnable package. Clean replay regenerates the evidence used to score the
scientific rubric. The displayed leaves and scores are illustrative. 
 
 
 We identify three coupled challenges.  First, scientific reconstruction:  papers are not executable specifications. Agents must translate prose, equations, figures, and domain conventions into a concrete experiment, identify the target observable, and resolve modeling choices that are not fully specified by the task contract.  Second, domain-native execution:  agents must operate specialized scientific software, select appropriate physical and numerical settings, interpret diagnostics, and determine whether a computation is stable and converged.  Third, scientific verification:  matching a reported value is not sufficient. The result must arise from a valid experimental workflow, and the evidence supporting it must be independently regenerable. These challenges separate scientific reproduction from either rerunning released code or producing a plausible final answer. 
 
 
 To study this setting, we introduce  PaperBenchX , a benchmark for paper-level scientific reproduction across disciplines. It contains 93 expert-constructed tasks spanning 12 research areas across electromagnetics, photonics, computational chemistry, computational materials science, computational biology and bioinformatics, and robotics and embodied AI. The tasks run in 10 domain-native scientific computing environments, including Ansys HFSS, Ansys Lumerical, Meep  ( Oskooi et al., 2010 ) , PySCF/GPU4PySCF  ( Sun et al., 2026 ) , ABACUS  ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , Quantum ESPRESSO  ( Giannozzi et al., 2009 ) , AutoDock Vina  ( Eberhardt et al., 2021 ) , Habitat  ( Savva et al., 2019 ) , SimplerEnv  ( Li et al., 2025 ) , and AI2-THOR  ( Kolve et al., 2017 ) . Each task is centered on a verifiable scientific claim from a published paper. The agent receives the paper, a public task specification defining the reproduction scope and deliverables, and the required scientific environment, but does not receive the private reference workflow, reference evidence, or evaluation rubric. Its goal is to reconstruct the experiment and deliver a runnable workflow that regenerates evidence supporting the target claim. 
 
 
  PaperBenchX  evaluates sustained, end-to-end scientific reproduction through replay-grounded verification: agents must maintain scientific intent, computational state, and evidence provenance while reconstructing experiments, running and diagnosing long-running simulations, and refining their analyses; after submission, each workflow is rerun from scratch in a clean environment, and only regenerated artifacts are scored against expert-validated criteria. This design distinguishes plausible implementations and successful software execution from actual reproduction of the target scientific result. Across 10 frontier agent configurations on the same 93 tasks, the strongest configuration exceeds the 90% full-reproduction threshold on only 13 tasks, while 71 tasks are not fully reproduced by any evaluated configuration; mean rubric scores range from 27.53% to 59.08%. Agents often make substantial progress in modeling and execution but fail at scientific validation, revealing a substantial gap between partial progress and reliably closing the loop from paper understanding to reproducible scientific evidence. 
 
 
 Our contributions are threefold: 
 
  •  
 
  Cross-disciplinary paper-level reproduction.  We introduce 93 expert-constructed tasks spanning 12 research areas and 10 scientific computing environments, each centered on a verifiable claim from a published paper. 
  
  •  
 
  Domain-native scientific execution.  Rather than reducing scientific problems to a common coding interface,  PaperBenchX  requires agents to operate inside the simulators, software stacks, numerical conventions, and resource constraints required by the underlying research. 
  
  •  
 
  Replay-grounded scientific verification.  We rerun every submitted workflow from scratch and score only regenerated evidence against expert-validated scientific criteria, distinguishing plausible outputs from reproducible scientific results.

  2.1  Machine-Learning Research and Paper Reproduction 

 
 MLAgentBench and RE-Bench evaluate long-horizon machine-learning
experimentation and research engineering, but their objectives are specified as
task-level metric improvement rather than reproduction of published
claims  ( Huang et al., 2023 ;  Wijk et al., 2024 ) . PaperBench and SA-Bench
move toward paper-level evaluation through reproduction or semantic-alignment
rubrics  ( Starace et al., 2025 ;  Hu et al., 2026 ) . They establish that a final
metric alone cannot measure fidelity to a paper, but remain centered on
relatively homogeneous machine-learning software stacks rather than
heterogeneous domain-native scientific environments. 
 
 
 
  2.2  Cross-Domain Scientific Benchmarks 

 
 Cross-domain benchmarks broaden the scientific scope but generally isolate only
part of the reproduction process. SciCode, DiscoveryBench, and
ScienceAgentBench evaluate scientific coding, hypothesis discovery, or data
analysis, while CORE-Bench recovers results by rerunning released
code  ( Tian et al., 2024 ;  Majumder et al., 2024 ;  Chen et al., 2024 ;  Siegel et al., 2024 ) . DISCOVERYWORLD evaluates
interactive discovery in a unified virtual world, and NatureBench constructs
paper-derived scientific-ML tasks  ( Jansen et al., 2024 ;  Wang et al., 2026 ) . ScienceIDE most directly evaluates domain-native
scientific execution by placing agents inside production scientific software,
but its tasks concern repository-level repair and implementation rather than
reproduction of a published experiment  ( Geng et al., 2026 ) . 
 
 
  PaperBenchX  targets the intersection left open by these benchmarks. It
requires  paper-level reproduction of key experiments , executes tasks
inside heterogeneous  domain-native scientific environments , and uses
 replay-grounded scientific verification . Submitted workflows must run
again from scratch and regenerate evidence that supports the target claim;
neither a plausible final answer nor a completed repository is sufficient.
Table   1   summarizes these distinctions. 
 
 
 
 
  3  The  PaperBenchX  Benchmark 

 
  PaperBenchX  evaluates whether an agent can turn a scientific claim into
independently replayable evidence in the domain-native environment required by
the underlying research. Figure   2   summarizes the complete
lifecycle, from the materials provided to the agent through clean replay and
evidence-based scoring. This section defines the task, describes the benchmark
composition and construction pipeline, and specifies the evaluation protocol. 
 
  
  Figure 3:   Coverage and evaluation structure of  PaperBenchX . 
 A , The 93 tasks span 12 research areas in six scientific domains.
 B , Their 93 source papers span 44 publication venues; bar colors
correspond to the 12 research areas in A.  C , The task rubrics contain
3,168 scorable criteria (median 38 per task); points are tasks and black ticks
mark research-area medians. 
 
 
  3.1  Task Definition 

 
 Each  PaperBenchX  task is centered on a verifiable scientific claim from a
published scientific paper. As shown in Figure   2  , the task
input has three parts: the paper; a public task specification defining the
scientific scope, target conditions and variants, observables, required
evidence, and delivery interface; and a scientific computing environment
containing the domain-native simulator, dependencies, data, and allocated
resources. The environment is part of the task definition rather than
incidental infrastructure, because model representations, numerical
conventions, execution procedures, and convergence evidence differ across
scientific software. 
 
 
 The agent must submit a runnable package containing all source, model-building,
simulation, post-processing, and analysis code needed for reproduction, with
 reproduce.sh  as the canonical entry point. During clean replay, the
evaluator refreshes the task container, restores only the submitted package,
runs this entry point, and collects the outputs regenerated by the workflow.
Those outputs, rather than the agent’s assertions, are scored against a hidden
scientific rubric. The private reference workflow and  reference
artifacts  are never exposed to the agent. Reference artifacts are
expert-generated simulator logs, raw numerical outputs, convergence records,
and derived metrics produced during task construction; they establish that the
task is executable and ground its expected evidence and scoring criteria.
Values reported in the source paper remain visible, but private tolerances and
reference evidence are withheld. The task therefore tests whether an agent can
construct a scientifically valid and independently replayable procedure, not
whether it can recover a hidden number. 
 
 
 
  3.2  Task Statistics 

  
  Figure 4:   Task construction and quality control. 
Experts turn a published claim into a runnable task by defining its scientific
scope, provisioning the domain-native environment, and specifying the public
task contract. Reference replay, calibration checks, and independent expert
review verify executability, fairness, and evidence requirements before the
task is admitted to the benchmark. 
 
 
 Benchmark composition. 

 
  PaperBenchX  contains 93 paper-reproduction tasks spanning
12 research areas and 10 domain-native scientific computing
environments, with 3,168 scorable criteria. The twelve research areas are
radio-frequency antennas and arrays; radio-frequency metasurfaces and
scattering; radio-frequency filters and frequency-selective surfaces;
integrated photonic devices; photonic crystals and topological photonics;
optical metasurfaces, gratings, and plasmonics; optical computing and signal
processing; optical resonators, filters, and tunable devices; computational
chemistry; computational materials science; computational biology and
bioinformatics; and robotics and embodied AI.
Figure   3  A shows the distribution of tasks across
these research areas. 
 
 
 The tasks run in ten domain-native scientific computing environments: Ansys
HFSS, Ansys Lumerical, Meep, PySCF/GPU4PySCF, ABACUS, Quantum ESPRESSO,
AutoDock Vina, Habitat, SimplerEnv, and AI2-THOR. The benchmark draws on 93
distinct source papers from 44 publication venues, as summarized in
Figure   3  B. Each task has an execution budget
determined by its simulation scale and resource requirements; agent time limits
range from     4     h   4\text{\,}\mathrm{h}    to     72     h   72\text{\,}\mathrm{h}   , with a median of     7     h   7\text{\,}\mathrm{h}   .
Figure   3  C shows the distribution of scorable
criteria across the same 93 tasks. 
 
 
 
 Release and benchmark integrity. 

 
 We release one representative task from each of the twelve research areas.
Nine tasks include complete, redistributable scientific computing environments;
the remaining three rely on commercially licensed software, for which we
release the task specifications and scoring details but not the corresponding
software environments. The remaining tasks are retained as a hidden evaluation
set to reduce test-set contamination and preserve the benchmark’s validity for
evaluating future agents. 
 
 
 
 
  3.3  Task Construction Pipeline 

 
 The pipeline proceeds in two stages (Figure   4  ): first
building a runnable candidate task, and then validating whether it can be
admitted to the benchmark. 
 
 
  Stage 1: Build.   Steps 1–2: paper and claim
selection.  A domain expert selects a
published paper, identifies a scientifically meaningful claim, and checks that
it can be reproduced under the available software, licensing, compute, and time
constraints. The expert then defines the scientific scope: the target figure or
table, model configuration, experimental conditions and variants, observables,
valid methodological alternatives, and evidence required to support the claim.
 Steps 3–4: environment and public contract.  The expert provisions the
domain-native scientific environment and writes the public task specification,
which states the scope, required outputs, submission location, and replay entry
point without disclosing the private rubric or reference solution.
 Step 5: initial execution check.  The expert implements a private
reference workflow and executes it in the assembled environment. This first
execution check verifies that the simulator can be invoked, the scoped
experiment can finish within the resource envelope, and the required reference
artifacts can be generated. A task reaches the candidate stage only after this
end-to-end workflow runs successfully. 
 
 
  Stage 2: Validate and review.   Step 6: rubric
construction.  The expert converts the evidence
requirements into independently scorable rubric leaves covering model
construction, parameter settings, execution, convergence, post-processing, and
claim validation. Each leaf specifies the evidence needed for credit and its
scoring rule, tolerance, and weight.  Step 7: clean reference replay. 
The private reference workflow is rerun from a clean copy of the final
container through the same replay interface used for submissions. Unlike the
initial check in Step 5, this stricter execution check verifies that the task
does not depend on stale state, undeclared files, or hidden setup; it also
confirms that the expected artifacts can be regenerated under the final
resource limits and consumed by the evaluator.  Step 8: calibration
checks.  Successful, partially successful, and invalid workflows are scored to
confirm that the rubric awards supported progress, withholds credit for missing
or contradictory evidence, and distinguishes a complete reproduction from a
plausible but scientifically invalid result.  Step 9: independent expert
review.  Two independent domain experts inspect the scientific scope, fairness,
reproducibility, evidence requirements, and scoring behavior. 
 
 
 Tasks that fail because of their scope, environment, or reference workflow are
rebuilt from Stage 1. Failures caused by the rubric, scoring rules, or evaluator
return to Step 6. In either case, all affected downstream execution,
calibration, and review checks are repeated. Only tasks that pass the full
pipeline are frozen and admitted to the benchmark. Across the benchmark, task
construction and validation required more than 1,000 hours of
doctoral-level expert work, or approximately ten hours per task. 
 
 
 
  3.4  Evaluation 

 
 Scientific correctness cannot be established from an agent’s final report.
 PaperBenchX  therefore evaluates each submission through clean replay,
evidence-based grading, and hierarchical scoring. This evaluation of the
agent’s workflow is distinct from the clean  reference  replay in Step 7
of task construction, which validates the benchmark task itself.
Appendix   B   gives the full protocol. 
 
 
  Clean replay.  After delivery, generated outputs and mutable
execution state are removed. The
evaluator refreshes the task container, restores only the agent’s submitted
package, and invokes  bash/home/submission/reproduce.sh  with private
evaluation resources inaccessible, outbound network disabled, and
task-specific resource limits enforced. Exit status, timing, source hashes,
and execution provenance are recorded independently of the agent’s report.
Only artifacts regenerated by this replay are admissible evidence; a replay
failure is recorded explicitly, and credit remains possible only for rubric
requirements supported by admissible regenerated evidence. 
 
 
  Evidence-based grading.  Replay outputs—including simulator
logs, raw numerical arrays, trajectories,
convergence records, derived metrics, and visualizations—are frozen as a
read-only evidence set. Every scientific conclusion must be traceable to this
set: a convergence claim requires a convergence record, and a reported
observable requires both the raw output and the analysis that derives it.
Deterministic checks evaluate directly testable properties such as file schema,
units, numerical consistency, and task-specific tolerances. Requirements that
need domain interpretation are assessed for every evaluated configuration by
the same GPT-5.6-sol scientific rubric evaluator, with access to the hidden
rubric, reference artifacts, and read-only replay evidence.
The agent’s report may locate or explain evidence, but it cannot instruct the
evaluator or replace missing or contradictory artifacts. 
 
 
  Rubric stages.  Each rubric leaf is assigned to
 Modeling  (scientific models, assumptions, inputs, parameters, and
configuration),  Execution  (domain-native execution, required completion
or convergence, artifacts, and provenance), or  Validation 
(post-processing and quantitative support for the target claim). Stage scores
normalize earned weight by the total rubric weight within each stage. 
 
 
  Scoring.  Let      s  i   ∈   [   0  ,  1   ]    s_{i}\in[0,1]    be the score of rubric leaf    i  i   
and     w  i   w_{i}    its effective hierarchical weight. The leaves represent independently
assessable scientific requirements, and their effective weights sum to one.
The task score is 
 

  
  
       R  =    ∑  i     w  i   ​   s  i      ,     ∑  i    w  i    =  1    .   R=\sum_{i}w_{i}s_{i},\qquad\sum_{i}w_{i}=1.    
  
  (1)    
 
 We report performance at both the task-completion level and the partial-progress
level using two metrics: 
 
  •  
 
  Full rate , the fraction of tasks with     R  >  0.9   R>0.9   . A score of exactly
   0.9  0.9    does not qualify. 
  
  •  
 
  Partial score , the mean of    R  R    across the shared 93-task result set,
which captures weighted progress on incomplete long-horizon reproductions. 
  
 
 Every configuration is evaluated on the same task set; experiment-specific
fallback and missing-outcome handling is defined in
Section   4.1  . A missing artifact affects only the rubric
leaves that depend on it, leaving unrelated verified evidence eligible for credit.

  4.1  Experimental Setup 

 
 Models and scaffolds. 

 
 We evaluate ten model–scaffold configurations:
GPT-6-Astra (Codex)  ( OpenAI, 2026b ) ,
Fable 5.1  ( Anthropic, 2026b ) ,
Fable 5  ( Anthropic, 2026b ) ,
Opus 5  ( Anthropic, 2026b ) ,
GPT-5.6-sol (Codex)  ( OpenAI, 2026b ) ,
Kimi-K3  ( Moonshot AI, 2026 ) ,
Qwen3.8-Max  ( Alibaba Cloud, 2026 ) ,
GLM-5.3  ( Zhipu AI, 2026 ;  Alibaba Cloud, 2026 ) ,
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash  ( DeepSeek, 2026 ) , and
HY3  ( Tencent, 2026 ) . Tasks are packaged as Harbor
environments  ( Laude Institute, 2026 ) . The two GPT models use
Codex  ( OpenAI, 2026a ) , while the other eight use Claude
Code  ( Anthropic, 2026a ) . All configurations use the maximum
available reasoning setting and receive the same public task materials and

 Evaluation protocol. 

 
 All configurations are evaluated on the same 93 tasks. When
Fable 5 or Fable 5.1 refuses a task, the system automatically falls back to
Opus 5: the original refusal is retained for the refusal rate, while the
fallback submission determines the task score. Missing outcomes and refusals
without a valid fallback count as zero. We report the  partial score  as
the mean rubric score, the  full rate  as the fraction scoring strictly
above 90%, and the  refusal rate  from the original model responses. All
available submissions are clean-replayed and graded by the same GPT-5.6-sol
evaluator  ( OpenAI, 2026b ) , supplemented by deterministic checks.

  5  Analysis 

 
 Partial Progress Rarely Composes into Full Reproduction. 

 
 Only 80 of 930 outcomes exceed the 90% threshold, and these successes are
concentrated on 22 tasks; 71 tasks are never completed by any configuration,
and 11 of the remaining 22 are completed by at most two. Figure 
  6  (a) localizes this composition gap. Modeling and
Execution have median scores of 73.4% and 73.5%, respectively, whereas
Validation has a median of only 40.0%. Even among the 304 outcomes scoring at
least 80% on both Modeling and Execution, only 53 (17.4%) exceed the
full-reproduction threshold, with a mean Validation score of 58.37%. These
results show that
current agents can often reconstruct and execute substantial portions of a
scientific workflow, yet still fail to compose those partial successes into an
end-to-end reproduction that produces credible evidence and validates the
paper’s claims.

 Interaction Efficiency Varies Substantially Across Agents. 

 
 Figure   6  (b) compares each configuration’s trimmed
mean interaction turns with its Partial score and finds only a weak negative
correlation (    r  =   −  0.14    r=-0.14   ). Fable 5.1 and Fable 5 average only about 113 turns yet
achieve Partial scores of 58.17% and 57.96%, respectively, close to the
59.08% attained by GPT-6-Astra with an average of 348.7 turns. By contrast,
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash averages 372.6 turns but scores only 45.47%. Longer
trajectories do not necessarily improve reproduction and may instead reflect
repeated trial and error, failure recovery, or continued execution of a
mis-specified workflow. These results indicate that interaction count alone is
insufficient to explain reproduction performance; the accuracy of early-stage
decisions may be an important factor shaping both interaction efficiency and
final scores. 
 
 
 
 Upstream Decisions Shape the Value of Execution. 

 
 We sample 50 trajectories from each of four models and divide tool-mediated
time into paper reconstruction, implementation, native execution, diagnosis
and tuning, and evidence and replay. Figure   6  (c)
shows that native execution accounts for 51.8–63.3% of elapsed time, but
models differ substantially in how effectively they convert it into valid
scientific evidence. Fable 5 allocates 37.1% of its time to paper
reconstruction and implementation, the largest upstream share among the four
models. 
 
 
 The F-stub UWB MIMO antenna task illustrates this pattern. Fable 5 scores
28.9% in 159 turns, versus 27.4% for GPT-6-Astra in 464 turns and 18.1% for
HY3 in 390 turns. It completes three antenna variants and recovers evidence for
port reciprocity, radiation patterns, and diversity gain. This case shows that
execution alone is insufficient. Sound reconstruction, parameter choices, and
workflow design shape whether computation yields verifiable evidence. 
 
 
 
 Final Outputs Alone Cannot Distinguish Scientific Failure Modes. 

 
 Failures take two qualitatively different forms. Some workflows execute
successfully but support an incorrect conclusion because of errors in modes,
ports, parameters, mechanism implementation, or result extraction. On the
polarization-insensitive LNOI edge-coupler task, GPT-6-Astra receives full
Execution credit but only 41.9% in Validation. Similarly, several models
complete replayable experiments for the eight-element smartphone MIMO antenna
but fail to reproduce its reported performance. 
 
 
 Other failures invalidate the evidence itself. Cached results can prevent
verifier-owned replay, privileged test-state information can invalidate
scientific results, and premature termination can leave no scoreable
submission. Final outputs obscure this distinction: one workflow executes but
reaches the wrong conclusion, whereas the other establishes no trustworthy
result. 
 
 
 Final-output agreement is therefore insufficient. By separately scoring
Modeling, Execution, and Validation and checking replay and provenance,
PAPERBENCHX distinguishes experimental-construction errors, incorrect
conclusions, and unverifiable evidence. End-to-end reproduction requires not
only an output, but one produced by a correctly constructed and independently
verifiable scientific workflow. 
 
 
 
 
  6  Conclusion 

 
  PaperBenchX  tests whether agents can turn published scientific claims into
executable workflows and independently verifiable evidence. Across 93 tasks in
12 research areas and 10 domain-native environments, we evaluate 10 frontier
agent configurations. The best achieves a     59.08  %   59.08\%    partial score but only a
    13.98  %   13.98\%    full rate; no configuration reaches full reproduction on 71 tasks.
Agents often build plausible models and run native simulations, but validation
remains their weakest stage, and more interaction does not necessarily improve
performance. These results make scientific reproduction an evidence-grounded
checkpoint for AI scientists and motivate better diagnosis, provenance, and
verification.

 From contract to evidence leaves. 

 
 The hidden rubric used during evaluation converts the public scientific
requirements into independent leaves. Representative leaves check whether
(i) the executed geometry contains the specified six layers and full-depth air
slots (Modeling), (ii) clean replay regenerates genuine Meep runs, raw arrays,
logs, and refinement controls (Execution), and (iii) power closure, pole fits,
mode agreement, and convergence satisfy the disclosed scientific conditions
(Validation). A missing item affects the leaves that depend on it rather than
silently imposing a global zero. 
 
 
 
 Evaluator policy. 

 
 Only evidence regenerated by clean replay is admissible. The evaluator accepts
equivalent documented data layouts and unit conversions, but does not infer
missing units, phase, provenance, or scientific quantities from a report.
Scientific failures receive zero on the affected leaves; evaluator read or tool
failures instead withhold the judgment for repair and re-evaluation. Each leaf
is judged against its stated requirement without targeting a model-level score. 
 
 
 
 Complete public record. 

 
 The pinned   06-gmr-grating-fano-meep   directory contains the full
agent instruction, scientific addendum, environment definition, judge prompt,
rubric, and reference materials.
