      Title: TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races 
      Authors:  Tom Sander ,  Pierre Fernandez ,  Itai Gat ,  Haiming Bao ,  Jiaxin Shi ,  Jason Park ,  Valeriu Lacatusu ,  Sylvestre-Alvise Rebuffi ,  Hongyan Chang ,  Hady Elsahar ,  Tomáš Souček ,  Tuan Tran ,  Surya Parimi ,  Alexandre Mourachko               View a PDF of the paper titled TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races, by Tom Sander and 13 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: We present TextSeal2, a distortion-free watermark for large language models that keeps its signal under speculative decoding: tokens that replace rejected drafts remain watermarked with the same keys, and the acceptance rate is unchanged. It also preserves output diversity and adds no measurable inference latency. Its predecessor, TextSeal, restores diversity in the Gumbel-max scheme by routing each token to one of two keys via a coin flip. This is suboptimal because the detector averages the scores from both keys without knowing which key was used. TextSeal2 instead merges two or more keys into a single virtual key and couples it to fresh noise through AutoMark's Gaussian copula. Any number of keys, including publicly shared keys, can be merged this way without diluting detection. Under speculative decoding, TextSeal2 verifies keyed drafts with one more exponential race, run on the leftovers of the draft races. By memorylessness, this race reproduces block verification, so the output follows the target model exactly. We evaluate TextSeal2 on three LLMs. At equal output token diversity, TextSeal2 detects 8 to 22 percentage points more 100-token answers than TextSeal at a false-positive rate of $10^{-3}$, and is comparable to textGrain while requiring no post-logits optimization. Under speculative decoding, it detects 18 and 22 percentage points more 200-token answers than TextSeal and textGrain, respectively, at the same acceptance rate.

page:https://www.anthropic.com/news/clau.text: How Claude's text watermarking works \ Anthropic                                   Skip to main content       News  Research     Policy     Commitments                          Company        Try Claude                                              Chapter   01 :  What is watermarking?             How Claude’s text watermark works         01  What is watermarking?      02  How does watermarking affect Claude’s outputs?      03  Which specific method of watermarking do you use?      04  What about cases where Claude has proofread or edited human text?      05  What about code?       06  What does this mean for users?       07  Why are you watermarking Claude’s outputs?      08  Other questions           Published   Aug 14, 2026     Category   Safeguards     Topics    Legal guardrails    Transparency    Privacy    Claude's character    Limits on abuse    See more...               Related articles       Societal Impacts  Sep 29, 2026     What do you want from AI?       View more         Future Claude models will generate text that contains a watermark. This is a way of determining the likelihood that Claude was involved in writing the text, and we, along with several other major AI providers, are implementing this change to comply with the EU AI Act.  In this article, we share answers to some of the questions we’ve received about how our chosen watermarking method works, whether it affects Claude’s outputs, and why we’re making this change. To summarize:   We use a method of watermarking that does not have any practical impact on the quality or content of Claude’s outputs;  The difference between watermarked and un-watermarked text will not be distinguishable to readers;  Nothing is added to the text and there are no hidden characters;  Watermarking doesn’t require extra tokens, and will not be more expensive;  Watermarking carries no identifying information and can’t be traced to a specific person, organization, or chat;  Watermarking won’t be specific to Claude. As of August 2, the EU requires AI providers serving its market to mark AI-generated content. Other major model developers have signed the same Code of Practice and will be implementing their own watermarks.   What is watermarking?  Large language models like Claude work by generating one word at a time. Each time the model decides on the next word, it chooses among a list of potential candidates, ultimately selecting the most sensible or likely based on the preceding text. Take the sentence “The weather today was cold and…”. The next word is very unlikely to be “sugary.” But it is quite likely to be “overcast” or “grey.” Under most circumstances, it doesn’t matter much to the reader which of these latter two words the model ultimately chooses—the meaning of the sentence is largely the same either way. In cases like this, the choice is settled by a random number.  Watermarking uses low-stakes choices like these—which occur many times over a piece of generated text—to leave a pattern in Claude’s responses. That pattern is undetectable to the reader, but  is  detectable to anyone who has a key that encodes it. When watermarking is used, choices are still made at random, but the  source  of the randomness is different. Instead of using an arbitrary random number generator to pick the next word, watermarking uses the key and a few words that come before to settle what word the model should pick. That is, the words that Claude picks are still random, but now, one can check the sequence of words and see if it’s consistent with the choices Claude would make if it was using the key. If it is, one can assign a probability that the text was generated by Claude.  Importantly, it isn’t that the model will now always be biased toward overcast or grey. Just as with non-watermarked text, overcast might be selected in one sentence, grey in the next, depending on the words that came before. And it’s not the case that the watermarking method pushes Claude to choose a word it wouldn’t have considered anyway (for instance, it wouldn’t make Claude pick a word like “nubilous”—an obscure  1   synonym for overcast or grey that Claude almost certainly wouldn’t use under normal circumstances).  How does watermarking affect Claude’s outputs?  Watermarking does not impact the quality of Claude’s output. To a reader, a watermarked response is indistinguishable from an unwatermarked one (in this way, AI watermarks differ substantially from their namesakes on banknotes, other physical objects, and some digital documents, which  are  visible to the naked eye).  In internal testing, we’ve seen no impact of watermarking on the content, level of creativity, or readability of Claude’s text. In the  SynthID-Text paper , which introduced the technique we use, Google DeepMind tested this impact by serving a model that used watermarking to a portion of their Gemini traffic and comparing thumbs-up and thumbs-down ratings. They found no statistically significant differences from the unwatermarked model. And in a controlled study, human raters comparing watermarked and unwatermarked answers side-by-side saw no difference in quality.  A useful analogy is to imagine you’re playing a game like Monopoly. On each turn, each player moves a random number of spaces around the board according to the roll of a die. Suppose that, instead of rolling the die to get this randomness, we decided to use a book of the digits of pi.  2   We start from a randomly-chosen digit (say, the 1,012,845th after the decimal place, which happens to be a 6), and from that point on each player simply uses the next digit in the sequence as their next “roll."  For all intents and purposes, the moves are still random: it makes no difference to the players—or to the outcome of the game—whether the randomness comes from pi or from dice rolls each time. But if we could see the sequence of all the moves after the game (and we knew the value of pi), we could work out whether this was a game that likely used pi to determine its moves. The game that used pi is, in a sense, “watermarked."  It’s the same for Claude-generated text. Watermarking doesn’t change the meaning or experience for the person reading it, but if you wanted to check after the fact whether the text was likely generated by Claude, the watermark allows you to do so.  Which specific method of watermarking do you use?  Claude’s text watermark is a version of the SynthID-Text approach published by Google DeepMind in a   Nature  paper  in 2024. It belongs to a family of approaches that go back to a proposal by Scott Aaronson in 2022, all of which share the same design principle that we described above—the watermark only changes the source of the randomness used to pick among words.   There are limitations to the effectiveness of watermarking. Using our key, one can only answer the question “What is the likelihood this was partly written by Claude?” It doesn’t confirm whether the text was human-written, and it can’t tell whether the text was written by a different AI (even if that other AI uses watermarking, it would have a different key; it might also use a different watermarking method altogether). Detecting a watermark also doesn’t work well on small samples, where there are fewer word choices and thus less information to go on. As a passage increases in length, confidence about Claude’s involvement increases too.  Watermarking is sparser on factual passages where there are fewer choices that can be made without decreasing the accuracy of the text. For example, take the sentence “Isaac Newton’s most famous work was called  Principia …”. It really matters whether the next word is “ Mathematica ” (it’s the only right answer), so the watermark would have nothing to act on. The same is true for proofreading. If you hand Claude a piece of writing and ask it to edit only the grammar and punctuation and nothing else, the watermark can only live in the handful of corrections, which might be too few to register.  What about cases where Claude has proofread or edited human text?  The watermark only applies to words Claude chooses. When Claude proofreads text written by a person, what it gives back has generally only been lightly edited; because nearly all the words are the person’s, there’s very little (if anything) for the watermark to attach to. Depending on the length of the text and how heavily Claude has edited it, those changes might not be enough to make Claude’s involvement detectable. The more Claude writes, the more decisions it has to make, and the more space there is for a watermark.  What about code?   As we noted above, AI watermarking takes advantage of decisions where either choice of a word would be equally good. Where an  exact  output is required—where there isn’t a choice, and something would be factually wrong or a piece of code would break if a different term was chosen—the watermark isn’t applied.  For example, once the model has written “2 + 2 =”, there is a very clear best choice for the next token (if the model is completing the sum, there isn’t an answer that’s equally as good as “4”; if it’s talking about George Orwell’s  Nineteen Eighty-Four , there isn’t an answer that’s equally as good as “5”). The “nudge” of the watermark wouldn’t be applied here. For the same reason, code—which in very many cases has to be exact—has generally less watermarking than some other forms of text.  Having said that, in areas where there  is  an arbitrary choice between particular words or terms within the code, the watermark can be used, such as comments within code. But by definition, it will have a negligible effect on the actual code produced.  What does this mean for users?   Does this slow the model down, or make it more expensive?  No. Watermarking has a negligible impact on the speed of models, and because it produces no extra tokens, the model is the same price to serve and use.  Can a watermark be traced back to me or my organization?  No. The watermarking applies to Claude and its outputs. It doesn’t identify anything to do with individual users. There’s nothing in the watermark, or its key, that would allow anyone to recover any information about the user, their organization, or their chats with Claude.   Why  are you watermarking Claude’s outputs?  We’re implementing watermarking to comply with the EU AI Act. Anthropic, along with several other major AI model providers and around  190 total signatories , signed the EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content in July 2026. This requires AI system providers to use methods of “marking” AI-generated text. We’re applying watermarking globally at launch because we don't yet have a durable way to scope it by region. However, we will continue to evaluate different approaches, and will share updates when we have them.  Other questions  How do I check if a piece of text was written by Claude?  We are releasing a detection API in private preview. It is currently available to eligible organizations as required under EU law (such as regulators, law enforcement, media, fact-checkers, independent researchers, educational organizations, and EU civil society groups). It is also available for enterprises who are similarly obligated to verify watermarking for their own compliance with the Act. We plan to expand access to the detection API over time. You can register interest in access  here .  What about images and other files?  When Claude produces a file of a supported type (such as a .png, .jpg, or .svg), it will attach a content credential in the form of a small, cryptographically signed note in the file’s metadata, saying that the file was made or processed with Claude. This is an open industry standard called  C2PA —the same used by camera manufacturers and in photo-editing software to record where an image came from. Any C2PA-aware tool can read it; we’ll be providing our own where you can drop a file and check.  This metadata label is very different from a watermark. Nothing in the file changes—it is not embedded or hidden. As with text, the credential only says Claude was involved in producing the file; it doesn’t include any identifying information.  Can’t someone just edit the text to get around the watermarking?  To some extent, yes. Light editing probably won’t remove the watermark completely; a complete rewrite where every word is replaced will. In the latter case, of course, it’s arguable whether the text can any longer be described as AI-generated.  What does a watermark actually prove?  A watermark can only determine that Claude was likely involved with the content at some point. It cannot distinguish “Claude wrote this” from “Claude heavily edited this.”  Do watermarks apply to translations?  Yes. A translation produced by Claude carries a watermark, because in this case every word is chosen by Claude.  What about older Claude models?  The EU law includes a transition period for Anthropic models launched before August 2, 2026, and we’re working to add watermarking for those models as well. This will be rolled out over the coming months.  How does this differ from AI detection software, like Pangram?  AI detection software uses a different method, because the companies that provide it don’t have our key. Among other things, those services look at aspects of the text like the subtle (and not-so-subtle) “tells” that often appear in AI’s phrasing. For example, AI models appear to be fond of the construction “this isn’t [X], it’s [Y]”, and use the word “quietly” a lot more than you might expect. Picking up on these patterns is fundamentally different from checking for a watermark.  Does this change who owns a given output, or who is legally responsible for it?  No. A watermark only helps test whether Claude might have produced or processed the content. It doesn’t say anything about ownership or authorship, and doesn’t change a user’s rights under our terms. We only apply the watermark when Claude was involved in processing the content or file.    Updated Sep 1, 2026:  Provided up to date information on the watermarking detection API.     Footnotes      01 Or, you might say, nubilous—which is also a synonym for “obscure.”        02 Pi is technically predictable, but any run of digits from somewhere in the middle of pi is indistinguishable from a run of rolls of a ten-sided die. Also, set aside the fact that the dice in Monopoly go from 1 to 6 whereas a digit of pi can be from 0 to 9; the analogy isn’t perfect.                                   Keyvan’s blog                   Subscribe  Sign in                    AI text watermarking and quality loss        Aug 24, 2026              5        1     1      Share                                   After the EU AI Act’s transparency guidelines went into effect, and following the announcement that most major AI labs will soon be watermarking their text output to comply, there has been some debate about how much of an impact this is going to have, if any, on the quality of the text produced by AI models.   Since the focus of AI labs shifted to code production, I think the written output of the models has gotten much worse.   1    But it’s still interesting to try to understand if watermarking could make it even worse.     I found the discussion around technology writer John Gruber’s recent post,   Anthropic’s ‘Watermark’ Text Adulteration in Claude Is a Perversion of Writing  , very interesting.   On watermarking, Gruber wrote:   It’s unacceptable for a tool to sacrifice an iota of clarity, coherence, meaning, quality, etc. for the purpose of embedding hidden clues within the text to suggest its provenance.   He got a lot of pushback, with many debating how you would even measure quality, or define it.    But some argued that watermarking does not affect quality at all: it’s essentially just using different random numbers to generate the text. Daniel Jalkut, whom Gruber linked to in his follow-up, published a piece titled   AI Can’t Adulterate its Own Writing  , in which he wrote:    …there are also ways of tweaking the algorithm that would not diminish its randomness. For example if a random number generator routinely reversed the order of the digits in a generated number, the randomness would remain the same.   Similarly, in another discussion, someone described it as essentially swapping two faces of a die.   In a   follow-up piece  , Gruber wrote:    I hope that’s true. I believe it’s possible that it is true. I think it’s highly unlikely that it is true.   I think Gruber is right.  Quality loss across responses            Anthropic make a bold claim: “  Watermarking does not impact the quality of Claude’s output.  ” The paper they link to and based their design on (Google’s SynthID-Text, published in   Nature   in 2024) assures everyone that the method “  preserves response quality  ”.   So it’s easy to assume there’s been a lot of fuss over nothing, that they really are just swapping some random numbers around.  But their no-quality-impact claim, which they tested with humans, is based on single responses. Not the way millions of people actually use these systems: as back-and-forth conversations, over time, over multiple prompts and responses.   The 56-page   supplementary PDF   they link to at the bottom provides some more info on the method used, and it suggests the no-quality-impact claim isn’t telling the full story. Notably, it says that there is a “diversity/detectability trade-off”:    While single-sequence non-distortion guarantees the quality of each individual response, it does not necessarily preserve diversity across multiple responses   Okay, so what does that mean? They go on to explain:   when sampling several responses to the same prompt, the similarity between the responses is greater for the watermarked responses than the unwatermarked responses.   Now, if they had truly only swapped one set of random numbers for another, we would not be seeing any such difference compared to the unwatermarked responses.  They go on to write:   This could be problematic in scenarios where inter-response diversity is important, or could lower the overall quality of a system which generates many responses then selects the best one   Okay, so in their own words, it can “lower overall quality” after all. But nothing to worry about, because this would only concern you if you cared about “inter-response diversity”, for which they only provide one example: a system which generates and selects responses.  But “inter-response diversity” affects how most people use these systems too. Especially for writing tasks where you want creativity.   In response to Gruber’s point about sacrificed quality, some argued that the model has no notion of the best next word to use for what each individual is trying to convey in their specific work, and so we shouldn’t get too hung up on the next word choice. But then surely they’d agree that you, the individual,   would   know if it’s suitable or not once you see it.    Let’s say you prompt: “I don’t like the ending to this sentence. Please suggest a new one: [sentence].” The model suggests an alternative, but you don’t like it. No problem, hit the retry button. Well, now you’re affected by watermarking, because you have hit the “inter-response diversity” problem: like throwing a loaded die, you’ll see similar responses more than you would with an unwatermarked model.   Natzir Turrado, a technical consultant,   actually tested this   (article in Spanish) by reproducing SynthID-Text on an open model with the paper's settings and a watermark key. He asked the watermarked model five times to describe a memorable trip to a coastal town. Four of the five answers he got back opened in a near-identical way: “My heart still sings/dances when I think back to my trip to the quaint coastal town of…”. For the unwatermarked model, three opened in different ways.   2    And though they don’t appear to have tested for it, the same thing that makes answers to the same prompt look similar could happen across different prompts too. The watermark only looks at a small sliding context window when choosing the next token, so any time two pieces of writing pass through the same short token sequence, they could be recreating the same context window, leading to a more predictable and less diverse output. And writing is full of identical short phrases that could trigger this behaviour.  Here’s another example of what this affects: one way people try to determine the confidence level of a response, to lower the chances of hallucinations, is to repeat the same prompt a number of times, to explore the different pathways the model takes. They then look at the results to see where the consensus lies. Well, this is also affected. With watermarking, you’re less able to trust the consensus you see forming, because the answers are now less independent: they’re steered by the watermark key.   What’s interesting is that while the SynthID paper points to the loss of quality across responses, I couldn’t find anywhere in the paper where they tested this particular aspect of the watermarking method with humans. If they didn’t, the wonderful human test results they point to did not involve testing the most affected part of the watermarking method.   3     So it seems to me that they   are   sacrificing quality, by limiting the creative range of their models through watermarking, and they don’t think you’ll notice or care much.   4     1    A pattern Jasmine Sun found looking at   why AI models don't write well.   Here’s what Katy Gero, a poet and computer scientist, had to say:     The same whimsicality that made GPT-2’s voice fresh also made it prone to other unpredictable behavior. “If you’re a big corporation like Google or OpenAI, you want a chatbot that’s going to make money. The chatbot that’s   not   going to make you money is the one that’s a weirdo,” Gero said.       2    Natzir Turrado pointed me to a   reply he received   on X from one of the SynthID paper’s authors, Sumanth Dathathri:     There's a lot of easy fixes to the diversity issue. I think if you tried the same prompt with Gemini/Claude   many times  , you'd get very diverse responses :)    It’s a bit ambiguous, but I wonder if his “easy fix” is shifting the problem to the user. It reads to me like he’s acknowledging that they’ve replaced the previous die with a loaded one, but the solution is just to roll it “many times” (my emphasis), and it’ll eventually land on each of its faces. If that is what he’s saying, why not admit that such a change does make the system worse than it was before for the user?   Turrado   responded  : “Curious: which easy fixes don’t trade off detection strength?”   No reply from Dathathri so far.     3    A   recent paper   recognised that this is an “understudied fundamental trade-off in LLM watermarks: quality-diversity-power, i.e., the trade-off between the quality of the watermarked text, the output diversity under the watermarking scheme, and the overall watermarking signal strength.”      4    There are ways to mitigate some of the effects to make them less noticeable to an individual using a chat app, e.g. by rotating watermark keys between each of their requests. But these are not fixes. They only dilute the effect, and have their own costs, e.g. making watermarking less effective on shorter texts, and more costly to detect. As another study   pointed out  : “achieving a perfect distortion-free watermark is impossible”.                  5        1     1      Share                Discussion about this post      Comments  Restacks                                                                       ChatGPT for All          Sep 17                The strongest move is using the paper's supplement against its headline preserves response quality holds for one response not the distribution, which is how people actually use these tools.       Title: L3G-World: Real-Time Infinite World Generation with Latent 3D Gaussian Memory 
      Authors:  Jinhyeok Choi ,  JoungBin Lee ,  Jongmin Lee ,  Minkyeong Jeon ,  Jiyoung Kim ,  Kaeun Han ,  Yoonjin Yoon ,  Seungryong Kim               View a PDF of the paper titled L3G-World: Real-Time Infinite World Generation with Latent 3D Gaussian Memory, by Jinhyeok Choi and 7 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Interactive world models generate visual content conditioned on user actions, yet maintaining spatial consistency over long-horizon exploration in real time remains challenging. Existing approaches rely on either temporal context or explicit 3D memory, both of which scale poorly because memory grows with the length of the generated stream. Moreover, explicit 3D memories condition latent video generators by re-encoding RGB renderings, which precludes real-time generation. In this paper, we introduce a Latent 3D Gaussian Memory (L3G) that combines the efficiency of feed-forward reconstruction with a compact, rapidly renderable scene representation. Building on this memory, we propose L3G-World, in which a memory updater and a video diffusion transformer (DiT) alternate autoregressively to generate spatially consistent worlds. The memory updater spawns Gaussians in newly observed regions and refines existing ones, so that the memory grows with scene extent rather than stream length. Each Gaussian further stores a VAE latent feature, allowing the memory to be rendered directly into the DiT's latent space without VAE re-encoding. Experiments show that L3G-World achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and long-horizon spatial consistency, with up to $38.6\times$ fewer 3D primitives, $3.2\times$ faster memory updates, and $359\times$ faster memory rendering relative to the most efficient prior 3D-memory baseline for each metric, enabling real-time world generation at 9 FPS.

      Title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers 
      Authors:  Jiongfan Yang ,  Weichen Fan ,  Haiwen Diao ,  Zhongang Cai ,  Ziwei Liu               View a PDF of the paper titled Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers, by Jiongfan Yang and 4 other authors 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.

Generated by thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. # Idol **A single image to 3DGS object model** Idol turns one picture of an object into a 3D Gaussian splat. Give it a render, a generated image or a photo: it removes the background, frames the object and generates up to 1,048,576 Gaussians, including the sides the picture never showed. It runs on consumer GPUs, using 7.2 GB of VRAM and can run in under 2 seconds.
[![Hugging Face](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Hugging%20Face-Model-yellow)](https://huggingface.co/speridlabs/idol) [![Hugging Face Spaces](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Hugging%20Face-Spaces-yellow)](https://huggingface.co/spaces/speridlabs/idol) [![Python 3.10+](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10+-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/downloads/)
| ![](assets/gallery/armchair.webp) | ![](assets/gallery/avocado.webp) | |---|---| | ![](assets/gallery/lamp.webp) | ![](assets/gallery/axolotl.webp) | Each pair: the input image and the generated object turning. The [demo](https://huggingface.co/spaces/speridlabs/idol) has 93 more examples ready to run and takes your own images as well. ## Model | | | |---|---| | Output | 3D Gaussians: 32,768 to 1,048,576 (default 262,144), standard 3DGS `.ply` | | DiT | 370M parameters | | Image conditioning | DINOv3 ViT-H+ and FLUX.2 VAE | | Decoder | 288M parameters | | Background removal | BiRefNet | | Sampler | Euler, 50 steps, classifier-free guidance 3.0, time shift 3.0 | ## Install ```bash pip install -e . # Python >= 3.10, PyTorch >= 2.5 pip install -e ".[demo]" # + Gradio, to run the demo locally ``` The weights are downloaded from Hugging Face on first use, you need to request access to [facebook/dinov3-vith16plus-pretrain-lvd1689m](https://huggingface.co/facebook/dinov3-vith16plus-pretrain-lvd1689m) and [black-forest-labs/FLUX.2-dev](https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/FLUX.2-dev) first, then log in with `hf auth login`. `flash-attn`, if installed, is used for attention; otherwise PyTorch's `scaled_dot_product_attention` is (same result, slower). Set `ATTN_BACKEND=sdpa` or `ATTN_BACKEND=flash_attn` to choose. ## Inference ```bash python -m idol.sample --image photo.jpg --mode real python -m idol.sample --image renders/ --mode synthetic --out outputs ``` For each image this writes `.ply` (open it in any Gaussian splat viewer), `_input.png` (the image the model saw, after background removal and cropping) and `_camera.json` (the predicted camera of the input). **Pick the mode for your input:** | `--mode` | for | |---|---| | `synthetic` (default) | computer generated images| | `real` | real world photographs | Other flags: | flag | default | | |---|---|---| | `--seed` | 42 | same seed, same object | | `--steps` | 50 | sampling steps | | `--cfg_strength` | 3.0 | classifier-free guidance | | `--rescale_t` | 3.0 | time shift: higher spends more steps at high noise | | `--num_gaussians` | 262144 | 32,768 to 1,048,576, a multiple of 32 | | `--dinov3_dtype` | bf16 | `fp32` runs the DINOv3 encoder in full precision (1.7 GB more memory) | | `--weights` | `speridlabs/idol` | a Hugging Face repo or a local folder | | `--no_optimize` | optimized | turn off the faster sampling (see below) | **Faster sampling is on by default on GPU** The first image in a process is slower while it pytorch compiles; the rest run at full speed. ### Python API ```python from idol import IdolPipeline pipeline = IdolPipeline.from_pretrained("speridlabs/idol") output = pipeline("photo.jpg", mode="real", seed=42, num_gaussians=1_048_576) output.gaussian.save_ply("photo.ply") output.preprocessed_image.save("photo_input.png") ``` ### Demo The Gradio app behind the [Hugging Face Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/speridlabs/idol) is in `demo/`, with the example images. It runs on ZeroGPU there and on any local GPU: ```bash pip install -e ".[demo]" cd demo && python app.py ``` ## More details about the model | Component | Parameters | Precision on GPU | Weights in VRAM | |---|---|---|---| | DiT (denoiser) | 370.6M | FP16 transformer blocks; FP32 embeddings and norms | ~0.8–1.0 GB | | Octree decoder | 50.8M | FP16 transformer blocks; FP32 embeddings and norms | ~0.1–0.2 GB | | Gaussian decoder | 237.3M | FP16 transformer blocks; FP32 embeddings and norms | ~0.5–0.9 GB | | BiRefNet (background removal) | 220.7M | FP16 | ~0.44 GB | | DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 | 840.6M | bf16 | ~1.68 GB | | FLUX.2 VAE | 84.1M | bf16 (FP32 checkpoint, cast on load) | ~0.17 GB | | **Full request** | **~1.80B** | mostly FP16 / bf16, some FP32 | **~3.7–4.4 GB of weights, 7.2 GB peak** | ## Benchmark Idol, TripoSplat, TRELLIS and LGM, scored at the input view (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, IoU) and at seven new views (DINOv2, CLIP, sharpness distance). Mean scores, 1 × H100 per model. Bold is the best in each column. | Model | Setting | PSNR ↑ | SSIM ↑ | LPIPS ↓ | IoU ↑ | DINOv2 ↑ | CLIP ↑ | Sharpness distance ↓ | Request time ↓ | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Idol** | 50 steps, 262,144 Gaussians | 12.25 | **0.726** | **0.213** | **0.862** | **0.781** | **0.885** | **0.81** | 6.8 s | | TripoSplat | 50 steps, 262,144 Gaussians | 11.76 | 0.712 | 0.225 | 0.860 | 0.743 | 0.868 | 1.03 | 9.9 s | | TRELLIS | Paper setting, 50 + 50 steps | 11.89 | 0.716 | 0.235 | 0.845 | 0.754 | 0.868 | 0.97 | 7.1 s | | LGM | Default, 65,536 Gaussians | **12.46**\* | 0.722 | 0.237 | 0.834 | 0.575 | 0.784 | 1.22 | **1.1 s** | \* LGM has the highest PSNR despite visibly blurry results, because PSNR averages squared pixel error. ## Across GPUs One image to 262,144 Gaussians in 3.4 s. Request time at 50 steps: median over 8 images, with the same code and settings on every GPU, one GPU per machine. | GPU | VRAM | Request time | |---|---|---| | B300 | 269 GB | 3.4 s | | B200 | 179 GB | 3.6 s | | H200 | 140 GB | 6.6 s | | H100 | 80 GB | 6.7 s | | RTX 5090 | 32 GB | 14.1 s | | A100 | 80 GB | 16.3 s | | L40S | 45 GB | 16.6 s | | RTX 4090 | 24 GB | 19.1 s | | RTX 3080 | 10 GB | 46.2 s | | L4 | 22 GB | 54.6 s | ## Acknowledgements Idol builds on [TripoSplat](https://github.com/VAST-AI-Research/TripoSplat). It uses [DINOv3](https://github.com/facebookresearch/dinov3), the [FLUX.2](https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/FLUX.2-dev) VAE and [BiRefNet](https://github.com/ZhengPeng7/BiRefNet). **Made with ❤️ by [speridlabs.com](https://speridlabs.com)**

Idol

A single image to a 3D Gaussian splat.
One picture of an object in, up to a million 3D Gaussians out, including the sides the picture never showed.

Idol turns one picture of an object into a 3D Gaussian splat. Give it a render, a generated image or a photo: it removes the background, frames the object and generates up to 1,048,576 Gaussians, written as a standard 3DGS `.ply`. It runs on consumer GPUs, using 7.2 GB of VRAM and can run in under 2 seconds.
## Examples Idol turns one picture of an object into a 3D Gaussian splat. Give it a render, a generated image or a photo: it removes the background, frames the object and generates up to 1,048,576 Gaussians, including the sides the picture never showed. It runs on consumer GPUs, using 7.2 GB of VRAM and can run in under 2 seconds.
## Get started **1. Get access to the image encoders.** Idol reads its input through two gated models on Hugging Face. Accept their terms with your Hugging Face account, then log in once with `hf auth login` (or set `HF_TOKEN`): - [facebook/dinov3-vith16plus-pretrain-lvd1689m](https://huggingface.co/facebook/dinov3-vith16plus-pretrain-lvd1689m) - [black-forest-labs/FLUX.2-dev](https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/FLUX.2-dev) (only its VAE is downloaded) **2. Install the code** ```bash git clone https://github.com/speridlabs/idol-sdk.git cd idol-sdk pip install -e . # Python 3.10+, PyTorch 2.5+, an NVIDIA GPU with CUDA ``` There is no separate download step: on the first run, Idol's weights (about 3 GB, from this repository) and the two image encoders download automatically into the Hugging Face cache. If the encoders are not accessible yet, Idol stops before downloading anything and says what is missing. **3. Generate a 3D object** ```bash python -m idol.sample --image photo.jpg --mode real python -m idol.sample --image renders/ --mode synthetic --out outputs ``` For each image this writes `.ply` (open it in any Gaussian splat viewer), `_input.png` (the image the model saw, after background removal and cropping) and `_camera.json` (the predicted camera of the input). Pick the mode for your input. It sets how much room the crop leaves around the object: | `--mode` | for | crop | |---|---|---| | `synthetic` (default) | renders and generated images of a single object | object fills 1/1.2 of the frame | | `real` | photographs | object fills 1/1.7 of the frame | From Python: ```python from idol import IdolPipeline pipeline = IdolPipeline.from_pretrained("speridlabs/idol") output = pipeline("photo.jpg", mode="real", seed=42, num_gaussians=1_048_576) output.gaussian.save_ply("photo.ply") ``` ## Flags | Flag | Default | What it does | |---|---|---| | `--seed` | 42 | Fix it to get the same object again. | | `--steps` | 50 | Sampling steps. Fewer are faster but lose some detail. | | `--cfg_strength` | 3.0 | Classifier-free guidance: how strictly the object follows the image. | | `--rescale_t` | 3.0 | Time shift: higher spends more steps on the overall shape, lower on fine detail. | | `--num_gaussians` | 262144 | 32,768 to 1,048,576, a multiple of 32. | | `--dinov3_dtype` | bf16 | `fp32` runs the DINOv3 encoder in full precision (1.7 GB more memory). | | `--weights` | `speridlabs/idol` | A Hugging Face repo or a local folder. | | `--no_optimize` | optimized | Turn off the faster sampling. | Faster sampling is on by default on GPU (~1.7x, same output quality): the denoiser is compiled with `torch.compile`, the guided and unguided passes run as one batch, and attention uses cuDNN with TF32 matmuls while sampling. The first image in a process is slower while it compiles. ## More details about the model | Component | Parameters | Precision on GPU | Weights in VRAM | |---|---|---|---| | DiT (denoiser) | 370.6M | FP16 transformer blocks; FP32 embeddings and norms | ~0.8–1.0 GB | | Octree decoder | 50.8M | FP16 transformer blocks; FP32 embeddings and norms | ~0.1–0.2 GB | | Gaussian decoder | 237.3M | FP16 transformer blocks; FP32 embeddings and norms | ~0.5–0.9 GB | | BiRefNet (background removal) | 220.7M | FP16 | ~0.44 GB | | DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 | 840.6M | bf16 | ~1.68 GB | | FLUX.2 VAE | 84.1M | bf16 (FP32 checkpoint, cast on load) | ~0.17 GB | | **Full request** | **~1.80B** | mostly FP16 / bf16, some FP32 | **~3.7–4.4 GB of weights, 7.2 GB peak** | ## Benchmark Idol, TripoSplat, TRELLIS and LGM, scored at the input view (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, IoU) and at seven new views (DINOv2, CLIP, sharpness distance). Mean scores, 1 × H100 per model. Bold is the best in each column. | Model | Setting | PSNR ↑ | SSIM ↑ | LPIPS ↓ | IoU ↑ | DINOv2 ↑ | CLIP ↑ | Sharpness distance ↓ | Request time ↓ | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Idol** | 50 steps, 262,144 Gaussians | 12.25 | **0.726** | **0.213** | **0.862** | **0.781** | **0.885** | **0.81** | 6.8 s | | TripoSplat | 50 steps, 262,144 Gaussians | 11.76 | 0.712 | 0.225 | 0.860 | 0.743 | 0.868 | 1.03 | 9.9 s | | TRELLIS | Paper setting, 50 + 50 steps | 11.89 | 0.716 | 0.235 | 0.845 | 0.754 | 0.868 | 0.97 | 7.1 s | | LGM | Default, 65,536 Gaussians | **12.46**\* | 0.722 | 0.237 | 0.834 | 0.575 | 0.784 | 1.22 | **1.1 s** | \* LGM has the highest PSNR despite visibly blurry results, because PSNR averages squared pixel error. ## Across GPUs One image to 262,144 Gaussians in 3.4 s. Request time at 50 steps: median over 8 images, with the same code and settings on every GPU, one GPU per machine. | GPU | VRAM | Request time | |---|---|---| | B300 | 269 GB | 3.4 s | | B200 | 179 GB | 3.6 s | | H200 | 140 GB | 6.6 s | | H100 | 80 GB | 6.7 s | | RTX 5090 | 32 GB | 14.1 s | | A100 | 80 GB | 16.3 s | | L40S | 45 GB | 16.6 s | | RTX 4090 | 24 GB | 19.1 s | | RTX 3080 | 10 GB | 46.2 s | | L4 | 22 GB | 54.6 s | **Made with ❤️ by [speridlabs.com](https://speridlabs.com)**

 Post training a model to explore Demoscenes 
 On the grammar of demoscenes and the possibilities of unfinished code 
 October 31, 2026 
 
 Lately, I have been fascinated by the world of demoscening and sizecoding and eventually I came across HellMood’s remarkable MS DOS demo  “   Memories   ”.  Whilst reading through his  writeup , I became interested in  how  the author had  arrived  at some of its visual effects. I was struggling to create any of my own, so I hoped to squeeze out a little bit of inspiration out of that.    

     

 I noticed that these effects could be traced back to earlier experiments consisting of alternative implementations and several ideas borrowed from previous demos. I began wondering how many other directions the same underlying ideas might have taken. I decided to start with a few existing demos, the simplest ones of all, and modify them character by character to observe how those changes can affect the visual feel.  

 I came across  Dwitter.net , which is like Twitter but for 140 character JavaScript demos. They already supported “remix”-ing any  dweet  so that we can build on top of them. Co incidentally, the most liked Dweet on the site shared the same effect as the parallax checkerboard effect from  Memories !  

     

 Digging a little deeper, I noticed some remixes shared substantial portions of their source code, differing by only a few characters, whilst others achieved similar visual effects through entirely different implementations.  

 Here is an example, I traced back d/36555 from d/367547 which in turn  is derived from d/36467. The gray underlined substrings show what is common across all of them. Blue shows what’s common in between the first two, and green shows for the next couple.  

     

 In linguistics, language is productive i.e. a finite vocabulary and a finite set of grammatical rules permit an  enormous  number of different expressions. Programming languages share this property too. Now let’s consider the aforementioned Dweets. They contain overlapping substrings, but their rendered results differ. Suppose you take a 140 character program, and remove its final 30 characters. Even with a hypothetical alphabet of just 64 character, there are almost 1.5 x 10^54 possible completion strings that can be formed. Almost all will be syntactically invalid or produce uninteresting results. Nevertheless, the number of possibilities is astronomical.  

 It’s not humanly possible to enumerate all of them exhaustively and it would be foolish to to generate and test all possible strings. However, the continuations of a partial program are not equally plausible. 

 Given a partial program, certain characters and expressions are considerably more likely to follow than others. This is pretty much how autoregressive language models work. I wondered whether I could use such a model to sample plausible continuations of unfinished Dweets and visualize the different directions each program could have taken.  

 And then, I could surgically delete substrings or mix-and-match them to my own aesthetic taste.  

 I had also grown rather frustrated with my own ability to “finish” a demo after starting one, so having an autocomplete that understood the peculiar language of Dweeting rather looked like an appealing prospect to me. 

 Around the same time, I came across  Mithil Vakde’s tweet  (you might have seen him on  HackerNews  recently). 

     

 That gave me another excuse to experiment - could I inject  my  own aesthetic taste as a prior into my autocomplete model? That’d be really amazing.  

 I understand that no one can write a function that determines whether a demo is beautiful, but people  can   express  their preferences by comparing examples, right?  

 With that in mind, I decided to put my GitHub Sponsors payout towards renting a GPU and post training a model of my own. 

 

 The first hurdle was finding a suitable dataset. I initially experimented with generating synthetic Dweets using Claude Sonnet 5.5 but found them not at all aesthetically pleasant. Fortunately,  Dwitter.net provides an API , which I used to build a modest dataset of 25k Dweets to be used for training along with ~1.3k more as a validation set. 

 I used Qwen2.5-Code-7B as the base model. It struggled to complete most of the Dweets I tested it on, which was understandable given how peculiar their syntax is. Dweets make extensive use of code golfing tricks and mathematical shorthand, which are rather unusual compared with the code a general purpose coding model typically encounters.  

 I decided to try continued pretraining (CPT) on the corpus, hoping to shift the model’s probability distribution towards the pecular language of dweeting. To see whether it had worked, I measured the  surprisal  of individual tokens before and after training. Surprisal is simply the negative log probability a model assigns to a token given everything preceding it. The less likely a token is, the more surprising it is to the model.  

 In the figure below, darker red indicates greater surprisal. After CPT, much of the code becomes noticeably less surprising (particularly the unfamiliar programming idioms).  

     

 Across 30 held out dweets, perplexity fell from 28.63 to 8.57, which means that the model had become substantially better at predicting the structure of these tiny weird programs.  

 Although the generated programs were more consistent, they still lacked a certain “charm”. Fortunately, Dwitter has an “awesomeness” score for every Dweet. I decided to use it to construct a curriculum.  

 I ranked the top 5k dweets by their “awesomeness” scores and constructed a curriculum that gradually favoured the more appreciated programs. Initially, every dweet had an equal probability of being sampled. Over 400 training steps, I progressively increased the weight assigned to higher ranked programs, until the top 1000 accounted for roughly 67% of the sampling probability. 

    Rank bucket  Step 1  Step 100  Step 200  Step 300  Step 400      1-1000  20.00%  35.89%  48.74%  59.01%  67.23%    1001-2000  20.00%  27.97%  29.60%  28.01%  24.99%    2001-3000  20.00%  20.03%  15.23%  10.41%  6.75%    3001-4000  20.00%  12.06%  5.63%  2.41%  0.99%    4001-5000  20.00%  4.05%  0.81%  0.16%  0.03%    

 This turned out to be a breakthrough! The generated continuations became much more visually interesting.  

     

 Interestingly, the improvements in token likelihood extended even to Dweets that had never been sampled during curriculum training. Perplexity fell from 7.42 to 5.65, although the gains were spread fairly evenly across awesomeness ranks. 

     

 Across 7000 Dweets, curriculum training improved token likelihood across all awesomeness ranks, including programs never sampled during training. The gains were particularly pronounced for programs the original model found difficult. 

 I now had a model that could produce rather beautiful continuations. I wondered whether I could take this further by incorporating my own aesthetic preferences. 

 In mid-September, I came across Surya’s article on  Training AI to Paint with Code , where they had used RL to produce watercolor paintings using p5js. They experimented with different reward functions before settling on pairwise comparsions against a collection of hand rated paintings. I remembered that idea and thought of trying something similar with Demoscener (it doesn’t feel alright to call it “the model” repeatedly).  

 I opted to do RLHF using GRPO, with myself acting as the reward function.  

 For each unfinished Dweet, I sampled a group of eight completions, rendered them side by side and selected the one I found most aesthetically pleasing. If none appealed to me, I skipped the group. I used these preferences to update Demoscener’s policy, then sampled fresh continuations and repeated the process over roughly 9–10 rounds of 500 groups each. Altogether, I manually inspected around 40,000 animations. 

     

 Somewhere around the 10,000th animation, I began to appreciate the existence of VLMs and HPSv3. Sadly, it was too late.  

 After several rounds of training, I wanted to see how much of my taste had actually rubbed off on Demoscener. I enlisted a rather unwilling friend to judge 400 sets of demos from a few of the checkpoints (I picked 4 randomly), without knowing which model had produced which. 

     

 The results showed that checkpoint 4 was the most favorable, so I used that to run inference on my Mac.  

 Now coming to the end of the side quest, I built a little interface where I could generate several continuations from the same prefix, render them side by side and branch off from whichever one caught my eye. I could then tweak the code, generate more continuations, and keep exploring. 

     

 Each branch represents a possible continuation, which I could compare visually, tweak by hand, and use as the starting point for further exploration. 

     

 There is something quite lovely about being able to wander through these possibilities. I think I'll be spending a little more time doing just that. 

 You can find  Demoscener-7B  and the  dataset  on HuggingFace. 

 
 
 
  Back to writing

HackerTube – karpathy 
   
  
    

     
     

    
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 
 
 



 
 
     
     

  
    

    
    
  
  
  
    
         
    



   
 

 
  
   
     
       
        karpathy
       
     
     
        Home   Blog  

     
   
   
    

    

    
         HackerTube 

         
             
                 
    31 Oct, 2026
 
             
         
    

     It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with:  hackertube.org ! 
   
 Opus downloaded all  comments of HackerNews , filtered them, ran Sonnet over them in a Workflow (Claude Code feature), got rid of spam, and narrowed everything down to 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila! 
 HackerTube: 
 
 Contains quality content 
 Uses the 50% thumbnail instead of the uploaded thumbnail 
 Custom and good ForYou recommendations without any user accounts, storing state in local browser session 
 Keyboard shortcuts 
 Export of the site's data available to give to your agent to easily create your own version 
 
 This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5  
 
  EDIT : A little bit more on my process. I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac). I use Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I don't actually  do  anything resembling traditional engineering anymore (read/write code, run commands in a terminal, or etc.), I only talk to Claude and have it do everything. In this case, the only "manual work" I did was: 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box and 3) I bought the domain name. I worked on this in between Claude's actual work so it still feels a little bit like team work :) Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, deploy, secure, harden and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

  I have the same experience, and I don't think it's just us. I suspect what's going on is we're experiencing the long-term effects of AI recommendation algorithms getting plugged into everything. I'm not anti-AI. I think neural nets are incredibly powerful tools and I really like using them as an aide for my coding work. But they clearly do only a first or second level of pattern matching(asterisk), and I think that has a fundamental impact on their overall usefulness and desirability. I can't explain this any better than Melanie Mitchell in her "AI for Thinking Humans," so I'd generally recommend that book to really understand the issues. But one way of thinking about it is that the AI keys in on patterns that are indeed there in its training data, but very often don't pick up on the same patterns as a human or treat patterns "not in the same way" as a person would. So you get the uncanny valley effect where the recommendations share some features of things you like and find interesting, but often miss the "soul" of the thing. A good example of this is I recently watched the movie "X-Men" (2000). I then got a bunch of superhero movie recommendations. On the surface, this makes total sense. I watched a superhero movie, I get more superhero movies. But the reason I like that movie is it portrays racism/nationalism in a way that isn't totally stereotyped while still being PG-rated and easy to watch, without the seriousness of something like "American History X" (it was also a Patrick Stewart tribute). It's very unlikely that an AI can make that level of inference. I actually  would  enjoy watching more movies like that (as opposed to your point about wanting variety and something more exploratory), but what are the odds it's going to recommend some vague theme like that instead of "more superheroes"? I also agree with your point that the underlying assumption we all want "more of the same" is a big thing that makes the modern internet feel more narrow. Memdoor

Your daemon agents on every door.
A lightweight coding and automation agent in a single CLI binary. Run it locally or connect over SSH to another machine — no Docker or Python required. Work interactively from a terminal, your IDE or phone, or start a run from a shell script, CI or a schedule and finish it from any of those, on a gateway you own. BYOK.

One binary to deploy. A headless-first CLI. Multi-step jobs kept as files in your repo, with checks, approval gates and resume. Less of your token bill, through a decision model in front of the chat model.

> **Five Qwen3.8-27B agents beat Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard, as a Memdoor workflow.** > [GVS5H](https://github.com/slee-persis/GVS5H)'s harness rebuilt with the authors' exact prompts and loop, > on the first ten problems of their list, five passes each: a mean of **9.8 of 10**, against 9.6 for the > authors' own harness and 8.0 for Fable 5 in a single call. All 50 runs are published: every request, > reply, program and grader output. The workflow is YAML and names no model: point it at yours, or at a > local one with `memdoor connect local` (Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, LM Studio; [how](https://memdoor.ai/docs/providers#a-local-runtime-no-key)). > [examples/workflows/team-solve](examples/workflows/team-solve/) · [the HN thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50320995) On this machine: ```bash curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-... # or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, … cd your-project && memdoor # the first run sets the machine up ``` Or on a box you can ssh to, with nothing installed there: ```bash curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash # here, once memdoor --gateway ssh://you@box # installs memdoor on the box, starts its gateway, opens the window on it memdoor --gateway ssh://you@box connect openrouter # your key, kept on the box; every turn there runs on it memdoor --gateway ssh://you@box run "fix the failing test" # the same box from a script or CI ``` The runs live on the box: close the laptop, the work goes on, and your phone or the next terminal opens the same conversation there. No account. Telemetry off unless you turn it on. macOS, Linux, Windows, one static binary, Apache 2.0. ### In GitHub Actions One step in a workflow, on your key, with nothing to add to your repo ([Marketplace](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/memdoor)): ```yaml on: pull_request jobs: review: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v5 - uses: guregodevo/memdoor-action@v1 with: workflow: pr-review openrouter-api-key: ${{ secrets.OPEN_ROUTER_API_KEY }} ``` Nine are built in: - **`pr-triage`** sorts a pull request for a maintainer: ready for review, needs work, or likely slop, from checks run in the job (the tests, claimed tests that are not there, functions nothing calls). - **`pr-review`** reviews the pull request, verifies each finding by running the code, and fails the job only on a blocker. - **`security-review`** does the same for security only: secrets, injection, path traversal, missing authorization. - **`write-tests`** writes tests for what the change touches, and fails the job when one shows the change is wrong. - **`pr-description`** writes the description: title, What, Why, How to test, Risk. - **`explain-failure`** reads a failed run's logs and the diff: the cause, file:line, and the fix. - **`issue-triage`** suggests labels, the kind, a summary and duplicates for a new issue. - **`fix-tests`** finds the test command, fixes the code until the tests pass, and leaves the fix in the working tree. - **`release-notes`** turns the commits since the last tag into Added / Changed / Fixed. No key at all: `local-model: Qwen3-8B-4bit` instead of the key runs any of them on a model inside the runner ([janis](https://github.com/guregodevo/janis), one file, the model cached), in one model call. It is a free first pass, not a reviewer: on a free runner it caught an obvious and a subtle bug in about a minute each, and can file a correct change's own fix as a blocker. Or `workflow: ` for your own, `.memdoor/workflows//` in the repo. The job ends with the run's outcome (0 done, 2 failed, 1 stopped, 3 stopped at an approval gate) and its summary shows the review, the fix or the notes. Trigger on `pull_request`, never `pull_request_target`: GitHub gives a fork's pull request no secrets, so a stranger's code never runs beside your key. On a ChatGPT Plus or Pro plan? Skip the key: `memdoor connect chatgpt` (or `/connect chatgpt` in the window) opens Sign in with ChatGPT, and your plan's allowance answers Memdoor's turns. A Claude subscription cannot be used this way (Anthropic's terms); Claude needs an API key. No key at all? The first `memdoor` signs you in with OpenRouter in the browser, a free account included (or with ChatGPT), from a gateway on this machine, over ssh or on a box. An account with no credit runs on a free model picked from OpenRouter's list, and the connect says so: 50 requests a day, and the free hosts train on what they are sent, so a trial, not private code. Or no key at all: `memdoor connect local` finds a model running on this machine ([janis](https://github.com/guregodevo/janis), Ollama, llama.cpp, LM Studio), and nothing leaves it. janis is ours: one Go server that runs the open models on a Mac's GPU through MLX or on an NVIDIA box through CUDA, serves chat and the decision model with no key, and runs Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B on a $0.71-an-hour Google L4; `memdoor --gateway ssh://you@box connect local` makes that box yours. And that box answers your laptop: `memdoor peers add box http://box:18789 --dir ~/app` names it, and `@box:coder …` in any conversation here runs the turn there, on the box's own model, and brings the answer back. Recorded on memdoor.ai: a laptop with no GPU asks, Qwen3.8-27B on an L4 through janis reads, patches and runs a Go program on the box, the window on the laptop shows it land.

Every run is a conversation on a gateway on your machine, whatever door it came in by: a terminal window, `memdoor run` from a script or CI, a cron schedule, your editor, or the page on your phone. The run a CI job started is the one you open with `memdoor resume `, watch live, and answer. One gateway, every door ([the walk through them, with exit codes](https://memdoor.ai/docs/headless)). ```bash memdoor run "fix the failing test" # one turn, no window; the exit code is the receipt of its checks memdoor workflow run release --wait # a workflow from a shell or CI, exit code the run's outcome memdoor resume --last # the same run, in a window ``` --- `memdoor` reads your files, writes patches, runs the build and fixes what it broke, in the directory you launch it from. Every model call goes from your machine to the provider you connected, on your account, at their list price. Two more things set it apart. **A decision model in front of the chat model.** Jev (TypeSafe) answers a typed question such as *is this hit relevant to the task?* with a calibrated probability in under half a second, and the harness acts on it: search, file and log reads return only what counts; only the tools the turn needs are sent; a turn that stops making progress ends instead of looping to a cap. Measured over 44 paired runs, decisions off and on: 22 of 22 passed each way; a question about the codebase went from 54,661 to 14,367 input tokens (−74%); an edit with a test and ten one-file fixes read the same files either way (within ±11%) ([`docs/features/DECIDE.md`](docs/features/DECIDE.md)). **Workflows.** Say the steps and the coder writes them as task files, one YAML per step, run as a graph by [`mario`](https://github.com/guregodevo/mario). Independent steps run in parallel; a step is done when its check passes, never because the model says so; a gate waits for your approval with the diff in front of you; a failed run resumes at the failed step. The files live in your repo, so a workflow is kept, shared and run again, by hand or on your local cron ([`docs/features/WORKFLOWS.md`](docs/features/WORKFLOWS.md)). Why workflows rather than skills: [the write-up](https://guregodevo.github.io/2026/10/06/workflows-not-skills/). Worked examples, each run before it was added: [`examples/workflows/`](examples/workflows/). One of them, the step that grades a trading rule (`examples/workflows/nightly-rule/steps/grade.yaml`), as it runs nightly; no code in it: ```yaml type: agent prompt: | Today's partition is {{.partition}}. Read rules/{{.partition}}.md and grade today's trading rule: assess it briefly (clarity, risk profile, plausibility) and write a JSON object {"score": <0-100 integer>, "verdict": ""} into grades/{{.partition}}.json (create grades/ if needed). requires: - table_pattern: build target: # run by the engine, not by the agent: the grade must exist and be newer than step 1's start stamp command: test "grades/{{.partition}}.json" -nt "rules/{{.partition}}.start" && test -s "grades/{{.partition}}.json" timeout: 10m ``` A recorded session of the review loop (findings verified by running, a gate, the fixes applied) plays at [memdoor.ai/workflows](https://memdoor.ai/workflows). ## Install ```bash curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-... # or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, … or /connect inside cd your-project && memdoor # the first run sets the machine up ``` macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel), Linux (amd64, arm64; static), Windows (`irm https://memdoor.ai/install.ps1 | iex`; the agent runs commands in Git Bash when it is installed, otherwise PowerShell). One binary, installed to `~/.local/bin`, no sudo, no Docker, no Python. The installer ([`scripts/install.sh`](scripts/install.sh)) verifies the SHA-256 of what it downloads. From a clone, with Go 1.25: ```bash git clone https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor && cd memdoor make build # ./memdoor, stamped with the tag it was built from cp memdoor ~/.local/bin/ # or anywhere on your PATH ``` ## In the window | Command | What it does | |---|---| | `/model` | Which model answers: the agent's ladder (cheapest rung first), or pin any model of your providers, with list prices | | `/connect` | Add a provider: OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, Baseten, Groq, xAI, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, your company's AI gateway; `/connect local` a runtime on this machine or the box (Ollama, llama.cpp, janis), no key; `/connect chatgpt` signs in with a ChatGPT Plus/Pro plan, no key | | `/workflow` | The project's workflows and runs; enter opens a run's graph, `a` approves a gate, `/workflow:` runs one | | `/usage` | This month on your key, per model, and what the decision model kept out of the bill | | `/remote` | This conversation on your phone: a link and a QR code, the terminal itself, end-to-end encrypted | | `/remote view` | A watch-only link: whoever opens it sees the terminal live and cannot type, no account, up to 200 at once; `?live=1` is the terminal alone, for a stream or OBS | | `/share` | A read-only link to the conversation, encrypted, secrets removed; `/unshare` deletes it | | `/files` or `ctrl+f` | The project's files, the ones this conversation read or changed first, each with what happened to it; enter previews, `ctrl+d` diffs, `ctrl+e` opens in `$EDITOR`, tab puts `@path` in the prompt | | `/graph` or `ctrl+g` | This turn as a graph: the reads, the edits that depended on them, the runs that depended on the edits, the failing check in red | | `/mcp` | Connect MCP servers from a URL, a command or a `.mcp.json` snippet | | `/help` | The rest | `Esc` interrupts a turn, `ctrl+f` opens the files panel, `ctrl+g` the turn as a graph, `ctrl+o` expands tool frames, `Shift+Tab` sets the reasoning effort, `@path` mentions a file. `MEMDOOR_APPROVE=changes` asks before every command and write, for machines whose policy requires it. ## In your editor `memdoor acp` serves the same coder over the [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com): Zed and JetBrains host it natively; VS Code through an ACP client extension (for example "ACP Client"), with one setting: ```json "acp.agents": { "Memdoor": { "command": "memdoor", "args": ["acp"] } } ``` Each editor session is a conversation on your local gateway; a prompt is a turn in the editor's workspace folder, and the turn's text, tool calls and approvals show as the editor's own. The steps: [memdoor.ai/docs/editor](https://memdoor.ai/docs/editor). ## From a script ```bash memdoor run "make the retry wait configurable and add a test" # a headless turn, no window git diff | memdoor run "review this diff; one line per finding" # stdin is the input memdoor run --json "fix the failing test" | jq 'select(.event=="done")' memdoor workflow run release --wait # progress on stderr, results on stdout memdoor remote --last # the link /remote gives, on stdout; the gateway holds the run for your phone memdoor remote --view --last # the watch-only link: an audience, or a pair of eyes ``` The exit code is the turn's receipt: 0 checked, 2 unverified or a failing check, 3 a question nobody answered (`--yes` answers it), 1 an error, 130 interrupted. The gateway starts if none is running; every run is a conversation `memdoor resume` opens. [Headless, then attached](https://memdoor.ai/docs/headless). A workflow in GitHub Actions is one step: [In GitHub Actions](#in-github-actions) above. ## Where your data goes Files, sessions and commands stay on your machine. What leaves is what the model reads, sent to the provider you connected; on OpenRouter every request carries `data_collection: deny` and hosts that train on paid inputs are kept out of the ladders. The one exception is a `:free` model, one you pin or the one an OpenRouter account with no credit answers on: its hosts train on what they are sent, the request says so (`allow`), and Memdoor says so at the pin or when the key is connected; use one for a trial, not on private code. On a vendor key or a company gateway nothing else is contacted: [`docs/SECURITY.md`](docs/SECURITY.md) lists every host the binary can name and a test fails the build on a new one. ## Documentation - [Getting started](GETTING_STARTED.md) - [Workflows](docs/features/WORKFLOWS.md) · [Scheduled checks](docs/features/cron-jobs.md) · [MCP servers](docs/features/MCP.md) - [Providers](docs/features/PROVIDERS.md) · [Security](docs/SECURITY.md) · [Decisions](docs/features/DECIDE.md) - [CLI reference](docs/reference/CLI.md) · [Architecture](docs/reference/ARCHITECTURE.md) · [Skills](docs/reference/SKILLS.md) · [ADRs](docs/adr/) - The served docs: [memdoor.ai/docs](https://memdoor.ai/docs/getting-started) ## Repository layout ``` cmd/cli/ the CLI (cobra): tui, model, workflow, cron, account, … gateway/ the local gateway: agent runtime, tools, providers, workflows pkg/ the domain: decision, metering, plan, workflow (the mario task factory), … web/ the memdoor.ai site and the served docs (React, Vite) scripts/ install.sh, install.ps1, deploy.sh docs/ features, reference, ADRs examples/ workflows built by the coder and run, to copy into a project ``` ## License Apache License 2.0 — [LICENSE](LICENSE), [NOTICE](NOTICE). The public repository is [github.com/guregodevo/memdoor](https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor); issues there.

 A multi-agent harness for programming problems, written as a
 Memdoor  workflow. Five roles (planner, two ideators,
solver, manager) and a repair worker each start from a fresh context and talk
only through files on disk. A shell script that runs the samples decides
success, not a model. It is the method of
 GVS5H  (Lee, 2026: five Qwen3.8-27B
models match Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard). 
 Rebuilt with the authors' exact prompts on Qwen3.8-27B, their loop scored a
mean of  9.8 of 10  over five passes on the first ten LiveCodeBench Hard
problems, against 9.6 for their own harness and 8.0 for Fable 5 alone
( below , every run published). 
 The coder wrote these files itself from a description of the method
(2026-10-25). Nobody hand-wrote them. 
  Five passes on the authors' ten (2026-10-31)     
 GVS5H's own harness, rebuilt as a Memdoor workflow on the same model:
Qwen3.8-27B, a 128K reply cap, the authors' prompts and loop. The first ten
problems of their LiveCodeBench Hard list, five passes, every program graded
on every public and hidden test with their corrected grader.

 Memdoor workflow 
 authors' 27B harness 
 Fable 5 alone

  10  / 10

  10  / 10

  9.8  
 9.6 
 8.0 
 
 
  
 The authors' columns are their repository's regraded result files
( q38_multiagent_pN ,  fable5_single_pN ), the numbers in their paper.
  bench/results/parity-5pass/   holds all 50
runs: every request and reply, the program, the grader's full output, each
call's cost and the host that served it, and every attempt that did not count.
49 of 50 solved; the 50 runs cost $35.79 (15.3M output tokens), $38.77 with
the 16 attempts that were cut by a clock, stopped for a fix or paused. 
  Note: ten problems, five passes each, not the authors' 100. The contests
date from 29 March to 6 April 2025, and the model may have seen them in
training: contamination cannot be ruled out. Fable 5's column is a single call per
problem from the authors' files; it was not run in this harness. The loop
sees only the public samples; the score is the hidden tests. A run took a
median of 40 minutes of model time (the longest 4 hours) and $0.39. All on
OpenRouter, not a local machine; Modal does not publish its precision.
Local paths in the run scripts and in four tracebacks a manager was shown
read  <scratch>  and  $HOME ; nothing else in the runs is edited.  
  Same as the authors'.  Every message, byte for byte:
  lib/test_parity.py  
runs their  multiagent_solve  and our workflow against one scripted model and
compares each request (four cases, all identical; a one-character change makes
them differ). The temperatures (plan 0.3, ideation 0.4, manager and worker
0.2), top_p 0.95 and top_k 20 (what their vLLM applied from the model's own
config), the 128K cap, up to 10 rounds, a cut-off worker summarized, and a
reply with no text answered by its reasoning. 
  Different.  The host. Theirs was their own vLLM in FP8. Ours is
OpenRouter, asked in the order Modal, CoreWeave, Parasail, Wafer until Modal
slowed to 14 tokens/s, then the FP8 hosts only (Wafer, Parasail, CoreWeave):
203 calls were served by Modal, 27 by CoreWeave and 115 by Wafer, every one
of the FP8 order's calls by Wafer. Three runs were moved mid-run, their
finished steps kept ( log/host-switch.txt ). 
  What it took.  The problem text was the mismatch: our first version wrote
its own task file around each problem, and the 27B planned worse from it than
from the authors' exact LiveCodeBench text (arc196_c's plan: 0 of 2 against 2
of 2). Four Memdoor changes let a workflow ask what their harness asks: a task
answers with the model's reasoning when it wrote no text,  top_p / top_k  on a
model line,  mark_cutoff  for a reply cut at the cap, and a call that runs on
its own four-hour clock. 
  Where it lost.  Twice, the same two gaps in the authors' loop: 
 
 Pass 5, abc399_e (32 of 44 hidden): round 1's program was right; the
manager invented a counterexample with a wrong expected answer, the team
rewrote it, and the new program passed the samples, which do not cover the
case. 
 Pass 4, arc196_c and arc196_d: a program passing every hidden test was
overwritten by a later round because the manager did not say done; both
got a correct program back before the loop's end (arc196_d at round 8,
arc196_c through the final call), at $3.44 and $4.24, the two most
expensive runs. 
 
 Both are fixable without changing the method (check a manager's counterexample
against a brute force on small inputs; keep the last program that passed the
samples). Neither is in these numbers. 
  Run it     
   curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash
memdoor connect openrouter                 # or anthropic, openai, gemini, chatgpt
# or no key at all: memdoor connect local   # Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, LM Studio on this machine
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor

mkdir -p ~/.memdoor/workflows
cp -r memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve ~/.memdoor/workflows/   # the library: any project sees it
mkdir my-problem && cd my-problem
cp -r ../memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve/sample/* .          # task.md + tests/1.in … 5.out
memdoor workflow run team-solve --wait   # progress on stderr, exit 0 when every sample passes
   
  /workflow  in  memdoor tui  draws the same run live. For your own problem,
replace  task.md  and put paired  tests/N.in  /  tests/N.out  files beside it.
The program is  solution.py , read from stdin, compared to the samples with
 diff . It needs Python 3 and bash. To keep it with one repo instead, copy
the folder into that project's  .memdoor/workflows/ . The project's copy wins. 
 The steps name no model. Whatever  /model  is pinned to answers, a local one
included ( memdoor connect local  for Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, LM Studio or janis:
 how to connect one ). 
  How it works     
   plan ──┬── ideate-a ──┬── solve ── test ── review ── repair ── verify
       └── ideate-b ──┘

 kind

  plan  
 agent 
  task.md  
  plan.md , and a  notes.md  ledger with one anchor per ideator 
 
 
  ideate-a ,  ideate-b  
 agent, in parallel 
  task.md ,  plan.md ,  notes.md  
 a proposal at its own anchor: A the most direct provable algorithm, B one from a different family of technique 
 
 
  solve

 the decision in  notes.md ,  solution.py  
 
 
  test

  tests/  
  test-output.log ,  test-status.txt  (never fails the run) 
 
 
  review

 the captured test output, not a model's claim 
  review.md , repair instructions in  notes.md  
 
 
  repair

 a fixed  solution.py , or nothing if the samples passed 
 
 
  verify

  tests/
