 Every agent prompt says "fresh context, read the files, do not rely on chat".
The paper credits that ledger discipline for the gain. There is one repair
round and no human gate. The last step is the whole verdict: 
   type: command
requires:
  - table_pattern: repair
command: |
  check=.memdoor/workflows/team-solve/check-samples.sh
  [ -f "$check" ] || check="$HOME/.memdoor/workflows/team-solve/check-samples.sh"
  bash "$check" > final-test-output.log 2>&1
  result=$?
  cat final-test-output.log
  exit "$result"
   
 Each step is one YAML file in  steps/ , the format of
 mario , the engine underneath.
 requires:  is the DAG. Changing a role means changing its prompt. 
  What the first run found     
 The sample: count the substrings of a string over {a, b, c} with equal
counts of each letter, up to 200,000 characters. Run on the default ladder
through OpenRouter: 
 
 8 of 8 steps, 5 of 5 samples. The solver took ideator A's prefix-state
method, O(N) with a dictionary of (a−b, a−c) pairs. A brute force on 300
random strings found no mismatch afterwards, and it runs in 0.04 s at
N = 200,000. The manager found nothing to repair. 
 One ideator's provider dropped the stream mid-answer. The coder had written
 max_retries: 0 , so the run died there. The agent steps now carry
 max_retries: 1 , and the run was resumed with  --partition , which kept the
planner's and the other ideator's work. 
 The ideator prompts the coder wrote named the sample's methods (A: a
streaming prefix-state count, B: sorting prefix states), which would steer
any other problem the wrong way. They now ask A for the most direct
provable algorithm and B for one from a different family of technique
(2026-10-28). 
 The first attempts failed every step in 0 s with "no agent named coder": a
run looked its agent up only in its own workspace. That was fixed in the
gateway the same day (v1.692.0).

# Prospero: a bloat-free, native AI coding harness with ImGui

Prospero is a native GUI application for Windows, macOS, and Linux that connects to an AI model provider, local or remote, allowing AI agents to drive your computer to develop software. It plows through intermittent errors and keeps at its task while unattended. It speaks the OpenAI Chat Completions API, used by llama.cpp, vLLM, LiteLLM, and providers with a compatible API. Also Anthropic's Messages API, with extended thinking and prompt caching. No providers are configured out of the box.

The UI is highly flexible, and you can rearrange the panes as you please with dragging and docking. Save your layouts for later in View -> Layouts. Unlike conventional ImGui applications, rendering is passive and will not consume resources while idle. It is a single executable, written in C++. In the typical case the engine runs in the same process as the window, and needs no daemon or server. The same executable can run headless, on another machine over ssh, or in the background after its window closes. The engine is lean and portable, and runs on computers and operating systems a quarter century old. Imagine a coding harness on Windows XP. Once it's connected to a provider, **you can ask Prospero for help with itself**. It will read its own embedded documentation, self-configure, and navigate you to any place in its UI. Prospero's desktop control features allow it to effectively develop, test, and debug native GUI applications. On Windows, it especially works well in [w64devkit][], making use of its shell and tools if available. You can start new sessions from the command line, even if there's already an instance, by invoking Prospero with a path where the new session will be rooted. For example, to start a session here: $ prospero . After no arguments, this is the second most common way to run Prospero. ## Documentation - [Usage](docs/usage.md): running it, sessions, the GUI, attachments, modes and the command line - [Configuration](docs/configuration.md): `prospero.ini`, endpoints, models, roles, instructions, skills, MCP servers and web search - [Desktop control](docs/desktop.md): letting the agent see and drive the screen - [Remote and background hosts](docs/remote.md): engines on other machines over ssh, and sessions that outlive the window - [Windows notes](docs/windows.md) - [Building](docs/building.md): building from source, and releases - [Development](docs/development.md): tests, and evals for comparing models Prospero also carries its own documentation, under Help, which an agent in it can read too. ## License Prospero is free and unencumbered software released into the public domain. See [UNLICENSE](UNLICENSE). Its programs include third-party code under its own licenses: Dear ImGui (MIT), FreeType (FTL), md4c (MIT), SDL3 (zlib), cpp-httplib (MIT), Mbed TLS (Apache-2.0), and Wuffs (Apache-2.0 or MIT, at your option), which every program with the engine includes. [w64devkit]: https://github.com/skeeto/w64devkit

Prospero: a new coding harness for a more civilized age 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
    Prospero: a new coding harness for a more civilized age  
   
    October 31, 2026
   
   
    nullprogram.com/blog/2026/10/31/
   

 I’ve been  fascinated with local LLMs  for a couple of years now.
The better open weight models, including some that inference on regular,
higher-end consumer hardware at tolerable speeds, are now reliable enough
to handle simpler programming tasks. This requires a coding harness, but
so far this year I’ve been disappointed by all the harness offerings. For
inexplicable reasons most are built with web stacks, and consume enormous
amounts of memory. At its core a coding harness is essentially curl glued
to  popen() . This should not require gigabytes of RAM. So I built my own:
  Prospero  . It’s written in  my C++ style  with a snappy  Dear
ImGui docking interface . It uses around two orders of magnitude
fewer resources than other harnesses without sacrificing features. 

   

 Dark mode aficionados are covered, too: 

   

 Note that Prospero comes with no model providers built-in. You’re expected
to supply that yourself, such as with  llama.cpp , a workplace on-prem
model, OpenRouter, Anthropic API, OpenAI API, etc. (You can’t use your
Claude subscription.) 

 For those unfamiliar with coding harnesses: In a chat interface you and
the AI take turns writing messages to each other. A coding harness extends
this concept, allowing an AI to “talk” to tools offered by the harness.
Tools “reply” with their outputs. A tool might read or write a file, or
run a shell command. An AI will go from tool call to tool call on its own,
looping on the results. Such an AI is called an  agent . Occasionally the
AI will send you a message to inform you of progress or to ask a question,
and the chat interface is still there. 

 Some harnesses, including Prospero, allow agents to spawn  subagents  to
do their bidding, to work in parallel or keep their  context  clean. That
is, to not fill their working memory with subtasks. Agents can message one
another and coordinate on tasks. Given SSH access to another machine, or
over plain WSL, Prospero can deploy a headless copy of itself to other
hosts so that agents can operate on those systems. The  Professional
Edition  embeds engines for combinations of x86/x86-64 and ARM64 on
macOS, Windows, and Linux. The Windows x86 engine even works on Windows
XP, and can play solitaire and minesweeper if you ask. 

 The last is because Prospero is one of the few harnesses with  desktop
control  capabilities. If your model supports vision — any any model worth
using does — then it can “see” your desktop and interact with it. It can
click, type, and drag to test and debug GUI applications live without a
specialized, per-app  MCP assist . 

 This headless engine is why no TUI is necessary. The harness engine runs
on the headless system, and the UI runs on your desktop or laptop. With a
little extra setup, the harness to run fully independently of the GUI, so
that it will continue without the GUI system attached — re-attachable
later. 

 Because Prospero is so lean, it may be the only harness that can drive a
 fuzz campaign , particularly on a headless system, without the
Linux OOM killer targeting  the memory-gobbling harness  rather than the
out-of-control fuzz target that triggered it. So many times I’ve checked
back in on a fuzz campaign hours later, to find nothing was accomplished
because the harness process is gone. 

 (Why have an agent run a fuzz campaign? Because it can fix discovered bugs
on the fly and keep the campaign going! It’s a no brainer.) 

 Configuration 

 The configuration lives at  ~/.config/prospero/prospero.ini . Easy to
edit. No JSON, thank goodness. Check it into source control, copy-paste
it. All the usual benefits. Alternatively, the Settings page can reach
every setting from the GUI, so you don’t have to edit the INI by hand. INI
files can also include each other, not just naming file system paths but
URLs: 

   include  = https://example.com/prospero.ini
  

 The idea is to allow a live shared or managed configuration. Includes by
URL are restricted in what they can set, with a hard rule against anything
which might appear in shell command. Some trust is still required, as a
configuration can extract an environment variable by using it as an API
key and supplying an endpoint it controls. 

 Prospero fetches a model list and other parameters like context size from
the endpoint, but you might want to tweak it. A typical configuration may
look like: 

   model  = falstaff/Qwen3.8-27B

 [endpoint falstaff] 
 url  = http://falstaff.local/
 key  = env:FALSTAFF_API_KEY

 [model Qwen3.8-27B] 
 edit_format  = replace
 template.reasoning_effort  = medium

 [model Qwen3.8-27B-xhigh] 
 like  = Qwen3.8-27B
 template.reasoning_effort  = xhigh

 [web] 
 search  = searxng
 url  = https://search.example.com/
 key  = env:EXAMPLE_API_KEY
  

 Passive rendering 

 The ImGui paradigm typically uses  active rendering , redrawing on vsync
like a video game. This is appropriate in some contexts, like interfaces
within video games. Less so for mostly-static text-oriented UIs, such as a
coding harness. Instead Prospero uses  passive rendering  with  settle
frames  to finish animations before going idle. When there’s nothing to
do, Prospero does nothing. It won’t chew on the GPU while the agent is
waiting on a build. 

 Never wait forever 

 An annoyance with most other harnesses is how easily they get stuck. I set
a long-running task, go to sleep, and in the morning find the harness hung
on a trivial issue two hours into the night, wasting the rest. Therefore
Prospero prime design principle:  Never wait forever .  Every operation
has a deadline.  This decision influences everything. If you’re not there
to grant a requested permission, the agent will get a denial by timeout
and must do without. To assist, Prospero will raise a system toast when an
agent requires your attention so that you’re less likely to miss it if
you’re attending. 

 The harness itself  plows through intermittent errors , trying its best to
drive the agent to complete its task. All network requests have timeouts,
and watchdogs prevent  endless waiting . Agent mailboxes  are
bounded . 

 Shell commands that hit their timeout convert to asynchronous background
commands. The agent can continue to wait on them, with a timeout, and so
will be woken at regular intervals to decide if it should continue. 

 The one exception is Plan mode, where it waits indefinitely after offering
a plan or requesting clarification ( ask_user  tool). It’s expected that a
user is attending to the agent during Plan mode. 

 No stray processes 

 The harnesses I’ve used have improved, but another regular annoyance
earlier this year was agents starting processes that never get cleaned up.
An agent kicks off a parallel build, hits a timeout because it was too
optimistic, the build “stops” by killing a piece of the build system. But
actually  the build continues anyway , at least in part. The agent tries
again, and now two builds are going, interfering with each other, making a
mess and bringing my system to its knees. 

 For awhile I was wary of letting agents run builds in certain harnesses,
which is a terrible outcome.  You want agents to close the loop  and
iterate independently. A human in the loop is like putting a ball and
chain on the agent, giving up most of its advantages. 

 Prospero promoting a synchronous timeout to an asynchronous task is a huge
improvement on its own, but there’s an additional principle at play: The
whole process tree lives and dies together. When a command is stopped,  it
stops . This is  trivial on Windows , though few harnesses seem to
take advantage of it. It’s more difficult on macOS and Linux, but Prospero
follows through. 

 Built-in self-help 

 Like every harness, Prospero supports  skills , a pre-packaged set of
instructions on how to accomplish some task (“I know kung fu.”). Prospero
contains a skill on itself and can read its built-in documentation. Ask
the agent how to do or configure something in Prospero, and the agent can
only answers your question, it can provide a hyperlink taking you to the
relevant place in the UI. It can also edit your  prospero.ini  and reload
it, to configure things on your behalf. This is not unique to Prospero,
but I’m not aware of any harness doing this nearly as well. 

 Choose your shell 

 On Windows, Prospero is designed to work well with  w64devkit , and will
prefer its shell if available. Models designed for coding know w64devkit
out-of-the-box, so these tools are complementary. Of course you’re not
locked into that shell, and you can freely choose a different default
shell. But Prospero is a rare harness where you can change shells mid
session. Sometimes PowerShell is more suited to the task, so you can pick
it out of the dropdown. The agent is informed of the change, and told
about known quirks (i.e. “this is an old Bash!”). On macOS you can switch
between bash and zsh. 

 The usual features 

 Prospero has the usual sorts of features you can expect from an advanced
shell. It can use Git worktrees, including subagent worktrees, so that
agents can share a repository. It speaks the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
It can search the web (if you allow). You can start side chats that share
context, realized as subagents. You can fork sessions. 

 For now there is no built-in terminal or editor. Instead Prospero will
open an external terminal or editor of your choosing. I’d rather use Vim
than a built-in notepad.exe-equivalent. With Ctrl+G you can edit your
prompt in an external editor. 

 Like all harnesses, the permissions system will not stop a malicious
agent. Agents are writing and running programs on your computer, and so
can ultimately access everything the harness can access. Permissions are
about gently reminding the agent of your wishes, and catching simple
mistakes. More like, “Whoa there, stay within the project” or, “Do not
control my desktop at this time.” If you want to lock an agent out, you
have to restrict the harness itself, putting it in a container or on a
Raspberry Pi, at the usual cost of inconvenience or cutting off useful
resources. 

 Community Edition versus Professional 

 I’m really excited about Prospero, and  I honestly feel it’s one of the
best coding harnesses available . It’s how such tools ought to be built,
but until now nobody else stepped up to do it. It would take a video to do
it justice, and maybe I’ll do that sometime, but that’s currently outside
my experience. 

 Most of the audience for my projects are hobbyists, even w64devkit. But if
Prospero goes beyond me and my little circle, I expect most users would be
professionals building commercial products. I’ve also invested more than
just my time into this project — already true for w64devkit, even more
true with Prospero. So while it’s an open source project, I’ve split it
into two tiers: 

 
   
     Community Edition: the build you find on GitHub at no cost. It has no
built-in headless engines, so remote deployments are limited. Plus a
little nag text to remind you you’re on the Community Edition. Suited
for hobbyists. 
   
   
      Professional Edition : Pay a nominal fee, get a DRM-free download
with free updates. All the headless engines are built in so you can push
remote deployments and remote sessions on other systems at the press of
a button. A serious feature for professionals. 
   
 

 Windows and macOS builds are code-signed in both cases (some of the cost).
If Prospero is useful for you professionally, even without the remote
deployment feature, you’re still encouraged to buy a copy to support my
ongoing costs!

  > I don't know why you needed a paragraph to say that 1000% memory inflation is a trade-off to optimize dev costs Because that's not what I said. My point was more that a "1000% memory inflation" is not a meaningful cost metric to begin with (to use just one toy example, perhaps you'd agree that going from 10% RAM to 100% has a very different impact than going from 1% to 10%, even though both are a "1000% inflation"). Memory (at least on a personal computer) is not rented by the hour on a per-MB basis; you buy it in bulk. What matters isn't how much memory you could have used but what you'd use the "saved" memory for. Also, when you buy a resource like RAM or CPU as a package, nominal values matter less than under what conditions one of these would reach 100% and your experience may be degraded. For example, if you have 16GB of RAM and you only ever run one program at a time, it doesn't matter to you at all if it uses 3GB or 3MB: you've paid for 16 and the total savings of the 3MB app are zero and in this hypothetical case, there's no tradeoff at all. Now, the average user on the average hardware doesn't use only one GUI app at a time, but they're also not using 200. The only relevant question pertaining to waste is what is the value of 3% memory to your users (integrated over all of them)? In many situations (again, not all), the answer is not much. (And BTW, some developers seem to care about 3% memory more than they do about 3% CPU, even though CPU is much more expensive). When it comes to agent harnesses, the analysis is clearer. On the one hand, people using coding agents are more likely than others to put even a little extra free RAM to some good use, but on the other hand, the cost of using the models themselves is so high that it makes the cost of RAM for the GUI negligible. Saying that a number going up by 1000% is bad is not good engineering. Good engineering requires thinking about the actual value and cost of that number. It varies over time, over app type, over different types of users, and over different kinds of deployments (i.e. how RAM is packaged and paid for).      reply                             neuroelectron    10 hours ago       |  root  |  parent  |  next   [–]

 Prospero is a native GUI application for Windows, macOS, and Linux that
connects to an AI model provider, local or remote, allowing AI agents to
drive your computer to develop software. It plows through intermittent
errors and keeps at its task while unattended. It speaks the OpenAI Chat
Completions API, used by llama.cpp, vLLM, LiteLLM, and providers with a
compatible API. Also Anthropic's Messages API, with extended thinking and
prompt caching. No providers are configured out of the box.

with dragging and docking. Save your layouts for later in View -> Layouts.

consume resources while idle.

runs in the same process as the window, and needs no daemon or server. The
same executable can run headless, on another machine over ssh, or in the
background after its window closes. The engine is lean and portable, and
runs on computers and operating systems a quarter century old. Imagine a
coding harness on Windows XP.

itself . It will read its own embedded documentation, self-configure, and
navigate you to any place in its UI.

and debug native GUI applications. On Windows, it especially works well in
 w64devkit , making use of its shell and tools if available. 
 You can start new sessions from the command line, even if there's already
an instance, by invoking Prospero with a path where the new session will
be rooted. For example, to start a session here:

         It's the memory latency, stupid 
         Making GROUP BY faster by doing more (CPU!) work 
         October 28, 2026 · Maor Kern 
       
       
  Disclaimer  no LLMs were harmed (or for that matter used) in the writing of this blog post  
 When you see your databases CPU at 100%, what is it  actually  doing? We like to act as though CPUs run code linearly for simplicity's sake, but in truth CPUs are incredibly complex beasts; they can potentially do many instructions at once, or sometimes none at all (despite our console showing 100%). Because CPUs can do so many things, one CPU at 100% may be doing much less than another at 100%. A CPU is considered "idle" only if no task (Linux task) needs CPU time; this does not mean the CPU itself is being fully saturated. So why would a CPU not be fully utilized, even if it appears to be at 100%? 
 The answer is usually  memory . 
 Memory accesses are orders of magnitude slower than internal CPU operations. To give a good picture of how much so, a modern CPU might be able to process somewhere in the realm of 4-8 instructions per nanosecond. A memory access to RAM can take somewhere in the realm of 50-100ns. To ease your mathing, that means a modern CPU can do around 400-800 instructions for every  one  memory access from RAM. 
     CPU     CPU core  4–8 instr / ns          L1 cache  ~1 ns   ~64 KB · ~4–8 instructions per access             L2 cache  ~3–4 ns   ~1 MB · ~15–30 instructions per access             L3 cache  ~10–15 ns   up to a few hundred MB · ~50–100 instructions per access             DRAM  ~50–100 ns   GBs · ~400–800 instructions per access         
 Given this, CPUs are built from the ground up to work their way around this. The most obvious way this is dealt with is CPU caches. CPU caches keep memory closer to the CPU than RAM, literally baked into the CPU chip. The closest cache (the L1 cache) takes around 1ns per memory operation- that's 50-100x faster than RAM! The "problem" here of course is that the CPU caches are fairly small; the L1 cache for a modern CPU is probably around ~64KB, while the farther caches max out at a few hundred MB for top end processors. A good database tries manipulating data in small "chunks" to take full advantage of caches, and you'll often hear cache utilization as being one of the top concerns of performance engineering. 
 Let's look at GROUP BY aggregations to get a better grip on cache utilization. In GROUP BY, we're looking to take a dataset, group it by a certain column (or more), and perform certain aggregations (for example, count, or sum on another column). The "naive" method might be to open a HashTable keyed by the group key that grows ever larger. For every new row, you would check if that key exists- if it does, go to it's corresponding aggregation and update the result. Simple, right? The problem is that if you have millions of unique groups, you're not utilizing your cache at all! Nearly every HashTable access will be a "cold" hit that goes to RAM. This means that although your CPU may /look/ like it's 100% utilized, in truth it'll constantly be waiting for cold memory accesses. 
 To demonstrate this, we'll take our state-of-the-art Pivot engine and ravage it! We'll remove all our complex logic and replace it with simplicity: 
    fn   consume (
    & mut   self ,
    batch:  RecordBatch ,
    _sender: & mut   dyn   Sender < RecordBatch >,
) -> unary:: Result <()> {
     let  group_keys = batch. column ( self .key_column). as_primitive ::< Int64Type >();
     for  &key  in  group_keys. values () {
         // If the Group Key doesn't exist- set it to 0 
         // Afterwards, add 1 to the group- this will give us a count(*) GROUP BY key_column 
        * self .counts. entry (key). or_insert ( 0 ) +=  1 ;
    }
}       
 We'll then run a simple query  SELECT count(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID  on the "hits" dataset ClickBench provides (99m rows). This query will give us a count per  UserID , meaning we'll have an entry in our HashMap per  UserID - I'll give a spoiler here that there are ~17m unique  UserID . 
Our performance checks will be on a bare metal server from our good friends over at CherryServers (AMD EPYC 9124 Genoa, 16 cores, 128 GB DDR5). We unfortunately can't use a common AWS/GCP machine because we want access to counters that aren't exposed there for security reasons (for example, we want to see how much memory is passing from DRAM controller to us). We'll confine ourselves to a single core, since this naive group by can't run on many cores. 
 To run it: 
    cat  > config.yaml << 'EOF' 
 server :
   bind : 127.0.0.1:5440
 workers : 1
 datastores :
   default :
     kind : pivotlake
     location : ./data
     default : true
 users :
   pivot :
     auth :
       method : trust
 EOF 
 taskset   -c  3  pivot  server  --config  config.yaml &
 taskset   -c  7  psql   -h  127.0.0.1  -p  5440  -U  pivot  -c   '\timing on'   -c   "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"        
 This takes... a whopping 3.9 seconds. Is that good? Is that bad? Everything in this world is relative, or so they say. If we run the query again (without restarting the server), it takes 3.6s. The second run is the one we're more interested in- there's no disk involved as everything is already sitting in our page-cache. 
 You'll notice we did  taskset -c . This pins the process to a given CPU; this will allow us to run  perf stat  on that CPU and see what's going on internally. We'll measure two metric groups- percentage of CPU slots stalling because of memory (and not doing anything in the meanwhile), and percentage of CPU slots actually retiring a micro-op: 
    sudo   perf  stat  -C  3  -M  backend_bound_memory,retiring --  taskset   -c  7  psql   -h  127.0.0.1  -p  5440  -U  pivot  -c   "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"        
 and we get back this 
   Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

        8364109137      ex_no_retire.load_not_complete   #     50.1 %  backend_bound_memory
       38233214040      de_no_dispatch_per_slot.backend_stalls
        8977647849      ex_no_retire.not_complete
       11861387798      ls_not_halted_cyc
       11431618219      ex_ret_ops                       #     16.1 %  retiring
       11858248045      ls_not_halted_cyc

       4.030148989 seconds time elapsed       
 This tells us that 50.1% of the time, the CPU couldn't do anything because it was stalling on memory! And only 16.1% of the time the CPU was actually retiring (aka doing) operations. 
 Another interesting stat to get is how many of our CPU memory loads are coming from DRAM (and not from caches): 
    sudo   perf  stat  -C  3    -e  ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near   --  taskset   -c  7  psql   -h  127.0.0.1  -p  5440  -U  pivot  -c   "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"        
 And the result: 
    Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

          76190837      ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near

       3.996301634 seconds time elapsed       
 Every load is 64 bytes (the minimum amount you can bring, a cache line), so we can multiply by 64 to see we pulled 4.5GB during this query from DRAM on CPU loads (this is without any prefetching). 
 Let's now try to improve our algorithm to take advantage of the CPU caches. To do this, we'll use a method called radix partitioning. The idea is to split the merge into two distinct phases: 
  Phase 1:  In this phase, we're simply going to separate the keys into 4096 different partitions (simply a Vec of SlabVecs- a SlabVec is a data structure similar to a Vec that is above memory that is already paged in. We don't use Vecs for raw memory in Pivot because it creates a lot of variance; not something for this blog post!). The partition will be decided by hashing the key and taking it's top 12 bits (2**12=4096). 
    fn   consume (
    & mut   self ,
    batch:  RecordBatch ,
    _sender: & mut   dyn   Sender < RecordBatch >,
) -> unary:: Result <()> {
     let  keys = batch. column ( self .key_column). as_primitive ::< Int64Type >();
     for  &key  in  keys. values () {
         let  hash =  self .hasher. hash_one (key);
         // Since we want top 12 bits, we shift the hash (a u64) 52 bits to the right 
         let  partition = (hash >>  52 )  as  usize;
         self .partitions[partition]. push (& mut   self .allocator, (hash, key));
    }
     Ok (())
}              UserID  hash(UserID)       7   0x 002 A91F3…     42   0x 000 7C4E2…     13   0x FFF 3B05D…     7   0x 002 A91F3…     5   0x 001 D6A88…     42   0x 000 7C4E2…     99   0x 002 E17B4…     7   0x 002 A91F3…     →   partition =  hash >> 52 , the first 3 hex digits     Partition 0  0x000000… – 0x000FFF…    42  42      Partition 1  0x001000… – 0x001FFF…    5      Partition 2  0x002000… – 0x002FFF…    7  7  99  7        …     Partition 4095  0xFFF000… – 0xFFFFFF…    13        
  Phase 2:  When all data has come through, go partition by partition, each time creating a HashMap, aggregating the partition into it, and then outputting it. This phase is very similar to our original algorithm, but we're going to use the hash from phase 1. 
    fn   into_outputter ( self ) -> unary:: Result < Option < Self :: Outputter >> {
     let   mut  groups =  Vec :: new ();
     for  rows  in  & self .partitions {
         let   mut  table:  HashTable <(u64, i64, u64)> =  HashTable :: new ();    // (hash, key, count) 
        rows. for_each (|(hash, key)| {
             match  table. entry (hash, |group| group. 1  == key, |group| group. 0 ) {
                 Entry :: Occupied ( mut  group) => group. get_mut (). 2  +=  1 ,
                 Entry :: Vacant (slot) => { slot. insert ((hash, key,  1 )); }
            }
        });
        groups. extend (table. into_iter (). map (|(_, key, count)| (key, count)));
    }
     Ok ( Some ( Outputter :: new (groups)))
}           Partitions, one at a time                                     0–1 done  2 in progress  3–4095 waiting     Partition 2    HashTable    Output   7  7  99  7   →    UserID  count    7  3    99  1    →    (UserID, count)    (7, 3)    (99, 1)      
 At first glance, this solution may seem rather odd. We're doing  more  operations here, not less! Every row, in both solutions, is hashed and sent into a HashMap. But in this solution, we're first pushing rows into seemingly meaningless vecs. 
 The key here (no pun intended) is to understand why we've done this; it's to make the aggregating HashMaps  smaller . By dividing our group by into 4096 pieces, we've made our working HashMaps much likelier to fit into our CPU caches. Every time we do a lookup on our HashMap, our CPU is more likely to find the relevant memory sitting in it's caches, which saves a big chunk of time. But why trust me? Let's run it! 
    taskset   -c  7  psql   -h  127.0.0.1  -p  5440  -U  pivot  -c   '\timing on'   -c   "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"        
 And... Boom! 3.3 seconds, and then on second run 2.7 seconds! We've definitely made an improvement. But to really drive this point home, let's run perf again: 
    sudo   perf  stat  -C  3  -M  backend_bound_memory,retiring --  taskset   -c  7  psql   -h  127.0.0.1  -p  5440  -U  pivot  -c   "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"        
 And our results: 
    Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

        3790955223      ex_no_retire.load_not_complete   #     23.5 %  backend_bound_memory
       20376118172      de_no_dispatch_per_slot.backend_stalls
        5442424751      ex_no_retire.not_complete
       10083617764      ls_not_halted_cyc
       19350459182      ex_ret_ops                       #     32.2 %  retiring
       10023435553      ls_not_halted_cyc

       3.575992317 seconds time elapsed       
 Now we can see the picture has completely changed- 23.5% of the time is spent on waiting for memory (as opposed to 50% before), 32% for actually retiring operations. You may notice we're actually doing  more  work, not less- in this run, we did 19350459182 operations (the  ex_ret_ops  counter), whereas before the database did 11431618219 operations. This is worth it though, because as we said before- if we can translate cold DRAM accesses into CPU instructions, it's nearly always a good trade to make. In this case, we went down from 8364109137 CPU slots stalled because of memory to 3790955223. 
 To complete the picture and really see we're pulling less memory from the DRAM, let's again check how many our memory loads come from DRAM: 
    sudo   perf  stat  -C  3    -e  ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near   --  taskset   -c  7  psql   -h  127.0.0.1  -p  5440  -U  pivot  -c   "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"            Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

          25688280      ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near

       3.009547012 seconds time elapsed       
 Whoo! That means that on demand we pulled 1.5GB from DRAM, instead of 4.5GB in the naive version. 
 That, of course, isn't the limit of how much we can utilize our CPU cache for GROUP BYs. And utilizing our CPU cache isn't the only way we can "hide" DRAM latency; another trick is prefetching memory to our cache before we need it, and yet another trick is creating algorithms that allow maximization of memory throughput- but that's not for this blog! We'll go into that in our next blog where we look at our /seemingly very weird/ implementation of JOIN probing. 
 For now, without explaining too much, I'll leave you with Pivot's speed for this query on a single core: 
   Time: 1848.353 ms (00:01.848)       
 and the amount of RAM we bring: 
    Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

          14917958      ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near

       2.182674864 seconds time elapsed       
 Which comes out to 954 MB. 
 Of course, Pivot knows to run in parallel on our 16 cores (where there are many other interesting cases), in which case it comes out to: 
   Time: 171.773 ms       
 nice :) 
 Try out Pivot if you want to have super speeds above parquets (OSS fun!), see you next time.

# Overview
This repository contains an annotated disassembly of the _Contra_ (US) NES ROM
and the build script(s) to reassemble the assembly into a byte-for-byte match of
the game.  This repo also contains supplemental documentation, diagrams,
scripts, and tools to help further understand the game.

A special thanks goes to Trax.  This project would not have gotten started
without the amazing initial disassembly by him for his [Revenge of the Red
Falcon](https://www.romhacking.net/hacks/2701/) project.

For the disassembly of _Contra_'s sequel, see
https://github.com/vermiceli/nes-super-c/

```
|-- docs - supplemental documentation
|   |-- attachments - files used in other documentation
|   |-- debugging - files used to help debugging
|   |-- diagrams - mermaid diagram files documenting program flow
|   |-- lua_scripts - lua scripts for mesen and fceux
|   |-- sprite_library - extracted sprites for ease of viewing
|-- src - the source code for the game
|   |-- assets - the compressed graphics data and encoded audio for the game
|-- assets.txt - a list of assets, their offset in baserom.nes and their length
|-- build.bat - build script for Windows Command Prompt (CMD) (no PowerShell)
|-- build.ps1 - recommended build script for Windows (PowerShell)
|-- build.sh - bash build script for Linux/macOS
|-- contra.cfg - memory mapping of PRG banks used when building
|-- README.md
|-- set_bytes.vbs - script used by build.bat to extract data from baserom.nes
```
# Building

In addition to _Contra_ (US), this repo can also build the _Probotector_ ROM.
To keep instructions simple, the section below only contains instructions for
building _Contra_ (US).

If you are interested in building a _Probotector_ ROM file, first read this
section to understand what is needed, then follow the instructions in the
section titled _Probotector_.

## Prerequisites
  * This repo does not include all assets (graphics data and audio data)
  necessary for assembling the ROM. An existing copy of the game is required.
  Place a copy of the US NES version of _Contra_ with the name `baserom.nes` in
  the project root folder.  The file will be used by the build script to extract
  the necessary assets.  The MD5 hash of `baserom.nes` ROM should be
  `7BDAD8B4A7A56A634C9649D20BD3011B`.
  * Building requires the [cc65 compiler suite](https://cc65.github.io/) to
  assemble and link the 6502 assembly files.  Please install it and ensure the
  bin folder is added to your path.

## Instructions
There are 3 build scripts in this repository. All of them do the same thing.  To
build the resulting .nes ROM file, simply execute the appropriate build script
based on your environment.

| Environment             | Command       |
|-------------------------|---------------|
| Windows                 | `.\build.ps1` |
| Windows (no PowerShell) | `.\build.bat` |
| Mac/Unix/Linux          | `./build.sh`  |

* `build.ps1` - PowerShell script recommended for building on Windows machines.
  Some users have reported needing to run the script as admin to access the
  `baserom.nes`, although I haven't experienced this.  Additionally, on older
  versions of PowerShell, you may need to adjust the execution policy with the
  command `Set-ExecutionPolicy`.
* `build.bat` - bat script that can be used on windows machines without
  PowerShell, but requires VBScript support.
* `build.sh` - bash script to be used in unix environments, or on Windows
  environments with bash support (Git bash, WSL, etc.)

### Video Instructions
If you prefer video build instructions, @jdsilva has published a video on
YouTube called
[Contra ROM Compiling Tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Sa1O3S5YK5U)

## Documentation

Supplemental materials have been added that help explain interesting features of
the code.  Below are some of the more important documents.

* [docs/Aim Documentation.md](./docs/Aim%20Documentation.md) - documentation on
  how enemy aiming works
* [docs/Bugs.md](./docs/Bugs.md) - bugs identified while disassembling
* [docs/Contra Control Flow.md](./docs/Contra%20Control%20Flow.md) - detailed
  look at the game routine and level routine flows.
* [docs/Enemy Glossary.md](./docs/Enemy%20Glossary.md) - documentation on every
  enemy type in the game
* [docs/Enemy Routines.md](./docs/Enemy%20Routines.md) - documentation on level
  enemy configuration and random soldier generation.
* [docs/Graphics Documentation.md](./docs/Graphics%20Documentation.md) -
  documentation on pattern tables, nametables, palettes, palette cycling,
  super-tiles, background collision, and compression.
* [docs/Native Port Coverage.md](./docs/Native%20Port%20Coverage.md) -
  bank-by-bank tracker for what the native port currently translates, uses as
  ROM-backed data, stubs, and still misses.
* [docs/Native Port Reliability.md](./docs/Native%20Port%20Reliability.md) -
  repeatable test, code coverage, and routine-ledger plan for increasing native
  port confidence.
* [docs/ROM Map.md](./docs/ROM%20Map.md) - detailed description of ROM file
  contents 
* [docs/Sound Documentation.md](./docs/Sound%20Documentation.md) - documentation
  on the audio engine used as well as information on all sounds from the game.

All sprites were captured and labeled for easy reference in
[docs/sprite_library/README.md](./docs/sprite_library/README.md)

### Getting Started

At first, there is a lot to take in and it may be confusing where to start.
The files in the repo under the `src/` folder are broken up based on the memory
banks in the game.  The _Contra_ cartridge is a
[UxROM](https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/UxROM) cartridge.  The game has 8, 16 KiB
banks of memory for a total size of 128 KiB.  Banks 0 through 6 are swapped in
and out of memory at address $8000-$bfff and bank 7 is always in memory at
$c000-$ffff.  Knowing this helps understand the code since only 2 banks are
available at any given time.  The start of the game and most of the game engine
logic exists in `bank7.asm` since that's in memory all of the time and where
the 3 NES interrupts are.

I think a good way to start reading this code is to look into
`docs/Contra Control Flow.md`.  That file shows the responsibilities of the game
engine loop routines and in what order those routines are called.

* `bank0.asm` - used exclusively for enemy routines. Enemy routines are the
  logic controlling enemy behaviors and settings: AI, movements, attack
  patterns, health, etc. Almost every enemy is coded in bank 0, but some
  enemy routines, usually those who appear in more than one level, are in
  `bank7.asm`.
* `bank1.asm` - responsible for audio and sprites.  The audio code takes up
  about 3/4 of the bank. The remaining 1/4 of the bank is for sprite data and
  code to draw sprites.
* `bank2.asm` - starts with RLE-encoded level data (graphic super-tiles for the
  level screens).  It then contains compressed tile data and alternate tile data
  and occasional attribute table data.  Then, bank 2 contains logic for setting
  the players' sprite based on player state.  Next, bank 2 contains the level
  headers, which define specifics about each level. Bank 2 then has the data
  that specifies which enemies are on which screen and their attributes.  Bank
  2 also contains the soldier enemy generation code.
* `bank3.asm` - starts with the data that specifies which pattern table tiles
  comprise super-tiles along with the color palettes.  This bank also has the
  routines to manage the end of levels.
* `bank4.asm` - mostly contains compressed graphic data. The rest of bank 4 is
  the code for the ending scene animation and the ending credits, including the
  ending credits text data.
* `bank5.asm` - mostly contains compressed graphic data.  The rest of bank 5 is
  the code and lookup tables for automated input for the 3 demo (attract)
  levels.
* `bank6.asm` - contains compressed graphics data, data for short text sequences
  like level names and menu options.  Bank 6 also contains the code for the
  players' weapons and bullets.
* `bank7.asm` - the core of the game's programming. Reset, NMI, and IRQ vectors
  are in this bank and is the entry point to the game.  Bank 7 contains the code
  for drawing nametables and sprites, bank switching, routines for the intro
  sequence, controller input, score calculation, graphics decompression
  routines, palette codes, collision detection, pointer table for enemy
  routines, shared enemy logic, score table, enemy attributes, and bullet angles
  and speeds, and the NES undocumented footer, among other things.

### Annotations

While reviewing the assembly, I used a notation to categorize unexpected, or
interesting observations.  You can search the code for these annotations.

* `!(BUG?)` - a possible bug
* `!(HUH)` - unexpected code or logic used
* `!(WHY?)` - unsure of why the code is the way it is
* `!(UNUSED)` - unused code or data that is never executed nor read
* `!(OBS)` - observation or note

# Debugging

One of the biggest advantages of building this ROM is that the build scripts
also build the debugging symbols.  Debugging symbols can be read by emulators
and be included in the source view while debugging the game.  For example,
[Mesen](https://github.com/SourMesen/Mesen2) will automatically load the
debugging symbols as long as the `contra.dbg` file exists in the same folder as
`contra.nes`.  Below is a screenshot of what debugging looks like with symbols.

![Mesen debugger screenshot](docs/attachments/mesen_debugger_screenshot.png?raw=true)

You can see that the debugging symbols file points to the source code to include
comments and labels.  If you move or delete the source files, you will lose all
the debugging information.

## FCEUX NameList

[FCEUX](https://fceux.com/web/home.html) doesn't support reading the debugger
symbols, but you can load NameList (`.nl`) files.  These files aren't as fully
featured as the debugging symbols file, but does at least allow you to label
jump/branch locations and ram addresses.  It doesn't easily support comments on
individual lines.

I've included the `.nl` files in `docs/debugging/fceux_namelists` for both
_Contra_ and _Probotector_.  These files were generated from the
`-m contra.txt -vm` command line parameter to `ld65`.  Then the that file was
converted to the `.nl` files with a custom script.  I can't promise to keep
these up to date as the source labels change, but I will try to.

# Project History
I first became interested in this project after watching the
[Summoning Salt](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCtUbO6rBht0daVIOGML3c8w) video
[The History of Contra World Records](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GgOE64kgjjo).
In the video starting at 35m 19s, there was a section where a speedrunner named
`dk28` died in the middle of level 1, and was advanced to level 2 for their next
life.  The video explains that there still isn't a known explanation as to why
this happened.  This got me interested in the assembly and thus this project
began.  Spoilers, I have not found the cause of the level skip bug.  It is still
unknown whether the bug is from some bug in the code, or whether it was a
hardware glitch.

The _Contra_ (US) NES ROM was disassembled using a NES disassembly tool. This
provided a starting point for code investigation.  The disassembler incorrectly
marked many lines of code as data and this had to be manually corrected.  At
this point, there was an .asm file for each ROM bank in _Contra_.

Build scripts were then created for both windows console (.bat), and powershell
(.ps1).  These scripts are equivalent and use ca65 to assemble the .asm files
and cl65 to link the .o files into a single ROM file. Creating these build
scripts required defining the memory addresses and bank layouts in the
`contra.cfg` file.

At this point, I had a repository that could be built that matched the NES ROM
byte for byte.  Then, I found and was able to incorporate the comments from
Trax's IDA Pro disassembly.  This was incredibly helpful, but more work had to
be done as Trax's disassembly couldn't be used directly for reassembly.  For
instance, it had a label for every line and all jump and branch statements were
hard-coded memory address offsets and not label references.

I then worked on updating all branch and jump offsets to point to label
addresses.  This helped ensure that the code was more readable.  At this point,
I also started updating data blocks that included memory offsets to use label
offsets.  The goal here was twofold:

 * make the code more readable and similar to what the original developers would
   have written
 * allow ROM hacking without breaking the entire build due to breaking
   hard-coded memory offsets

When all of this was done, the project could assemble and be byte-for-byte
exactly as the _Contra_ (US) ROM.  However, this was just the prerequisite to
documenting the codebase.  Every label had to be given an appropriate name, and
each line of assembly had to be documented.

# Probotector
This repo can also produce a _Probotector_ ROM file.  _Probotector_ is the
PAL-specific variation of the _Contra_ (US) game.  It is mostly identical except
different sprites.  For a full list of differences, see the document
`docs/Probotector.md`.

## Building

First read the section above for building _Contra_ (US) in general.  The process
is very similar.  Place a _Probotector_ ROM in the root folder with the name
`baserom.nes`.  It should have a MD5 hash of `7127F616C13B58087481DD9E93AEB2FF`.

Then, depending on your environment, run one of the following commands.

| Environment             | Command                         |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------|
| Windows                 | `.\build.ps1 -Game Probotector` |
| Windows (no PowerShell) | `.\build.bat Probotector`       |
| Mac/Unix/Linux          | `./build.sh Probotector`        |

Notes of caution, especially for people building both _Contra_ (US) and
_Probotector_.

1.  Be sure you have the correct `baserom.nes` for the game you are building.
Otherwise, the generated ROM will be incorrect.
2.  If you have _Contra_ (US) assets in the `/src/assets/` folder and are
building _Probotector_, or vice versa, the build scripts will delete the graphic
asset data and re-extract it from the `baserom.nes`. This prevents accidentally
using the wrong game's assets in the result ROM.

# Build Details

The build scripts accomplish the following tasks:
 * extracts necessary data from `baserom.nes` into `src/assets`
 * assemble each bank .asm file into a .o file
 * assemble constants.asm and ines_header into .o files
 * link all output .o files into a single .nes ROM file

The build scripts all utilize [cc65 compiler suite](https://cc65.github.io/) to
assemble and link the 6502 assembly files.  The asset data is pulled from
`baserom.nes` as specified in `assets.txt`.  Each line in `assets.txt` specifies
the file name of the asset, its offset into `baserom.nes`, and its length.

## 1. Assembly
Each .asm file is assembled into a .o object file.  This section outlines what
is happening as part of that process.

### Import Export Validation
During assembly, if any symbol is undefined and not explicitly defined in an
`.import` directive, an error will be generated.

## 2. Linking
Linking is the concept of combining the various .o object files into a single
.nes ROM file.  This is done by the cl65 linker.  Its job is to replace labels
with actual CPU memory addresses where the labels will exist when loaded. These
are then stored in the resulting contra.nes ROM file. This is aided by the
linker configuration file contra.cfg.

This file specifies the layout of the .net ROM file.  Without this file, or with
a misconfigured file, the linker would not generate an identical .nes file.
There are two parts to the contra.cfg file: MEMORY layout and SEGMENTS layout.

### Contra.cfg MEMORY Layout
This section tells the linker where in memory each bank will exist.  The linker
needs this to know to replace a label with the correct address.  For example,
the opcodes that get generated for `jsr zero_out_nametables` depend on where in
memory the label `zero_out_nametables` will exist. This is what the
configuration file memory section specifies.

### Contra.cfg SEGMENTS Layout
This section specifies defines in which order the .o files should appear in the
resulting .nes ROM file.

# References
 * Trax's [Disassembly of _Contra (US)_](https://www.bwass.org/romhack/contra/)
 * Trax's [documentation on romhacking.net](https://www.romhacking.net/documents/713/)
 * [Tomorrow Corporation's Retro Game Internal Series on Contra](http://tomorrowcorporation.com/posts/retro-game-internals)
 * [Overview of NES Rendering by Austin Morlan](https://austinmorlan.com/posts/nes_rendering_overview/)
 * [Rom Detective article on Contra](http://www.romdetectives.com/Wiki/index.php?title=Contra_(NES))

  For the Multiplayer part: It's deterministic lockstep. Both browsers run the same C core (compiled to WebAssembly), and the only thing sent over the network is each player's button bitmask per frame. Local input is delayed by 4 frames (~67 ms), which hides normal internet latency; if the other player's input for a frame hasn't arrived yet, the game waits for it. Every 2 seconds both sides compare a hash of the game RAM to catch desyncs. Transport is a WebRTC data channel via PeerJS (its free cloud server handles matchmaking with a room code), with Google's STUN server for NAT traversal and Metered's free-tier TURN relay as a fallback when a direct connection isn't possible. For AI usage: It was all done by Claude/Codex, but it wasn't that straight forward. First: i started in April and the models weren't good enough and would make errors. You could see those immediately in glitches. Then, i spent some time in building a harness and collect telemetry data in Mesen. 	 *     @type string $source             The full path to the source the files were installed from.

	/**
	 * Construct the upgrader with a skin.
	 *
	 * @since 2.8.0
	 *
	 * @param WP_Upgrader_Skin $skin The upgrader skin to use. Default is a WP_Upgrader_Skin
	 *                               instance.
	 */
	public function __construct( $skin = null ) {
		if ( null === $skin ) {
			$this->skin = new WP_Upgrader_Skin();
		} else {
			$this->skin = $skin;
		}
	}

	/**
	 * Initializes the upgrader.
	 *
	 * This will set the relationship between the skin being used and this upgrader,
	 * and also add the generic strings to `WP_Upgrader::$strings`.
	 *
	 * Additionally, it will schedule a weekly task to clean up the temporary backup directory.
	 *
	 * @since 2.8.0
	 * @since 6.3.0 Added the `schedule_temp_backup_cleanup()` task.
	 */
	public function init() {
		$this->skin->set_upgrader( $this );
		$this->generic_strings();

		if ( ! wp_installing() ) {
			$this->schedule_temp_backup_cleanup();
		}
	}

	/**
	 * Schedules the cleanup of the temporary backup directory.
	 *
	 * @since 6.3.0
	 */
	protected function schedule_temp_backup_cleanup() {
		if ( false === wp_next_scheduled( 'wp_delete_temp_updater_backups' ) ) {
			wp_schedule_event( time(), 'weekly', 'wp_delete_temp_updater_backups' );
		}
	}
